title: Three Players the Ravens Need To Move On From Before the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens have reached a crossroads way before the mid-season point, losing two straight in truly ridiculous fashion -- shutting out their opponents in the first half and then getting shutout and overtaken in the second.
Thus, the Ravens currently sit with a 4-3 record in last place in the AFC North -- a division they were heavy favorites to win -- and with a road game in Buffalo on the horizon, things could start to unravel quickly for Baltimore.
With the NFL trade deadline less than two weeks away, the Ravens must consider unloading a few players in order to either acquire some immediate help in return, or start loading up on draft capital for next year. Either way, several names on Baltimore’s roster just don’t make any sense for the team anymore, regardless of what eventually becomes of the 2026 campaign.
Here are three players that the Ravens should consider trading away before the deadline:
As hard as it is to say goodbye to the top pass-catcher in franchise history, it’s time.
Andrews hasn't just become a non-factor in the Ravens’ offense , but also a liability with dropped passes. Sure, there is no clear successor at the tight end position, and Baltimore wasted a huge opportunity by letting Isaiah Likely walk in free agency, but Andrews is just not cutting it anymore (averaging $13M/season makes it tough).
Rookie Matthrew Hibner was, at one point, playing on more than half of the Ravens snaps, and fellow-rookie Josh Cuevas has seen his usage go up steadily as the season has progressed. Veteran Nick Vannett took some snaps away from Hibner once he was promoted from the practice squad in early October, but that was expected. Blocking specialist Durham Smythe, on the other hand, will miss the rest of the season due to an Achilles’ injury.
The depth chart might not be in a great place, but Andrews is not making very much of a difference anyway. He hasn’t reached 50 receiving yards in any game (he's done it once since the start of last season), and has a single receiving touchdown for the season. He’s also recording personal lows of 7.8 yards per catch and 5.5 yards per route run.
Baltimore really needs to spread out Andrews’ targets among the remaining three tight ends and rookie wideout Ja’Kobi Lane, and see who will step up as the passing game’s safety net of the future.
At an average of just 20 rushing yards per game and 12 receiving yards per game -- as a pass-catching alternative to Derrick Henry in the backfield -- Hill is just not working out. At his current pace, he would finish the season with under 350 rushing yards and just over 200 receiving yards, and he hasn’t scored once either way. He hasn’t logged a broken tackle for the year, either.
The Ravens haven’t been great at maximizing Hill, either. He’s averaging 3.0 yards before contact per rush -- compared to Henry’s 1.9 -- and 6.7 yards per rushing attempt, but Baltimore isn’t giving him enough carries to make a difference or at least find a rhythm.
The market for soon-to-be 29-year-old running backs with limited production and no previous experience as the top guy will be miniscule, but Hill does contribute on special teams and is considered a reliable blocker. It’s just that he’s not taking enough of the load off Henry’s shoulders .
Adam Randall is still on IR with no word on when he might be coming back, and the Ravens have Jonathan Ward on the practice squad, so looking for a street agent option could work. The pool of available guys with experience as primary runners is attractive for a team looking at a one-year rental, including Raheem Moster, Alexander Mattison, Kareem Hunt, Antonio Gibson, Miles Sanders and Joe Mixon, and each one of them should have an accessible price tag.
Walker’s case is truly strange. A 25-year-old fourth rounder from 2024 who has the same number of touchdown catches than starts in his pro career (five), but just 11 receptions over 20 games played.
His 0.75 yards per route run this year seem almost impossible to believe, yet here we are.
It seems Baltimore’s passers just don’t trust Walker, because his usage on the field isn’t dramatically low. He’s played in almost 40 percent of the Ravens’ offensive snaps this year, yet has managed just nine targets and four catches. All this despite top wideout Zay Flowers missing one game and top rookie Ja’Kobi Lane missing four this year , so there have been some chances.
If the Ravens aren’t going to try and develop Walker, they should trade him to a team that will. Rookie fourth-rounder Elijah Sarratt has played in just one game and sorely needs some of the reps that Walker has been handed with no returns. The compensation for Walker will be very low, but his production after two and a half years has been even lower.
Rafael brings over two decades of experience writing about all things football.

title: Ravens Film Room: Why The Secondary's Failures Are Likely To Keep Getting Exposed
full_text:
There was every reason to suspect that Joe Burrow was going to carve up a suspect Ravens pass defense, which was struggling in critical areas even against lowly quarterbacks. And sure enough Burrow threw four touchdown passes with a perfect passer rating in the second half, as the Bengals mustered 35 unanswered points.
Is there any reason to think it will be any different against former MVP Josh Allen on Sunday? Or a quality Jaguars passing attack on a short week after that? Was there anything in the film against the Bengals – or in obvious passing situations late in games or when attacked in the slot or when managing third-and-long situations – that would portend a turnaround anytime soon?
This secondary has not been good for quite some time, and it is not good under rookie head coach Jesse Minter, no matter how much money failing general manager Eric DeCosta spends on certain players and no matter how high he picked them in the draft. It’s screaming out for a shakeup, but Baltimore already has a $370M payroll, they overpaid for lineman Cam Jurgens in trade and would have to find someone to take a big salary (like this defensive player’s for instance ) off their hands to make a meaningful addition.
These DBs do not get their hands on the football, they are not scheme disciplined they look like man corners who are lost in many of Minter’s zone concepts in the most important times. At this point it’s fair to expect this to be who they are, once again, unless the pass rush ramps up in a remarkable way.
A year ago, $19M corner Marlon Humphrey and recent first-round pick Nate Wiggins were one of the three most exploited corner duos in the NFL; it’s not nearly that bad this year, but they also haven’t faced many quality QBs, and Wiggins, who had been stout against the Bengals in the past, struggled mightily on Sunday (six completions on eight targets for 80 yards and a TD) and needs to slough that off, because Humphrey isn’t ascending in any way shape or form.
“He's played better football,” longtime NFL coach and defensive coordinator Marvin Lewis told me on “The Daily Flock” of Wiggins after watching Sunday’s film. “And he just has to get back, in my opinion, to doing that. Some of the things that have happened in  a lot of their games, they've been having some communication errors in the back end.
“And I think that's you see that across the NFL quite a bit. That's why you see the offenses motioning into all these bunches and stacks and formations to make guys communicate on the perimeter. And if one guy doesn't see it the same or communicate it, then you leave a guy wide open. And that happened a little bit … Yeah there's some things probably, technically, I would clean up um guys coach people differently in today's NFL.”
Many of these issues are lingering and deeply embedded and Minter tweaking the scheme hasn’t changed nearly enough. The Ravens are 20th in the NFL in opposing passer rating (95.5). but when you filter out the linebackers – who account for all three interceptions on this team (none in the second half of a game) you see how acute the coverage problems are.
Minter, who badly needs someone with head coaching experience like Lewis to join him on staff , is averse to blitzing and is now down a starting edge defender for the season (sack-leader Tavius Robinson). If $30M pass-rusher Trey Hendrickson doesn’t start operating like the “closer” he was hyped up to be , this defense is cooked.
Wiggins has never had strong ball skills, they refuse to move Humphrey to the slot (perhaps that will come if TJ Tampa gets activated from IR this week), and free safety Malaki Starks (another recent first-round pick) has yet to look anything like a ballhawk despite this defense being set up for him to, in theory, be just that.
Ravens corners and free safeties in coverage this season:
Opposing QBs : 91/ 135 (67.4%), 1139 yards (8.4/att.), 7 TD – 0 INT, 110.7 rating
7 Pass Break Ups, 12.5/comp, 17 comp 20+,  55 1st Downs
Minter said: “You could look at a bunch of different plays where it's something different - where it's certain coverage one play, certain coverage another play, certain guy one play, certain guy another play, playing a coverage one way versus the same route, or playing a coverage two different ways versus the same route even though we're in the same coverage … To me, it just starts with us putting them in a better position. [It] always starts with the coaching, in my opinion, and I'll leave it at that.”
Minter is playing in dime nearly a third of the time, which is nearly twice as much as anyone else in the AFC, and it’s not working. He’s going to end up shifting to more nickel (five defensive backs), and better hunt better match-ups in the slot. Blitzing and playing man better become more a part of this mix, too.
We’ve been writing this for weeks,  but if Humphrey can’t help this team in the slot, then where can he? Should be his strength. This had been a failure from scheme and execution.
Burrow didn’t lean into the slot as much as we thought he might, but did go 5/6 for 51 yards and TD when targeting those pass catchers. On the season the Ravens are among the NFL’s worst, allowing a 121.9 rating on slot targets (27th), and 75% completions (48/64), with four TDs.
Minter needs to switch it up in there.
He probably needs linebacker Teddye Buchanan, working back from season-ending ACL surgery, to help more in coverage against bigger bodies and try to free up Kyle Hamilton to hunt the ball more. If Minter ends up having to move Hamilton more to a free safety role, it’s a bit of a white flag about how this defense was supposed to function, and time to wonder if 2026 is going to end up far closer to 2025 than anyone has the stomach for.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: It's Time To Start Worrying About Derrick Henry. History Says Ravens Better Limit His Workload
full_text:
The Ravens’ default in Derrick Henry’s first two seasons in Baltimore, when times got tough, were simply to ride the workhorse back to stabilize the offense and keep the defense off the field.
And perhaps, once Lamar Jackson returns from an ankle injury that rookie head coach Jesse Minter insisted on calling “day-to-day, ” the combination of those two in the backfield will reignite a staggering run game. But there is also serious reason for concern that this 2027 offensive line will be general manager Eric DeCosta’s biggest failure of them all, and that a desperate trade for Cam Jurgens won’t be a panacea, and that Father Time is creeping in on Henry unlike at any time prior in his career.
What has been bread-and-butter – gutting teams with outside zone, winning in short-yardage, and the expected surge from a renewed emphasis on under-center runs – is now more like a moldy croissant – Henry is starting to look like a 32-year-old running back (historically when careers expire at that position as 55 years of data pointed to ). And at a time when the Ravens let All-Pro fullback Pat Ricard leave as part of their talent exodus, and with powerful blocking tight end Durham Smythe lost for the season and with this line struggling and their best lineman Vega Ioane, looking a potential absence due to injury, Jackson is likely going to have to boost this thing with legs more than anything else.
Henry’s body language looks different, during and after Sunday's debacle.
He seems to know holes are going to close before they open and he almost sounds defeated. Whether or not his football mortality is peering back at him remains to be seen, but rookie coordinator Declan Doyle is riding him hard – 147 carries leads the NFL and are second in NFL history through seven weeks for a 32-year-old back since the 1970 merger – and now feels like a good time to scheme up some stuff for his understudies.  Doyle threatened to run Henry 300 times or more – would be first time in Henry’s career he’s done that three years in a row – but perhaps they need a rethink .
“Got to be better,” Henry said after averaging 2.9 yards/carry Sunday. “It's not good enough. Terrible. I'm looking at myself. I think every man can look in the mirror, but as far as myself, I can speak on me.
“It's not good enough at all. We got to figure it out. Everybody evaluates themselves, coaches are going to evaluate and we can go from there. It's just not good enough at all for us to be able to win games and be able to string drives together [and] have an impact on the game as far as the running game."
Henry needs help at this stage of his career and he’s not getting it. Baltimore’s 1.33 yards before contact are the team’s lowest since 2010, their 4.7 yards/carry as a team is the lowest since 2018, before Jackson was the full-season QB. Defenses are picking up keys and tells and shutting down inside runs and the pitch plays. Minter seems to think Doyle needs to find solutions.
“Any time you look at specifically the run game, to me, it's - what are you asking the guys to do,” Minter said Monday. “Can they do what you're asking them to do when you go to the line, to the tight ends, to the wide receivers?
“Obviously, we lost one of our key blocking tight ends a few weeks back, and so it's like, what are we asking some of these younger guys to do? Can they do it? Can we be good at the things that we're asking them to do? So, I think it's just a constant search for the schemes, the plays, what you're asking the guys to do.”
Henry is averaging 3.9/carry – 26th in the NFL and his lowest through seven games since 2019. These three areas beg major questions:
This was a cheatcode for Henry his first two years here. And maybe when Jackson comes back it will be again. But left tackle Ronnie Stanley isn’t special anymore, and the interior offensive line, sans Ioane, has a chance to be one of the worst in the NFL.
The Ravens averaged 5.9 yards/carry running outside zone in 2024-20425, which had a lot do with Henry winning a quadruple crown in that span – most carries (632), most rushing yards (3516, nearly 300 more than anyone else) with 32 rushing TDs and 5.6 yards/carry. That run will not continue this season.
Henry's 3.9 yards/carry is the average for all 32-year-old backs since 1970, and Baltimore is at 4.9 yards/carry on outside zone. The last three weeks Henry has 94 yards on 27 carries on outside zone (3.5/carry). They have faced bad perimeter rushing defenses in recent weeks and bad defenses against outside zone, and been stymied, anyway.
“We (have) to search for those better answers on how people are playing us,” Doyle said after Sunday’s’ game when the offense failed to score again in the second half.
Henry ran more under center than anyone in the NFL in Tennessee before joining the top shotgun offense in the NFL, in terms of usage, in Baltimore. Doyle made getting under center a major emphasis this offseason, but DeCosta let an All-Pro center leave in free agency and replaced him with cheap journeymen who got hurt and now they have no under-center run game.
We’ll see how much Jurgens helps. Baltimore averaged a season-low 0.30 yards before contact Sunday. The last four weeks he is averaging 3.7/carry on under-center runs, 27th in the NFL.
Third-and-1 has been a disaster around here since around the middle of last season. Turns out firing Todd Monken as offensive coordinator – he is a front-runner for NFL Coach of the Year in Cleveland nearing the midpoint – wasn’t a solution there. This is now worse than ever.
The Wild Cat stuff works every once in a while, but I suspect Jackson on bootlegs and keepers will be a calling card when he comes back. The Ravens third-down run conversion rate (40.9) is their lowest since 2003 – yeah, 2003 – and they rank 29th in the NFL in third-and-one and fourth-and-one rushing this season.
A bad offensive line undermined this offense a year ago. It could do so on a much grander scale this year.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Marvin Lewis Could Help Fix The Ravens' Defense. If Jesse Minter Calls, He'll Listen
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens badly need someone with NFL head coaching experience on their staff, ASAP, to try to help the franchise pull out of a seven-season funk with a collapsing second-half defense.
Rookie head coach Jesse Minter seems overmatched and bewildered right now – allowing 35 unanswered points to the Bengals Sunday was a nadir for the once-proud defense  – and some alarming missteps from the offseason are already coming to roost. Building one of only two coaching staffs in the NFL that included no one with former NFL head coaching experience was really something, especially for how novice most of the staff was , and there are obvious issues with players being undisciplined to the system once playing with a lead, repeated communication mishaps, pathetic tackling and massive issues with pass rush and coverage.
The general manger is out of his depth, too, and already made a ridiculously desperate trade for a slumping offensive lineman in concussion protocol, and who has been running the team as if his job might be in the balance. Eric DeCosta should have been fired when head coach John Harbaugh was, and he seems to be squirming now . The building in tense, the GM, coach and players have proven to be chokers; the two-time MVP quarterback (Lamar Jackson) is injured, the team can’t manage its messaging about his high-ankle sprain in a coherent manner ( abhorrent PR is very much their brand ) and they’ve blown 13-point leads in successive weeks to division foes.
Worst of all, they have DeCosta-ed – losing a game in which they lead by double-digits in the second half – a record 17 times since the start of 2019 (he is the constant) – and already done it three times this season in Minter’s first seven games. As always, we have a plan to help the perpetually underachieving franchises in this town; the Ravens should have hired Marvin Lewis when they put the staff together and they need to call him now (like I did Monday).
The Commanders just brought in former head coach Steve Wilks to help their overwhelmed young defensive coordinator and the Cowboys brought in Mike Pettine to do the same thing and head coach DeMeco Ryans took over play calling on defense in Houston and the Broncos, who nearly went to the Super Bowl last year and could do so this year, turned things around once head coach Sean Payton took over offensive play calling.
Lewis ran the Ravens defense at its heights, had a great run as Bengals head coach, helped young head coach Antonio Pierce as an assistant head coach with the Raiders in 2024, and follows the league closely doing syndicated calls of NFL games on the radio. He’s watching Ravens film, he knows their culture and history like few could, and he is at a stage in his career where it’s not about his padding resume, but rather helping young coaches succeed in a place he cares deeply for.
So when I tooK the pulse of the Ravens systemic issues with Lewis on “The Daily Flock Show” (a deep dive on their defensive woes) Monday I had to ask if he’d try to help his buddy Ozzie Newsome out and be a resource for Minter if the team reached out. Lewis wouldn’t consider leaving his home in Arizona for much, but this would pique his interest should the Ravens do the right thing.
“Well, I would be remiss in saying I wouldn’t listen,” Lewis said about any hypothetical Ravens interest. “You’ve got to listen. And there are people you want to help, and more important than me; it’s somebody I would want to help and support. That’s what’s important more than anything.”
When former Ravens defensive mastermind Mike Macdonald left to become head coach in Seattle – the one that got away – he didn’t bring in a family member to be his mentor, he secured the services of successful former head coach and defensive coordinator Leslie Frazier. They won a Super Bowl in Year Two. It should have been a prerequisite for Minter’s staff, and the Ravens have a history of doing this sort of thing in-season, be it Dean Pees and Jerry Rosburg rejoining the franchise out of quasi-retirement .
He was invaluable for Pierce, he has recent experience at Arizona State University as well so still understands how to relate to young players and his wealth of experience is unlike anything on this staff currently. He did special projects for Pierce, helped with inactives and was a sounding board for him to sit in on coordinator meetings throughout the week and offer insight to the head coach in private.
“Thursday and Friday he gave me about four minutes in practice where I could go over a special situation that may come up in the game, where it’s a backed-up situation for the offense or the offense threw a big pass and now it has the ball at the 25-yard-line. And I wouldn’t tell those coordinators what the situation was going to be for the day, because we wanted them to think on their feet and be ready to call it that way …
“A lot of things like that I did, and I was a part of the defensive meetings and I’d look at the opposing defense and would go in and talk to the offensive coaches. “When you do this, this is always their response.’ We saw a little bit of that yesterday (in the Ravens game) I think in how Cincinnati kept building their formations.”
The Ravens badly need new eyes and ears in their meeting rooms. Here’s their second half rankings:

INT/Att .: 0.00% (T-last) First Downs : 12.3 (30th) 3rd Down: 44% (24th)
QB Rating: 117.0 (28th) Comp % : 71.3% (28th) TD-INT : 8-0 (32nd)
Both of Minter’s starting corners were embarrassed by the Bengals Sunday, Lewis noted in our discussion how much Nate Wiggins was attacked, while Marlon Humphrey lost the plot in coverage and suffered in tackling. Their corners and safeties do not have an interception all season; their culture is warped and on Monday Minter hinted at how deep it runs.
“We have guys that care and want to do it right,” Minter said, “but there's also moments in the game where it's like, 'Who's the guy that's going to grab everybody together, get them together on the sideline? I think as a team, we're working through who that is.
“Who is that person? Who are those players? There’s guys that want to do it, and then there's guys that maybe they're dealing with something, or they're not playing the way they want to play, so they don't feel like they can do it in those moments.”
Maybe a former head coach could help the rookie figure out how to bring it out of them.

title: Were Ravens Surprised Lamar Jackson Missed Bengals Game? Could He Play Sunday? Jesse Minter Explains
full_text:
Ravens rookie head coach Jesse Minter continues to speak in guarded and cryptic tones about the status of two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson ahead of a critical game at Buffalo in Week 8. The team is nearing the midpoint of the season in a downward spiral and Jackson, recovering from what he called a "high-ankle sprain," has arguably a greater impact on regular-season wins and losses than any NFL player.
Minter’s defense is getting overrun in the second half of games – allowing 114 points in the second half, most in the NFL – with some in rival NFL front offices believing the young coach needs help from a former head coach/defensive coordinator to fix systemic issues in their game-day process. In two straight weeks the offense has failed to score in the second half with back-up Snoop Huntley filling in, while the defense blew a 13-point lead to the Browns and Bengals.
The Ravens have an NFL record 17 losses with a double-digit lead since 2019, the collapses have only gotten worse under Minter – allowing 35 unanswered points Sunday at hom e was a new low – and while general manager Eric DeCosta’s rosters are undoubtedly a major part of the problem ( his job security should be under intense scrutiny after head coach John Harbaugh was already fired for all the late-game debacles), Minter is in the crosshairs now and badly needs his best player back.
After asserting for three weeks – during which Jackson never once practiced fully – that the star was “day-to-day” with an ankle injury that the team was certainly couching as not too severe – Minter stayed away from that wording on Monday. But he uttered it again as recently as Friday, although Jackson made it clear in his remarks on Friday that the injury was extremely painful, saying he still has been unable to run normally since suffering the injury in Week 4.
“I think he’ll be in a decent spot but we'll know a lot more on Wednesday,” Minter said.
It’s fair to assume at this point that Jackson will not play until he is able to practice fully with no setbacks. The CBS broadcast of Week 7’s game referred to “swelling” over the weekend after limited practice Wed-Fri as the cause for Jackson being downgraded to out on Saturday after being listed as questionable on Friday’s injury report.
“I’m not going to speak really on the details of anybody’s injury,” Minter said. “… Look, if he’s able to play and is healthy enough to play and play the way he needs to play, then he will play.”
The CBS broadcast also asserted that the Ravens were surprised that Jackson was not able to face the Bengals. To that Minter said, “I would say a little bit,” pointing to an ongoing feeling-out process with the ankle.
Of course, the backdrop to the situation is the fact that Jackson is the rarest of superstar quarterbacks in his prime who has reached a point in his contract with no future guarantees beyond this season. He carries an untenable $85M cap hit in 2027, with a no-trade clause and a no-franchise tag clause, which gives him NBA levels of leverage over where he plays next season and how much he makes .
Minter continues to say that Jackson is “working his butt off” to return as soon as his body will allow him, and he has repeatedly refereed to this decision as one the team and QB and medical staff would make together. The Ravens win 70% of their regular season games that Jackson starts and are a losing franchise without him since he took over as starter midway through the 2018 season.
His career arc with them has been highly unusual throughout, demanding a trade at one point and getting no interest as a de-facto free agent on a non-exclusive tag, which later become fodder in an NFLPA collusion case. Given the strange backdrop between player and team, calling this a “day-to-day” injury for the better part of a month seems to have been another unforced error by this franchise.
Beating Buffalo coming off a bye would be a stretch and the Ravens have a quick turnaround hosting Jacksonville on Thursday night in Week 9.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens GM Eric DeCosta Should Have Been Fired With John Harbaugh. Another Playoff Miss, He Has To Go
full_text:
It’s fair to wonder at this point if the Baltimore Ravens historic proclivity for choking away double-digit leads will change until general manager Eric DeCosta is fired.
The only clear-eyed move for detached owner Steve Bisciotti (“I don’t spend as much time around here as I did,” he crowed in January) to have made when he fired John Harbaugh just shy of 20 years on the job was to also fire Decosta – who had arguably more to do with the team’s malaise than anyone. An invested owner would have started fresh with outside evaluators who didn’t play favorites and try to prop up preexisting bloated and bad contracts and play politics like DeCosta has perfected. It was time to bring in someone else leading personnel whose brand wasn’t building the worst fourth-quarter rosters in the NFL and failing to maximize Lamar Jackson’s talents in his 20s; someone who could actually get Jackson signed to a contract extension that DeCosta and team president Sashi Brown whiffed on all of 2025.
But that’s not what Ravens fans got.
Bisciotti opted to outsource this decision to DeCosta and Brown, with former GM Ozzie Newsome still involved. So as the Ravens sit at 4-3, getting outscored 35-0 in the second half at home by the Bengals, having Decosta-ed now 17 games since 2019 (losing despite a double-digit lead) and with their hand-picked novice head coach Jesse Minter (who was always getting this job as I began reporting back in November on air in Baltimore) an overmatched mess, DeCosta needs to be on notice. As Harbaugh and former Ravens offensive coordinator Todd Monken make the case as NFL Coach Of The Year at the midpoint, and Minter gets run over every Sunday ( better get him some help , DeCosta!), let’s point the finger right where it belongs.
Here’s Bisciotti telling you exactly how the hiring process would work , why he wouldn’t be sitting in on every Zoom with every candidate and why he was perfectly comfortable letting the real work unfold without him while he chilled on his yacht:
“I want very much this person to be picked by Eric and Oz and Sash, more than me. When I come in, when they call me in for these five (finalists), I'm going to already know why they love them. I'm going to come back, and I'm going to give just them my honest opinions, my reservations – if there are any – on individuals that may be a red flag that they didn't see.
“So, I would hope that when I spend a lot of time with these people, that I might unearth some things; which I think I'm really good at unearthing some details that maybe others missed. I think that I'd like to feed that into them, and if it changes their top five, then great. And if it doesn't, I want these guys to be partners.”
He’d better start getting a shortlist together of potential new “partners” for Minter. Bisciotti’s franchise is becoming a joke after a guy who created generational wealth by starting a staffing company in his basement thought it was in his season-ticket holder’s best interest to allow a self-serving GM to the run show to replace a coach who might be headed to Canton.
This mess belongs to DeCosta and Brown.
Baltimore has blown four leads of 10-or more points, it’s long-pathetic fourth-quarter defense is worse than ever, $30M pass rusher Trey Hendrickson (signed after DeCosta reneged on a Maxx Crosby trade) has done nothing in the second half of games and a roster that is supposed to have the best secondary in the NFL – loaded with DeCosta’s highest paid guys and overhyped first-round picks – does not have an interception in all season (none for corners or safeties) despite being thrown on more than anyone and mostly by bad quarterbacks.
Minter is apparently so bad at being a head coach that he suddenly can’t call plays worth a damn anymore, either. The players looked to be quiet quitting on him Sunday, it’s clear he had a far better roster with the Chargers and the lack of accountability is glaring. Kyle Hamilton shouldn’t be the person calling out this joke defense all season – that’s what a real head coach would do.
(I publicly championed Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores or Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo to get this job when it opened; of course DeCosta wouldn’t ask for an audience with either, because they wouldn’t put up with his BS. When Sean McDermott was fired by Buffalo, any serious front office would have altered their search – that was jerry-rigged for Minter all along – to get him in front of their owner ASAP. But this was about power and job security, not about truly trying to win in 2026.)
DeCosta (employed by the Ravens his entire adult life; GM since January 2019) is running a $370M payroll, highest of Bisciotti’s tenure, and somehow has exactly one playmaker on defense, again (Hamilton) thus far. Minter’s inability to adjust anything at halftime, and the insistence on playing copious amounts of dime defense (nearly twice as much as any other AFC team) while getting shredded on the back end and offering zero impactful pass rush at the same time is quite a combination. He won’t blitz. He’s lost.
When former Ravens defensive coordinator Mike Macdonald – the one that got away – built a staff that would win a Super Bowl in Year Two in Seattle, one of his first hires was former successful NFL head coach Leslie Farzier. We got Rick Minter, the coach’s daddy, in that role and twice-failed offensive coordinator Joe Lombardi to try to prop up rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle.
That’s how you get a -70 second half scoring differential that keeps getting worse. Devoid of meaningful corrective measures, and players who fear no consequences because many of the biggest culprits are made-men by the joke of a GM.
Instead of a break from the past, Ravens fans get all the worst parts of the end of the Harbaugh regime, only amplified.
You get DeCosta and Brown (3-7 in their last 10 home games) with virtually full autonomy over the building getting to handpick a novice (cheap and young!) coaching staff loaded with rookies who wouldn’t rock the boat or pushback on all of his aging and overpaid veterans clogging up the ability to win in the clutch on offense and defense. (Letting Isaiah Likely, a top three NFL tight end, walk in his prime so DeCosta could try to shame him by giving his contract offer to broken down Mark Andrews ? More fake tough guy stuff from an egomaniacal GM who likes to stalk the sidelines and pretend he’s a coach on game day – without any of the accountability).
You get zero pushback on Brown – who went 0-16 as Browns GM, you can look it up – making data their beacon and losing sight of scouting principles and the checks and balances that made them great under Newsome. You get stuck with a failing GM from Newsome’s ugly personnel family tree (it is to GMs what Bill Belichick’s is to head coaches – it’s just a fact).
You get one of only two NFL coaching staffs that entered the season with no former NFL head coaches on staff ( tanking Miami is the other ). You get an unserious organization led by over-empowered charlatans, co-signed by a half-interested owner who should have sold the team by now. Makes you wonder if any reasonable standards still apply in Owings Mills.
“If we fail, then I'll assess his contribution to that failure,” Bisciotti said of his next coach before hiring Minter. “Because like I said, this is an 'all-hands on deck.' When we fail, we fail together.
"And so, yes, it's Eric’s job to mentor him and guide him in our culture, hope he understands it and can add to that culture. What we do on the field, it will play a role, but I certainly hope to get back to the playoffs, and I certainly hope to overachieve.”
Good luck with that, brother. You run a sham process; you get sham results.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Rookie Coach Jesse Minter Is Getting Exposed: Hiring Outside Help Could Save The Season
full_text:
Jesse Minter, the aspiring head coach, is undermining Jesse Minter, the proven defensive coordinator. Or perhaps, Jesse Minter, the esteemed defensive play caller, isn’t nearly skilled enough to overcome Jesse Minter, the guy who is still pretending to be an NFL head coach.
However you want to frame it, Minter is getting exposed in the second half of games in embarrassing fashion and general manager Eric DeCosta is getting unmasked for being fraudulent with another suspect roster and for hiring a staff full of novices who are collectively failing at a historic rate. Minter and his band of start-ups are blowing 10-point leads in a flurry that fired head coach John Harbaugh couldn’t ever touch their lack of cunning and expertise is eviscerating this team in the clutch. To call them overmatched right now would be complimentary.
Minter needs to do something about it, and do it now.
Maybe the Ravens players weren’t quitting as they allowed 35 unanswered points after leading, 13-0, at the half over the Bengals, but they damn sure weren’t trying their best either. They are making Minter look like a naïve joke; their lack of tackling and mental focus in the second half is not NFL caliber. It appears as if they are walking all over this staff, making them look silly for all the boastful talk about this roster all offseason long . It’s an ugly look.
“Not really good enough, starting with me,” was the joist of what we got from the rook coach, who was getting abused by garbage QBs so of course he got utterly punked as Joe Burrow for four touchdown passes and a perfect rating in the second half against his impotent pass rush and utterly predictable schemes. Mind you, Minter is handcuffed by another roster devoid of sufficient playmakers in their prime - a $19M corner who wouldn’t start for a real contender, a $20M linebacker whose been maybe $6M guy the last three years, and a $30M edge rusher who has yet to show up in the second half of a football game and whose former team, the Bengals, do not miss him one bit.
The season might be slipping away as Minter hinted ahead of a trip to Buffalo: “Right now, I think it's just a big point in the season for us to determine what type of team we want to be.” Unless this organization takes major corrective action to try to prop Minter up in a way that should have been emphasized when the staff was originally put together (a former head coach or two on this staff; Miami is the only staff without it), expect more of the same results.
They had best take one of the measures we suggest below, immediately. First, let’s first quantify the extent of Minter’s defensive failures.
Coaches are judged in no small degree based on how they adjust at halftime and how they change tendencies and tactics from week to week. Minter seems entirely lost in the second half as a coordinator despite having incredibly favorable game conditions on that side of the ball, and the pressure is breaking him; passing on chip-shot field goal to go up 16-14 with the game sliding away, instead having Snoop Huntley (with Lamar Jackson out three weeks with what Minter kept calling a “day-to-day injury ") try a fourth-down pass was telling.
Minter probably knew his garbage second-half defense was cooked anyway, but how about doing something about it instead of playing ridiculous amounts of dime coverage with inept defensive backs with zero ball skills? Sitting back in nickel/dime over 80% of the time, again, being scared to blitz (30%), again, isn’t working. Selling out to keep a shell on everything and giving up the fifth-most big plays in the second half doesn’t look very smart.
The Ravens have a +65 first-half scoring margin and a -70 in the second half – that appears to be a first in NFL history through seven games of a seasons. Coupled with the fact the Ravens have now DeCosta-ed 17 times since 2019 – blown a double-digit lead to lose  – and three times already this season including back-to-back weeks against division foes, Minter needs to show he is cut out for this soon if he doesn’t want this to be a lost season with the upcoming schedule.
They have allowed 114 points in the second half, most in the NFL, and the next-worst scoring differential is -51. Here are their second-half rankings:
Yards Per Play: 6.0 (29th) Passing Yards : 147 (29th) Yds/Att.: 8.0 (30th)
INT/Att .: 0.00% (T-last) First Downs : 12.3 (30th) 3rd Down: 44% (24th)
QB Rating: 117.0 (28th) Comp % : 81.3% (28th( TD-INT : 8-0 (32nd)
He is failing at both parts of his job, he is in a difficult position with a Machiavellian GM pulling his strings, but the idea he could put together a staff this short on proven NFL chops with his dad, Rick, as the sage shoulder for him to lean on was a joke.
There are many reasons why Minter’s best buddy Mike Macdonald hired Leslie Frazier for his staff, and it was a blight not to lean into this (longtime NFL head coach and coordinator Todd Haley explained on “The Daily Flock Show” ). And there’s a reason we have seen a slew of coordinator moves already this season, like the Cowboys bringing in Mike Pettine (remember him) or Texans coach DeMeco Ryans taking over defensive play calling or Sean Payton (mentor to Ravens OC Declan Doyle) doing the same in Denver.
More such moves are coming around the NFL, we can all remember when the Ravens brought back Chuck Pagano or Dean Pees or Jerry Rosburg to the fold to assist in some capacity. It worked better at some times than others, but this staff needs real help, right now.
Marvin Lewis might not want anything to do with being in an NFL building trying to bail out some kid who probably got hired too soon who should have been all over him in February to join his staff. He has seen it all and done it all and has oodles of AFC North head coaching and coordinating experience and saw this Ravens defensive lineage at its birth.
He knows Ozzie Newsome incredibly well and this front office is losing all touch with that era (check out Solomon Wilcots, who knows Newsome well, breaking it down here ). Lewis can take things off Minter’s plate and help him immeasurably. This is an ongoing defensive crisis and needs to be dealt with as such.
Wink Martindale has his faults, and he hasn’t been a head coach, but I got news for you, he knows firsthand what a fraud DeCosta is building defensive rosters and he would be a vital check on the front office. Minter better realize the same thing Martindale and Zach Orr and others around here did – all the money in the secondary and all the over-drafted corners with no ability to impact the ball in flight won’t win for you.
Few can dial up the blitz like Martindale, he has Harbaugh and Michigan ties like Minter and the Cowboys should have hired him and not Pettine. Having him help create man-coverage pressure looks that run counter to Minter’s pansy schemes is necessary; his zones were picked apart by bad QBs, and the real gauntlet has just begun.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Allow 35 Unanswered Points To Bengals: Key Takeaways For A Team On The Brink
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens have been the NFL’s most pathetic chokers throughout Lamar Jackson’s tenure with the team, dating back to 2018.
Even by their lowly standards, giving up 35 unanswered points to the Bengals in the second half is a new low for general manager Eric DeCosta (ties worst in franchise history), the one constant in all those heartless losses that now span seven coordinators and two head coaches after Sunday’s epic meltdown.
DeCosta’s rosters have done it with regularity and reckless abandon many, many times with the two-time MVP on the field, and without him, it feels almost inevitable. Rookie head coach Jesse Minter – yet to prove he is remotely ready to run a sideline and call a defense at the same time – blew a double-digit lead for the fourth time in seven games, and lost doing so two weeks in a row; Minter is a master at this, doing it twice at home already this season and three times in 2026.
Minter’s feeble scheme and weak-minded players blew a 13-0 lead Sunday as Joe Burrow destroyed them like lesser QBs like Tyler Shough and Cam Ward have in the past. The Ravens now have lost 17 games with a double-digit lead since 2019, Minter has proven to be far more adroit and adept at it than anyone else, the fraud GM who builds these awful defenses year after year got platitudes from the owner when coach John Harbaugh was fired, and this 35-13 loss at M&T Bank Stadium is as ugly as any of them, even if it was Snoop Huntley at QB.
Imagine getting DeCosta-ed now at 17 times-and-running in this short a period of time and thinking swapping out a veteran staff for a bunch of rookies coaches who are younger and cheaper and way more malleable was going to fix Baltimore’s clear, systemic problems of which DeCosta and team president Sashi Brown are prevailing culprits. Oh well. Steve Bisciotti has been yammering about selling the team for years. Maybe they will finally get a real GM in charge then. Maybe DeCosta can hide the standings from his boss (John Harbaugh and Todd Monken look like they can coach after all).
The Ravens (4-3, last in AFC North) have won three times in their last 10 home games, they are remarkably devoid of anything approximating a true playmaker on defense, Minter’s scheme has been an utter failure in the second half and they face Josh Allen in Buffalo off a bye next week. Jackson returning might not be enough.
“Starting with me, just a bad effort by the defense in the second half,” Minter said.
The Ravens dominated the first half but didn’t have enough to show for it, stalling twice deep in Bengals’ territory and settling for field goals. They built a 13-0 lead into the half but settled for three after an 18-play, 78-yard march that took 11 minutes off the clock and stalled at the 16. And then went 13 plays and 82 yards on their next drive, taking six minutes off the clock and reaching the 6 before settling for three. Six offensive penalties in the first half – including four false starts and a delay of game – led to some of that stalling out.
It’s truly pathetic what must go on in the Ravens locker room during halftime with a big lead. They ceded momentum in the second half like they can’t wait to hand a game away. It’s staggering, really, but it’s their brand. Sunday they wasted no time swinging the tenor of the game after owning the Bengals in the first half and holding the ball for nearly 23 minutes.
How’s this sequence – Burrow carves them up in the underneath passing game for a TD drive to make it 13-7, Ravens offensive line gets swallowed up again on the next drive with a three-and-out that ends on a sack and then a huge return on the ensuing punt that forces the long-snapper to make a tackle.
And that was followed up by Baltimore’s secondary getting absolutely carved up – and no semblance of a pass rush – on Cincy’s second drive of the second half, this capping it with a TD pass to Tee Higgins to make it 14-13. Burrow was 9/10 for 100 yards and two TD passes on the first two drives of the second half.
Baltimore’s tackling was once against atrocious in the second half, even Kyle Hamilton fell prey to it several times including on a TD run (Marlon Humphrey, a $19M corner, made an even bigger a mockery of “tackling”’ the net drive), and this team will have to win shootouts when Jackson returns because the defense is just as fraudulent in 2026 as it was in 2025 and 2024.
Burrow was 16/18 with four TD passes and a perfect 158.3 rating in the second half. Joe Flacco got to play the final four minutes in this debacle.
"it was the tale of two halves," defensive lineman Calais Campbell said of what could be their motto.
"We have complete control over that mentality," Minter said, admitting he isn;t sure how to correct their mentality.
Minter has been fairly atrocious in the second half of games and seems to be suffering trying to run the team and call the defense at the same time. He also has become a big part of Baltimore’s choking tendencies and it’s in his head now, too, and he made a failed decision to open the fourth quarter that blew up in his face.
Minter opted to eschew a chip shot field goal to re-take the lead after having a full timeout at the end of the quarter to think about it. If he really thinks his defense is any good – and its one of the worst in the NFL in the second half – he grabs the lead.
Instead, they had the back-up attempt a pass on fourth and two and it fell woefully incomplete and never had a chance of working. And Burrow went right back to picking apart this secondary with short passes, and when he did have to step away from pressure he found Tee Higgins for 40 yards.
He entered this game with a bottom five second half defense in points per drive and points allowed and pressure rating and sacks, and hit new lows Sunday. He has made no adjustments and has no answers and his players with the Chargers were better than DeCosta’s bloated mess of a roster; his defenses there were never this bad.
Overpaying in a desperate trade for Cam Jurgens, while in concussion protocol no less, wasn’t likely to fix much overnight . And it didn’t. Baltimore could not operate the under-center rushing game, Derrick Henry remains an ineffective running back on the inside – like all season – but also now on the outside as linebackers sell out to take away outside zone and whack Henry behind the line of scrimmage before he gets going.
Henry ended up with 17 carries for 46 yards and an unthinkable 2.6 yards/carry average..  He once again was a non-factor on short-yardage plays and the return of Jackson may open up the run game some for sure, but Henry has been a blow-average back, at age 32 he needs major help from the line, and rookie guard-center-guard Vega Ioane was ruled out in the first half with a knee injury.
“I’m certainly concerned about that,” Minter said of the run game. “We've got to search for those better answers in how people are playing us.”
Look one guy can’t muster a pass rush all on his own, but when you give an oft-injured, older pass rusher who isn’t good against the run $30M a year to just rush the passer , dude needs to make some big plays. But DeCosta – a failure at quite a bit but especially pass rush and offensive line construction – doesn’t find those guys and Hendrickson’s revenge game was a dud.
Hendrickson is well removed from the hand procedure he underwent and he did get close to Burrow a time or two early in the game but Baltimore’s second-half defense has been a joke because the overrated corners and safeties never touch the football and their defensive front never gets home. Hendrickson was lauded as a ”closer” but hasn’t sniffed a QB in the fourth quarter in his Ravens career (Bengals have the NFL’s best fourth-quarter pressure rate without him) and Burrow cough laugh in this defensive line’s face the entire second half.
They couldn’t make him flinch. Hendrickson has two sacks all season and just two pressures in this game and the Ravens had an inept 22% pressure rate, which will get…

title: Four Ravens X-Factors For Clash vs. Bengals
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens will continue the 2026 regular season back at home against the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 7 , and the difference in the game could come down to how an individual player performs when it matters most or over the course of the game by capitalizing on their opportunities when presented with them.
With a win, the Ravens improve to 5-2 and could move back into the top spot in the AFC North division standings. A loss could drop them to last place after the Pittsburgh Steelers' overseas win, especially since the Cleveland Browns play a one-win team on Sunday.
Here are four players who could wind up tilting the scales in favor of the Ravens and first-year head coach Jesse Minter.
Even before fourth-year pro Tavius Robinson went down with a season-ending pectoral injury , the second-round rookie was already following in his footsteps by playing regularly on defense in a rotational edge-setting role on early downs in his first season. Now that the Ravens' sack leader through six games is out for the year, Young will likely be asked to assume an even larger role as a pass rusher moving forward, starting in this game.
The two-time Pro Bowl center will finally be making his debut for the Ravens after being acquired via trade a couple of weeks ago from the Philadelphia Eagles. His insertion into the starting lineup couldn't have come at a better time, as the Ravens will be facing a revamped Bengals interior defensive line that features a pair of multi-time Pro Bowlers in Jonathan Allen and Dexter Lawrence, whom he faced twice a year in the NFC East when he played against the New York Giants.
Jurgens' presence will allow standout first-round rookie Vega Ioane to return to his natural spot at right guard, where he began the season before a litany of injuries at center caused him to spend the last three games playing out of position.
With veteran safety Jaylinn Hawkins out for a couple of weeks due to a knee injury, the second-year pro and special teams ace will likely not only get to see his first defensive snaps of the season but could emerge as a difference-maker in DIME packages. The Ravens could play him in the box near the line of scrimmage as a blitzer and heat-seeking missile in underneath coverage while allowing three-time All Pro Kyle Hamilton to play further back in a somewhat more traditional safety role to help the unit better cover the middle of the field.
Despite having last week off while on bye, the Bengals still lead the league in most receiving yards allowed to the tight end position this season with 451 yards through six weeks. While the Ravens have a pair of exciting young rookies at the position who have shown impressive flashes when called upon to play bigger roles this year, the three-time Pro Bowler remains a fixture in Baltimore's passing attack, leading all tight ends in offensive snaps played, targets, receptions and receiving yards. Andrews has had some of his best career games in this rivalry against the Bengals, where he has terrorized their off-ball linebackers and defensive backs alike.

title: Five Pivotal Ravens Matchups to Watch vs. Bengals
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens' Week 7 bout against the Cincinnati Bengals could ultimately be decided by battles between specific position groups or individual players outperforming their counterparts on the other side of the ball.
It'll be the team's first game back at M&T Bank Stadium after a two-week road stint and second straight clash with an AFC North rival. With two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson out for a third straight game with an ankle sprain , they're entering this matchup as slight home underdogs.
If the Ravens prevail, they will improve to 5-2 and could be in a two-way tie for first in the AFC North standings, depending on how the Cleveland Browns fare on the road against the one-win Tennessee Titans this week. Here are the five matchups that can either make or break this game:
To avoid getting into a shootout with his backup quarterback, Tyler Huntley, under center, Baltimore and head coach Jesse Minter will need their tandem of Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey to continue their strong start to the season. They're going to be facing arguably the most lethal wideout duo in the league and one that has given their defense fits and put up prolific numbers over the past half-decade. While Chase has been the more dangerous of the two in their previous matchups and is a threat to take it to the house any time he touches the ball, Higgins has been the more productive of the two, leading the team in receiving with 134 more yards than the next closest pass catcher.
It'll be interesting to see if the Ravens have Wiggins follow Chase to whatever side he lines up on, since that's best-on-best. From a physicality standpoint, Humphrey would be a good matchup against Higgins, although both excel at attacking the ball at the catch point.
Both teams turned one of their most glaring weaknesses from last season into a strength this year by importing new blood and multi-time Pro Bowlers. For the Bengals, it was trading for star nose tackle Dexter Lawrence and signing Jonathan Allen as a salary cap casualty, while the Ravens reunited with left guard John Simpson in free agency, selected stud rookie Vega Ioane in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft and traded for Cam Jurgens a couple of weeks ago . Lawrence and Jurgens have history and are used to clashing twice a year as former members of opposing NFC East teams and will continue to do so in the AFC North. Since most games are won and lost in the trenches, this matchup could truly wind up tipping the scales in favor of the team whose unit imposes its will and consistently executes at a high level.
This game will mark the first time that four-time Pro Bowler Trey Hendrickson will be playing against his former team since his five-year stint in Cincinnati came to an acrimonious end. After half a decade of not getting to hit or even get too close to Joe Burrow in practice, he'll be free to terrorize his former teammate as often as he's on the field. In order to do so, he'll have to get past and around a fellow four-time Pro Bowler and former Raven, Orlando Brown Jr. On the opposite side, Ravens second-year edge defender Mike Green will have his hands full in obvious passing situations going up against Bengals third-year right tackle Amarius Mims, whose 96.1% pass-block win rate in one-on-ones is the highest mark among offensive tackles with a minimum of 150 snaps this season, according to Pro Football Focus .
The Bengals have struggled mightily to limit the impact of opposing tight ends due to their young second-year off-ball linebackers still not being adept at having a natural feel in coverage. Through five games, Cincinnati has allowed 451 receiving yards to tight ends this season. The Ravens have a three-time Pro Bowler in Mark Andrews and two rookies at the position in Matt Hibner and Josh Cuevas, who has flashed this and will likely get ample opportunities to exploit that trend, especially off of play-action if they can get the run game going with Henry.
With fellow starting safety Jaylinn Hawkins out for this game due to a knee injury, the Ravens could have their three-time All Pro playing further back this week. This would allow Minter to deploy other aggressive downhill defenders closer to the line of scrimmage, such as fourth-year breakout inside linebacker Trenton Simpson and second-year safety Keondre Jackson. Having Hamilton assume more coverage responsibilities could help the Ravens defend the middle of the field better in the zones behind the linebackers where Deshaun Watson feasted on last week. Burrow won't hesitate to follow suit and try to exploit as well, given how high a level of processor he is at reading and carving up defenses.

title: Will Lamar Jackson Return to Face Bills? Doctor's Opinion vs. Ian Rapoport's Report
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills know their next opponent is the Baltimore Ravens.
As to whom the opponent will start at quarterback on November 1 in Orchard Park, it doesn't appear that even the Ravens know that at this point in time.
Two-time NFL MVP Lamar Jackson has missed the last three games due to what Dr. David Chao believes is a left ankle eversion sprain . Conventional wisdom suggests Jackson will return for the Week 8 game against the Bills, but there's certainly reason for doubt.
There was a thought that Jackson, although not 100 percent, could have played against the Cincinnati Bengals on October 25. After limited participation in practice, the QB1 was tabbed as questionable to play on Friday's injury report. On Saturday, the Ravens ruled him out.
Meanwhile, Chao, a former San Diego Chargers' team doctor who now offers expert injury analysis, gave Jackson a one-in-three chance to suit up in Week 7.
This week, Chao has issued a 50 percent probability that Jackson returns to game action against the Bills.
"I don't think he's for sure playing this week yet. I think this is a 50-50 week," said Chao on Monday. "Let's see how it develops. It's a big game, Bills, etc., but I don't think it's a guarantee that he's playing. I think it's 50-50 right now."
Lamar Jackson keeps trending closer to a return. Week 6: I had him at 85% no-go Week 7: 66% no-go Week 8: 50-50 This is his best chance to return since the ankle injury. pic.twitter.com/kxbYA7udrK
On Tuesday, NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport appeared on ESPN's Big Day , and proceeded to make a strong declaration.
"I expect, based on the people I've spoken with, that Lamar Jackson will play this week.  He will be on the field this week against the Buffalo Bills," said Rapoport. "He is believed to be as close to 100 percent as he has been, and the Ravens do expect him to play."
As for Ravens' head coach Jesse Minter, his comments did not reach that same level of confidence.
"Lamar's working his butt off to be back, to be out there," said Minter one day after losing to the Bengals. "I'll think he'll be in a decent spot, but we'll know a lot more on Wednesday."
It's also worth noting that Rapoport called Jackson's ankle sprain "a two-to-three week injury."
Quite frankly, it's foolish for him to speak so matter of factly. There have been plenty of instances where this type of injury, depending upon severity, can take up to four weeks, especially when the player relies as heavily on his legs as Jackson does.
There's also reason to question Rapoport's sources in this situation. Last week, Jackson called out the talking head for apparently mis-reporting the injury.
"Ian Rapoport said that? He part of the training staff?" said Jackson during his media availability .
The Bills are 2-2 against Jackson as a starter in the regular season and 2-0 in the playoffs.
While Jackson is probably more likely to play than not, the Bills must prepare in case backup Tyler Huntley gets the call again.
Huntley, who can also tuck it and run effectively, owns an 8-11 record as a starter. He has 34 career appearances under his belt, accounting for 17 touchdown passes and 11 interceptions.
Last time out against the Bengals, Huntley completed 67.6 percent of passes for 298 yards and one touchdown. He was sacked four times and intercepted once in the 35-13 loss.
While the QB choice is TBD, the Ravens will almost definitely be without starting guard Olaivavega “Vega” Ioane due to injury.
As for the Bills' injury outlook , they appear to be nearing full strength in Week 8.

title: Bills' Next Opponent Receives Worrisome Injury News as Ravens Take Another Hit
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills’ players and coaches may have been on a bye week over the last several days , but that wasn’t the case for the majority of teams in the league in Week 7 as the NFL was jam packed with plenty of exciting action last weekend .
For Buffalo’s upcoming opponent—the Baltimore Ravens—things weren’t so exciting on Sunday, though, as the AFC North squad fell short at home to the Cincinnati Bengals, 35-13, after originally leading 13-0 at halftime. The loss marked the team’s second straight in its division to fall to 4-3 on the season under first-year head coach Jesse Minter.
Furthermore, Baltimore appears to have lost an important member of its offensive line during the last matchup with Cincinnati, as well, as NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo reported on Tuesday morning that Ravens’ starting offensive guard Olaivavega “Vega” Ioane, who was selected at pick No. 14 overall in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft out Penn State this past spring, suffered a MCL sprain against the Bengals.
A 22-year-old native of Graham, Washington, Ioane was the fourth offensive lineman selected in the first round of April’s draft, but he was also the first guard to go off the board.
Seen by many talent evaluators as a sure-fire NFL starter, Ioane seamlessly transitioned into the starting lineup for Baltimore this offseason.
Making starts at right guard and center out of necessity due to various other injured players going down earlier this season up front for the Ravens, the former Nittany Lions’ lineman has been a solid presence along the offensive line during his first season as a professional.
In fact, according to the NFL’s Next Gen Stats , the 6-foot-4, 326-pound thumper allowed only a 4.6% pressure rate entering Week 6, and he surrendered zero sacks in 163 pass-blocking snaps ( 84 at RG, 79 at C ), as well, making him the highest-rated rookie guard in the NFL in that critical department.
For that reason, the news of Ioane being sidelined for at least “a little bit” is certainly brutal information to receive at this juncture of the season, especially considering that Baltimore’s franchise veteran quarterback Lamar Jackson is likely set to return to the lineup after missing the past three games with an apparent ankle injury.
If the rookie stalwart is unable to suit up against the Bills this weekend at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, then it will mean that the Ravens will be trotting out their sixth different offensive line combination through the first eight weeks of 2026 campaign.
And, while that’s a sight that Buffalo’s AFC counterpart likely doesn’t want to see this weekend, it’s certainly a situation that the Bills and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard will have to capitalize on .
Whether it be up-and-coming defensive star Deone Walker or former top-10 pick Ed Oliver on the interior of Buffalo’s defensive front, someone on the defensive line needs to dominate their battle with Baltimore’s backup at right guard on Sunday.
The matchup between the Bills and Ravens has future playoff implications written all over it, so it’ll be imperative that Buffalo takes full advantage of any areas of weakness that their upcoming opponent might have.
The objective for first-year head coach Joe Brady has seemingly always been to reach the No. 1 seed in the AFC during his inaugural season as the head man in charge in Western New York, and that goal appears to be more in reach than ever before entering November 2026, especially after the Kansas City Chiefs just dropped their first game of the season on Sunday Night Football against the Seattle Seahawks.
Out of the bye week, Brady and Leonhard must create a plan of attack to push forward with vengeance over the final 11 games of the season.
Exploiting Baltimore’s shortcomings up front would be a great place to start on Sunday.

title: Quenton Nelson Trade Gives Bills Urgency to Make Deal With Colts Immediately
full_text:
We are two weeks away from the NFL trade deadline but one big move has already gone down and that's a stark reminder for the Buffalo Bills that they can't sit around and wait much longer.
On Tuesday, the Indianapolis Colts traded All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
This obviously shows the Colts are not waiting around to start the fire sale everyone was expecting and this should add urgency for the Bills, who need to immediately call the Colts if they want to acquire players Indy is willing to sell off.
Three Colts players the Bills should have interest in are defensive linemen DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart and wide receiver Josh Downs, all of whom ESPN's Adam Schefter believes could get moved before the deadline.
"I think the players that could be on the move for the Colts are DeForest Buckner, Josh Downs, and Grover Stewart," Schefter stated on The Pat McAfee Show . "DeForest Buckner is the one that I think will be dealt next."
While the defensive line certainly isn't the most dire need the Bills have on defense, it's still a position group general manager Brandon Beane should consider adding to.
Ed Oliver and Deone Walker are great, but the Bills are lacking a third starting-caliber player at the position and Oliver has been banged up this season , which only makes adding depth more necessary.
Buckner would be the better option of the two because he's not only a plus run defender, but an elite interior pass-rusher, also. In seven games this season, Buckner has posted four sacks.
The Bills have had major issues stopping the pass this season and beefing up the pass-rush is a good way to fix that.
Stewart would be a cheaper option and a fine consolation prize, although he doesn't offer much as a pass-rusher. He would, however, be an upgrade for Buffalo's run defense.
At wide receiver, the Bills don't have a dire need there, at least not yet. Keon Coleman has done a great job stepping up in 2026 and Khalil Shakir and DJ Moore give Buffalo a strong trio.
However, Moore has been battling a shoulder injury and the Bills are just one injury away from being in a precarious spot at the position because Joshua Palmer simply can't be relied upon.
Adding Downs would give the Bills some strong insurance and a player who can do just about everything Moore can.
If the Bills want any one of these three players or someone else on the Colts' roster, they need to strike quickly or else they could miss the boat.

title: Tre'Davious White Projects When He'll Be Ready to Boost Bills' Subpar Defense
full_text:
Veteran cornerback Tre'Davious White is back in town with the Buffalo Bills for his 10th season as a pro.
The 2017 Bills' first-round draft pick has ditched his couch for one more run in Orchard Park. Buffalo signed White to its practice squad at the start of its Week 7 bye.
"This was a different kind of offseason for me. I've been sitting on the couch, drinking ginger ale and eating popcorn for a while," said the 31-year-old White as a guest on Eric Wood's Centered On Buffalo podcast .
White, a former All-Pro and well-liked locker room presence, provides leadership upon his arrival, but when will the grizzled veteran be able to contribute on field in a game situation for a struggling defense that ranks next to last against the pass?
"For me to be able to go out there and play in a NFL game at the position that I play, at defensive back, uhh, I got so much respect for the position, I'd disrespect the position just thinking I can just come off the couch and come out there and be Tre White," said White.
Naturally, White, who hasn't seen game action since Buffalo's divisional playoff loss last January, needs some sort of ramp-up period, especially considering he did not attend a training camp this past summer.
One has to think White will require at least four weeks of practice to get back up to speed in both the physical and mental aspects of the game.
"It's gonna be a process, which I know. We've been talking about it for a while. It's gonna be a process. I'm going to go into practice and just to go out there and move around a little bit. See where I'm at," said White.
Coming out of the bye, the Bills will hold their first Week 8 practice on Wednesday, October 28. It'll be White's first opportunity to get on the field in coordinator Jim Leonhard's defense.
"The best thing for me, I know these guys. I know a lot of these guys on the team," said White.
White's familiarity with multiple teammates coupled with his experience should speed up his acclimation period to some extent.
"The main thing with me is gonna be getting the reps with the guys, getting comfortable with who I'm around. Learning where my help is in this defense and learning where I can make some plays," said White.
If the plan is to give White at least four weeks of prep, then that means the earliest he would suit up is the Week 12 home game against the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night. Of course, this is sheer speculation, and a lot can change after White returns to the practice field on Wednesday.
White is another year older, but he still had some gas left in his tank as recent as last season.
Initially brought back as cornerback insurance during Spring 2025, White wound up as the full-time starter opposite Christian Benford as first-round rookie Maxwell Hairston spent the first six weeks on Injured Reserve.
White maintained his starting role as the Bills began to ease Hairston into the rotation, and the grizzled veteran was more than serviceable throughout the year. Over 16 regular season starts, he made 40 tackles, 6.0 TFL, one interception and nine pass break-ups. Opposing passers averaged only 5.1 yards per attempts and completed 51.1 percent when targeting White.
While he has thrived playing zone coverage for most of his career, White is a true technician, and student of the game, with plenty of capability in an aggressive man coverage scheme.
"I'm just gonna be playing ball," said White.

title: Week 8 NFL Power Rankings Roundup: Bills Move Up During Bye Week
full_text:
Week 7 was a well-timed bye for the Buffalo Bills . They're off to a 5-1 start, but they've been playing in multiple tight games. That's primarily been due to their defensive shortcomings.
Buffalo is currently first in the league in points scored , but their defense is 30th in points surrendered. They have been able to win despite this, but they hopefully found some answers during the bye week.
The Bills also saw their stock rise despite not playing. With the previously undefeated Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers both losing, Buffalo is climbing up many NFL power rankings. Let's check out where they stand with our weekly roundup.
Connor Orr moved Buffalo up to No. 1, due to two of the undefeated teams losing. The Bills now have a chance to get fully healthy, but they also have a couple of tough games ahead of them with the Baltimore Ravens and Minnesota Vikings up next.
"Coming off the bye, the directive for Buffalo was simple: improve ball security, weaponize this defense and try to keep Josh Allen packed in a sheet of ice like a fish purchased from Pike’s Market to help him absorb a massive stretch of games in which he will have to be Superman," Orr wrote.
ESPN picked the best offseason addition for each team and for the Bills, it was DJ Moore. Nick Suss said they have survived without him as he's dealing with a shoulder injury, but added that Moore takes the offense to another level when he's on the field. That's encouraging since he has a chance to be back in Week 8 .
"No player this season is averaging more yards per route run (2.47) with as deep of an average depth of target (15.9 yards) as Moore. He was acquired from the Bears for a 2026 second-round pick this offseason," Suss wrote.
Chad Graff and Josh Kendall of The Athletic moved Buffalo up two spots as well, giving them the No. 1 position. Still, they're concerned about the pass defense, which has been suspect all season. They did bring back Tre'Davious White , which should help, but won't fix everything.
"There was hope for the Bills’ defense after they hired Jim Leonhard to lead the unit. But six games into the season, Buffalo has the fourth-worst pass defense in the league based on EPA per dropback and the third-worst defense overall. They’ve allowed more than 250 passing yards in five of six games this season,"
Kristopher Knox says the Bills needed the bye week as they have been fighting to win one-score games to start the season. This break could be exactly what they need to get the defense back on track, because as he said, winning with a porous defense is not sustainable.
"Allen and the offense have been more than capable of offsetting that suspect defense when playing mostly mistake-free football. However, the Bills' early-season formula may not be sustainable against top-tier teams in January," Knox wrote.
Pete Prisco ranks Buffalo second overall, but like most analysts, he's worried about the defense. There's a huge test coming up against Lamar Jackson, which is a chance for Jim Leonhard and his unit to prove themselves worthy.
"They come off the bye with a big one against the Ravens, who should have Lamar Jackson back. The defense has to be better than it was before the bye," Prisco wrote.

title: Surprising Stat Shows How Clutch Bills' WR Keon Coleman Has Been in 2026
full_text:
Keon Coleman entered the league in 2024 and had a lot of pressure put on his shoulders. Not only was he the first selection for the Buffalo Bills that season (in Round 2), but he had some big shoes to fill.
Buffalo had just moved on from WR1 Stefon Diggs , and Coleman was tasked with taking over. He struggled throughout his first two seasons, and was even benched at one point in 2025 for multiple games.
This led to speculation that he would be cut or traded this offseason, but that never happened. Instead, Coleman has become the team's most consistent pass-catcher , filling in for an injured DJ Moore. After six games, Coleman has 19 receptions for 283 yards with three touchdowns. Most importantly, Josh Allen's job has been easy when targeting No. 0.
Through the first six weeks, Allen's quarterback rating when targeting Coleman is 139.8, which is the fifth-best in the NFL. His name is up there with elite players such as Justin Jefferson and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. That said, here's a look at which receivers make up the top five :
The Bills were off in Week 7 and will take on the Baltimore Ravens in Week 8. It's another tough test, but Buffalo has been up to the task throughout the season, thanks primarily to its offense.
Entering Week 8, Buffalo is first in points scored and fourth in yardage. Compare that to 30th in defensive points and 31st in defensive yardage and it's clear that the offense is doing the heavy lifting.
That offense can get even better starting this week. Moore has missed two full games and part of another two already this year. That's left the Bills thin at receiver and while Coleman has risen to the challenge, this offense will only look more dangerous when Josh Allen has Moore, Coleman, Khalil Shakir, and Dalton Kincaid all on the field together. That's without even considering what James Cook and Ty Johnson offer out of the backfield.
The only question now is whether defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard can get the defense on track. If so, the Bills could be an unstoppable force.
