title: Cowboys Week 7 Report Card: Williams Runs to Perfect Grade, Defense & Coaching Barely Pass
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys snapped their two-game losing streak on Monday night by notching a 38-21 victory over their NFC East rivals, the Philadelphia Eagles.
While it's obviously good for the Cowboys to get the win, it's hard to get excited about what we saw on Monday night.
After all, the Eagles are ravaged by injury and were missing key players on both sides of the ball, and especially on offense, with Jalen Hurts, DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks all out. As a result, this was hardly a measuring stick game.
Now, let's dive into the details a bit more and see how we graded the Cowboys following their Week 7 victory.
Prescott threw for 212 yards and three touchdowns, and those three scores were beautiful passes , but he also had some bad to really bad throws throughout the contest and barely finished with a completion rate above 50%. That was particularly surprising because Dallas' pass protection was very good.
CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens each had a touchdown grab, and Lamb found pay dirt twice. There was also a Ryan Flournoy sighting, with the young wide receiver finishing second on the team with 70 yards.
Someone wake us up when Jake Ferguson shows up this season. He was out-produced by Brevyn Spann-Ford for a second straight week, with the former not securing a single catch while the latter posted two for 11.
Not only was this the best game of Javonte Williams' season, but also of his career, with his 155 yards amounting to a new career-high for him. He also added a touchdown for good measure and his 6.2 yards per carry were more than he has averaged in any contest this season, and it was just the second time he has recorded more than four yards per tote in a game.
Williams showed great patience and vision, and he ran tough. The Cowboys' offensive line also had its best showing of the 2026 season in run-blocking.
Dallas needs to see this more often moving forward.
Still to many easy completions out there for an Eagles offense that had Tanner McKee, who threw for 211 yards, under center and Hollywood Brown and Makai Lemon as his best options at receiver.
A better quarterback would have had a field day, so the Cowboys were fortunate to face McKee.
According to Pro Football Focus , Dallas did muster up 18 pressures, but only two of those were turned into sacks, with Quinnen Williams and Donovan Ezeiruaku getting them.
There was even a pick! DeMarvion Overshown's leaping grab was one of the best plays of the entire game. Dallas now has two interceptions on the season, tied for the second-fewest.
Saquon Barkley was torching the Cowboys whenever he had the ball in his hands and finished with 8.8 yards per carry. However, the Cowboys were lucky because Barkley just couldn't stay on the field as he battled multiple injuries throughout the game.
Dallas did a good job limiting Dameon Pierce to under four yards per carry, but that's not exactly difficult to do, especially with the Eagles' short-handed offensive line. In all, the Eagles averaged a healthy 4.8 yards per tote.
This game might have gone much differently if Barkley was able to play his full allotment of snaps.
Bryan Anger had one solid punt that landed inside the 20 and one lackluster one when the Cowboys were buried deep in their own territory. Brandon Aubrey was a perfect 3-for-3 on extra points and field goals, and he knocked through a long of 55 yards.
The return game was OK without KaVontae Turpin , with guys like Jonathan Mingo and Tyler Goodson averaging 25 and 21 yards per kick return, respectively.
Mingo did nothing in the punt return game and let one bounce that allowed the Eagles to down the ball and set the Cowboys up deep in their own territory.
Head coach Brian Schottenheimer's failure to call a timeout near the end of the first half gave the Cowboys one less opportunity to score a touchdown. Dallas ended up settling for a field goal and went into halftime with the unused timeout, which is inexcusable.
We saw the embattled Cowboys head coach call a pair of give-up plays on third downs throughout the game, with the first coming on Dallas' second-to-last drive of the first half when he called a handoff to Williams on third-and-8. The bigger head-scratcher was dialing up a run to Hunter Luepke of all people on another third-and-8 in the fourth quarter at Philly's nine-yard line.
It was more of the same for Christian Parker, who is married to rarely blitzing. Parker gets a reprieve this week because Dallas' defense didn't implode, but a more competent quarterback is going to pick this unit apart every time.
Luckily for Parker and Co., the Cowboys won't face many of those over the next five weeks.

title: Dallas Cowboys Troll Eagles With Meek Mill Locker Room Celebration After MNF Win
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys entered Week 7 in a must-win situation, after getting embarrassed two games in a row in the primetime spotlight. On Monday night, the team capped off another busy week of action by taking down the NFC East rival Philadelphia Eagles in convincing fashion at Lincoln Financial Field.
Dallas secured the 38-21 win, positioned themselves to take control of the division, got the offense back on track, and even witnessed the defense pitch a shutout in the fourth quarter.
You have to take all of the wins, no matter how big or small, whenever you can get them, so the Cowboys were eager to celebrate closing out October with a win. And when the team made their way back to the locker room, they found a brilliant way to troll their arch rivals.
A video shared by Jon Machota of The Athletic showed players leaving the field and marching into the locker room, while "Dreams and Nightmares" by Grammy-nominated Philadelphia rapper Meek Mill blasted over the speakers in the locker room.
They’re playing that Eagles Meek Mill music in the Cowboys’ postgame locker room pic.twitter.com/pPkYQTMGpF
Bumping Meek Mill after beating the Eagles is a next-level troll move.
The vibes were high for Dallas after snapping their two-game skid, and Dak Prescott described the positive energy inside of the locker room during Brian Schottenheimer's post-game celebration.
“That's the time to celebrate. All the work that you've put in, a hard week of preparation, you take them one by one. You understand that you haven't won in a couple of weeks and some letdown games," Schottenheimer said when speaking to media after the game, via Todd Archer of ESPN.com.
"It's just an exciting (time). It's the culmination of all your hard work and you winning that game just coming together and that's the brotherhood showing and that's what makes it special is it's just that group in there. It's just a group that sweats together, sacrifices together and they get to celebrate together. And so that's what makes it fun, but that time doesn't last. Short week being this is a Monday. Take care of our bodies and we've got to be just as hungry as we were in approaching this week, last week as we need to do this.”
Now, we'll have to see if the Cowboys can keep that momentum rolling into next week when they return home to host the Arizona Cardinals at AT&T Stadium.

title: Jensen's Judgment: Jonah Coleman Has Forced Broncos' Hand
full_text:
Bo Nix finally snapped out of his slump in Week 7 , totaling nearly 300 yards from scrimmage, including a rushing and passing touchdown of 50-plus yards.
The Denver Broncos defeated the Arizona Cardinals handily, 30-16. Coinciding with Nix's get-right game was the return of rookie running back Jonah Coleman.
Coleman led the Broncos in rushing, with nine carries for 54 yards, and he outearned all of his fellow running backs in touches and snap share . It's unusual to see a rookie go from the training table on injured reserve to leading a team in rushing in a single game, especially one coached by Sean Payton.
But there's a reason why Payton immediately inserted Coleman into the lineup. The rookie has forced the Broncos' hand, and that's the subject of this week's Jensen's Judgment column.
The bitter truth is that Dobbins hasn't looked like the player we saw for 10 games last season. His burst has diminished, his vision is lacking, and his patience in allowing blocks to set up has gone from virtue to a vice. He's waiting too long to hit the hole.
The bottom line is, Dobbins wasn't getting it done, and the Broncos' 26th-ranked rushing offense (going into Week 7) was only prolonging Nix's funk. Dobbins only received six carries against the Cardinals, rushing for 23 yards (3.8 avg.), but Payton made sure to get him a goal-line carry, which he punched in for a touchdown.
That gesture didn't seem to mollify Dobbins, though, as he ran back to the sideline and sat down on the bench as soon as he got to his feet, instead of celebrating the score with his teammates. On the ensuing possessions, Coleman took over as the Broncos' second-half closer, much like he did in Week 2.
The difference between Week 7 and Week 2, though, was that Dobbins was a little banged up against the Jacksonville Jaguars. He was completely healthy in Sunday's game in Arizona.
Dobbins leads the Broncos with 87 carries for 293 yards and three touchdowns, but he's averaging a career-low 3.4 yards per carry. His explosiveness seems to have evaporated, and whether that's due to his age (turning 28 in December) or the cumulative effect of the major injuries he's suffered is anyone's guess.
When it comes to explosive runs, Dobbins has only five on 87 carries, giving him a 6% explosive-run rate, per NFL.com's Michael F. Florio . On 24 carries this season, RJ Harvey has zero explosive runs.
Coleman has four explosive runs on just 19 carries. In other words, the rookie is delivering a run of 10-plus yards on 21% of his carries. He moves the needle when he's on the field, and his burst simply gives the Broncos' offense an additional gear that's been absent with Dobbins as the No. 1 running back.
In Dobbins's defense, he did have an explosive run of 13 yards wiped out by an illegal shift penalty against the Cardinals, but it would have only improved his explosive-run percentage to just shy of 7%. The consistent ability to pick up positive yardage on the ground has played a big role in the Broncos' struggles on third down, creating way too many third-and-longs, and exacerbating, again, the Nix issue.
This offense ranks 31st in third-down efficiency, converting just 31.1% of its attempts. The one-yard-and-a-cloud-of-dust approach with Dobbins simply hasn't worked, and it's put Nix way behind the sticks with too many third-and-longs (defined as needing at least seven yards to convert).
Now, don't get it twisted; Dobbins should still have a role in this offense. His body language wasn't good on Sunday, but if he can get his mind right, his leadership and energy provide an emotional lift to the Broncos' offense — and that's valuable.
When Payton took back the play-calling duties going into Week 5, Dobbins saw his touch share skyrocket. He had 18 carries in Week 5, followed by 17 totes in Week 6.
Alas, the increase in touches did not result in better efficiency. After beating the Seattle Seahawks in overtime, Dobbins pointed to the murderer's row of defenses the Broncos had faced up to that point in the season, and he had a valid point.
But Dobbins didn't look any better against the Cardinals. Meanwhile, Payton was running out of time to inject some life into this rushing offense, and Coleman's return from injured reserve was staring him in the face.
It brings me no pleasure to write this. Dobbins was given a two-year, $16 million contract extension this past spring, and is being paid to play like a top-10 running back, but the results aren't there.
It's a disappointment. But the NFL is a production-based business, and Dobbins, of all people, understands that.
Payton has now seen the explosive element Coleman brings to the table in two games this season. 19 NFL carries isn't the biggest sample size to go on, but until he gives Payton a reason to think differently, the rookie should continue to outearn Dobbins in snaps and touches as this team's RB1.
Dobbins may get the start, once again, as a sort of consolation for his demotion, but Coleman must lead the way. The rookie has already proven himself as a runner, as a receiver, and as a trusted role player in pass protection.
If Dobbins wants to earn back the RB1 duties, he's got to show it on the field. Otherwise, it's the Jonah Coleman show behind Nix moving forward.
Whether Coleman's emergence has cooled the Broncos' jets on the NFL trade winds remains to be seen. The Broncos were linked to Jonathan Taylor by Adam Schefter , but that was before Coleman's big return game in Arizona.
Meanwhile, the Indianapolis Colts' fire sale continues apace, with All-Pro right guard Quenton Nelson being dealt to Seattle on Tuesday. Stay tuned.

title: Broncos Sign WR Ahead of Week 8 Tilt vs. Chiefs
full_text:
The Denver Broncos made a pair of roster moves in the lead-up to their Week 8 home showdown with the Kansas City Chiefs.
The team announced Tuesday that it has signed wide receiver Eli Pancol to the practice squad. In a corresponding transaction, Denver released defensive back Ugo Amadi — who joined the club on Oct. 9 — from the taxi squad.
Undrafted in 2025 and yet to appear in an NFL game, Pancol spent his rookie campaign with the Jacksonville Jaguars and Indianapolis Colts, with whom he signed a reserve/future contract in January. The Colts waived him at final cuts and eventually released him again last week following a second stint on the practice squad.
Due to injuries, the 6-foot-3, 205-pound wideout was a five-year collegiate contributor at Duke, catching 130 passes for 1,710 yards and 14 touchdowns from 2019-2024. He added seven rushes for 40 yards and two scores on the ground.
In 2024, he earned third-team All-ACC honors while taking home the Brian Piccolo Award, given to the “most courageous” football player in the Atlantic Coast Conference.
Pancol ran a 4.40 forty-yard dash and recorded a 36-inch vertical jump at his Pro Day prior to turning pro.
"Any team that gets Eli Pancol is getting a relentless hard worker," Pancol told The Draft Network in a 2025 interview. "I’ve proven that no matter how much adversity comes my way, I’m always going to overcome the obstacles. I’m coming to work every single day to get better. I love the game of football. I love feeding off the energy of the fans. I use that to energize my teammates. I’m also a physical receiver who loves to block. I’m ready to work. You can’t go wrong with somebody like me."
Interestingly, Pancol becomes the fifth WR to land on Denver's practice squad, joining the likes of Dane Key, Cameron Ross, Kolbe Katsis, and Michael Bandy. None of these incumbents have been promoted to the active roster in recent weeks.
Speaking of the 53, the Broncos could be a little shorthanded at the position in Week 8 with Pat Bryant still on short-term injured reserve and Jaylen Waddle emerging from Sunday's win over the Cardinals with an apparent chest issue.
Head coach Sean Payton indicated Monday that Marvin Mims might see an uptick in usage going forward, as he's seemingly leapfrogged Troy Franklin on the depth chart.
“We’re trying to get him touches. He’s one of our explosive playmakers," Payton told reporters via conference call on Monday. "Quite honestly, we need to get him more touches on offense, and we’ll do that. A lot of it had to do with the way they were kicking off. We kind of, you noticed, went more to a single returner and certainly that first one (return) that puts us at midfield was a big one for us.”

title: Sean Payton Reveals Why Broncos Never Lost Faith in Bo Nix Amid Bench Calls
full_text:
The noise around Bo Nix reached a fever pitch entering the Denver Broncos' Week 7 road game against the Arizona Cardinals.
On the heels of a concerningly slow start to the season, Nix passed for just 107 yards against the Seattle Seahawks on primetime, and critics came out of the woodwork to pile on the third-year quarterback. We heard from network pundits like Ryan Fitzpatrick that Nix's performance was "almost disrespectful to the quarterback position," while former teammates joined in the pile-on .
Then the calls for Denver to bench Nix began. From the local airwaves and blogs to a vocal segment of Broncos Country, people genuinely wanted Sean Payton to take action at quarterback.
The din has quieted after Nix's historic performance on the road against the Cardinals. He threw for just 222 yards, but he had four explosive passing plays , including a 52-yard screen that RJ Harvey took to the house.
What seemed to open the floodgates for Nix was his 62-yard rushing touchdown in the second quarter. He had a different vibe and energy about him from there on out, and became only the fifth player in NFL history to post a rushing and passing touchdown of 50-plus yards in the same game.
After the game, Payton explained why he and the Broncos never considered sitting Nix down amid his slump, even, say, to give him a mental breather.
"The confidence inside the building relative to his abilities hadn't changed at all," Payton said on Sunday. "And I appreciate some guys—sometimes you're answering questions about whether or not, and there's not one time where we were [thinking about making a change]— he's our guy."
To his credit, Payton never wavered on Nix publicly. He backed his young quarterback in the immediate aftermath of that Seahawks game — which the Broncos won, by the way.
After seeing the brutal day Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs had against Seattle's defense, the entire NFL world softened its opinions on Nix and his 107 passing yards. Mahomes passed for just 165 yards and zero touchdowns, with an interception.
And that was with Kansas City playing from behind the entire game. A big difference between Mahomes's day against Seattle and Nix's was how the Broncos' quarterback was able to lead to touchdown-scoring drives early in the game to build a two-score lead.
Not only that, but Nix and the Broncos did not turn the ball over against Seattle. The Chiefs had three turnovers.
It kind of puts things in perspective, doesn't it? What made the Nix cacophony so wild to behold was that the Broncos actually won the game.
For the third straight year of his career, Nix defeated the defending World Champions, and people wonder why Payton and company never considered making a quarterback change.
The calls to bench Nix began after his Week 4 performance against San Francisco, and with each passing week, they grew. As I wrote back then : Bench Nix? Don't make me laugh.
This kid is now 29-12 as a regular-season starter and has a career winning percentage of .707. It's not always pretty, but Nix is a winner; he's a gamer, and he performs at his best when the chips are down and his back is against the wall — just as we saw on Sunday at State Farm Stadium.
Nix was always the one in control of how long his slump would last, but the Broncos kept on winning games. It was no coincidence that in his breakout game, his supporting cast finally rediscovered their complementary playmaking ability.
"It was good to see him play well, and it was good to see us block well and make some plays down the field," Payton said of Nix and the offense.
They say that a franchise quarterback is "the tide that raises all ships." Guys like RJ Harvey, Courtland Sutton, and Marvin Mims Jr. were suddenly executing, getting open, and making would-be tacklers miss, but they took their cues from Nix, whose confidence and aura seemed to come flooding back in waves after his 62-yard touchdown romp.
By the way, did you know that Nix's huge touchdown run was the longest by a quarterback in franchise history? These aren't the first records Nix has set, and they won't be the last.
The Broncos now sit at 5-2 and they have the chance to overtake the Chiefs in the AFC West this week if they can get the win. Nix has never lost to the Chiefs at Mile High, and given the stakes and his newfound momentum, don't be surprised if he gets the last word on Mahomes and company after Week 1's ugly loss at Arrowhead Stadium.
The toughest opponents on the Chiefs' schedule have only just begun. Besides the Broncos this week, the Chiefs still have to face the 49ers, Los Angeles Rams, Cincinnati Bengals, Buffalo Bills, and New England Patriots.
The Broncos have already faced the entire NFC West, going 3-1. The Broncos have a few more tough opponents left on the schedule, but the worst is behind them.
If Nix leads the Broncos to a win over Kansas City this week, they could run away with the division and set themselves up to repeat as AFC West champions.
All of the Broncos' goals for this season are still very much on the table — even more reason why benching Nix was unthinkable inside the walls at Dove Valley.
He's always been Denver's guy.

title: Broncos Are 5-2, But These 3 Veterans Could Still Be Traded
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is approaching on November 10 , leaving the Denver Broncos with two more games until the big date.
The Broncos have a chance to take the lead in the division with their rematch with the Kansas City Chiefs this week, followed by a road trip to face the Carolina Panthers. These next two weeks, not just for Denver but for every team, will be critical in determining whether to be buyers or sellers at the deadline.
As we saw with the Seattle Seahawks on Tuesday, when they acquired All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts , winning teams often hunt for an extra piece to push them over the top, while struggling teams look to move players for draft picks to help with their future.
Even at 5-2, the Broncos are in a somewhat weird spot, as they have the oldest roster in the NFL when weighted by snaps. They also have an expensive roster with some core pieces set to be free agents, and they won't be able to keep everyone.
Not only could the Broncos look to add a player at the deadline, but they should try to move on from a few of their own. That's what we're talking about today.
The Broncos should try to deal two of these players, with the third depending on how the team feels about its depth at the position. Let's get into it.
Dobbins is the first of two players Denver should be looking to trade. His contract is only a one-year commitment (2026). The second year of his deal comes with a $12 million cap charge, but his salary isn't guaranteed. Suffice it to say, his level of play hasn't justified his contract, and certainly not a second year at $8 million.
Dobbins's play has been a detriment to the offense. He's leaving yards on the field.
Dobbins ranks second-to-last on RYOE (rush yards over expected) with a -77, meaning he's expected to have 77 more rushing yards than he actually has. But the rationale to trade him goes beyond his play and into his attitude, as we've seen on the sideline and in the locker room after games.
Dobbins had issues with his lack of touches when Davis Webb was the play-caller, and though he may have celebrated Sean Payton taking over beginning in Week 5, his efficiency only got worse, despite his coach feeding him a touchdown in three straight games. On the sideline, Dobbins seems a bit standoffish of late.
Dobbins isn't celebrating scores and big plays with teammates, like RJ Harvey's 52-yard touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals, or even his own score at State Farm Stadium.
Jonah Coleman took over as the closer against the Cardinals, while Dobbins sat on the sidelines with a look of frustration anytime the cameras panned to him. Coleman is on his way to taking over the top job, and with two games left before the deadline, Dobbins losing the RB1 job seems inevitable.
If the Broncos can find a taker on Dobbins, they shouldn't hesitate to move him.
This one is tough, given Mims's explosive plays against the Cardinals and Payton saying he wants to get him more involved in the offense. The issue has been Mims's effort.
Outside of the Cardinals game, his lack of intensity has been problematic on offense on plays where he isn't designed to get the ball. And when there have been plays designed to get him the ball on deep shots, the effort hasn't been there, as if he didn't expect his quarterback to actually target him.
The added issue is Mims's play as a returner, although he's been an All-Pro twice in his first three years. He's been excellent as a returner, but he's been less reliable this season, especially as a punt returner. His ball security has been poor, with a costly fumble against the San Francisco 49ers, and his decision-making when fielding punts has been even worse.
Mims is also in the final year of his rookie deal, and the Broncos haven't seemed intent on extending him. Granted, they like to do extensions during the bye, and that's coming in Week 10, but they were quiet during the offseason and preseason. With wide receiver Pat Bryant set to return from injured reserve soon, the Broncos could make room on the roster for him by trading Mims.
However, one potential hold-up to trading Mims is the Broncos' depth. Offensively, it would be as difficult to replace him with Troy Franklin waiting as a reserve.
But Franklin has struggled more often than not this season. As a returner, Kolbe Katsis would be the immediate Mims replacement, but he's on the practice squad. It's tough to justify a spot on the 53-man roster and 48-man game-day squad for a returner-only player.
If the Broncos don't plan on extending Mims, a trade would make a lot of sense. However, given that Mims was Payton's first draft pick as Broncos head coach, the symbolism in play could cool the team's trade heels. Time will tell.
Kris Abrams-Draine and Jahdae Barron have done well enough that Denver could explore trading Moss or Ja'Quan McMillian. Moss would make more sense due to the usage of the two depth players.
Now, unlike Dobbins and Mims, I'm not straight-up advocating for a Moss trade; it's more of an explore-the-possibilities idea to see what the Broncos could get on the trade market. If an offer wows them, they could pull the trigger.
Moss and McMillian are both free agents after this year, and Denver will be hard-pressed to keep them both. The Broncos are in a spot where they'll likely have to pick one or the other.
Moss is a good cornerback who gets a bad rap, but he'll likely be the more expensive of the two soon-to-be free agents because he plays on the boundary. Some projections have Moss commanding $20 million per year on his next deal, with some even suggesting $25 million per year as a high possibility, given how much the cornerback market has grown.
Again, Abrams-Draine and Barron have done well. Denver should feel confident in turning to either of them for a larger role without the coverage unit falling off, especially with Patrick Surtain II coming back from an injury. Neither player has really done much in the slot, which is another reason why Moss is more likely to be dealt than McMillian.
Many teams could use some corner help, and Moss would not only cost Denver more than McMillian to keep, but would also likely net them more in a trade. This could allow the Broncos to be more flexible with their draft picks when it comes to trading for a player at the deadline, if they so choose.

title: Broncos' Snap Counts vs. Cardinals Hint at Major Shakeup
full_text:
The Denver Broncos went into State Farm Stadium on Sunday and blew out the Arizona Cardinals , 30-16. Denver's 14-point margin of victory was its highest of the season.
Week 7's game also wrapped up the Broncos' four NFC West frames; Denver went 3-1 against arguably the toughest division in football.
As we continue sifting through the aftermath of the Broncos' fifth win of the season, let's examine the snap counts to see what we can glean about playing time trends and individual player outlook. Keep in mind, quarterback Bo Nix and the Broncos' five starting offensive linemen played 100% of the game, totaling 61 snaps.
Alex Palczewski saw a season-high 14 snaps in Week 7, as the Broncos ran a lot of jumbo packages. With that said, we'll start on the offensive side of the ball with the running backs, where we see a major shakeup in snap share.
Coleman went from the training table on injured reserve to the starting lineup, essentially. Dobbins started the game, but Coleman's snap share doubled the veteran's.
That's how it shook out in touch share, too, with Coleman finishing with 11 touchdes (nine carries/two receptions) to Dobbins's six. Coleman produced 69 yards of offense with his 11 touches, while Dobbins had 23 yards and a touchdown.
Adding what Sean Payton said about Coleman earning the playing time he received, and the Broncos may have a new RB1. Not to be outdone, though, Harvey had five touches for 60 yards, including a 52-yard touchdown catch on a perfectly timed and executed screen pass.
Note that Prentice's 10 snaps were a season high. This accounts only for offensive snaps, but the fullback also made some hay with his special teams snaps, blocking a punt in the second half.
Sutton again led the way in snap share, finishing with three catches for 45 yards. He caught a 20-yard pass on the Broncos' first play of the game, an explosive harbinger of what was to come in this game.
Waddle had the second-highest snap share, finishing with four catches for 48 yards on a team-high seven targets. His 27-yard catch down the right seam was one of four explosive passing plays on the day.
Waddle suffered an injury late in the game, falling on a fumble. He did not return.
It was great to see Mims make some hay with his snap share on Sunday. He played with intensity, taking a 20-yard completion and turning it into a 47-yard gain by making an initial would-be tackler miss. More of this, please , Coach Payton.
Franklin had his opportunities, including on a well-executed flea-flicker, but he couldn't come down with the ball despite it hitting him in the hands. He was held to zero catches on two targets. Meanwhile, Humphrey caught his second pass of the season — a five-yard gain.
This was a rough game for the tight ends. Trautman had two costly penalties, though he did play a part in springing Nix on his 62-yard touchdown run by tricking the defensive back covering him into thinking the quarterback was still in the pocket, even though he was about to blaze past him on his way to pay-dirt.
Engram was the only targeted tight end in the passing game, finishing with one reception on three targets for two yards. Nix just doesn't throw to the tight ends.
Adkins saw a season-high snap share, doing some big-time blocking in the Broncos jumbo packages and multi-tight-end sets.
Uwazurike led the way, although Allen did get banged up late in the game. It was easily Uwazurike's best game of the season, though, totaling four pressures and two QB hits, with four tackles.
Allen was a monster in the middle once again, registering five pressures and three QB hits. He didn't get a sack, but he was a force all game long, and he totaled three tackles.
Roach was an absolute best, with three pressures, two hits, and a sack. He also chipped in three tackles (two solo). He received a game ball for a reason.
D.J. Jones was able to generate one pressure and just one tackle. It was a quiet day for Denver's nose tackle. But the other Jones — Sai'vion — had a career-high 28 snaps and notched the first sack of his career. Sai'vion also contributed two tackles.
In Cooper's first game of the season, he came only two snaps away from Bonitto's 47 snaps. Cooper totaled three pressures and one tackle.
Bonitto was an animal, totaling a team-high six pressures and one QB hit. He also chipped in just one tackle, but he impacted Jacoby Brissett throughout the game, making life tough on the Cardinals' quarterback.
The Broncos continue to rely on Robinson, and he doesn't disappoint. He didn't register a sack, but he did have three pressures and a QB hit, while chipping in three tackles.
Tillman saw a healthy snap share once again, even amid Cooper's return, because Jonah Elliss was placed on IR. Tillman played well, with two pressures and one QB hit, along with two tackles. He was excellent in this game .
Singleton played 100% of the snaps, and he filled up the stat sheet, with 19 tackles, a sack, and three pressures. He went sideline to sideline making plays for the Broncos.
Strnad also had a good game, finishing with six tackles. He was targeted five times in coverage, allowing four completions, but it was for a total of just 19 yards because of how quickly he wrapped up the receiver. He's having a great season.
No more part-time snaps for Moss; he received 100% of the playing time in his first full game back from his rib injury. He was targeted five times, but only gave up two completions. One of them was a big gain, though.
Barron checked in next, in terms of snap share, and it may have been his roughest game of the season. But he was often asked to shadow Trey McBride, and Barron was on the losing end of that matchup. At least Barron totaled five tackles, though he gave up four completions on five targets for 41 yards.
McMillian had several opportunities for an interception hit him in the hands. He usually capitalizes on those opportunities, but not on this day. Still, he totaled five tackles and gave up four completions on eight targets for 46 yards. He was very good in coverage.
Abrams-Draine took his tackling and physicality to another level in this one. He finished with three solo tackles, and allowed just three of his five targets to be caught for 16 yards. He didn't have an interception, but it was overall his best game of the season.
Jones played 100% of snaps, but it wasn't his best game. He gave up two completions on three targets for 34 yards, and totaled nine tackles. He was also penalized.
Rapp was elevated from the practice squad once again and essentially played starter snaps. He wasn't quite as good as he was last week, but he was often the Broncos' high safety and wasn't officially targeted. He had two tackles.
Key's day was a bit rough. He saw plenty of snaps but didn't impact the box score. In coverage, he was targeted twice, allowing one catch for 14 yards. He was a little bit late to react at times.

title: Broncos HC Sean Payton Gets 'Quite Honest' About Using Marvin Mims Jr.
full_text:
Among the footnotes included in the Denver Broncos' 30-16 victory over the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday was the deployment of Marvin Mims, who returned to his prior role as the team's primary returnman.
Whereas the team had two players back deep in recent weeks, Mims was flying solo against the Cardinals , returning two punts for eight yards and four kicks for 103 yards, including a 39-yard scamper, at State Farm Stadium.
Perhaps more importantly, Mims saw an uptick in usage on the offensive side, catching two passes for 53 yards — highlighted by a 47-yard catch-and-run — across 16 snaps, running as the No. 3 WR behind Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton.
This was perhaps by design, as Broncos head coach Sean Payton reiterated his long-standing desire to craft additional opportunities to get the ball in Mims' hands.
“We’re trying to get him touches. He’s one of our explosive playmakers," Payton told reporters via conference call on Monday. "Quite honestly, we need to get him more touches on offense, and we’ll do that. A lot of it had to do with the way they were kicking off. We kind of, you noticed, went more to a single returner and certainly that first one (return) that puts us at midfield was a big one for us.”
It was an overall banner day for both units; Denver's offense hung three touchdowns on Arizona's hapless defense, one of which was preceded by a blocked punt. Kicker Wil Lutz also made all of his extra points and went three-for-three on field goal attempts.
“I think the quickest way to improve your team is in the kicking game and then in your defensive and offensive fronts," Payton said. "If you talk about taking care of the football and playing well on special teams, you’re going to give yourself a chance. I think [Special Teams Coordinator/Assistant Head Coach] Darren [Rizzi] and his group have done a real good job.”
The stakes become ratcheted much higher for the Broncos on Sunday, when they'll welcome the rival Kansas City Chiefs to Empower Field at Mile High for a battle of 5-2 versus 5-1. Winner takes sole control of the AFC West around the midway point of the 2026 campaign.
With WR Pat Bryant (ankle) expected to miss another game, and considering Patrick Mahomes is on the other sideline, Denver may look to lean on its passing attack — and Mims is likely to see a handful of targets.
Payton should make good on his vow and find ways to get Mims more involved. He's proven to be a reliable deep threat with reliable hands and a knack for the clutch. The All-Pro special-teamer could even be the deep threat if Waddle (chest) is forced to miss Week 8.
“I’ve said this a hundred times, but divisional games are always important and they typically kind of move," Payton said Monday of the upcoming tilt. "I don’t see rivalry weeks in the NFL. They’re generally divisional games where you have an important game against a division opponent. So I don’t see the Auburn-Alabama. I don’t see the Ohio State-Michigan. That’s just from being in this league long enough and doing it long enough.”

title: Sean Payton Offers 'Explosive' Take on Jonah Coleman's Growing Role
full_text:
If you watched the Denver Broncos' 30-16 win over the Arizona Cardinals, you could feel a big shift .
Bo Nix looked like his old self , shaking off the rust from the broken ankle he suffered back in January and regaining his confidence. He made history with his 62-yard touchdown run and 52-yard touchdown pass to RJ Harvey.
The Broncos' offense still showed a few warts of inconsistency, but overall, it was a big step forward, and exactly the type of get-right game Nix and company needed. One of the reasons it felt so different offensively was the presence of rookie running back Jonah Coleman.
After spending four weeks on injured reserve, the Broncos activated Coleman for this game , but we weren't sure how the rookie would fit into the offensive flow of things. It's rare to see a player — let alone a rookie — go from the training table on IR to leading the team in offensive touches, but that's what happened.
Coleman led the team with nine carries for 53 yards and caught two passes for 15 yards. He also showcased his proficiency as a pass protector , further earning the trust of Nix and his coaches.
After a night to sleep on it and watch the film, Broncos head coach Sean Payton shared his thoughts on Coleman's performance in the desert amid Mile High speculation over who this team's No. 1 running back is.
“He played well. The touches he had were explosive," Payton said of Coleman on Monday morning.
Payton doesn't go out of his way to compliment rookies, but he gave Coleman some love. That says a lot.
It could be a sign of things to come, as Payton said that Coleman's 11 touches in Week 7 came the hard way; the rookie earned the role he was given on Sunday, and he absolutely capitalized on the opportunity.
"Like anything else, I think it’s something you earn," Payton said of Coleman. "He’s done a good job of that."
Coleman has only been active for three games this season. He's touched the ball in two of those games, and his impact has been palpable.
The Broncos' run game was much more productive with the rookie in the backfield. Coleman's burst and vision set him apart from Dobbins and Harvey. Unlike his Week 2 performance against the Jacksonville Jaguars , Coleman showed down-to-down consistency against Arizona.
As a veteran, Dobbins has good vision, but he's lacked burst this season. Harvey has burst in spades, but he lacks vision. The two backs only combined for nine carries against the Cardinals, matching Coleman's total number of totes.
On one third-quarter scoring drive, Coleman kept moving the chains with three runs for 18 yards. Once the Broncos made it to the goal line, Dobbins was inserted into the lineup, and he was able to punch it in from one yard out.
Fantasy football people would say that Dobbins "vultured" a touchdown that should have gone to Coleman, given how the rookie carried that drive as a between-the-tackles runner. But Payton has to play the political game, and he very much appreciates Dobbins.
So even though Coleman's touch and snap share outpaced Dobbins, Payton made sure to give his veteran back the opportunity to score a touchdown for the third straight game. To his credit, Dobbins didn't let his coach down, but the back's energy seemed a bit off.
For example, after his third-quarter touchdown at State Farm Stadium, Dobbins didn't celebrate with teammates in the end zone, but instead trotted off to the sideline and immediately sat down on the bench. That vibe will be something to monitor moving forward, especially given the rumors coming out of the Broncos' locker room post-game that Dobbins didn't make himself available to the media.
In the Broncos' season-opening loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, Coleman dressed but didn't touch the ball. Dobbins actually had his most proficient day as a runner against the Chiefs, averaging 4.5 yards on eight carries.
I would expect to see a heavy dose of both Coleman and Dobbins this Sunday in the Broncos' rematch with the Chiefs. After Kansas City lost to the Seattle Seahawks in Week 7, this next game at Mile High will determine which team leads the AFC West.
Given the burst and playmaking ability Coleman has shown this season, it wouldn't be a surprise to see him once again out-earn Dobbins in touches and snaps. The rookie is a complete back, which means he doesn't have to come off the field on third down, though that's often when Payton will look to get Harvey involved in the offense.
Entering Week 7, the rumor mill was rife with nuggets connecting the Broncos to various running backs ahead of the November 10 trade deadline, including Jonathan Taylor . With two games left until the deadline, Coleman's emergence may have cooled Denver's jets on the possibility of trading for a running back.

title: Film Room: Bo Nix's Cardinals Performance Changes the Conversation
full_text:
The Denver Broncos offense finally came alive, blasting the Arizona Cardinals 30-16 on Sunday afternoon at State Farm Stadium. This was the perfect “get-right” game for the Broncos, as Arizona’s defense ranks among the worst in the league at allowing explosive plays.
Despite some inconsistencies throughout the game, this was by far Bo Nix’s best performance since the AFC divisional round playoff game against the Buffalo Bills last season. He unlocked the passing offense early, finally found his legs as a runner, and took advantage of his opportunities to make plays within the structure of the offense.
Nix finished the game 15-of-29 for 222 yards and a touchdown, and added another 73 yards on seven carries with a 62-yard touchdown run .  That touchdown run was massive because it allowed the offense to relax and exhale, jolting some confidence into a maligned unit that has struggled to get anything going all year.
We’re taking a long look at the explosive plays in this week’s film room.
This might be the best throw Bo has made all year. He hasn't shown the confidence to rip the Dig over the head of the LB at all. This was a great way to start the game. pic.twitter.com/aMOn5DXEOu
Sean Payton’s offense features a lot of dig routes, and Nix hasn’t connected on them nearly as often as he should. It’s a staple of the passing game, and the Broncos have several receivers who succeed when running them.
Denver opened the game in an empty shotgun set, and the Cardinals run a quarters coverage shell. Notice how deep the safeties get in their drops, opening a huge window over the middle of the field for Courtland Sutton on the in-breaker.
This might be Nix’s best throw of the year. Watch as he uses a subtle pump fake to freeze linebacker Jack Gibbens, then rips a throw right over his head. I hope this throw gets plastered all over the locker room to prove to Nix that he doesn’t need to be hesitant to “let it rip” over the middle of the field.
The longest rushing touchdown by a QB in Denver Broncos history. Nobody had their eyes on Nix. Kudos to Adam Trautman for manipulating his defender downfield. pic.twitter.com/xqxe6vRBXD
Welcome back, Bo Nix! This 62-yard touchdown run was the longest rushing touchdown by a quarterback in Broncos history, the longest rush by a quarterback since Justin Fields ripped a 67-yard touchdown run in 2022, and the longest rushing touchdown of any player in the league this year.
This is a great process from Nix, as he navigated a muddy pocket and slashed through the Cardinals' defense at a top speed of 19.9 miles per hour. Arizona was in man coverage across the board, and nobody had their eyes on Nix when he escaped the pocket.
The Broncos run a sail concept to the right side of the field, drawing nearly every defender to that side and opening up a ton of grass for Nix to exploit.
Watch tight end Adam Trautman carefully. He does a fantastic job of manipulating his defender while Nix is taking off. He even flashes his hands to show a target, even though Nix is already several yards downfield. There wasn’t a defender within four yards of Nix until he got inside the 5-yard line.
This one felt good. It breathed life into the offense as a whole, but it also breathed confidence into Nix.
This is a perfect play call into the blitz. The OL has nobody to block downfield. Troy Franklin with a huge block, as well. pic.twitter.com/8lXpp0sb97
On the Broncos’ first possession of the second half, they executed a beautiful screen pass to running back RJ Harvey for a 52-yard touchdown. This play was historic for Nix, as he became the fifth quarterback in NFL history to record a 50-yard rushing touchdown and a 50-yard passing touchdown in the same game.
This is a beautiful play call by Payton. The Cardinals sent Mack Wilson and Kalen King on a blitz, and the Broncos' offensive line executed perfectly. Left guard Ben Powers is the only player with anybody to block for the first few yards, and Harvey was instantly off to the races.
Explosive run and screen plays can only happen if receivers are doing their job as blockers down the field. Watch Troy Franklin work over Garrett Williams and allow Harvey room to the inside. That’s textbook execution.
Shout-out to Erick Trickel, who called a 50-yard Harvey touchdown on a screen play in his bold predictions this week . Erick pulled some great numbers on the Cardinals' defense against screen plays for Dove Valley Deep-Divers Podcast , and nailed this prediction square on the head.
Cover 2 Hole shot. Burke bites on the out route and Bo puts a good ball on Mims before the safety can rotate over. pic.twitter.com/b8rSkQbJ3J
On the following offensive drive, Nix beats the Cardinals with a hole shot in Cover 2. Good things happen when Marvin Mims Jr. gets involved in the passing game, and Nix makes cornerback Denzel Burke pay for biting on tight end Evan Engram's out route.
Nix’s eyes are in the right place here, which helps to draw Burke to Engram. This is a good throw and an even better play by Mims, who slips a tackle in open space and scampers for a 47-yard catch-and-run.
Rip the seam into Tampa 2. Mack Wilson can't even get his head turned around. Excellent throw on the back-shoulder. This is promising stuff. pic.twitter.com/9fI4CljqRb
Our last play is incredibly exciting stuff from Nix. Arizona is in Tampa Cover 2, and Nix rips a back-shoulder throw to Jaylen Waddle up the seam. This is a tight-window throw, and Nix had the confidence to put it on Waddle with the safety crashing down.
First, Nix does a great job identifying the matchup, with Waddle drawing coverage from Mack Wilson running the pole. Nix hits his back foot and lets it fly, putting a great throw in the perfect place for Waddle to come down with it. Wilson doesn’t even get his head turned around, and Waddle makes a great catch for a 27-yard gain.
Nix still had a lot of frustrating issues this week, but I really liked the confidence he played with for most of the game. He showed better poise in the pocket, stepped into a handful of throws, and gave his playmakers opportunities downfield.
This was a great building-block game for Nix, as several of these plays suggest. His early-season timidity was hampering the offense, so it was a breath of fresh air to see him let his hair down and hunt with the football.
Nix got active with his feet to open things up and stayed aggressive when he had the opportunity. If he can keep this level of play, this offense has a chance to right the ship and be a dangerous unit for the rest of the season.

title: Broncos' Player Grades From 30-16 Win Over Cardinals
full_text:
The Denver Broncos took care of business by beating the Arizona Cardinals 30-16 , a team now at 2-5 and viewed as one of the worst in the NFL this year as they undergo a rebuild.
The Broncos were expected to win, and they did, with great play on both sides of the ball, but they still had concerning moments they need to correct before the Kansas City Chiefs arrive next Sunday for a rematch.
This week, the Broncos' player grades are mostly positive, but it's a one-game sample size. Some of these performances, even a few of the good ones, will need to be even better next week.
This game could be a springboard for greater consistency, especially on offense. That said, let’s get into the grades.
Both Broncos linebackers were all over the field against the Cardinals. Strnad didn’t have as productive a game in the box score, but he played well in coverage, rallied to the ball when he allowed a catch, and played well against the run, finishing with six tackles.
It's time for the Broncos to turn to Coleman fully, and not just because of what he did in this game, but also because of the play and attitude of J.K. Dobbins. In his first game back from injured reserve, Coleman ended the day with 11 total touches for 69 yards — nine for 54 rushing and two for 15 receiving — and was trusted late in the game to run out the clock.
Nix's first-half performance wasn't great, especially through the air, but he flipped the script in the second half and showed he's still a threat with his legs, with a 62-yard rushing touchdown .
BO NIX 62-YARD TOUCHDOWN RUN DENvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/sxC4uWF33r
Nix's pocket presence still needs improvement, though. He's still bailing the pocket when there isn’t pressure, but this could be a springboard for improvement, as it was a step forward with several explosive passing plays.
Alex Singleton | LB | Grade: 78.9
Singleton had some coverage lapses, as expected, but he wasn’t a liability and was flying around the field in the run game. He added pressure and big hits, which brought energy to the team, and finished with 19 tackles .
Dondrea Tillman | OLB | Grade: 76.4
Tillman had a great game on a limited snap count and has become an effective weapon when he sees the field. He could probably go to another team and thrive as a third rusher, but he sits as the fourth outside linebacker in Denver, but he does his job consistently whenever he hits the field.
Ja’Quan McMillian | CB | Grade: 76.3
McMillian has issues in coverage, especially against bigger matchups, but he has a nose for the ball and for generating takeaways. He didn’t have one against the Cardinals, but he got close a couple of times and stays mostly consistent in coverage. He is looking for a big extension.
RJ Harvey | RB | Grade: 74.8
Harvey is an explosive player who thrives in space, and he showed that with a big touchdown on a screen pass. There are still issues as a rusher, but the coaches just need to accept that Harvey isn’t a between-the-tackles runner and that they need to get him into space.
Quinn Meinerz | RG | Grade: 71.8
Meinerz was a mauler up front and did well in pass protection. He remains the Broncos' best offensive lineman and led the interior unit to its best game of the season.
Center Luke Wattenberg and left guard Ben Powers also played well, while the tackles, including Garett Bolles, were poor against the Cardinals.
Marvin Mims Jr. | WR | Grade: 70.1
Mims finally showed some effort on offense, even when the ball wasn’t going his way. That has been a concern with his play since 2024, and this was the first game he looked like he gave 100% on every snap he was out there. His returner inconsistencies have raised some questions, though.
Jahdae Barron | CB | Grade: 28.1
Barron had a tough task covering Trey McBride often, but he made it easier on Arizona at times. Barron was grabby throughout the game, and the Cardinals kept going to the refs about it, which may have led to two late defensive pass interference calls against him.
Devon Key | S | Grade: 30.6
The Broncos got a good game out of Key against the Seattle Seahawks, but he struggled against the Cardinals, as did Taylor Rapp. The play of both fill-in safeties made it clear that the Broncos need Talanoa Hufanga back as soon as possible.
Mike McGlinchey | RT | Grade: 32.4
There were multiple plays where McGlinchey had to choose between two rushers and ended up blocking no one. He has always had issues in pass protection, but normally made up for it as a run blocker. That didn’t happen in this game, and it isn't happening this season.
Troy Franklin | WR | Grade: 40.5
Weirdly, Franklin's blocking kept his grade from being even worse. As a receiver, both his routes and after the catch, he was, to be blunt, lazy. He didn’t put in the effort to get the ball, and yes, he was dealing with contact, but not enough to keep him from giving more effort to the catch, as shown on the botched flea-flicker at the end of the first half.
Adam Trautman | TE | Grade: 42.3
Trautman's best play came on Nix’s touchdown run, where he really sold the route and pass to keep his defender in coverage with his back to the ball as the quarterback streaked downfield. Were it not for Trautman, it probably wouldn't have been a touchdown. Suffice it to say, his best block in this game came without actually blocking a defender.
D.J. Jones | NT | Grade: 45.6
Jones played well overall, but a handful of plays hurt his grade. Without these five snaps, Jones's grade would have been 60.3. His struggles against double teams are a consistent issue, but the Cardinals didn’t put him in that position often.

title: Broncos' Biggest Winners and Losers From 30-16 Victory Over Cardinals
full_text:
The Denver Broncos defeated the Arizona Cardinals 30-16 on the road to get to 5-2 in the standings. It sure didn't look or sound like an away game, with the overwhelming number of Broncos fans at State Farm Stadium.
With the Kansas City Chiefs losing to the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday night, the stage is set for the Broncos' rematch with Patrick Mahomes and company next week at Mile High. The Broncos have the chance not only to balance the scales against the Chiefs and avenge their Week 1 loss, but also to make headway at the top of the AFC West at the halfway point of the season.
As we sift through the aftermath of the Broncos' fifth victory of the season, let's talk about this team's biggest winners and losers.
Nix finished with 295 yards from scrimmage, but it was his 62-yard touchdown run that seemed to reignite his confidence. He also tossed a 52-yard touchdown pass to RJ Harvey, becoming the fifth player in NFL history to record a rushing and passing touchdown of 50-plus yards in the same game.
Nix finished 15-of-29 passing for 222 yards and a touchdown. After the game, Nix toyed with a local media corps that had been skeptical that he had fully healed from his fractured ankle suffered back in January.
"You believe me now?" Nix asked with a smile from the post-game podium.
BO NIX 62-YARD TOUCHDOWN RUN DENvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/sxC4uWF33r
Nobody should be questioning Nix's health anymore, and his big game in the desert seemed to salve whatever was ailing him between the ears in his recovery from that serious injury.
Barron deserves a lot of credit for holding down the fort amid Patrick Surtain II's injury, but he had a rough game against the Cardinals. Barron was penalized twice for pass interference, and he allowed four of five targets to be completed for 41 yards.
Barron did finish with five tackles, and while his coverage was sticky, Jacoby Brissett was able to exploit him, especially one-on-one against tight end Trey McBride. Let's hope this game doesn't affect Barron's confidence too much because he's been a plus player over the past month.
The rookie returned from injured reserve and made a huge impact in his first game back. Coleman's burst brought an energy to the Broncos' ground attack that had been missing.
He also did well as a receiver out of the backfield and in pass protection. He finished with 69 yards from scrimmage on 11 touches, and averaged 6.0 yards per carry as a rusher.
The rookie Jonah Coleman making something out of nothing DENvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/wjeHrq6ZEi
The Broncos' run game is looking up with Coleman back on the field.
Dobbins went from getting 17 carries last week to just six on Sunday, mainly because Coleman was efficient when he was on the field. Alas, Dobbins was only able to generate 23 rushing yards on those carries, though he did find the end zone on a 1-yard touchdown.
Dobbins did have a nice 13-yard run erased by an illegal shift penalty, so he did have a few nice runs. But his burst is nowhere close to that of the rookie.
I expected Sean Payton to balance the running back touches, but not in the rookie's favor. It could be a sign that there's a new RB1 in the Broncos' backfield.
Bonitto was a terror all day long, finishing with a team-high six pressures on Brissett. Alas, Bonitto wasn't able to get home for a sack, but his presence was felt all game long.
With a solid head of steam built up over the past few weeks, it's very possible it could culminate in a big Bonitto night next week against the Chiefs and their undrafted rookie left tackle.
Waddle makes the "losers" side of the ledger, though it wasn't all his fault. As a receiver, he was solid, catching four of his seven targets (team high) for 48 yards, including a long of 27 down the right seam.
Alas, with the Broncos trying to protect a lead and kill the clock late, Payton decided to get cute and run an end-around, and Waddle bobbled the tossed exchange, fumbled it, and then fell on the ball as Josh Sweat landed on top of him, injurying his chest.
The injury didn't look good for Waddle, who was shortly thereafter escorted to the locker room never to return. With how well Coleman was running the ball late, it was an unnessary risk that Payton has already accepted the blame for, calling the play call "dumb." Let's hope Waddle's injury isn't as serious as it looked.
Harvey only carried the ball three times for six yards, but his two catches for 54 yards and a touchdown made a big difference in this game. On his 52-yard touchdown, Payton perfectly timed a screen to exploit the Cardinals' blitz-happy defense, and Nix, Harvey, and the Broncos' offense executed it to a 'T.'
RJ Harvey takes the screen pass 52 yards for a TD! DENvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/symyT3Qo6D
It was Harvey's first receiving touchdown of the season and well deserved. Given the burst he shows as a runner, he's deserving of more carries than he's gotten of late, but it appears he's going to take a back seat in that department to Coleman and Dobbins.
Singleton finished with a season-high 19 tackles (12 solo), and was a whirling dervish out there. He was penalized for a ticky-tack roughing the passer call, but the veteran linebacker was a difference-maker out there.
In coverage, Singleton didn't hold up so well, allowing four of five targets to be completed for 38 yards, but he cleaned up those plays well. The team captain has a legitimate chance at notching 200 tackles this season.

title: What It Would Cost Lions To Trade For Charvarius Ward: And Is He Worth it?
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have the opportunity to make a move that could help their defense prior to the Nov. 10 trade deadline.
Through the first six games of the season, the Lions' biggest area of weakness has been their secondary. While things trended up in their win over the Green Bay Packers in Week 7, the Lions could do wonders for their secondary stability by adding a player before the deadline via trade.
There are several intriguing options thought to be available, and one team has already begun to deal off key players in anticipation of a rebuild. On Tuesday, the Indianapolis made a pair of deals trading two key veterans in offensive lineman Quinten Nelson and defensive end De'Forest Buckner.
With those deals appearing to be the start of a sale, the Colts could be willing to listen on their cornerbacks. Sauce Gardner is the headliner of the group, but he doesn't fit the Lions financially having signed an extension just last year.
However, Charvarius Ward has emerged as a intriguing target for the Lions, as his value fits what the team may be willing to spend in a trade come the deadline.
Under general manager Brad Holmes, the Lions have not pursued the traditional splash trade and instead have targeted value within the margins. Ward fits that mold, and could offer exactly what the Lions need from both a play-style and experience standpoint.
Now in his ninth season, Ward has started all seven games up to this point for the Colts. The veteran has recorded 21 tackles and five passes defensed thus far for a team that has sputtered to a 2-5 start.
Ward is well traveled, having began his career with four seasons playing for the Kansas City Chiefs before moving on to the San Francisco 49ers. After three years playing for the 49ers, he joined the Colts last season on a three-year deal.
The Middle Tennessee State product is under contract through the end of next season, but his deal is not guaranteed next year and the Lions could take on $18 million in cap savings if they elected not to keep him according to OverTheCap .
As a result, the contract makes sense to add for Detroit, who has some potential big extensions on the horizon in addition to the moves they've already made under Holmes.
To acquire Ward, the Lions would need to part with a pick in the later rounds, most likely a pick later on Day 3. Detroit is uniquely equipped to make this deal, as they hold their own sixth-round pick in addition to a projected compensatory pick for the loss of cornerback Amik Robertson as well as three seventh-round picks.
It's not a guarantee that Detroit gets that extra sixth-rounder, but with all their late-round picks Detroit could put together a package in lieu of trading a fourth- or fifth-round pick.
If the cost for Detroit is in that range of a late Day 3 pick, it's absolutely a move worth making as Ward would give them another veteran presence with a contract that has a manageable out following the sea
Sports journalist who has covered the Detroit Lions the past three NFL seasons. Christian brings expert analysis, insights and an ability to fairly assess how the team is performing in a tough NFC North division.

title: Detroit Lions Release WR, Sign DL To Practice Squad
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have announced a practice squad shakeup, releasing wide receiver Lawrence Keys and inking former Minnesota Vikings defensive lineman Taki Taimani.
Taimani is an interior defensive line presence that came into the league in 2024 as an undrafted free agent. He earned a spot on the Vikings' initial 53-man roster and appeared in seven games as a rookie.
He visited the teams Allen Park Performance Center last week for a tryout and eventually found a new landing spot.
Earlier this month, the front office has continued to add practice squad depth along the defensive line. Chris Smith was let go, while Aidan Keanaaina and Jeffrey M'ba were added.
Keys was added as an undrafted free agent out of Tulane. He was waived with an injury designation during training camp before eventually being brought back to the practice squad in late September.
Additional Detroit Lions NFL Insider Analysis: 8 Winners, 3 Losers From Week 7 Win Against Packers at Ford Field
Head coach Dan Campbell began his media session on Monday praising the efforts of the defense against the Packers.
Detroit's defense only gave up 17 points and largely held Packers quarterback Jordan Love in check.
"That was a really good outing, man. That's two weeks in a row. I feel like our defense is playing pretty good football now, gaining a lot of confidence. Our coverage units, man, much improved. Really all of those guys really stepped up and played pretty good for us. We looked like we played as one unit. We were disruptive upfront. Thought (Aidan Hutchinson) Hutch's sack early in that game was, that was big, man," said Campbell. "Just kind of set the tone a little bit. And it was good to see . Knocked out the run and really kind of kept that pass game down considerably from what they've been doing all year.
"We were efficient in that regard and really had an opportunity for three other interceptions that were in position close enough to make that we could have. So, that was good. We were good in the red zone."

title: Detroit Lions Could Be NFC's Most 'Dangerous' Team
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have won back-to-back games for the first time in a calendar year.
Sports Illustrated NFL insider Albert Breer recently examined why Dan Campbell's squad look increasingly dangerous, following a gutsy victory against the Green Bay Packers.
As Breer explained, "The bigger thing, though, is the reminder of how that roster was assembled, and how the young core is filled with smart guys like (Jahmyr) Gibbs who now have the experience to match. It’s also why, before that 10-play, 71-yard drive, the team could survive a Dan Campbell dice roll, where he left the offense on for a fourth-and-1 from the Lions’ own 24 in tie game with 4:53 left."
The NFC is not as strong as it once appeared, as the Los Angles Rams have stumbled out of the gates.
After early struggles defensively, Kelvin Sheppard has improved the play of the secondar,y, largely through the improved play of D.J. Reed and the emergence of rookie Keith Abney and third-year cornerback Ennis Rakestraw.
Safety Brian Branch gave the defense a spark and there is still hope Kerby Joseph will return to action at some point this season.
Detroit's roster is used to their head coach taking calculated risks, so the debate on the outside regarding Campbell''s in-game decisions do not impact the former NFL tight end.
Additional Lions NFL Insider Analysis: What Week 7 Snap Counts Revealed Against Packers
"As a result, they’re getting closer to controlling the NFC North. Next week, they’ll get the undefeated Vikings at home," writes Breer. "And they couldn’t be more ready for that after riding out some bumps, and injuries, early in the year. Branch and Cade Mays are back now. Joseph will be soon. The team, coming together and beginning to illustrate how Campbell and GM Brad Holmes built it, is starting to roll."
Quarterback Jared Goff Goff has steadily inserted himself into MVP conversations the last couple of weeks. He has tossed 14 touchdowns without throwing an interception yet this year.
Detroit's offensive line only allowed five pressures against the Packers and are expecting to gel with the return of Cade Mays to the lineup. This season, the veteran signal-caller has only been sacked 12 times.
"I mentioned this all the time. Good teams win multiple games at multiple points in a season," said Campbell earlier this week. "And so this is a step in the right direction. We have got back-to-back wins. We need to try to put – stack some more here together. So, this was big. That was against a good opponent that was hot in our division. So those are good things , man. And so we have got to build off of it. And obviously we have got another hot team coming in right now, Minnesota, that we're going to have to be on top of our game. We have got to play a lot cleaner than we did against Green Bay.
"But man, there's some things we are definitely getting better at. I'm excited about this O-line playing together. I mentioned this before, but now that we've kind of got those guys going here, we can get this five settled in and let them just soak them with reps together in real games and let them grow," Campbell added. "And then I'm excited for the defense where it's going. We are improving right now. And this is going to be a big task. This is a tall task against a really good opponent with some weapons, but it's another, man. We're excited about this, man. Second division game at home. So it's good, man. It's good to get a win.”

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly of Lions 20-17 Win Over Green Bay Packers
full_text:
On Sunday, the Detroit Lions squeaked by Green Bay at the bell, 20-17. Jake Bates kicked the game winner after DJ Wonnum deflected Trey Smack’s go-ahead attempt for the Packers about three minutes of game time prior.
The game got off to a solid start, but the expected shootout did not occur, as the Lions and Packers defenses each got the stops needed to keep in striking distance.
Here are the good, bad, and ugly as the Lions jumped to 4-2 on the young season.
Player Awareness and Discipline
The Lions showed superb situational awareness on Sunday. Jahmyr Gibbs was relied upon as the feature back, but his pass blocking set up a next play touchdown on the opening drive of the game. Then, when the back got two free chances at a touchdown late, he refused to run the ball in, sliding down to drain the clock over his accolades.
In addition, the Lions refrained from a defensive pass interference or defensive holding penalty, which has rarely been seen with the secondary.
Another showcase of player awareness was with offensive lineman Penei Sewell. The All Pro tackle was given a package where he could be eligible to run routes, and Sewell took advantage, running a hitch and shuffling to open grass, forcing a linebacker to cover him. That freed up Jameson Williams for his second touchdown of the game on a Jared Goff scramble drill.
Normally, special teams would be the category here, but a pair of kick return penalties soured the special teams day. On the kicking and kickoff front, however, the Lions executed well. Bates made all his attempts, and none of his kickoffs put the Packers in advantageous positions.
On a day where the Packers miss two field goals, the Lions can be thankful that their kicker stood tall to hit the game winner.
Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams decimated the Packer secondary on Sunday. The two receivers found more holes in the defense than on the foam cheese headgear the Packer fanbase is known for.
St. Brown was the driving force of the first half, hauling in seven of his eight targets for 135 yards. He helped set up both Lions’ scoring drives, along with being in position for a third scoring drive before a Gibbs fumble. The All Pro pass catcher was held in check in the second half, only adding less than 20 yards, but still finished with his fifth career game over 150 yards receiving.
Williams, meanwhile, contributed both touchdowns for the Lions during the contest, his second straight game with a pair of scores. The former Lions first round pick did his damage, racking up 91 receiving yards on the day.
The offensive line squared off against an extremely strong Packer front seven, but it did not execute at the level expected. The Lions, fresh off of a bye week and adding Cade Mays into the lineup, struggled. Jahmyr Gibbs averaged four yards per carry, which only occurred after the Packers gave up nearly 20 yards at the very end to try to encourage the back to score.
Mays had a shaky game, with a bad exchange to open the second half causing a turnover, missing the cadence on another play, and being knocked into Gibbs for a fumble at the end of the first half.
Christian Mahogany contributed his own false start in a critical situation, moving at a defensive flinch to try to give the Lions a free first down. If it was not for the strength in the Green Bay front four, this likely gets an “ugly” grade.
The Lions surrendered 274 passing yards on Sunday, or 264 yards after taking out sack yardage. That is progress compared to their Arizona game, but it is still a high amount. While Green Bay had 46 drop backs, it was not a lockdown effort with Brian Branch back in the lineup.
Branch did record an interception on the day, and the secondary added a few crucial Khalil Dorsey coverage plays with Ennis Rakestraw Jr. missing time with injury. DJ Reed has a solid game as well. However, this game was much too close to consider the day an overwhelming success.
The worst passing defense in the NFL took a step forward, but there is much more progress to be made.
When the Packers were forced to trot out their third string center making his offensive debut by the second drive of the game, the Lions were expected to rack up pressure. Instead, the Lions were held to a single sack. Outside of Aidan Hutchinson, the Lions hit Jordan Love exactly once.
Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams could not take advantage of an inexperienced center with the duo of defensive tackles on fresh legs. Love had 46 drop backs and only got sacked once, which is concerning when the Lions take on the undefeated Vikings next week.
The Lions had all the momentum after forcing multiple defensive stops in the first half, including a tackle for loss in the red zone. However, the team could not capitalize.
In an attempt to make it a two score game at the halftime break, Jahmyr Gibbs fumbled. On the ensuing drive to open the third quarter, Cade Mays and Jared Goff botched an exchange. The Lions fell flat, and the Packers got their first lead of the game.
Detroit grabbed the lead back, but the game went from a potential blowout to a last second win. In multiple key moments, the Lions fell flat. In the third quarter, the Lions could not finish in the red zone. The very next drive came courtesy of a Brian Branch turnover near midfield, and the Lions went three-and-out.
In a crucial third-and-one, the Lions offense went backwards and failed to convert in two plays. They wound up needing Wonnum’s outstretched hand to barely deflect a field goal and keep the score tied late. A strong finish was only necessitated by critical missed assignments and failures to execute starting with the final drive of the second quarter.

title: The Perfect Trade Target For the Lions May Have Just Become Available
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have a glaring need at the cornerback position if they desire to get into the mix of the Super Bowl contenders.
A 4-2 start to the 2026 season has brought plenty of optimism back to the organization, which had won two straight NFC North titles before missing the playoffs last year. Still, there are concerns surrounding the secondary and whether or not the defense can hold up against the best of the best offensively.
As a result, the pressure is heating up on general manager Brad Holmes to make a move for reinforcements at the cornerback position. Veterans D.J. Reed and Roger McCreary have been better of late, and Khalil Dorsey flashed some potential in the win over the Packers on Sunday.
However, an ideal veteran rental option may have just become available in Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen. Signed to a one-year contract, Woolen could be the missing piece for Detroit's cornerback room.
The Eagles lost on Monday to the Dallas Cowboys, falling to 2-5 on the season. With quarterback Jalen Hurts on injured reserve due to blood clots and now sitting three wins out of first place, the Eagles could be sellers at the trade deadline.
Backup Tanner McKee has had intriguing moments, and Saquon Barkley is one of the NFL's most accomplished running backs. However, the Eagles will have a major challenge battling back in the NFC East without their starting quarterback and a team that appears to be in disarray.
As a result, Woolen could be an ideal veteran for them to deal in an effort to add some late-round draft capital ahead of next year's draft. This also makes perfect sense for the Lions and how they've operated in the past, opting to add veterans on short-term deals as opposed to making huge splashes.
Woolen calls to mind an addition the Lions made two years ago at the trade deadline, when they traded for Za'Darius Smith. While Smith wasn't a high-priced, ultra-productive edge rusher, he was a proven veteran who provided stability after Aidan Hutchinson suffered a season-ending injury.
Formerly a fifth-round pick of the Seattle Seahawks in the 2023 draft, Woolen's career started with a bang as he earned Pro Bowl honors after picking off six passes as a rookie. He helped the Seahawks win the Super Bowl last year, but wasn't re-signed as the team committed its resources to retaining 2024 first-round pick Devon Witherspoon.
Woolen's free agency market wasn't what he'd hoped, and ultimately he ended up signing a one-year deal with the Philadelphia Eagles. While he hasn't had eye-popping production, Woolen has provided some stability in the secondary for the Eagles and could benefit from a change of scenery moving forward.
Ultimately, the Lions have a need for a veteran, and a trade for Woolen fits how they have operated in the past. This could be an ideal move for Detroit ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.
