title: Colts' Future Comes Into Focus After Parting Ways With Two Trench Staples
full_text:
When it rains, it pours. And it's coming down in buckets over Indianapolis.
The Colts have made two major changes to their roster, trading away two of their most recognizable players as the franchise looks to chart a new course after a disappointing season.
After sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, Indianapolis also traded defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for 2027 fourth-round pick.
With both veterans gone, Indianapolis faces significant questions about both its immediate and long-term future. Let's attempt to answer what the next several months may look like.
The Colts have little time to adjust after trading away two of the most established players on their roster. There's still football left to play, but with Nelson and Buckner gone, Indianapolis is officially headed for a lost season.
Rather than mail it in, the Colts should use the remaining games to evaluate the players who are still there. The departures create opportunities for younger players to take on larger roles and show whether they belong in the team's plans moving forward.
Indianapolis could also make more moves before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. Veterans such as Keenan Allen, Grover Stewart and Charvarius Ward could attract interest from contenders if the Colts decide to pursue additional draft compensation for their next general manager to work with.
By the end of the season, Indianapolis should have a clearer picture of which players can contribute to its next competitive roster and where reinforcements will be needed.
Trading Nelson and Buckner leaves significant holes on both lines. Each was an established starter and leader at his position, making their departures consequential beyond the immediate impact on the depth chart.
Offensively, Indianapolis must find a replacement for Nelson at left guard. Rookie Jalen Farmer, a fourth-round pick in the most recent draft, is one option. He should receive a 10-game trial run the rest of the season so the Colts can determine whether he can be part of the team's long-term plans.
Buckner's departure creates a similar challenge on the defensive line. More responsibility will fall on the remaining interior defenders, including Stewart and Adetomiwa Adebawore. The Colts have to find out if Adebawore, a free agent at the end of the season, is a pillar they want to build around.
How Indianapolis handles those vacancies will be a crucial part of its roster evaluation. The goal isn't necessarily to find direct replacements for two established stars, but to build offensive and defensive lines capable of supporting the team's next competitive window.
The Colts' longer-term outlook will depend heavily on who takes over as general manager and how that person chooses to approach the roster. Indianapolis still has talent, but the new decision-maker will have to identify which players he or she deems as viable options moving forward.
The trades also provide additional draft capital. Indianapolis acquired a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick for Nelson, adding to the compensation received for Buckner. However, the Colts still don't have their 2027 first-round pick after sending it to the New York Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner.
That makes the team's remaining draft assets especially important. The next general manager will need to weigh the value of adding young talent against the opportunity to address immediate needs through free agency.
Moving veteran contracts could also create more financial flexibility, depending on the details of each deal. That would give the next GM more options to retain key players, pursue outside additions or continue reshaping the roster.
Ultimately, Indianapolis has created an opportunity to take the team in a different direction. The next general manager will have to decide how much of the current foundation is worth keeping around. Those deemed to not be worth retaining must make their way out of the building one way or another.
Needless to say, primary owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has a big hire to make in the not-so-distant future.

title: Thank You, Big Q: Remembering a Colts Legend
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts traded their longest-tenured player to the Seattle Seahawks on Tuesday for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. Two mid-round picks for one of the greatest offensive linemen in franchise history.
I always thought Big Q would retire in Indianapolis. I thought he would spend his entire career wearing the Horseshoe, walk into the Hall of Fame one day and have the Colts attached to his name forever.
Instead, one of the best players to ever put on a Colts uniform is heading to Seattle.
Nelson was the No. 6 overall pick in 2018, and it did not take long to realize Indianapolis had something special. He became the first guard in NFL history to win Offensive Rookie of the Month and immediately helped change the identity of an offensive line that desperately needed one.
From there, the accolades became almost automatic.
Nelson made the Pro Bowl in each of his first eight seasons, becoming the first player in Colts history to accomplish that and only the second offensive lineman in NFL history to do it, joining Hall of Fame tackle Joe Thomas.
He was also a three-time First-Team All-Pro from 2018-20 before adding three Second-Team selections in 2021, 2024 and 2025.
That is six All-Pro selections in eight completed seasons.
And somehow, the awards still do not tell the entire story.
Nelson brought an edge to this offense that is hard to quantify. He didn't just block defenders; he punished them, played through the whistle, and made sure everyone around him played with that same intensity.
Seriously, how many offensive guards have a highlight tape you would willingly sit down and watch? Big Q was different.
The consistency was just as ridiculous. Nelson started 136 games for Indianapolis and missed only four, all during the 2021 season.
Even at 30 years old, he was still playing like one of the best guards in football. Through seven games this season, Nelson had allowed zero sacks and only six pressures, while his 86.6 PFF grade ranked third among qualified guards.
I understand the business side. Nelson is in the final year of his contract, the Colts are 2-5, Chris Ballard is gone and this franchise is clearly looking toward what comes next.
But some players mean more than the draft picks attached to their name.
Nelson was toughness. He was consistency. He was the backbone of this offensive line for nearly a decade and represented everything you could ask for in an Indianapolis Colt.
In my eyes, Big Q is a future Hall of Famer and one of the best Colts to ever wear the Horseshoe.
Man, I am going to miss watching No. 56 in Indianapolis.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Next Colts Player Most Likely to be Traded After Quenton Nelson
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have started their trade deadline activity with a major move , sending left guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
With the team sitting at 2-5 and facing questions about its direction, more changes could be on the way.
Jonathan Taylor, Josh Downs and Grover Stewart are among the other players who could draw interest from contenders. However, DeForest Buckner stands out as a particularly intriguing candidate, especially with a familiar NFC contender potentially in the picture.
The San Francisco 49ers have already emerged as a potential landing spot for DeForest Buckner.
San Francisco has a clear need up front after dealing with injuries along its defensive line. The 49ers have also been one of the NFL's best teams this season, starting 6-0 despite those absences. Adding Buckner would give them an established interior pass rusher as they look to maintain that success.
As for the financials, San Francisco entered the trade-deadline period with approximately $41.3 million in salary cap space, the most in the NFL. That flexibility puts the 49ers in a strong position to pursue a veteran like Buckner without having to make significant financial sacrifices elsewhere on the roster.
And of course, there's familiarity between the two parties. The 49ers selected Buckner with the No. 7 overall pick in the 2016 NFL Draft, and he spent the first four seasons of his career with the organization, playing a key role in their run to Super Bowl LIV.
San Francisco traded him to Indianapolis in March 2020 in exchange for the 13th overall pick, which became defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw. Now, six years later, the two sides could reunite under very different circumstances.
Buckner is 32 and in the final year of his contract, while the Colts are gearing up to start a rebuilding phase. A return to San Francisco would give Buckner an opportunity to compete for a championship while allowing Indianapolis to recoup draft capital for a veteran who could leave in free agency next offseason.
The Colts are actively shopping Buckner, whose connection to San Francisco makes the 49ers seem like a trade partner of destiny.
Buckner isn't the only Colt who could be dealt before the Nov. 10 deadline.
Jonathan Taylor is the biggest name among the Colts' other potential trade candidates, although Indianapolis appears more inclined to keep him than move him. Ownership reportedly views the star running back as a key piece of the team's future, but that shouldn't make him untouchable.
If the right offer comes along, the Colts should be willing to pull the trigger. The 2022 Christian McCaffrey trade offers a useful benchmark, as Carolina received second, third and fourth-round picks in 2023 along with a fifth-rounder in 2024 from San Francisco.
Taylor remains one of the NFL's top running backs, and Indianapolis should demand a substantial return rather than trade him simply for the sake of moving him. At the same time, the team shouldn't pass up a significant package of draft capital just because Taylor is a player it wants to retain.
Josh Downs is another possibility as he enters the final year of his rookie contract. The 25-year-old receiver could appeal to contenders looking for a reliable slot target, although moving him would leave Indianapolis with fewer established options in the passing game.
Defensive tackle Grover Stewart could also draw interest from teams seeking help against the run. Like Buckner, the veteran defensive tackle is playing on an expiring contract, making him a potential rental for a contender and another opportunity for Indianapolis to add draft capital.
Either way, Nelson’s trade is just the first of a few to come as Indianapolis strips its operation down to the studs, ready to start fresh.

title: Let the Fire Sale Commence: Biggest Domino in Colts Rebuild Falls First
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are staring down a full-fledged organizational reset after parting ways with longtime general manager Chris Ballard following their Week 6 loss to the then-winless Tennessee Titans.
After assistant general manager Ed Dodds took over for Ballard to become interim GM for the remainder of the 2026 season, the mission from ownership was clear: start shopping the entire roster ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline .
A near decade of mediocrity left the Indianapolis Colts at a crossroads, and they've decided to tear the roster down to its studs as they embark upon a new era.
This rebuild has officially kicked off a fire sale of sorts, with the departure of longtime future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson being the first domino to fall.
The Colts traded Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, according to NFL insider Tom Pelissero.
So, how did we get here, was the compensation fair, and where do we go from here?
I break it all down below.
Quenton Nelson has been one of the league's most consistent, productive, and accomplished players since the Indianapolis Colts drafted him sixth overall in the 2018 NFL Draft.
Nelson has earned Pro Bowl honors in each of his eight seasons in the NFL and has added six All-Pro selections (3x First-Team, 3x Second-Team).
On top of that, Nelson has only missed four games in eight seasons.
Nelson has epitomized what it means to be a future Hall of Fame candidate, so why on earth did the Colts let him walk out the door?
For starters, it's more than likely that Quenton Nelson was fed up with how the organization continues to find itself in rebuilding scenarios and wanted no part in running it back.
Nelson is 30 years old and is in the final year of his four-year deal, so not wanting to sign up for a full-blown rebuild in what could very well be his final NFL contract is understandable.
Of course, the Colts would love nothing more than to have Nelson around for their first official rebuild in over a decade, but unfortunately for them, it's a two-way street.
It takes two to tango, after all.
Nelson likely wanted to start fresh elsewhere, particularly with a contender, before he entered his first free agency as an unrestricted free agent.
Given what the Seahawks gave up for Nelson, I think it's fair to assume he was not interested in re-signing with the Colts.
Some may feel strongly about the Colts not netting at least a second-round pick for Quenton Nelson's services, but at the end of the day, Indianapolis's hands were tied.
The Colts have been famously inching towards a fire sale of their roster, and Nelson's pedigree has revealed him as a popular trade candidate.
In theory, a future Hall of Famer should at least net a first-round pick in return, but it's not quite that simple.
The offensive guard position is one of the biggest examples of non-premium talent, and even though Nelson sports some of the best talent said position has ever seen, teams across the league remain hesitant to value it that way.
A current third-round pick and a future fifth-rounder may seem scoff-worthy at first glance, but when you break down the history of traded compensation for other guards across the league, Nelson's haul starts to make more sense.
You may not like it, but the Colts did as best they could.
Indianapolis' return of a 3rd and a 5th for Quenton Nelson is the most pure draft capital for a guard since at least 2011, per Spotrac. only 4 have netted a 4th: 2013: G. Carimi, 4th 2014: L. Mankins, 4th + player 2021: B. Bredeson + 5th + 7th, 4th 2025: J. Thuney, 4th
I think this is both the best example of why the return for Quenton Nelson isn’t as irresponsible as some are suggesting, and also why the Chris Ballard era needed to end: non-premium positions.
It's precisely why Nelson's return seems so weak, but also why star running back Jonathan Taylor will not be netting a first-round pick in return.
Not only were the Colts dealt the tough task of netting worthwhile compensation for one of the league's least-valued positions, but they also had the added layer of Nelson's expiring contract to deal with.
Unless they re-sign him, the Seattle Seahawks have signed up for 11 weeks of Quenton Nelson.
When you consider Nelson's age, expiring contract, and unwillingness to sign up for a true rebuild with the organization that's failed him, this seems like one of the best-case scenarios for Indianapolis.
The only argument against this process I can think of is that the Colts could have potentially netted more compensation if they had waited closer to the deadline.
In theory, this would've driven up the price, but realistically, how much of an overpay could the Colts have gotten out of this hypothetical hard bargain?
Nelson leaving in free agency would've netted a third-round compensatory pick; therefore, it's almost as if the Seahawks rented his services for a future fifth-round pick.
This may sting on the surface, but you also can't guarantee that the Colts would not have made any deals in free agency that would've negated their compensatory return.
Again, it's more than likely that Nelson didn't want to be here, so it makes sense that the Colts wanted to do right by their longtime offensive pillar and ship him somewhere that's best for both parties.
It's borderline disgusting to watch a homegrown future Hall of Famer get dealt elsewhere, but this is the bed the Colts have made, and now they must sleep in it.
As far as the 2026 regular season goes, the Colts have admitted that playoffs are no longer an option.
Nelson's departure lowers the offense's floor more than you can imagine, so trying to maintain playoff aspirations while preparing for the future is no longer a feasible outcome.
The Colts will continue selling off as many assets as possible as they look to enter a new era, but at least their future can get a good look for the rest of this season.
The left guard spot will likely see rookie Jalen Farmer fill the void at some point in the near future, and this is a massive opportunity for OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr. to turn his most recent draft crush into yet another successful project across the Colts' offensive line.
Sparano Jr. has churned out successful draft-and-stash projects in recent years, such as LT Bernhard Raimann, G Will Fries, G Matt Goncalves, C Tanor Bortolini, and RT Jalen Travis, and Farmer could become the next installment of sorts.
Sparano Jr.'s conviction in the former Kentucky guard led the Colts to draft him in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft.
Sparano Jr.’s conviction in Jalen Farmer is so apparent, not only by his own words, but also by the #Colts war room’s reaction when he arrives to celebrate said draft selection. 🎥: @Colts https://t.co/RxH86gKHkC pic.twitter.com/EFmmsUSYYe
Farmer has yet to play this season, given the Colts' offensive line has been held down by a veteran unit, but with Quenton Nelson's departure leaving a gargantuan-sized hole, the rookie now has a huge opportunity to prove himself as a building block for the next regime.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts Week 7 Stock Report: 2 Risers, 3 Fallers as Offense Falls Apart
full_text:
A third straight loss leaves the Indianapolis Colts facing an uncomfortable reality: the season is slipping away, and the offense is now a major reason why.
For once, the defense held up its end against the undefeated Minnesota Vikings. Indianapolis still walked away with a 16-10 loss and a 2-5 record.
There aren't many players trending upward right now, but a couple deserve some credit. Here are my two risers and three fallers from Week 7.
With Sauce Gardner sidelined, Walley stepped into a bigger role at outside corner and delivered his best performance of the season.
He earned a 94.2 coverage grade from Pro Football Focus, the highest in the NFL in Week 7. Walley allowed just 16 receiving yards and forced a fumble.
Unfortunately, he suffered an injury and never returned. That's a tough way to end a breakout game, because outside corner looks like exactly where he belongs.
Facing one of the NFL's most aggressive defenses, Raimann was one of the few Indianapolis offensive linemen who didn't look overwhelmed.
He posted an 89.5 pass-blocking grade, the third-highest among NFL offensive linemen in Week 7, and helped spring Jonathan Taylor's 38-yard touchdown with a downfield block.
The Daniel Jones situation is getting more concerning by the week.
He finished 13-of-22 for 108 yards, zero touchdowns and a game-sealing interception, earning a 46.5 PFF passing grade.
Through seven games, Jones has 1,398 passing yards, four touchdowns and seven interceptions while completing just 59.6% of his passes.
Yes, he's missing weapons, and Minnesota's pressure was absurd. But his mobility has vanished, the missed throws keep piling up.
The calls for Anthony Richardson are only getting louder.
This is a name I never expected to see on the fallers list.
Shrader entered Sunday without a missed field goal this season, then missed from 56 and 48 yards in the second half. Both were long attempts, but Indianapolis desperately needed those points in a six-point loss.
He's been too reliable for us to panic after one game. Still, this was an uncharacteristically rough afternoon for a guy who has made a habit of drilling everything.
Minnesota's pass rush was a nightmare for this offensive line, and Travis had his share of struggles at right tackle.
He allowed six pressures and finished with the 134th-ranked pass-blocking grade among 157 offensive linemen who played in Week 7, according to PFF.
That's simply not going to cut it, especially with Daniel Jones already struggling to operate under pressure.
Indianapolis finally got a defensive performance good enough to win. If this offense doesn't figure things out soon, that won't matter much.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Face Difficult Decision With Josh Downs as NFL Trade Deadline Approaches
full_text:
To trade, or not to trade.
The Indianapolis Colts find themselves at a crossroads, with the direction of the franchise suddenly far less certain than it appeared just weeks ago. As the organization looks to chart its next steps, decisions made over the coming weeks could have lasting implications for its future.
One intriguing question now emerging is whether Indianapolis could part ways with a player who has been a key piece of its offense.
The Indianapolis Colts could have some difficult decisions to make ahead of the NFL trade deadline. With DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson and Keenan Allen among the players whose names have surfaced in trade discussions, Josh Downs is another name worth watching, per ESPN's Jeremy Fowler.
Fowler mentioned Downs as a potential trade candidate Monday while discussing the wide receiver market ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline. His comments came less than a week after Indianapolis fired general manager Chris Ballard, leaving interim GM Ed Dodds to navigate an uncertain future for the franchise.
The Aftermath top stories, including the Chiefs potentially adding WR help via trade and a look at Aaron Glenn in New York and Shane Steichen in Indianapolis. pic.twitter.com/ctDMRjtDSn
At 2-5, the Colts have fallen well short of expectations, raising questions about whether the organization should prioritize salvaging the 2026 season or begin positioning itself for the future. Fowler has also reported that rival teams believe Indianapolis could be open to making deals before the deadline, particularly involving players approaching the end of their contracts. Downs fits that profile as he plays out the final year of his rookie deal.
Fowler's report does not mean the Colts are actively shopping the 25-year-old receiver, but the combination of Indianapolis' struggles and Downs' contract situation makes him an intriguing candidate to monitor.
Downs' recent performances have offered little encouragement as the Colts' season has gone off course. After recording 77 receiving yards against the Houston Texans in Week 3, the fourth-year receiver has failed to reach 50 yards in any of his four subsequent games.
That decline is particularly notable given the circumstances. Alec Pierce has been sidelined with a heel injury since Week 2, leaving Indianapolis without one of its primary downfield threats. His absence should have created opportunities for Downs to assume a larger role, yet the receiver has managed just 58 yards over the past two games. He caught four passes for 40 yards against the Tennessee Titans before recording two receptions for 18 yards in Sunday's loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Downs has yet to record a receiving touchdown this season.
His production is not the only thing worth watching. Downs' demeanor over the past few weeks has also stood out, with the receiver appearing increasingly frustrated at times. That reaction would be understandable given Indianapolis' struggles, particularly for a player whose future with the organization is uncertain.
Body language alone cannot establish whether Downs wants out of Indianapolis. Still, his recent performances and apparent frustration provide additional context as questions emerge about his future with the Colts.
If Indianapolis believes a significant roster reset is necessary, Downs could be a logical candidate to move. His established production and potential appeal to contenders give the Colts an opportunity to address their longer-term needs while helping another team immediately.
Downs recorded at least 58 receptions in each of his first three NFL seasons, establishing himself as a reliable slot receiver. That experience could appeal to a contender seeking another pass catcher without committing significant resources to an older veteran. However, with Downs in the final year of his rookie contract, an acquiring team would be taking on a potential rental unless it could reach an extension with him.
Several teams could make sense as potential suitors. The Kansas City Chiefs have been looking around for receiver help amid injuries at the position, while the Pittsburgh Steelers have also been identified as a potential fit. Downs' ability to work primarily from the slot could give either team another option in the passing game, depending on its needs and willingness to pursue a deal.
Indianapolis has its own reasons to consider a move. The Colts lack a 2027 first-round pick after acquiring cornerback Sauce Gardner from the New York Jets, making the prospect of replenishing their draft capital particularly relevant if the season continues to unravel.
There is also the question of whether Downs would want to remain in Indianapolis beyond this season. His recent frustration could simply reflect the team's struggles, but if it signals broader dissatisfaction with the organization's direction, an extension could become more difficult to negotiate. Downs said in July that he wanted to boost his stock throughout the season before determining what came next, leaving his long-term plans open.
The Colts cannot assume Downs intends to leave, but they also cannot ignore the possibility of losing him in free agency without receiving anything in return. If the organization does not believe an extension is realistic, exploring his trade market now could be a sensible way to recoup value rather than risk his departure for nothing.
Trading Downs might make sense from a long-term roster-building perspective, but it would leave Indianapolis with an even greater need at wide receiver.
Pierce's absence has already exposed the position's lack of depth, leaving Downs among the Colts' most established receiving options. Indianapolis has also traded Michael Pittman Jr. and AD Mitchell over the past year, further thinning its receiving corps. Moving Downs would put even more pressure on the remaining players and leave the franchise with substantial work to do at the position heading into 2027.
There is a longer-term cost to consider, too. Downs has demonstrated that he can be a productive NFL receiver, recording at least 58 receptions in each of his first three seasons. Although his recent production has declined, he is still young enough to remain a useful part of the offense well beyond this season.
That is what makes the decision so difficult. A trade could bring back draft capital and help the Colts avoid losing Downs for nothing, but it would also mean surrendering a proven player at a position that already requires significant investment. Indianapolis still has games to play in 2026, and removing another established pass catcher would make it harder to field a competitive offense for the remainder of the season.
Any offer would need to account for both sides of that equation. The Colts have reasons to consider a deal, but they should not create another roster problem simply to acquire additional draft picks.
Ultimately, the decision comes down to how Indianapolis evaluates Downs' long-term future and what another team would be willing to offer. His contract makes a trade worth considering, but his age and track record give the Colts a legitimate reason to retain him.
If Indianapolis believes Downs would be willing to sign an extension and remain part of the team's plans, keeping him makes sense. The receiver room already needs significant help, and trading away another established option would complicate the rebuilding process.
If the Colts instead believe an extension is unlikely, the calculus changes. With the deadline approaching, a reasonable offer could give Indianapolis an opportunity to recoup value rather than risk losing Downs in free agency. That possibility deserves consideration, particularly if the organization is preparing for a broader roster overhaul.
Still, the price matters. Downs has shown enough to warrant meaningful compensation, and moving him for a late-round pick simply to avoid losing him for nothing would be difficult to justify.
The Colts should explore the market…

title: Colts Week 7 Snap Count Analysis: 3 Takeaways From Vikings Loss
full_text:
A box score can only tell you so much about an NFL game. Snap counts offer another perspective, showing which players coaches trusted most , who saw their role change and where opportunities opened up.
The Indianapolis Colts ' 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings provided plenty to examine beneath the surface. With seven games in the books, the latest snap counts offer a closer look at how the roster is taking shape as the team tries to salvage its season .
The Colts' search for consistency at linebacker continues. Sunday's loss to the Vikings offered another example of how unsettled the rotation remains.
Only Akeem Davis-Gaither has solidified his place as the unit's every-down MIKE linebacker. The WILL spot has been a revolving door.
Davis-Gaither played 57 of 59 defensive snaps against Minnesota, but three different linebackers split time next to him: Jaylon Carlies played 23 snaps, Germaine Pratt played 20 and Austin Ajiake saw 18.
The circumstances explain some of the rotation. Rookies CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher were inactive with injuries, Carlies was returning from a two-game absence, and Pratt had just been elevated from the practice squad after joining the team earlier in the week. Still, the Colts have struggled to establish a consistent pecking order at the position through the first seven weeks of the season.
Carlies opened the year as a starter but has missed time with injuries. Boettcher had been part of the rotation before his latest setback, while Ajiake has really only played when options have been thin. Pratt's arrival added another name to the mix without necessarily providing a long-term answer.
Davis-Gaither has earned his workload, but the same cannot be said of anyone competing to play alongside him. With Indianapolis sitting at 2-5, the team is running out of time to establish continuity. Allen's eventual return could give the Colts another opportunity to evaluate their options, although he has primarily played the MIKE.
For now, the rotation remains a question mark. Injuries have complicated the situation, but the Colts really need someone to seize the opportunity and give the defense some much-needed stability.
The Colts' wide receiver rotation has become difficult to understand.
Keenan Allen saw his playing time drop significantly against Minnesota despite leading Indianapolis in receptions, while Laquon Treadwell continued to play a major role in an offense that desperately needs more production through the air.
Josh Downs led the receivers with 52 snaps, followed by Treadwell with 45 and Allen with just 30. Allen played 49% of the offensive snaps after seeing 71% against Tennessee, a notable decline for a veteran who caught all three of his targets for 31 yards against the Vikings. He led the Colts in both receptions and receiving yards.
For context, the run-heavy game plan likely played a role in Allen's reduced workload. Still, that explanation only goes so far. Allen's experience and size should make him a useful option in a game plan that requires receivers to block on the perimeter, particularly when Downs, a smaller player, is one of the primary alternatives.
Treadwell's continued involvement is also worth questioning. He played 45 snaps but managed just two catches for 19 yards. This season, Treadwell has logged just 15 catches on 358 snaps.
Downs wasn't much more productive, finishing with two receptions for 18 yards on four targets. With Alec Pierce unavailable, Indianapolis was already short on proven receiving options, yet Deion Burks played just seven snaps and Ashton Dulin saw only one in his return from a hamstring injury.
There may be legitimate reasons for the distribution, including the specific packages Indianapolis wanted to use and the need to manage players returning from injury. But the results were hardly encouraging. The Colts scored just 10 points, and no receiver managed more than 31 yards. No Colts wide out has caught a touchdown since the team's last win, a 19-17 victory over Houston.
Indianapolis needs to find ways to keep its most reliable receiving options involved, particularly as the offense struggles to move the ball.
Tyler Warren's absence created an opportunity for the Colts' other tight ends to step up, but the distribution of playing time against Minnesota raised some questions about how Indianapolis views the position.
Mo Alie-Cox led the group with 39 offensive snaps, playing 64% of the team's offensive plays. That was a significant increase from the 31 snaps he recorded against Tennessee.
Will Mallory went in the opposite direction. After playing 43 snaps against the Titans, Mallory saw his workload fall to 21 against Minnesota, a notable shift considering Warren's absence had created an opportunity for Mallory to establish himself as a reliable option.
The results didn't exactly justify the rotation, either. Mallory was targeted three times but failed to record a catch, while Alie-Cox was targeted twice without a reception. Drew Ogletree was the lone Colts tight end to catch a pass, finishing with two receptions for 12 yards.
Warren's eventual return should restore some order to the position, but Indianapolis still needs to figure out what it wants from the players behind him.
Alie-Cox has experience as a blocker, while Mallory offers a different skill set. With the offense struggling to produce points, the Colts need to make better use of their available personnel rather than simply cycling through options without much production to show for it.

title: Colts Week 7 Position Grades: Offense Falls Flat Against Vikings
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts finally got a respectable performance from their defense Sunday. Unfortunately, the offense completely fell apart against Minnesota's relentless pressure.
Minnesota walked away with a 16-10 win, dropping Indianapolis to 2-5, and Brian Flores' defense was the story.
Flores is a mad scientist, and watching his pressure packages connect is like watching a piece of art come together in real time. The Vikings blitzed on an NFL-record 85.2% of Colts dropbacks in the Next Gen Stats era, and a one-dimensional Indianapolis offense had absolutely no answer.
A Colts fan could only wish. Here are my position grades from Week 7.
Daniel Jones finished 13-of-22 for 108 yards, zero touchdowns and one late interception, earning a 53.2 offensive grade and 46.5 passing grade from PFF.
Jones faced pressure 16 times and took four sacks. He completed 9-of-11 passes for 83 yards from a clean pocket, but his completion percentage dropped to just 36.4% when under pressure.
Whether Jones had nowhere to go with the ball or Minnesota's pressure simply got there too quickly, he looked like the old Giants version of Daniel Jones again.
Jonathan Taylor was basically the entire offense, rushing 18 times for 95 yards and a touchdown while gaining 64 yards after contact.
Seth McGowan also had a strong afternoon with 46 yards on 11 carries and provided a major spark in the return game.
No Colts receiver finished with more than Keenan Allen's 31 yards, and the entire room combined for only 10 targets and 79 yards.
Jones did not always have time, but this group still made almost no impact. Indianapolis desperately needs some explosiveness back in this receiver room.
Drew Ogletree caught two passes, while the rest of the tight end room went without a catch on five targets.
This offense badly needs Tyler Warren back. The pass blocking was also rough, including a 30.4 PFF pass-blocking grade from Mo Alie-Cox.
Bernhard Raimann and Quenton Nelson held up well in pass protection, but the rest of the line struggled against Minnesota's constant pressure.
Indianapolis allowed four sacks on 16 pressures, while Tanner Bortolini, Nelson and Matt Goncalves averaged just a 45.8 run-blocking grade.
For once, this defense gave Indianapolis enough to win.
Minnesota finished with 136 rushing yards but no rushing touchdowns, while the Colts' defensive line generated 11 pressures and two sacks. The defensive ends played particularly well, although DeForest Buckner had a quiet afternoon.
Akeem Davis-Gaither showed real improvement in coverage with a 70.2 grade, but the rest of the linebacker room averaged just 43.9.
Run defense also left plenty to be desired outside of Jaylon Carlies, but limiting Minnesota's overall production was still a step in the right direction.
Justin Walley had his breakout game with a 94.2 PFF coverage grade, while Kenneth Harris also played well.
Charvarius Ward struggled, but the group missed zero tackles and held Minnesota to only 150 passing yards and one touchdown without Sauce Gardner. This was a good showing for this group.
Defending the run wasn't the issue for this unit. Pass coverage was a completely different story.
The unit averaged a 44.5 coverage grade and allowed a reception on every target, while Cam Bynum and A.J. Haulcy surrendered passer ratings of 118.8 and 152.1 when targeted.
Spencer Shrader missed two field goals for the first time in his career, from 56 and 48 yards.
The expectations are high because Shrader has been so reliable, so those misses hurt in a six-point loss. I still have zero concern about him going forward.
For most of this season, the defense has been the problem in Indianapolis.
Sunday was the exact opposite, and until this offense becomes more than Jonathan Taylor and hope, performances like this are going to keep happening.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts' Season Is Spiraling. These 5 Quotes Tell the Story
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have hit a wall. Three straight losses have dropped them to 2-5 and put their season in serious jeopardy.
Sunday's 16-10 defeat to the Minnesota Vikings left Indianapolis with plenty of questions to answer. In the aftermath, several members of the organization offered revealing comments that provide a closer look at where the Colts stand following another disappointing loss.
Steichen Remains Committed to Daniel Jones
Head coach Shane Steichen has no plans to make a change at quarterback, despite having every reason to.
Following Sunday's 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, Steichen was asked whether he had considered benching Daniel Jones. His answer?
"I have a ton of faith in Daniel."
As the season progresses and Jones shows few signs of improvement, that faith is beginning to become unwarranted. Jones completed just 13 of 22 passes for 108 yards against Minnesota, took four sacks and threw an interception on Indianapolis' final possession to seal the defeat. He has now thrown seven interceptions against just four touchdowns through seven games.
"I got a ton of faith in Daniel (Jones)." #Colts head coach Shane Steichen said he has not thought about a quarterback change. pic.twitter.com/VF5j10SKaE
Steichen pointed to the game plan's emphasis on running the football, but the passing attack's continued struggles have become difficult to ignore. With Indianapolis sitting at 2-5, sticking with Jones is a significant gamble for a coaching staff that needs results. Anthony Richardson Sr. remains an alternative, though he has yet to play this season and Steichen has consistently dismissed him as a possible option.
Even if it's borderline delusional, Steichen's confidence in Jones is obvious. For a guy coaching for his job the rest of the way, it's easy to see that if Steichen is going to bow out, he's doing it on his terms.
DeForest Buckner has been very forthcoming regarding his frustration with the Colts. After yet another loss, the veteran defensive tackle had little patience for questions about a team that continues to fall short.
When asked if he's frustrated, Buckner kept things blunt. "I don't know. How about you guess. Yeah, I'm frustrated. Same thing, we lost," he said.
Asked where the Colts go from here and what was missing from the team, Buckner offered little optimism, responding, "(I) couldn't tell you" and "I don't know."
It's a troubling place for Indianapolis to be. The Colts have no clear answers for how to reverse their slide. Buckner has been through years of disappointment with the franchise, and his comments reflect the frustration of a veteran who has yet to see the sustained success the organization has been chasing.
If I spent my prime years playing for a consistently mediocre team, I'd be seething too.
If there's a silver lining for Buckner, it's that the loss puts the Colts one step closer to a full roster clean out before the Nov. 10 deadline, which is expected to include the 32-year-old.
Jonathan Taylor's Future in Indianapolis Is Uncertain
Jonathan Taylor is trying to tune out the noise surrounding his future with the Indianapolis Colts, but the trade speculation isn't going away.
Taylor's wife, Ayanna, fueled the conversation over the weekend by discussing the possibility of her husband being traded on social media. Following Sunday's loss to the Minnesota Vikings, Taylor was asked about her comments and largely brushed them aside.
"It's been out there already, so I think her adding (to it) doesn't really change anything. You know everybody's on TikTok these days. So, you just gotta … stay focused," Taylor said.
Part 2 from #Colts RB Jonathan Taylor’s wife, Ayanna, on his trade rumors: “How are they gonna get new leadership to come in when they really have no options? …” “That’s what brings us back to my husband. Do they keep him? … Or do they just cut their losses and trade him?” https://t.co/hs5S81hKLS pic.twitter.com/WQJrBC435R
Given how the past few weeks have gone in Indianapolis, it's easy to understand why the speculation has intensified. With the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaching, the Colts face major questions about their direction and whether moving veteran players could help them rebuild.
Still, Taylor has remained indifferent to a trade. He signed a two-year, $44 million extension in August that keeps him under contract through 2028, making a trade a significant decision for the franchise. But his wife's comments have put his future in the spotlight at a time when little appears settled in Indianapolis.
Interestingly, reports from ESPN's Adam Schefter indicate that Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon is inclined to retain Taylor. "Irsay-Gordon views Taylor as a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," he writes, adding the Colts would have to receive a near-too-good-to-be-true compensation package to move their superstar running back.
Quenton Nelson Is Still Holding Out Hope
Offensive guard Quenton Nelson is urging the Colts to keep believing they can turn their season around.
"Everyone needs to believe that we can do it. That we can get a win," he said postgame. "All it takes is one to go on a run."
It's an understandable message from one of Indianapolis' veteran leaders, but the Colts need more than just belief to change their trajectory. Their recent stretch of defeats that has raised serious questions about the team's direction, and Sunday's defeat marked another missed opportunity to get back on track.
Nelson is right that one win can change the tone around a struggling team. But with the Colts running out of time, results need to come quickly.
Anthony Richardson's Comments Raise Questions About His Judgment
Anthony Richardson has yet to see the field for the Indianapolis Colts this season, and his latest comments aren't likely to help his chances of earning another opportunity.
Richardson was asked Sunday about his recent misdemeanor marijuana possession charge, which stems from an October traffic stop. He declined to discuss the ongoing legal matter in detail but offered an answer when asked whether he regretted the incident.
"I enjoy life. I don't really regret a lot of things I do. I appreciate my life. I appreciate God waking me up every morning," Richardson said.
Richardson is entitled to let the legal process play out without commenting on the specifics of the case. But his broader response raises larger questions about his judgment at a time when his NFL future is in the balance.
The former No. 4 pick is in his fourth season and has made just two appearances since the start of 2025. With Daniel Jones struggling and the Colts falling to 2-5, Richardson could theoretically have an opportunity to get back into the quarterback conversation. Instead, this is just another example of how he can't seem to get out of his own way.
Richardson's comments don't establish whether he regrets the specific incident, and it would be unfair to treat them as an admission that he doesn't. Still, with his career at a crossroads, he needs to give the organization confidence that he's prepared to make the decisions required to earn another chance.
Right now, they don't seem keen on giving him one.

title: Shane Steichen Doubles Down on Daniel Jones Despite Poor Results
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have lost three straight games, fallen to 2-5, and watched their season spiral out of control. Yet head coach Shane Steichen apparently has no interest in reconsidering his quarterback situation.
Following Sunday's 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, Steichen reaffirmed his confidence in Daniel Jones, saying he has a “ton of faith” in the veteran quarterback.
At this point, that faith is unjustifiable . Jones has struggled all year and is a shell of the player the Colts had for 10 games a season ago.
Jones has thrown just four touchdowns to seven interceptions through seven games this season. Sunday's performance was another low point: he finished with 108 passing yards, no touchdowns, and an interception on the Colts' final drive.
The contrast with last season is stark. In 13 starts in 2025, Jones threw for 3,101 yards and 19 touchdowns against eight interceptions while completing 68% of his passes, giving the Colts a reason to believe he could be their answer at quarterback.
The current version of Jones has done little to warrant Steichen’s dogged commitment.
Despite those struggles, Steichen is digging his heels in, determined to do anything but entertain the possibility of benching Jones. When asked after Sunday's loss whether he had considered a quarterback change, Steichen said he had not, reiterating his confidence in the veteran.
Here’s the problem. Everyone can see that Jones isn’t producing the results necessary. That is, everyone but Steichen.
Steichen’s response is difficult to defend. Coaches should stand behind their players, but that support cannot come at the expense of making necessary decisions. Jones has had seven games to affirm last year wasn't a fluke, but he's done next to nothing to inspire confidence.
At 2-5, the Colts have reached a point where continuing to roll Jones out there with the starters week in and week out borders on malpractice.
The bigger question is what Steichen's refusal to consider a change says about Anthony Richardson. If Jones' struggles haven't been enough to prompt a serious evaluation of the alternatives, it raises questions about how the coaching staff views the former fourth overall pick and whether he has any realistic path back into the starting lineup.
Richardson hasn't exactly made his own case easier .
In addition to swinging and missing at his first chance as the starter, Richardson’s recent marijuana-related charge and subsequent comments expressing no regret have added another complication to an already uncertain situation.
Still, those issues shouldn't eliminate the possibility of giving him another chance. If Steichen no longer believes Richardson can be a viable option, the organization needs to confront that reality. If he does, it's difficult to understand why the Colts wouldn't at least explore a change with their season slipping away.
Richardson doesn't need to be the long-term answer to justify giving him another opportunity. With the season slipping away, there is little to no downside to finding out whether he can offer something Jones hasn't.
Even if Richardson fails to capitalize, Indianapolis would have a clearer picture of its quarterback situation heading into the offseason.
Ultimately, Steichen's unwavering support for Jones says as much about the coach as it does the quarterback. At 2-5, Steichen has every reason to reevaluate his approach. Instead, he appears determined to stick with his guy regardless of the results.
If Steichen is going down with the ship, he's making it clear that he'll do so on his own terms.

title: The Jaguars' Perfect Trade Target Isn't Actually Even an Option
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- There is one NFL Trade Deadline target that makes perfect sense for the Jacksonville Jaguars ... who also seemingly has zero chance of landing in Jacksonville.
The Indianapolis Colts are in a complete tailspin , and their fire sale began on Tuesday as they sent future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a third-round pick and a future fifth-round pick. As a result, it only makes sense for the Colts to make the perfect trade deadline target available: defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.
With that said , Buckner's talents should not be expected to land in Jacksonville for a simple reason: the Colts and Jaguars do not do business with each other when it comes to trades.
There are a million reasons why Buckner would make sense for the Jaguars. Even at 32, he is still one of the best interior pass-rushers in the NFL, and he would lead the Jaguars in both pressures and sacks. The Jaguars have lacked any sense of an interior rush for years now, and Buckner would be a more appealing option to boost the Jaguars' pass-rush than most other interior defenders. He is also in a contract year and would likely help the Jaguars earn a compensatory draft pick in March if he serves to only be a rental for the rest of 2026.
Buckner is exactly the kind of player the Jaguars need in the middle of their defense, the Colts are seemingly set to be willing to move on from all top players, and the Jaguars have the picks to make a compelling case and offer. With that said, there just isn't a chance the Jaguars are going to land the veteran defensive tackle. Whenever Buckner is traded (likely to the San Francisco 49ers or Chicago Bears), one should not question why Jaguars general manager James Gladstone didn't make it happen.
Sources: The #Colts are also actively shopping DT DeForest Buckner. I expect him to be moved soon if the right offer comes in. https://t.co/U36PCN9an3
Instead, it is clear that the Jaguars' AFC South connection with the Colts makes them disqualified from the Buckner sweepstakes to start. Buckner looks like he is bound to be the next player the Colts and placeholder general manager Ed Dodds deals, but that does not mean the Colts are going to help Jacksonville anytime soon.
Yes, the Colts have already conceded their place in the AFC South race. And yes, the Colts will likely lose to the Jaguars twice in 2026 even if Buckner wasn't on the Jaguars' defense. But history says that a Buckner trade to Jacksonville isn't just unlikely, but it it would break all historical precedents the AFC South has set over the last few decades.
The Jaguars have engaged in player trades in the AFC South just twice: in 2025 when they traded Christian Kirk to the Houston Texans for a seventh-round pick, and in 2020 when they traded the Tennessee Titans a sixth-round pick for linebacker Kamalei Correa, who played six games for the 1-15 Jaguars and made seven tackles.
So trades have happened, but it has only been trades that contain absolutely zero consequences. The Jaguars knew that Kirk was never going to impact their race for the AFC South title, just like the Titans knew that giving Correa to a bad Jaguars team would make no difference. A Buckner trade wouldn't fall into this category at all, though. It would be a legit game-changer in the short-term, and Dodds doesn't want to be the interim general manager who helped the Jaguars find playoff success in a wide-open AFC.
In a perfect world, Buckner would make a ton of sense for the Jaguars. He fits everything they need on and off the field. But in this world, Buckner to the Jaguars is nothing more than a pipedream and a wish upon a star.

title: Ranking the Jaguars' Top NFL Trade Deadline Targets: From Realistic to Delusional
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL Trade Deadline is officially two weeks away, and the Jacksonville Jaguars are certainly a team to watch once Nov. 10 rolls around.
Part of that is due to the situation surrounding wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., who could draw interest from teams in need of an offensive spark. Part of it is also due to the fact that the 4-2 Jaguars look ready to go on a run, which would mean it makes all the sense in the world for them to be buyers once the deadline is officially here.
So, which trade deadline targets make the most actual sense for James Gladstone's front office to go after? And which are, well, pipedreams? We break it down below.
If there is one move that just makes sense for the Jaguars, from fit to need, it is likely Khalil Mack. The Jaguars have a talented pair of defensive ends in Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker who should get more productive as the year goes, but their pass-rush depth behind the duo is minimal. The Jaguars have not gotten much production from backup defensive ends Danny Striggow and Bryan Thomas Jr., while Dennis Gardeck might be better off as a rotational piece than as a key part of the pass-rush rotation.
Mack makes a ton of sense for a contender like the Jaguars, he is cheap and in a contract year, and likely would take what amounts to a fifth-round pick to land in a trade. He is getting up there and his production has taken a small dip as a result, but he can still get the job done. He would fit the Jaguars' culture and mentality on defense, while also allowing Travon Walker to play pass-rushing snaps inside more frequently.
While Moro Ojomo did get sidelined with an injury against the Dallas Cowboys on Monday Night Football, he still makes a ton of sense for a team like the Jaguars as long as it wasn't anything overly serious. The Eagles are sitting at 2-5 and their season looks closer and closer to being over with each passing week. With big money tied up to Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, it has always been clear the Eagles would not re-sign Ojomo, making him an easy trade candidate.
Ojomo is young, can give the Jaguars a boost both against the run and the pass, and would allow the Jaguars to have time to figure out whether he is just a rental and a compensatory pick formula chess piece, or if he is instead a long-term option. Not many players, if any, make more sense for the Jaguars to call about.
While Zach Sieler has been a productive player for a long-time, he is in a different stage of his career than Ojomo. He is older, less productive as a pass-rusher right now, more expensive, and is under contract for several more seasons. With that said, he has connections to the Jaguars' staff, would improve their depth at defensive tackle, and likely would not take much to pry from the Dolphins considering where they are at with their rebuild.
Do the Jaguars actually have a use in their scheme for a true designated pass-rusher who is more of a speed threat than anything else? That remains to be seen considering the traits the Jaguars have been adding at EDGE over the last two years. With that said, both Will McDonald and Josh Uche are guys who can really go off the edge, and they would give the Jaguars the fastball pass-rusher off the edge that would mesh well with Hines-Allen and Walker.
This would be all about cost, both in terms of draft compensation and cap space needed. The Jaguars would need to create a few million in terms of cap space to fit Payne's deal on the books, while he is also closer to being a blue-chip player than most others on this list. Payne would make a big, big impact for the Jaguars due to his production as both a pass-rusher and a run-stopper, but this seems unlikely unless it is something like a straight Payne for Brian Thomas Jr. swap.
We already mentioned one Los Angeles Chargers pass-rusher as a trade option. Tuli Tuipulotu is another gifted Chargers defender who could be shopped as they continue to lose games due to his status as a contract-year defender at a premium position. With that said, chances are he would cost a good bit more than Mack due to the fact that he is a much younger player at the same position. He would also be more of a starter-type, while Mack can be more rotational.
Outside of Jacksonville, the AFC South is a mess right now. All three other AFC South teams lost in Week 7, bringing the combined AFC South record for non-Jaguars teams to 5-16. The 2-5 Indianapolis Colts look like they could be major sellers ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline, and the result of their battle with the Jaguars in Week 8 could play a big role in that. The Houston Texans seem unlikely to be sellers since they will believe they can make a run, while the Tennessee Titans have the NFL's best defensive tackle once again playing on its worst team
With that said, do not expect for the Jaguars to land any potential departures from the AFC South such as DeForest Buckner, Grover Stewart, Quenton Nelson, or whomever else. In-division trades do not happen often unless they are ones of little-to-no consequence, like the Jaguars trading Christian Kirk to the Texans last season. That is just how these things go, and the only real way the AFC South's movement at the deadline will impact the Jaguars is by weaking the division as they try to go on their run.

title: Liam Coen Has 1 Simple Solution for Jaguars to Avoid NFL's Referee Debacle
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- As the Jacksonville Jaguars surely know by now, the NFL has a referee problem.
The Jaguars have seen officials make some dramatic, and even simply flat-out wrong, calls against them during their 4-2 stretch in the first six weeks of the season. This includes five touchdowns negated by penalties since Week 3, including a Bhayshul Tuten touchdown in Week 6 against the Houston Texans on a phantom hold. A few plays later, Trevor Lawrence threw a red-zone interception and the Jaguars failed to score, eventually losing 34-31 on a walk-off field goal.
With the NFL's officials under more fire this week after a complete debacle of a performance in the Green Bay Packers' loss to the Detroit Lions, it is only natural for the focus on the NFL's penalty problem to once again shift toward its officials. As a result, Jaguars head coach Liam Coen has one simple solution for the Jaguars to avoid penalty issues at they look to make a run: l eave no doubt.
“Leave no doubt is really what it comes down to. Play above it, leave no doubt," Coen said Monday when asked about what he preaches to his locker room when it comes to recent penalty issues.
That is of course easier said than done, especially with some of the calls that have gone against the Jaguars this season. But no matter how valid the penalties are, the flags are the biggest reason the Jaguars are 4-2 right now and not 5-1. The numbers make it clear that, outside of the Packers, no team has been impacted more by judgement calls from officials than the Jaguars.
What you are feeling is real weezy The Packers rank last in penalty "luck" through 7 weeks. Mostly due to defensive holding and roughing the passer calls on the defense https://t.co/CytDRjyAhP pic.twitter.com/g42tXv7wWG
"Fundamentals, and you guys hear me say it ad nauseam, but regardless of results, right, the fundamentals and techniques in which we coach, teach… We’ve got to continue to detail those even when fatigue sets in and whether it's mental or physical fatigue that sets in, we have got to be at our best in terms of detail, fundamentally sharp, disciplined in order to leave no doubt that we control our destiny," Coen said.
"We control the outcomes of games at the end of the day in terms of win or lose, and we can live with those results. You just can't go there. It's hard not to. It's human instinct and nature to do so, but it really doesn't do anybody any good to go down that path. Trust me, I've been there.”
Coen, of course, is right. There is nothing the Jaguars can do about the called-back Tuten touchdowns or Josh Cameron's negated kickoff return against the Eagles or Travis Hunter's negated interception against the Bengals, or any of the several questionable pass interference calls against the Texans. All the Jaguars can do is play through it, starting with Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts.
Penalties are a huge reason the Jaguars lost to the Texans in London, but they are not the only reason. The Jaguars still made their fair share of self-inflicted mistakes that they must avoid in the weeks to come, which is the message Coen and his staff has stressed.
"We got to be on our P's and Q's, and that just makes us better football players," Jaguars cornerback Jourdan Lewis said on Monday.
"And I think that's what kept me in the league a long time, is just understanding how to adapt to different styles of how the game is being played and called just understanding the rules, because at the end of the day we got to go out there and play. Regardless of how it's being officiated or things are being called, we got to be out there and give it our all and play our best.”

title: Jaguars Know The Magic Number in the AFC South, and Now They Can Make Their Run
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ready to make their run.
The bye week turned everything around for the Jaguars a year ago, and the comparisons to this year can certainly be drawn. Jacksonville was 4-3 and coming off a tough loss in London at last year's bye week, and this year the Jaguars were 4-2 entering their bye and coming off an emotional last-second loss to the Houston Texans in London.
Adding Jakobi Meyers at the trade deadline certainly helped, but overall the Jaguars were a different team post-bye last season. Jacksonville went 9-1 after last year's bye week to set themselves up with a 13-4 record, an AFC South title, and a home playoff game.
Now, they will need to make the same thing happen now that they know what the magic number in the AFC South is : 13 wins.
The math is simple. If the Jaguars go 9-2 over the next 11 weeks, they will win the AFC South. With the Houston Texans and Indianapolis Colts sitting at 2-5 after Week 7 , the Jaguars can ensure an AFC South title with 13 wins ... a number the Colts and Texans can not reach. Now, winning 9-of-11 games is difficult and something most teams do not do over the second-half of a season, but the Jaguars will be coming out of their Week 7 bye hoping to not be like most teams.
It helps that the Jaguars got quite a bit of help from the AFC South in Week 7. The AFC South went 0-3 on Sunday, and the Jaguars' three rivals have just five wins combined this season. The Texans have made runs before, and nothing is ever secured, but the Jaguars' chances of winning the south increased on a Sunday where the Jaguars were at home.
“It helps. It definitely helps. I did keep some eye on some of the opponents that we will be seeing in the future. To see the type of game style that they play and how they're doing," Jaguars cornerback Jourdan Lewis said Monday. "The AFC South helped us. We’re still number one in the division and just trying to make sure that we don't have any skids to where we let anybody get any opportunity to take that from us.”
To ensure the Jaguars avoid those skids and make a run, the Jaguars have a few clear areas to improve. Head coach Liam Coen noted some of these areas Monday, pointing out red-zone penalties on offense, explosive plays allowed through the air on defense, and kickoff and punt coverage units.
Each of these aspects of their team came up big in their lone two losses, especially in the Week 6 loss to the Texans. That is where the Jaguars' bye week comes into play. Last year, the bye week was about improving Trevor Lawrence and the passing game, and the Jaguars did exactly that. Now, their focus moving into Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts and beyond is clear.
"Anytime you get a little bit of an opportunity to reset, gather your thoughts, also get away from it a little bit. Sometimes absence makes the heart grow fonder in ways, and no different in football. I couldn't sleep last night," Coen said Monday.
"Excited about getting back in the building and getting back with these guys and attacking these next 11 games together and really getting after it. It also came a little earlier this year than last, if you will, right, in terms of the way it played out and how many games we've played. But six weeks in and you see all the stuff that happens on any given Sunday, specifically within our division, it should only allow you to have a mindset and mentality to come in here and attack this thing with a division game up this week.”
The Jaguars have one of the NFL's easier schedules over the next 11 weeks, facing the Colts and Titans twice, the 2-5 Texans once more, the Washington Commanders, and some other very winnable games against the Dallas Cowboys, Baltimore Ravens, New York Giants, and the Pittsburgh Steelers. The toughest game left looks to be the Chicago Bears in Week 13.
But the Jaguars, more than anything, need to avoid those skids that Lewis mentioned. They can't take anything for granted, and they are still facing their own injury questions and pre-trade deadline chatter. It is, however, clear what it will take for the Jaguars to reach their goals.
Nine more wins, and the Jaguars will play a playoff football game in Jacksonville. It is time for the Jaguars to make their run.

title: The Colts Have Already Given the Jaguars the Perfect Week 8 Blueprint
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a big game coming up in Week 8, and they may have been given some early help in the form of the Minnesota Vikings.
The Jaguars are set to host their AFC South rival Indianapolis Colts in Week 8 as Jacksonville comes off their bye week, and they will be getting a Colts team that is fresh off a 16-10 loss to the Vikings. But beyond the fact the Jaguars are getting a slumping Colts team at the right time, the Jaguars also got a boost from the Vikings via a blueprint for disrupting the Colts, Shane Steichen, and Daniel Jones.
No team in football is blitzing more than the Vikings, who are led by defensive guru Brian Flores. Flores is going to send the house every single week, and he made sure to really turn up the pressure against the Colts and Jones. The plan clearly worked, with Jones going 11-of-18 for 101 yards and an interception against the blitz: giving him a passer rating of 53.2 and just 5.6 yards per attempt. Jones was one of the worst quarterbacks in the NFL this week against the blitz by most metrics, numbers that track with season-long averages.
The Vikings defense blitzed on 85.2% of Daniel Jones' dropbacks, the highest blitz rate by a defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). Minnesota generated pressure on 60.9% of those blitzes, with all four its sacks coming when blitzing. #INDvsMIN | #Skol
This season, Jones ranks No. 21 out of 33 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA/Dropback against the blitz, No. 26 in passer rating, No. 33 in sacks, No. 27 in pressure rate, and No. 29 in air yards per attempt. In short, he gets sacked a ton against the blitz and, when he does throw it, he isn't exactly pushing the ball downfield. Jones is not accurate enough or a quick enough processor to consistently win as a quick-game passer, and Flores was able to get after this flaw on Sunday.
Simply put, the blueprint has been out on Jones for some time. But the performance he put together against the Vikings, combined with the fact that the Colts have the NFL's slowest receiver room with Alec Pierce injured, makes it clear that to secure a win on Sunday, Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile should take a page out of his former bosses' playbook.
Campanile has worked for a number of top defensive minds, including Flores, Vic Fangio, and Jeff Hafley. While there is no coach quite like Flores, he has certainly made an impact on how Campanile sees the game and structures his defense, which means it might not be overly difficult for Campanile to attempt to replicate some of the things the Vikings did against the Colts.
“I think a lot of people had a huge influence on me. I'd say recently, obviously working with Jeff Hafley, I thought we had a very similar belief system and style. We see things very similarly and then Vic Fangio is probably a guy who—he had a tremendous impact on me, just in seeing certain things in the game and how you call the game," Campanile said last year. "And even in terms of how you practice things, so he's been somebody that has been a great resource for me, was a huge help to me. And he definitely had a big effect on me as well. Jeff's one of those guys and Flo [Vikings Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores] too. Coach Flores had a huge impact on me. And you can probably see a lot of the things that we do,  they may show up  for some of those teams as well.”
There are different factors to work in, of course. The Jaguars have an elite shutdown cornerback in Travis Hunter who can impact the math when it comes to blitzing and the defensive approach. The Jaguars have also not blitzed anywhere near as much as the Vikings, with Minnesota blitzing on 68.9% of passing plays (No. 1 in the NFL) compared to 30.5% from the Jaguars (No. 14). The highest rate of blitzing the Jaguars have done in a game this season was 45.2% against the Denver Broncos in Week 2, which would still fall below the Vikings' lowest blitz rate of the season (54.35).
But the blueprint is there, and the Jaguars can spin things in their own way to get home. Against the Colts a year ago, the Jaguars blitzed Jones twice on seven drop backs in his limited time on the field. Expect that number to go up after the success that Flores and the Vikings had, because it is clear that Jones and the Colts' offense as a whole simply can not handle it.

title: 4 Realistic IDL Trade Targets for the Jaguars Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- For the last several years, it feels like there has been a common trade deadline theme for the Jacksonville Jaguars: defensive tackle help.
The Jaguars' defensive tackle room has been productive in some facets this season, with Jacksonville's interior defensive line playing a large role in the unit being one of the NFL's best against the run. But there are other aspects of the unit that have disappointed, such as the lack of a consistent interior pass-rush.
So, if the Jaguars opt to use the trade deadline to improve the middle of their defensive front, who would make the most sense? We break it down below.
We have talked up Moro Ojomo as a logical fit for the Jaguars for a few weeks now, and it is easy to see why. Ojomo is only 25-years-old, his cap hit is $1.84 million, he is a productive interior rusher, the Eagles are trending towards a firesale, it is highly unlikely the Eagles would extend him since they have two big-money defensive tackles ... do I need to keep going? He has one of the most clear trade cases in the entire NFL, and he would serve as a nice boost to the Jaguars' interior pass-rush potential.
Adding a player like Ojomo would give the Jaguars a rental for the next 11 games to pair inside with Arik Armstead, Travon Walker, and Josh Hines-Allen on third-downs, while also giving the Jaguars some options for the future. If Ojomo impresses with Hamilton and Armstead in contract years, the Jaguars could re-sign him and make him a pillar of the defensive line moving forward. If they have other plans, they could see him walk in free agency and likely nab a high compensatory pick depending on the size of the deal he signs in free agency.
It remains to be seen i f the Jaguars could actually afford to trade for Daron Payne . He would cost about $9 million to add to the roster, and the Jaguars would need to create some space to do that. With that said, Payne is still uber-talented at 29-years-old and he is right up there for Ojomo in terms of the ability to be an X-Factor and actually change the trajectory of the Jaguars' interior defensive line moving forward.
Payne is in the last year of his deal, so the compensatory pick formula game would once again apply. He is having a solid year as both a pass-rusher and a run-defender and would give the Jaguars quite the formidable talent inside their defense for what would likely amount to an all-in on a rental veteran before he hits free agency for the first time.
A player who has a few connections to members of the Jaguars' defensive staff, Zach Sieler would make sense for a lot of reasons. He may not be at the level of Payne or Ojomo in terms of impact, especially as a pass-rusher, but he would give the Jaguars improved depth at defensive tackle from both a run-defense and pass-rush perspective. It would also make a ton of sense for the Dolphins to move him, even after their first win against the New York Jets on Sunday.
Simply put, the Dolphins are clearly still all-in on building toward the future in terms of draft picks and flipping veterans for the right price. They have hung onto a few young playmakers, but otherwise they look like they are open for business. Unlike the opther players on this list, he is still under contract for a few years and would have $10 million be guranteed next year, so he would have to be seen as a long-term option.
The Los Angeles Chargers have other appealing trade candidates on their roster, especially along the edge defender spots on the depth chart. With that said, Tomlinson is an experienced veteran who is an immediate impact as a run-defender, and he could quickly help boost the depth chart for a team with an open window like the Jaguars. He would give the Jaguars a better run defender at the backup spot than Matt Dickerson has provided this year, and he would come cheap.
With that said, Tomlinson is the worst pass-rusher on this list by a healthy mile and it is clear the Jaguars would still have the issue of an interior pass-rush moving into the future. But this is about winning games no matter what it looks like, and Tomlinson would make the Jaguars a slightly better team at a cheap cost.

title: 2 Jaguars Players Who Make Sense to Surprisingly Be Traded Before the Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL Trade Deadline is quickly approaching, and the Jacksonville Jaguars have the ability to make quite a few moves.
Most of the trade deadline chatter when it comes to the Jaguars is going to focus on wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr., or whether the Jaguars will add needed depth pieces on the defensive side of the ball. But what if the Jaguars are also looking to unload a few players?
With the Jaguars the clear favorites in the AFC South and a legit contender in a wide-open AFC, it stands to reason the Jaguars shouldn't want to move many, or any, of their non-Thomas Jr. contributors. With that said, what if it could help the Jaguars land ammo for a trade for a defensive lineman or defensive back? That is at least worth consdiering.
With that in mind, here are two players who I think could qualify as surprise trades from the roster who could help the Jaguars accomplish exactly that ahead of the trade deadline.
Trading away a starting offensive lineman right after losing left tackle Anton Harrison for the year would be odd, which, of course, is why it qualifies as a surprise option. I do think there is a scenario that even with the loss of Harrison that the Jaguars could see Cleveland as expendable as he enters his final 11 regular-season games under contract with the team, in part due to the contract situation and in part due to the other linemen on the roster.
Cleveland has never really been seen as an extension candidate after this season, so trading him for value now instead of hoping to potentially get a compensatory pick for him after next year's free agency would make long-term sense. In the short-term, the Jaguars have multiple other options they could slot in at right guard and likely get similar production as they have gotten from Cleveland this season.
Wyatt Milum, the current swing tackle, is more of a guard than a tackle. Same goes for backup lineman Daniel Faalele. Add in the impending return of Patrick Mekari from injured reserve, and the Jaguars can still have solid offensive line depth without Cleveland, who could fill in for a more offensive line-needy teams. This would also give the Jaguars a chance to package picks for defensive depth or an actual swing tackle option.
Jourdan Lewis has been a good soldier for the Jaguars since he signed with the team in free agency last March, but there is reason to believe the Jaguars could benefit by looking to move him at the deadline. Teams are always needing cornerbacks at the deadline, and Lewis is a productive and experienced veteran who has made a lot of plays in this league. The flip side, and why this would be a surprise, is the fact the Jaguars are one of those teams that needs cornerback help as well.
The difference here is that Lewis is a nickel cornerback, and the Jaguars could sustain losing his spot on the depth chart if it means improving the other outside cornerback spot across from Travis Hunter. Jarrian Jones has been more productive from the slot than on the outside, and he would give the Jaguars more speed at nickel than Lewis is able to give them right now. They would need Montaric Brown to return to form on the outside or need to add another outside cornerback to make it work, but it makes sense.
It is a bit tough to see Lewis on the roster beyond this season so, like Cleveland, it could be a short-term move to benefit in the long-term. It would be tough to trade a leader and a captain, but it is worth considering under the right circumstances.
