title: Jaguars Get the Perfect Week 7 Outcome Thanks to AFC South Rivals
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- As far as bye week Sundays go, this one could not have gone much better for the Jacksonville Jaguars.
The Jaguars had some clear games they needed to see go their way in Week 7 as they enjoyed their bye week after a 4-2 start, and that is exactly what they got. Of course, they got some welcomed help from their AFC South rivals in the process.
The AFC South went 0-3 during the early afternoon slate of games on Sunday, with the Houston Texans losing at home in overtime to the New York Giants, the Tennessee Titans losing on a walk-off field goal against the Cleveland Browns, and the Indianpolis Colts losing yet another game, this time against the Minnesota Vikings.
The Jaguars were always going to remain in firm control of first-place in the AFC South regardless of Sunday's results, but their position was made even stronger by the fact that every single other team dropping their Week 7 game. As a result, the Jaguars gained a bit of a cushion against the rest of their rivals, with the space between them and the Texans as the highlight.
The AFC South through 7 weeks: pic.twitter.com/ltUY5NJ9BT
The Jaguars will get another chance to take a big step in the AFC South over the next few weeks, starting with Week 8's game against the Indianapolis Colts. With the Colts now at 2-5 and offseveral brutal losses, it certainly stands to reason the Colts could shop some of their key veterans and look very different a week from now as their season continues to slip out of control.
The Colts are already a cursed team when it comes to playing games in Jacksonville, but they could reasonably trade any of Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, or DeForest Buckner over the next week as they prepare for next year's rebuild. If the Colts are without any of those players, a scenario that was made more possible by Sunday's loss, then they are an even easier target for the Jaguars to hit next week.
As for the Texans, they are on a bye next week. This means a Jaguars win over the Colts in Week 8 would bring the Jaguars back to being three games ahead of Houston in the AFC South, which was the exact spot the Jaguars were in before they lost to Houston in Week 6. Few teams start 2-5 and win their divison. Even if the Texans are still far from done, they took a big hit this week.
The Jaguars play three AFC South games in their next five weeks, with next week's game against the Colts and then two games against the lowly Titans in the next four games after that. In part due to today's results, the Jaguars can make things look very, very good for their playoff chances by December.
Outside of this week's news about left tackle Anton Harrison being ruled out for the rest of the season , the bye week went about as good as the Jaguars could have hoped. Consider this a winning weekend for Duval and Liam Coen's squad.

title: 4 Players the Jaguars Desperately Need to Step Up After the Bye Week
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' bye week is almost over, and it is nearly time for the Jaguars to turn their focus to the rest of the 2026 season.
The Jaguars are in a good place as they enter the final day of their bye week, but things can always get better, can't they? The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 right now and in first-place of the AFC South, but they will need a team effort to continue their winning ways over the next few months.
For the Jaguars to keep taking strides after the bye week, though, they will need to see a few players take some big steps to pave the way. Here are those players they will need to seize the moment the most:
Walker Little is set to be the Jaguars' starting left tackle after Anton Harrison's season-ending injury , and the Jaguars will need him in a big way. Little played very well against the Houston Texans in the Week 6 loss in Houston against the NFL's best pass-rush duo, and he has a long history of being a productive blindside protector. When comparing their careers, it doesn't look like the numbers indicate there is much of a drop-off from Harrison to Little, if one at all.
Still, the Jaguars will need Little to step up and be at his best down the stretch. They still have to play the Texans and some other fierce pass-rushes this season, and Little will be an important piece of Liam Coen's offense as they look to continue set up Trevor Lawrence for an MVP-caliber season like the one he has had to this point.
The Jaguars' secondary has plenty of questions entering Week 8, and one of the biggest questions might be Jourdan Lewis -- especially when the Jaguars get Montaric Brown back from his hamstring injury. Lewis has done some good things for the Jaguars in the run game and he has recorded two interceptions as their primary nickel cornerback this season, but he has also given up some big plays in the process in the Jaguars' only two losses.
With the amount of attention teams clearly have on Travis Hunter, who they have been avoiding in coverage for the most part, more and more passes are going to come Lewis' way. The Jaguars will need Lewis to become more consistent and cut-down the explosive plays allowed in coverage if they are to fix their secondary issues.
If the Jaguars' pass-rush is going to get home more often over the second-half of the season, it will likely hinge on the interior pass-rush. Defensive ends Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen are consistent pass-rushers who bring plenty of pressure off the edge, but it is easier for quarterbacks and offenses to negate their impact when the Jaguars are not getting much of a pass-rush from the interior group.
Armstead has had some games where he has absolutely taken over, and other games where he has been just marginally productive. If the Jaguars are going to start ramping up their pass-rush production as the stakes increase each week, they will need Armstead to help lead that charge in a big way.
If the Jaguars trade Brian Thomas Jr. , it is clear that they will need Josh Cameron to step up in a big way. Even if the Jaguars do not trade him, they still likely need to see Cameron be ready to step into a larger role than the limited, but impressive, role he played for the Jaguars during the first six weeks of the season. Cameron has stepped up each time the Jaguars have gone his way, and he needs to continue this trend moving forward.
Cameron very easily could be the Jaguars' WR3 after the bye week, depending on how they view Thomas and his place in the offense. That would mean more on his plate than his duties over the first six weeks of the season, and the Jaguars will have to ensure that their sixth-round rookie wide receiver is ready for the moment if it comes to that.

title: What the Jaguars Can Realistically Afford at the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The 2026 NFL Trade deadline is just a few weeks away, and the Jacksonville Jaguars could certainly be a big factor.
Most of the trade talk around the Jaguars understandably centers around third-year wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. , but what if the Jaguars are buyers at the deadline?
The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 and in first-place in the AFC South during their bye week , and they could reasonably look to add a potential difference-maker or depth piece at a number of positions before the trade deadline hits.
But what can the Jaguars afford when it comes to the deadline , both in terms of cap space and draft picks?
As things stand today, the Jaguars are set to have nine picks in the 2027 NFL Draft: six of their own original selections and three picks via the compensatory draft pick system after they saw Devin Lloyd, Travis Etienne, and Greg Newsome depart in free agency. The Jaguars have used the draft compensatory formula to give themselves more at bats in the draft, as well as give themselves more chances to trade for depth pieces such as Tim Patrick last season and Daniel Faalele this season.
"I think that's something in the spring we highlighted quite a bit about the idea of going down the compensatory picks approach and not signing immediately some of the street free agents. Really where we were going to turn our attention to was during training camp and the regular season, knowing that we had a larger stock of future draft picks to utilize to answer any questions that we might need to in those moments," Jaguars general manager James Gladstone said at the conclusion of training camp this summer.
"Yeah, that gives us more flexibility to pursue those paths and those options. I think that that's an ever-evolving strategy as to whether or not you're going to deploy that one year after the next. It was where we found ourselves this past cycle, and I think that's why you probably saw some willingness there, not to say that we weren't unwilling a year ago, because we were. I think the equivalent of that was probably [WR] Tim Patrick and using a sixth-round pick to get him from Detroit. We still have avenues for pursuing those into the regular season."
Compensatory Pick (Devin Lloyd)
Compensatory Pick (Travis Etienne)
Compensatory Pick (Greg Newsome)
When it comes to cap space, things are a bit tighter. The Jaguars can always work to create more room, but a lack of cap space now means that players on hefty deals, such as Daron Payne, may be tougher to trade for than players on their rookie deals still like Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo.
The Jaguars did some work to create cap space with restructures ahead of Week 1, and Spotrac has the Jaguars currently at $4,659,858 in available cap space, which ranks No. 25 in the NFL.
"I think that's a move to make so that we're not forced to do anything should we pursue an avenue. We want to make sure we have the flexibility we need to keep things on the table as the season progresses," Gladstone said before the season began.
"In the same breath, we're always going to do our part to consider all options, and through that lens not all those are going to come to the table or to the public's understanding. I think the understanding that we are always going to turn over every stone is certainly going to be the case."
In short, the Jaguars have plenty of flexibility before the deadline to be aggressive from a draft pick standpoint. From a cap space standpoint, a player either on their rookie deal or a cheaper contract makes the most sense.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: Were the Chiefs Actually Exposed in Seattle?
full_text:
Things couldn't have gone much worse for the Kansas City Chiefs in their Sunday Night Football loss against the Seattle Seahawks . Still, KC remains at the top of the AFC with a 5-1 record and a lot of football still to be played.
What questions rose to the top of the Chiefs' list of uncertainties after their first loss of the year? Let's answer a few in this week's edition of the Chiefs On SI mailbag.
After this Seattle debacle, how bad have the Chiefs been exposed? - @MrEd315
I like the phrasing of this question, and I think I may surprise some people with my answer. How badly were the Chiefs exposed on Sunday? I'm not sure they were exposed at all!
The Chiefs' flaws in that game were glaring. Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong are not a legitimate 1-2-3 trio of wide receivers, and the Chiefs know that. The Seahawks knew that.
The injuries at offensive tackle—down to OT3 on the left side and OT4 on the right—were no secret either. The Seahawks may have "exposed" the fact that if you can stop Kenneth Walker, you can stop that version of the Chiefs' offense , but we talked about that issue all week, leading up to the game.
The pass rush wasn't nearly good enough at rattling Sam Darnold, but it was the fourth game this year where they failed to record a sack; that's not a new issue either.
This whole winding road leads me to a potentially unsatisfying point: the Chiefs lost that game more dramatically than I would have expected, but not for any reasons that weren't already top-of-mind. Is that enough to soothe all of your Chief concerns? Absolutely not. But it is a silver lining, and better than losing a game for some surprising, unforeseen reason.
How would you divvy up blame for the poor offensive performance between QB play, personnel, and scheme? I feel like the QB play is not a given to be Tier 1 like it was prior to 2024. - @broccolirabe.bsky.social
Patrick Mahomes has been excellent this season, but I do think the Seattle loss included his worst game of the year . With memories of the way he's been caught "pressing" in the past as he's tried to overcome his surroundings in recent years, I think the uncertainty at offensive tackle and lack of any legitimate separation from his pass-catchers allowed Mahomes to rediscover some bad habits in Seattle .
Still, late in the game, Mahomes seemed to find his groove again before being let down by his supporting cast. The quarterback is, by far, the least of my worries.
I do think the coaching staff could have given Kenneth Walker a few more tries on the ground before completely giving up on the running game (though it was unproductive when they did try it), and I'd love to see Cyrus Allen get a longer look when none of the other pass-catchers are standing out. Ultimately, I think that the deficiencies of the players who were thrust into action on Sunday night played the biggest role of the three options presented in the question.
How do they get to 10 wins? - @joeybeckley.bsky.social
Keep playing the games. They're 5-1. They have plenty of issues to solve, and this mailbag has detailed several, but I'd be absolutely floored if they're not a playoff team with double-digit wins.
With the injuries at WR and tackle and the lack of any sort of pass rush, could the Chiefs actually do a little selling at the deadline instead of adding? - @mrproctober.bsky.social
If some team wants to acquire a non-vital piece from KC, Brett Veach should hear them out, sure. In the meantime, they're currently the No. 1 seed in the AFC. Even if that seems unlikely to hold, a 5-1 team quarterbacked by Patrick Mahomes will not and should not be "sellers" at the deadline.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Several Young Players Drop in Week 8
full_text:
Seven weeks into the 2026 NFL campaign, the Kansas City Chiefs finally suffered their first loss . There are no moral victories in this sport, although one potential silver lining is that the defeat came at the hands of an NFC club that very well could contend for the Super Bowl once again.
In the aftermath of an ugly showing on the road, Kansas City is sent back to the drawing board prior to a critical Sunday showdown against the Denver Broncos. The club's young players will surely be asked to contribute in an AFC West clash — which ones are trending in the right and wrong directions?
Following Week 7, let's break down the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each qualifying 53-man roster member in tiers. Be sure to return to this series each week to see who's moving and shaking.
Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott isn't included due to him currently being on the physically unable to perform list . Left tackle Josh Simmons isn't included after going to injured reserve . The same applies to running back Brashard Smith .
When you notch an interception to potentially save a touchdown, you get kudos. When you do so in a game that was bordering on getting out of hand and your return sets up the team for an end-of-half field goal try, you get mentioned in this group. Cornerback Nohl Williams' impressive season rolls on thanks to his pick of Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold in Week 7.
NOHL WILLIAMS END ZONE INT AND A BIG RETURN KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/K42foMAhQy
First-round corner Mansoor Delane had a couple of rough reps against last season's Offensive Player of the Year, wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba, although one was simply a remarkable throw and catch. There's no need to worry about the LSU product moving forward. His third-down pass breakup and separate nice play on Smith-Njigba on a second-and-10 in the second half provided plenty of reason for continued optimism.
Rookie pass rusher R Mason Thomas and sophomore defensive end Ashton Gillotte were both shouted out in this week's stock watch story for their performances at Lumen Field. Thomas flashed more of his ability to put pressure on opposing signal-callers, whereas Gillotte's run defense was one of the few bright spots on Sunday Night Football .
Dropping down after temporarily being bumped up a tier are undrafted rookie offensive tackle Kahlil Benson and first-round defensive tackle Peter Woods. The former had one of his worst showings as a pro, albeit against a ruthless defense, but he was partially responsible for quarterback Patrick Mahomes being pressured at a top-five rate for his career. The latter played 33 snaps, good for nearly 48% of those available, but made a minimal impact.
First-year halfback Emmett Johnson didn't receive a single carry on offense for the second time in three games, but he did make a pair of nice plays in the passing game. One was a critical catch on a seemingly lost drive, and the next was a block that allowed Mahomes to pick up a rushing first down.
Wide receivers Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen both had moments that reminded those in Chiefs circles why they have yet to break out to this point. Allen, in particular, is a fan-favorite piece who many want to see the field more, but he's occasionally had trouble even navigating plays correctly.
UDFA defensive tackle Bryson Eason logged five snaps on defense and had an assisted tackle. He doesn't play special teams, so he can't move down a tier, but he's the least-noticeable player in this group.
The split of special teams versus offensive reps for tight end Jake Briningstool is up to 84-52 in 2026. In the last three games, it's 39-23. In Week 7, it was 12-5. Among this "primary special teams tier," he's the player it's easiest to see getting a promotion with a bit more involvement in future contests. Without someone above him getting hurt, safety Xavier Nwankpa's role seems capped, which is a shame considering the juice he brings to the field.
Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa is moderately similar to Nwankpa, although his role for special teams coordinator Dave Toub is more significant as a trusted option who's also made some plays this season. Given the shuffle at his defensive position, though, an increased snap count appears unlikely.
With Simmons on IR, UDFA tackle Diego Pounds technically was active for Week 7 but didn't play a single snap. He's here until further notice, joined by fourth-round rookie corner Jadon Canady , seventh-round rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier and UDFA defensive end Jack Pyburn . Nussmeier has routinely been the club's emergency third field general, but him not getting any live reps is a good thing.

title: Chiefs Stock Watch: Multiple Risers and Fallers After KC's First Loss vs. Seahawks
full_text:
No good run lasts forever, which the Kansas City Chiefs learned the hard way in Week 7 against the Seattle Seahawks. Going on the road to face the defending Super Bowl champions proved to be too tall a task for head coach Andy Reid's crew, resulting in an embarrassment on the Sunday Night Football stage.
Multiple players on both sides of the football struggled to make a positive impact. On the flip side, others' arrows might be pointing in the right direction despite the 20-3 defeat.
Let's dive into the good and bad from Week 7's Chiefs loss against Seattle and single out three players whose stock is trending up, as well as three who could use a better showing in Week 8 and beyond.
These players stood out for positive reasons over the weekend, potentially changing the trajectory of their seasons in the process.
Coming into the regular season, many had questions about how viable of an option second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte would be. After all, he was on the heels of an underwhelming debut campaign and also sustained a plantar fascia injury in August. After a quiet start to 2026, those concerns were only amplified, but Gillotte's been improving since then.
According to Pro Football Focus , the former third-round pick logged three pressures in back-to-back games against the Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Chargers. The outlet didn't credit him with one in Week 7, but he logged a season-high four "stops" on SNF . For reference, that's a quarter of his 2025 total.
Speaking of pressures, rookie D-end R Mason Thomas racked up four of them against a tough Seattle squad. He was one of just four Chiefs to notch a statistic in that category and trailed only fellow pass rusher George Karlaftis' six on the night.
Thomas, a second-rounder out of Oklahoma , is the best athlete in the room and wins quicker than anyone else. He's an excellent change-of-pace piece whose sack numbers aren't there yet, but there's no denying his raw ability. He has 14 combined pressures in his last three games and isn't getting washed out in run defense as often as he did earlier in the season.
Not all tackles are created equal, especially in the modern NFL. Elements like depth in relation to the line of scrimmage, pursuit versus crashing downhill, whether a player was in coverage and so much more go into the value of that box score stat. Linebacker Nick Bolton knows that better than anyone, evidenced by him sitting in the double digits in four of his last five contests. The Missouri product had another 11 tackles on Sunday, but this game felt a bit different.
Bolton was a huge factor in run support in Seattle, including a TFL on halfback Velus Jones Jr. on the club's fifth possession and a couple of other stops. He did whiff on an attempt that comes to mind, but this was the fully realized version of the heat-seeking missile Kansas City needs. Add in that Bolton was fighting through some obvious discomfort down the stretch, and you get a bang-up job for the leader of the defense.
This group of three didn't meet the standard in Week 7 and desperately need to recover moving forward if the team is to remain successful.
No one — and I mean no one — had a rougher Week 7 for the Chiefs than cornerback L'Jarius Sneed. I almost feel bad for him, as this shouldn't have been the plan for him when the club reunited with him on a one-year deal during the offseason. His rough year continued on Sunday night, even on just 14 defensive snaps, which underscored just how colossal of a failure this stint was against wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba.
Sneed routinely lost to the reigning Offensive Player of the Year on in-breakers, including a third-and-7 on Seattle's second possession for a gain of 33 yards. At that point, Sneed had been targeted three times in coverage and surrendered 53 yards. The aging Cooper Kupp, too, got his game off against Sneed by way of a third-and-9 conversion on that same drive.
The bad moments didn't stop there for Sneed, who ceded a nine-yard reception despite committing defensive holding on a play with less than a minute left in the first half. This was a game to flush for the veteran defensive back; only time will tell if his play improves.
Back to the theme of all good things coming to an end. With how otherworldly impressive he was to begin the year, running back Kenneth Walker III was eventually bound to stumble. There's no shame in doing so against a defense that, according to RBSDM , ranks second in rush success rate (32.1%) and third in EPA per carry (-0.196) allowed. Walker rushed for 36 years on Sunday, and each of them was about as hard-earned as it gets.
A 2.6 yard-per-carry average was nothing for a player who's averaging 4.10 yards after contact per tote in 2026. Walker's patented wiggle didn't allow him to break strings of tackles in tight spaces in prime time, nor was he able to escape around the edge and record explosive rushes. His longest carry was seven yards, easily his worst in a single contest this year.
Better days are ahead for Kansas City's best player this season.
Week 7 was an ugly one for quarterback Patrick Mahomes, seeing him complete just 19 of his 33 passes for 165 yards, no touchdowns, an interception and a 58.3 passer rating. The two-time MVP looked like anything but that under the bright lights at Lumen Field, missing multiple throws in various fashions and also bailing on a couple of clean pockets.
Mahomes admitted following the loss that he can be better, and everyone expects him to. It's also difficult to place too much blame on him considering he was down both starting offensive tackles and perhaps his two best receivers. Running an offense at a high level while shorthanded and being under duress roughly half the time is virtually impossible.
We'll honor the stock watch component and list Mahomes here, but don't expect to see his name too many times.

title: What Matters (and What Doesn't) from the Chiefs' Brutal Loss in Seattle
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' Sunday Night Football loss to the Seattle Seahawks was a drubbing in all three phases, leaving plenty of questions unanswered about how the Chiefs can recalibrate for the next act of their season.
However, not all of the Chiefs' issues that were exposed in Seattle are worth worrying about. Following a loss that thorough, let's take a look at some issues that do matter and some that don't—at least until further notice.
For the fourth time in six games, the Chiefs' defense failed to record a sack of the opposing quarterback. Even though some of the underlying metrics have supported the KC pass rush due to better performances in statistics like pressure rate , they've allowed opposing quarterbacks to be too comfortable, too often. With Sam Darnold as the target on Sunday night, the Chiefs just needed enough pressure to rattle Darnold, forcing him to start making characteristic mistakes. Instead, he threw and ran for several long third-down conversions.
Meanwhile, the Chiefs' only sacks since Week 1 came against a completely battered Los Angeles Chargers O-line last week.
Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane had a couple of "welcome to the NFL" moments against Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but nothing about Delane's losses indicate that he's anything other than an excellent young player who got beaten by a superstar.
JSN WHAT A CATCH FOR A TOUCHDOWN KCvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bN6IT22fM4
Similarly to the long completion Delane allowed last week to Chargers wide receiver Quentin Johnston, the rookie was in excellent position, had his hand between the ball and the receiver's hands, and just couldn't land the final fingernail to break up the pass. Delane would love to have those plays back, I'm sure, but even elite cornerbacks lose to the best receivers at times. Delane looked like a near-peer to Smith-Njigba, not like a rookie out of his depth.
If you would have told me before the game that rookie Cyrus Allen would lead the Chiefs' wide receivers in receiving yards, I would have been thrilled. Allen has seen very limited work to begin his first year in the pros, and a chance to break out through a heavily injured Chiefs WR room would have been well-timed.
Well, he did lead Chiefs wideouts in receiving yards, but he only had one catch for 18 yards—reeled in on the second play of the game.
With Rashee Rice (hamstring) sidelined again and Tyquan Thornton (ankle) remaining on IR through at least the vast majority of the regular season , the Chiefs needed someone to step up. Tight ends and running backs led the receiving box score with paltry stats, while Allen's 18 yards narrowly outpaced Xavier Worthy's three catches for 11 yards, Justin Watson's one for seven, Andrew Armstrong's one for three and Jalen Royals' zero for zero.
The Seahawks' defense is excellent, but those are not the stat lines of a functional unit.
Rice is the Chiefs' most reliable wide receiver, while Thornton was the most explosive. Worthy's role is murky, as his blazing 40-yard dash speed doesn't quite seem to translate to game speed, and much of his potential remains theoretical. Royals and Armstrong may have roles as "dirty work" receivers, but the Chiefs still need to find significantly more firepower in the passing game.
As disappointing as Kenneth Walker's 14-carry, 36-yard performance was, there's no reason for his underwhelming stat line to overshadow his impact on the Chiefs' offense or what can be expected of him going forward.
With O-line uncertainty and the aforementioned woes in the passing game, the Seahawks knew what we all knew: the Chiefs' best chance for offensive success (and explosive plays) came with Walker, so the Seattle D played accordingly. While the star running back has shown that he can jump-start the Chiefs' offense against middling opponents, it's too much to ask for him (or any individual player) to thrive as the focal point of an otherwise-struggling unit against an excellent defense.

title: After Flopping vs. Seahawks, Patrick Mahomes Knows Chiefs' Offense Must Bounce Back
full_text:
No matter how you slice it or what you chalk it up to, there's absolutely no denying that the Kansas City Chiefs' offense did nothing short of flop against the Seattle Seahawks.
Add in that KC came into Week 7 with an undefeated record and had a chance to extend that streak on Sunday Night Football , and you get an even bigger disappointment in terms of performance.
From opening kickoff until the final whistle, head coach Mike MacDonald and his Seahawks defense completely bottled up a Chiefs offense that rolled into the evening as one of football's best per-play, per-drive and per-game units. There's tons of blame to go around, although it's no surprise that the team's best player spent the first moments after the 20-3 loss reflecting.
Quarterback Patrick Mahomes didn't sugarcoat Sunday's shortcoming, but he knows it's time to get right back to work and right some wrongs.
"You got your tail kicked," Mahomes said. "Didn't execute offensively, especially around that midfield area. Kept us away from a lot of points, or at least enough points to be competitive. But it's stuff you've got to learn from. That's obviously a really good defense, and we didn't execute at a high enough level to have success."
By Mahomes' normal standards, he delivered a terrible showing at Lumen Field. On 38 plays, per RBSDM , he averaged -0.13 EPA and had a -9.8% completion rate over expected. Over his last three contests, No. 15 has completed just 61.3% of his passes with an 81.0 passer rating, two touchdowns, two interceptions and an average of 220.7 passing yards each week.
It didn't really matter what the situation was, either. On early-down passes, Mahomes led Kansas City to -0.08 EPA/play (25th percentile) compared to -0.21 (37th percentile) on late-down passing plays. Ahead of Monday's Week 7 finale between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles, the two-time MVP is 14th among all quarterbacks in adjusted EPA/play (0.139) but is just 25th out of 35 players with 50-plus plays in the same metric (0.023) in Weeks 4-7.
The Chiefs are the only NFL team in the Super Bowl era to have a game with: no 10+ yard rushes no 20+ yard passes no red-zone drives no touchdowns multiple missed field goals
Has pressure factored into Mahomes' lackluster play? Outsiders would argue yes; he thinks on Sunday it was more so him not setting the right tone from the start.
"Obviously a little bit, but I thought especially early in the game, I thought my feet were kind of getting me into trouble where I could have maybe sat in the pocket and made some of the throws down the field," Mahomes said. "I got better a little bit later in the game. But at the same time, when you play a team like that, you can't let them get ahead and get into a game they want to play. Obviously they've had a lot of success doing that, and so [we've] got to be better starting faster — especially with me — and then try to do better throughout the entire game."
According to TruMedia , Kansas City has allowed the sixth-lowest pressure rate on the year at 31.4%. In Weeks 4-7, though, that's 19th at 37.6%. The club is actually being blitzed at a lower per-dropback share (22.8% versus 24.2%) in that sample, so it's a reflection of poor tackle play through and through. Jaylon Moore missing Week 7 and Josh Simmons missing all season hasn't helped.
As currently constructed, the Chiefs' passing attack simply isn't dynamic enough. It owns football's third-lowest average in yards to the sticks on throws (-2.6), and that's down to -4.5 yards in the last two weeks. Injuries can again be at least partially credited here, as Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ) is on injured reserve and Rashee Rice ( hamstring ) hasn't played in weeks.
At the end of the day, not everything falls on Mahomes. He can only put his Superman cape on so frequently, and it's impossible to do others' jobs for them. With that said, he undoubtedly could be playing better, which might just in turn raise the floor of a suddenly struggling offense.
Whether he can do so, fair or unfair, will determine whether Sunday was a blip on the radar or a reason to slam the panic button.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From the Chiefs’ 20-3 Loss to the Seattle Seahawks
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night in Seattle, and it wasn't close.
The 20-3 final score told the story of a night when the Chiefs struggled in all three phases against a Seahawks team that reminded the country exactly why they held the Lombardi Trophy eight months ago.
Seattle came in at 3-3 and struggled on offense, but their play felt much more dominant and urgent than Kansas City's. The Chiefs were outplayed from start to finish, and the winners column is notably short this week.
Here is the full breakdown.
If there was one moment Sunday night when it felt like the Chiefs might have something going, it came with seconds left in the first half. Seattle led 10-0 and lined up on a second-and-goal from the three, with the ball set to return to them to open the third quarter. A 17-0 halftime deficit would almost certainly have been insurmountable.
Instead, Sam Darnold targeted Rashid Shaheed, and Nohl Williams jumped the route, picked it off, and took it 65 yards the other way. His only mistake was not finding the end zone, which loomed large when Butker missed the ensuing field goal as time expired.
It was Williams's first career interception, notable for a corner known as a ball-hawk coming out of California. He finished the night as the Chiefs’ best defender by a wide margin, recording double-digit tackles, including a tackle for loss, and allowing just two catches for 22 yards on three targets, according to PFF’s preliminary grades. In a game short on positives, Williams stood out.
With tight end Travis Kelce dropping two passes and Patrick Mahomes missing him badly on the opening drive, his backup led the Chiefs in receiving. Noah Gray caught all three of his targets for 44 yards, including a 19-yard reception, continuing what has quietly become a bounce-back season for the six-year veteran.
He is now just nine catches and 20 yards away from surpassing his 2025 season totals, and he has caught 12 of his 14 targets this year, making him one of Mahomes’ most reliable options in a season where reliability has been hard to come by at receiver. On a night with little to celebrate, Gray’s consistency was a welcome constant.
The Chiefs generated just nine pressures on Darnold all evening, and Karlaftis accounted for five of them. That he was the lone bright spot along the defensive line says more about how poor the rest of the group was than it does about how good he was, though he was good.
He hit Darnold twice, batted down a pass, and recorded a tackle for loss, becoming the only Chiefs pass rusher to register a quarterback hit all night. Former All-Pro Chris Jones had zero pressures on 24 pass-rush snaps, according to PFF’s preliminary grades.
The other four pressures belonged to rookie R Mason Thomas, leaving a goose egg for the rest of the group. Karlaftis has been this defense's more consistent performer all season, and Sunday was no exception, even if the unit around him was subpar.
The matchup was billed as strength-on-strength, and Seattle won it in a landslide. Kenneth Walker , who had rushed for 665 yards in his first five games and topped 100 yards in four of them, was held to 36 yards on 14 carries, both season lows by a wide margin.
He averaged just 2.6 yards per carry and forced only one missed tackle, compared to nearly double digits in every previous game this season. The Seahawks bottled him up all night, and without the run game generating momentum, the play-action attack never materialized. Mahomes finished with just 165 passing yards, his lowest output of the season.
To make the optics worse, Seahawks running back Emanuel Wilson ran for 100 yards and a touchdown on the other side of the ball, flipping the entire pre-game narrative on its head. The Chiefs will learn from this, but it was a humbling night for the NFL’s No. 1 offense.
The kicking situation has moved from a concern to legitimate alarm territory. Harrison Butker now sits at just 69 percent on field goals this season after missing two more Sunday night. The first was a 45-yarder, the shortest miss of his season, that went wide right. The second was a 58-yarder at the end of the first half that he hit straight down the middle but left short of the uprights.
The latter is the more troubling miss because it raises questions about leg strength, not just accuracy. The Chiefs never reached the red zone all night, so two made kicks likely wouldn't have changed the outcome, but 13-9 midway through the fourth quarter rather than 13-3 with two missed kicks makes the game look entirely different.
Dave Toub and the Chiefs need to determine quickly whether this is a physical issue, a mental one, or both. For a three-time Super Bowl champion and one of the most decorated kickers in NFL history, the decline has been sudden and significant.
It is hard to single out one defender on a night when Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught nine passes for 150 yards, and the Chiefs allowed 11-of-16 third-down conversions, many on third-and-medium or longer. But cornerback L’Jarius Sneed stood out for the wrong reasons, and Spagnuolo clearly noticed.
Sneed allowed all five of his targets to be caught for 83 yards in just 14 defensive snaps before being benched for Chris Roland-Wallace in the second half, when the defense performed considerably better. Smith-Njigba piled up 129 yards in the first half, with Sneed on the field for much of it.
Sneed surrendered four first downs, three of them to Smith-Njigba and one to Cooper Kupp. The fact that Darnold was actively targeting whoever Sneed was covering in a game that was never particularly close suggests the league has begun to view him as a liability in coverage, and that Roland-Wallace may need to be the answer moving forward.

title: Andy Reid Defends Chiefs Kicker Harrison Butker After Rough Night: ‘He’s Off a Bit’
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks during Sunday Night Football can hardly be attributed to one player's mistakes. It was a putrid showing in all facets of the game for KC, and Mike Macdonald's squad came out dominant from the get-go.
With that said, kicker Harrison Butker's shortcomings continued to loom large on special teams. It's become a consistent theme for the 31-year-old, who has slipped significantly from his prime and endured several rough seasons in a row. Butker's first field-goal attempt of the evening came from 58 yards out. He wasn't able to connect. There's nothing dishonorable about missing a near-60 yarder, but the kick would have split the uprights had it traveled the distance.
That raises real questions about Butker and what has been causing this prolonged slump. He's only two months removed from drilling a record-shattering 69-yard kick in the NFL Preseason that had fans believing he was back to his elite self. Is there a lapse in focus with his kicks, a mechanical issue, or even an underlying injury?
He partially redeemed himself in the third quarter, hitting his second field goal from 50+ yards this season. However, he squandered that momentum by missing a 45-yard attempt wide right with more than eight minutes remaining in the final quarter. The kick would've cut the Chiefs' deficit to seven points and given them a chance to get back into the contest, but Butker couldn't capitalize on the opportunity.
In his postgame press conference, head coach Andy Reid acknowledged that Butker hasn't been himself lately but maintained that he remains confident in his longtime placekicker. "Listen, he's been one of the most consistent kickers in football," Reid said. "He's off a bit. So, we've got to fix that."
The numbers don't necessarily back Butker's reputation as one of football's most "consistent kickers," though. As noted by Associated Press writer Josh Dubow , his 15 missed kicks since the start of the 2025 campaign lead the NFL. That many failed attempts in that span is a far cry from the consistency Reid described.
Harrison Butker's 2026 field goal percentage and ranks via @TruMediaSports : Overall: 71.4 (29th) FG40%: 100% (T-1st) FG50%: 20% (28th) XP%: 93.3% (T-24th) @KCSportsNetwork pic.twitter.com/U9Gbiy1YNg
Dating back to the 2024 season, Butker has converted exactly 50% (9-of-18) of his field-goal attempts from 50 yards or deeper. While raw leg strength has long been his trademark, the fact that he's falling multiple yards short on long-distance tries now indicates that his value is no longer what it once was.
Reid has consistently defended Butker through his recent struggles, and there was a point when it was reasonable to believe the veteran could return to form. However, he's getting closer to the point of no return, having statistically performed like a bottom-tier kicker in recent years despite his penchant for coming through in clutch moments. Kansas City isn't exactly in a position to simply cut ties with the Georgia Tech graduate, who is signed through 2028 and ranks as the NFL's fourth-highest-paid kicker. Regardless, his current production is no better than what the Chiefs could get from the average practice squad kicker. If he continues costing the team games, a serious conversation about his future will have to be had.

title: Andy Reid Clears Air on Reported Spat With Josh Simmons in Team Meeting
full_text:
In the aftermath of their most embarrassing performance of the 2026 season by an insanely wide margin, the Kansas City Chiefs have bigger fish to fry than engaging in hypotheticals regarding those who aren't even on the active 53-man roster.
Given the lack of consistency or clarity with one particular player, however, it was only a matter of time before head coach Andy Reid was asked about left tackle Josh Simmons once again.
Just days removed from Kansas City placing the 2025 first-round pick on IR , a national report from ESPN revealed that Simmons had a back-and-forth with Reid on Wednesday and was asked by him to leave a team meeting. Did that incident have anything to do with the transaction the following day?
Speaking to the media after a 20-3 loss on Sunday Night Football to the Seattle Seahawks, Reid shot down any correlation between the two.
"Listen, Sam (McDowell), I've said so much on him," Reid said of Simmons. "Rick (Burkholder) has talked about him, this and that. Things happen. That's no reason that he was put on IR. He's got a bad back. He's got to get that worked out, and that's the main thing. I'll leave it at that, and that's where we're at with it."
According to the aforementioned report, Simmons was called out for having his feet up while sitting during the meeting and told Reid it was because of an aching back and hips. Upon being directed to seek treatment if he was indeed in pain, the former Ohio State star allegedly "disrupted the meeting" and even led to quarterback Patrick Mahomes to urge Simmons to step out as well.
Burkholder, vice president of sports medicine and performance, provided a statement to lead off Thursday's media availability and described Simmons' Wednesday absence from practice as something that allowed him to "get with his people" and decide next injury-related steps. After all, the second-year man is attempting to recover from a bulging disc in his back that's bothered him since mid-August.
With the Seattle game in the books, Simmons will miss at least the club's next three contests against the Denver Broncos, New York Jets and Atlanta Falcons. Mike Garafolo of NFL Network reports that the team holds out hope for Simmons eventually hitting the ground running again with the "right attitude and healthy, ready to go" for the stretch run of the season.
Reid appears to share that same end goal. Even if it's been an awkward week on the Simmons front, the leader of the team reiterates that the focus remains solely on the back injury and subsequent recovery.

title: 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs' Ugly Week 7 Loss to Seahawks
full_text:
Before the Kansas City Chiefs even took the field in Seattle to battle the Seahawks, most figured it would be a trying night for one of football's last undefeated teams. That certainly proved to be the case in Week 7, as head coach Andy Reid's crew got throttled in prime time.
The hosts came out firing on the Sunday Night Football stage, taking advantage of the visitors' shorthanded offense and also making the most of favorable matchups on the other side of the ball. Kansas City did attempt to snap out of its funk in the second half of play, yet it never got close and wound up dropping a brutal game by a final score of 20-3.
Here are 10 instant observations and Chiefs takeaways from Week 7.
It feels like forever ago that fifth-round rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen was dazzling during the summer and becoming a fan-favorite player, but in reality, it's only been a few months. Given the injuries to wideouts Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ) and Rashee Rice ( hamstring ), the door was opened for the Cincinnati product to make an impact. After logging a pair of catches for 27 yards in Week 6, he stood out from the jump on Sunday.
On just the second play from scrimmage for Kansas City, Allen hauled in a pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes down the left sideline and gained 18 yards. It was a dead silent half for him the rest of the way, however, which raises questions about his true involvement in the offense. Is Allen a scripted player or a difference-maker?
Look, it was glaringly obvious that finding a way to slow down someone who came into Week 7 with 49 catches for 717 yards and seven touchdowns would be super difficult. Flat-out stopping the reigning Offensive Player of the Year? Forget about it... which the Chiefs seemed to do at first whistle.
Receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba wasn't fair in the opening half of play, routinely burning cornerback L'Jarius Sneed in the slot and even providing first-round rookie Mansoor Delane with two "welcome to the league" moments. He finished the first two quarters with six snags for 129 yards and a touchdown, serving as a walking nightmare for Steve Spagnuolo's defense.
That defense was downright terrible on late downs in this one; JSN was a top force in that unfolding.
It's always difficult having a nuanced dialogue about Mahomes' play. On one hand, he's held to such a high standard by many that it seems fair to point out when he doesn't meet the bar. On the other hand, he rolled into Week 7 without the aforementioned receivers and both of his starting offensive tackles.
There's room to meet in the middle. According to RBSDM , he owned an ugly mark of -0.39 EPA per play in quarters one and two. No. 15 missed plenty of throws on SNF , leaving many of them short and also putting too much mustard on one pass that got picked off. That said, constant duress made his life much more difficult.
It's impossible to consider Mahomes' shortcomings and not directly jump into the offensive line situation. In our Week 7 preview, we briefly touched on how Kansas City has typically operated a quick-game passing offense and relied on explosive rushes and play-action to help open up the occasional deep shot. With no Jaylon Moore ( and with Josh Simmons still out ), operating a functional offense seemed far more difficult than it needed to be on Sunday.
Undrafted rookie free agent Kahlil Benson whiffed on multiple occasions, and right tackle Joshua Ezeudu also had his fair share of rough moments. Sure, Reid didn't do a ton to protect his linemen and Mahomes was far from perfect, but this can't be sustained for much longer.
After he missed an extra point last week, I opened the floor for there being an active Harrison Butker problem on the Chiefs' hands. He's years removed from producing a season that lives up to his prime, and his variance from long range makes him far from the slam-dunk kicker he used to be. That trend continued into the Seahawks game.
In a vacuum, there's no shame in missing a 58-yard field goal. When Butker left his short to end the first half, though, that sent KC into the break scoreless. He redeemed himself temporarily with a 50-yard connection in the third frame, only to push a 45-yarder midway through the fourth quarter. The more the sample size grows, the worse this looks.
Speaking of the Butker miss, that opportunity was only presented due to a brilliant play on the ball by cornerback Nohl Williams on defense. He picked off quarterback Sam Darnold's pass in the end zone and returned it for 64 yards, followed by a run and timeout by the offense. Had Seattle put up seven points on that drive, it would've been far more demoralizing than facing a 10-point deficit.
With the Chiefs driving in the fourth quarter, a drop by receiver Xavier Worthy and a holding penalty on left guard Kingsley Suamataia put the offense in a second-and-20 situation. The following two plays may fade into the void over time, but rookie running back Emmett Johnson 's 12-yard catch made third down manageable. He then threw a critical block on a scramble by Mahomes for the first.
Butker wound up missing the 45-yard boot at the end of the drive, but Johnson deserves props for being a gamer when needed.
The unfortunate thing for Worthy is he just recorded seven targets and 70-plus receiving yards in back-to-back games. On the surface, he looked like he was building some significant momentum, and he even acknowledged such this week. Gifted a massive chance to be the X-factor in Week 7, however, he flopped.
It wasn't just the fourth-quarter drop, either. The former first-round pick displayed minimal or no awareness on multiple plays, including one where he ran out of bounds and another in which he failed to throw a block on a reception by running back Kenneth Walker. The latter play could've been the most explosive of the night. Unless he's getting the ball in space and given some runway, Worthy just isn't a huge impact piece.
Anyone hoping for the third-year man to blossom into a WR1 can officially call it. They can likely sell stock on him being a high-end WR2, too, even in KC.
Through five games, Walker had fully justified the Chiefs' investment in him and then some. He's been the team's best player to this point and almost singlehandedly transformed the offense from a player standpoint, leading the sport in a variety of statistics on the ground. Citing a lackluster showing in the box score is in no way an indictment on him — it's more of a praise of the home team.
Walker finished Sunday Night Football with 14 carries for a measly 36 yards, throwing him off pace and also ignoring just how hard he had to work for that output. Week 7 wasn't a talent problem for the star halfback, as just about anyone would've failed to thrive in these conditions.
At the end of the day, the Chiefs were never going to run the table, even if fully healthy. Considering the circumstances of a lack of health on offense and facing a Super Bowl-caliber team, it shouldn't be a complete and utter shock that the Seahawks looked good. It is a surprise that the Kansas City offense looked so inept.
It's this writer's view that only a handful of teams truly matter at the moment. The Chiefs are still one of them and had to face off against a member of that group on the road in prime time. The sky isn't falling in the slightest, although this is a wake-up call for many.

title: Complete Chiefs Inactives for Week 7 vs. Seahawks: Jaylon Moore & Others Sitting Out SNF
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs return to prime time in Week 7, this time for an interconference tilt on the road against the reigning Super Bowl champions. The Seattle Seahawks await on Sunday Night Football , with Mike Macdonald's 3-3 club looking to gain some ground in the NFC West standings and defend home turf.
Neither team rolls into this one fully healthy, which is to be expected at this point in a grueling season. The hosts had multiple players carrying questionable designations entering the weekend, whereas the visitors ruled out a pair of key offensive starters while also shuffling the roster quite a bit.
With that in mind, here's who's inactive for Kansas City and Seattle in Sunday's matchup.
Here are the Chiefs’ inactives for tonight’s game against the Seahawks: WR Rashee Rice OT Jaylon Moore QB Garrett Nussmeier DB Jadon Canady FB Ben VanSumeren DE Jack Pyburn
Earlier this week, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid revealed that wide receiver Rashee Rice and right tackle Jaylon Moore wouldn't be suiting up on Sunday. Rice still hasn't returned to practice since sustaining a hamstring injury in Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders, and Moore got knocked out of Week 6's win over the Los Angeles Chargers and has been in concussion protocol ever since. Joshua Ezeudu steps in for Moore at right tackle.
Cornerback L'Jarius Sneed, who didn't originally travel with the team on Saturday due to a personal issue before joining everyone on Sunday, is active. Sneed (knee) was previously questionable to play in Week 7 after being limited in practice all week.
On Saturday, the club placed second-year running back Brashard Smith on injured reserve with a hamstring issue. Undrafted rookie free agent Jadyn Ott was signed to the 53-man roster to take his spot.
At the same time, wide receiver Justin Watson was elevated from the practice squad and linebacker Cooper McDonald came off IR and is set to play for the first time since Week 1 .
Left tackle Josh Simmons doesn't appear on Sunday's inactives because he's now on IR. Earlier on Sunday, a report shed light on the day leading up to him eventually being placed on the list, including being told to leave a team meeting by Reid and quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Tonight’s @Seahawks inactives; QB Drew Lock will serve as the emergency 3rd quarterback. pic.twitter.com/OzEKzer0eH
After being non-participants in practice on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday, the Seahawks ruled linebackers Chazz Surratt (calf) and Drake Thomas (ankle) out. Five other players were questionable, with four being on the defensive side of the ball. title: Chargers' Ladd McConkey Could Emerge as Trade Target for AFC Contender
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have exercised a plan to stand pat and hold off trade calls despite being 0-6. They will play two more games before the November tenth trade deadline and the calls will not stop anytime soon and if they fall to 0-8, the front office will have serious decisions to make.
It is no surprise that the Chargers would be receiving trade calls on their best players who may be on expiring deals and not part of the immediate or future plans. Trade rumors have been ongoing since the Chargers started 0-3 and will continue as they look like the walking dead on offense.
Veteran edge rusher Khalil Mack is the most mentioned named amongst NFL insiders and trade rumors circulating the NFL landscape. NFL insider Tomy Pelissero floated ten potential Chargers who could be moved at the deadline, but it appears Mack and running back Kimani Vidal are the only names that have been recurring in discussions.
It is no surprise that other players, including the Chargers' best, are now being floated in trade discussions on sports shows and media segments around NFL-focused media platforms. Given the Chargers' direction and current position to land the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft it would not be a shock if teams tried to inquire about seemingly off-limits players.
One Chargers player sure to be floated as a potential trade target is Ladd McConkey. This is especially clear with teams like the Pittsburgh Steelers out there as possible buyers and McConkey would be a good fit and target for Aaron Rodgers' style.
To be clear, it's all speculation on whether the Steelers would reach out to the Chargers to engage in any form regarding McConkey’s availability. If the Steelers front office does try to reach out to Chargers general manager Joe Hortiz regarding the availability of Ladd McConkey, Hortiz should laugh and hang up the phone.
It is clear, the Chargers offense has been a train wreck through the first six weeks of the season. However, Ladd McConkey, who is not healthy right now, has been the only functional target for Justin Herbert when he has been on the field. McConkey is in year three of his rookie contract and has been a reliable target for Justin Herbert since he entered the NFL, he is not a player that should be traded.
There may come a day where the Chargers entertain trade offers from McConkey but it will not be in the middle of this season. If the Steelers are looking for wide receiver help, they will likely look elsewhere.

title: Chargers Miss Out on Quenton Nelson, But Draft Favorite Waiver Target Emerges
full_text:
It has been buzzing for a few weeks that the Los Angeles Chargers could be in contention for the All-Pro guard, Quenton Nelson . Even with the team at 0-6, they have reported to the media the belief in their squad giving reason for the belief they could actually make an offer for the Colts legend.
As of today, Oct. 27, that was not true. The Chargers were reportedly not one of the teams interested in Nelson, with the Seattle Seahawks being the winners of the sweepstakes, giving up a fair price of a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
This does not mean that the saga is over. The Chargers could very well look into the Seahawks player who was released in the corresponding move.
Christian Haynes is a 26-year-old offensive guard who was drafted in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft with the 83rd overall pick. Since being drafted, Haynes has started five games for the Hawks, all of those games coming this season.
His 210 offensive snaps of playing time thus far have earned him a 59.7 overall PFF grade, 43rd among 74 qualified offensive guards. His PFF pass-blocking grade of 46.0 ranked 62nd among 74 qualified offensive guards. His run-blocking grade is 62.5, ranking 33rd among the same 74 qualified candidates.
Christian Haynes (RG #64) I did not know he had this in his bag #seahawks pic.twitter.com/FLQfOd4hYW
For reference, Chargers starting right guard Cole Strange , on 387 snaps, which is nearly double Haynes, ranks 67th in overall PFF grade, 69th in pass blocking and 50th in run blocking. Haynes is better in every PFF category.
Furthermore, Haynes has allowed 11 total pressures in pass protection. That total included one sack and three hits allowed to opposing pass rushers. He was flagged for zero penalties over the course of the season.
Strange has allowed one more pressure, two fewer hits and the same number of sacks. He has also been penalized five times with the Bolts. Even if Haynes is only marginally better than Strange, an improvement is still an improvement.
Overall, it is very fitting for the 0-6 team led by Joe Hortiz to go bargain-bin shopping on the second-hand market. Haynes has been released by the Seahawks, making him available on the waiver wire. The Chargers are the worst team in the NFL, with the only week they have not lost being their bye week.
After acquiring All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson, the Seahawks waived guard Christian Haynes to make room on their 53-man roster.
This means the Bolts get the first selection on the waiver wire. If you are going to be the worst team in the NFL, you might as well take advantage of the perks that come with it.

title: Desperate Patriots Could Help Chargers Offload Quentin Johnston, More at NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
When thinking about NFL trade partners for the Los Angeles Chargers , the usual suspects come up.
For example, good luck ducking chatter about the Chargers sending Khalil Mack to the Chicago Bears .
And the Chargers could always go after Brian Thomas of the Jacksonville Jaguars , if they end up wanting to be buyers at the deadline while aiming at finding pieces that help create a long-term fix.
Most likely, though, the 0-6 Chargers limping out of the bye have eyes on acting as big sellers at the NFL trade deadline. That’s especially the case for Mack, who they should do right by as his career winds down.
And it should be the case for guys with any sort of value who might not be around after this season. Quentin Johnston is one name who comes to mind in this category.
Elsewhere in the AFC, the New England Patriots might be able to help the Chargers out.
Those mentioned Patriots are 4-3 in the AFC East, just behind the 5-1 Buffalo Bills. They’re 2-0 in division play, so they’re right there in the hunt.
Mike Vrabel and Co., too, are desperate to prove this year isn’t a bust. The Chargers happen to roster some very Patriots-like players, too.
That’s something recently brought up by Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer, who mentions Mack and Johnston as obvious Patriots fits.
“I think stylistically he would really fit Mike Vrabel as a bigger, more rugged edge,” Breer said, according to Michael Hurley of NBC Sports Boston. “Quentin Johnston's another player that you could look at, somebody that may not have a future in Los Angeles."
Mack signed another one-year deal with the Chargers this past offseason after weighing retirement. Shipping him to a possible contender would make plenty of sense, even if the return wouldn’t be that big now.
When it comes to Johnston, the former first-round pick had the team pick up his fifth-year option. The Chargers saw a deal, but Johnston’s limitations as a route-runner and drop issues have popped up again. Through five appearances, he’s third on the Chargers in receiving with just eight catches on 21 targets.
Even if the Chargers don’t keep rolling with Mike McDaniel’s system for the rest of the year or even into 2027, it wouldn’t make sense to keep Johnston. At this point, the non-Ladd McConkey aspects of the depth chart probably need thrown out, especially if they remain on track for Jeremiah Smith at No. 1 overall in next year’s draft.
For the Chargers, a team like the Patriots is a really good example of a franchise worth calling often over the next few weeks, even if it’s just used as a leverage play against other buys while trying to find the best value possible at the deadline while selling.

title: Ranking Chargers' Top NFL Trade Deadline Targets From Realistic to Delusional
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-6 and the front office's plan to stand pat will be put to the test before the November 10th trade deadline. The Chargers have no business being buyers at the trade deadline with the season essentially lost and the injury list substantial . However, could they convince themselves to make moves for the future? Potentially, but at what cost?
NFL insiders such as Jordan Schultz have been adamant that he believes the trade market will be very active this year. Historically, the NFL trade deadline has been an overhyped affair with few trades actually taking place. That historic trend has started to shift to move activity on the trade market in recent years. If the Chargers for some reason want in on the action, here are some trade targets they could pursue if they want to get wild.
Former first-round pick Brian Thomas Jr is in his third year in the NFL and has not found a home with Liam Coen's offense since Coen's arrival in Jacksonville. After posting a 1,200-yard season as a rookie in 2024, Thomas has seen his target share decline almost weekly.
Thomas is off to a very slow start in 2026 despite the Jaguars winning and throwing the ball all over the field with Trevor Lawrence. Thomas has only nine receptions on the year for 105 yards and could clearly benefit from a change of scenery. However, the Jaguars are winning and have eyes on contending.
Jacksonville will not part with one of their starters while he is on a rookie contract simply because he hasn't fit into the offense as well as they hoped. Wide receiver depth is needed in the NFL. If they were losing, this would be a different story.
Is it possible the Jaguars would entertain the right offer? Sure, but because of his production or lack thereof, his value is at an all-time low. Chargers wide receiver Quentin Johnston has been more productive than Thomas this season.
For the Jaguars to move off of him midseason as they are trying to reach the playoffs and contend they would have to get undeniable draft compensation. Considering the going rate for a struggling former 2024 first-round wide receiver is a second-round pick, Thomas would like cost the Chargers their third-round pick. I doubt the Jaguars will move Thomas midseason but NFL insider Adam Schefter did mention Thomas as a name to watch before the deadline but this feels more like an offseason move.
Some names to watch ahead of the NFL’s Nov. 10 trade deadline: pic.twitter.com/6THEK7IFqT
Cowboys owner Jerry Jones loves to wheel and deal. The Cowboys are in a relatively weak division this season with the Giants surprisingly in first place so moving off of their swing guard is not in their best interest for this season with a winnable division in front of them.
However, the Cowboys have been experiencing some injuries to the depth in their defensive back and linebacker rooms and the Chargers have been starting rookies all over their offensive line but have depth at both safety and linebacker. Jones has already shown a willingness to trade to address the defense, could there be a deal to reunite former Oregon teammates TJ Bass and Justin Herbert?
More than likely any potential trade would be a player for player swap plus draft pick. Bass is scheduled to be a unrestricted free agent in the coming offseason and the Chargers could take the rest of the year to gauge whether Bass would be a good fit moving forward while trying to keep quarterback Justin Herbert standing long enough to see 2027 in one piece.
The Colts have signaled they are open for business by trading away All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson. Keenan Allen was a late signing for the Colts and he has slowly become a reliable receiving target with Alec Pierce done for the season. The Colts have other wide receivers that could fill in if Allen was no longer there.
It is no secret that Justin Herbert trusts Keenan Allen. Ladd McConkey has been injured all season and with Herbert completely out of rhythm in Mike McDaniel's offense, it may be worth bringing Allen back to help give Herbert any semblance of confidence. Acquiring Allen would not cost much given his circumstances, potentially a late-round swap. It may be worth it to help Herbert get back on track and head to 2027 with some positive momentum.

title: Chargers Should Aggressively Take Advantage of the Endless Bears Trade Rumors
full_text:
Every public suggestion around the Los Angeles Chargers says Jim Harbaugh, Joe Hortiz and the organization out West won’t host a fire sale at the NFL trade deadline .
It’s not a shocking public stance right now. It also won’t be shocking when actions speak louder than words and they end up selling big. Harbaugh’s Chargers are the worst team in football at 0-6 and top the NFL draft order for good reason .
In related news, every public suggestion hints that the Chicago Bears are about to be big buyers at the upcoming NFL trade deadline.
This is related for one simple link between the teams: A guy named Khalil Mack.
For those out of the loop, the Bears are 5-2 and just behind the 6-0 Minnesota Vikings in the NFC North. The need for more pass-rushers and other all-in moves is obvious.
Among the many bits of reporting, Jordan Schultz appeared on The Pivot and linked the Bears and 49ers to Mack.
“Two teams I’m watching very closely, the 49ers and Bears,” Schultz said. “I’ve heard both teams connected to several defensive players, including rushers Josh Sweat, Khalil Mack and also DeForest Buckner…I’d be shocked if they don’t make a move before the deadline.”
Chargers fans don’t need to be told that Mack going to the Bears would be a reunion. In the process, the Chargers would do right by him by letting him go contend for a title.
Mack, after all, pondered retirement before coming back to the Chargers for at least one more year on an $18 million contract. He’s still playing at a high level for a defense that is slowly morphing into form after an adjustment period since the arrival of new coordinator Chris O’Leary.
In theory, the Chargers could sweeten the pot on a trade and up the return a bit by offering to absorb some of Mack’s remaining money on the one-year deal. But the overall return will be minimal. Even multiple teams interested in Mack won’t drive up the value that much.
The silver lining on a Mack trade, beyond just doing right by him, means even more developmental reps for the likes of Tuli Tuipulotu and first-round pick Akheem Mesidor.
And at this point, 0-6 is 0-6. A few wins won’t change this soon-to-be-selling outlook for the Chargers. But it’s especially true with Mack, as there’s no real reason to keep him around on a sinking ship after what he’s done for the franchise. Shipping him out to a franchise he’s familiar with and giving him a shot at a title is a no-brainer, especially with the rumors stressing just how active the Bears want to be at the deadline.

title: The Perfect Trade Target for the Chargers May Have Just Become Available
full_text:
Brian Thomas Jr. is a name worth keeping an eye on as the NFL trade deadline approaches, and the Chargers could have a legitimate opportunity to add a receiver who still has plenty of potential.
Between his place in the offense, the receivers competing for targets and the struggles that have followed an incredible rookie campaign, Thomas has become a fascinating trade candidate.
According to NFL insider Adam Schefter , Thomas Jr. is a name to watch out for. Also stating that the Jags “might be willing to listen” to offers.
It is easy to forget just how impressive Thomas looked as a rookie. He finished the 2024 season with 1,282 receiving yards and 10 touchdowns. Establishing himself as one of the most exciting young receivers in the league. He had the speed to get behind defensive backs, the length to make difficult catches and the ability to turn a routine pass into a game-changing play.
The problem is that the production has not continued at that level. His numbers fell considerably in 2025, and his involvement has become even more limited this season. The recent decision to keep him on the sideline for an entire second half only added to the uncertainty surrounding his future.
But the bigger question is whether Thomas is in the right situation to get the most out of his abilities.
Liam Coen’s offense has evolved around the players who are producing consistently, and Thomas has struggled to take advantage of his opportunities. His issues with drops and consistency cannot simply be blamed on the scheme. At the same time, an offense that has found other reliable options has less reason to keep forcing targets toward a receiver who is not making the most of them.
Jakobi Meyers and Parker Washington have earned important roles, while rookie Josh Cameron has also started to receive more opportunities. Travis Hunter adds another layer to the receiving picture as well. With more competition for snaps and targets, Thomas no longer has the same clear path to opportunities that he once did.
That is what makes a potential trade interesting. A change of scenery would not automatically fix his problems, but it could give him a chance to rebuild his confidence and find a role better suited to his strengths. Herbert would be an intriguing quarterback for that process. His arm strength and willingness to attack downfield could allow Thomas to get back to doing what made him such a dangerous receiver in the first place. The Chargers would not need to reinvent the player. They would need to help him become a more consistent version of himself.
The biggest question is what the Chargers would have to give up to make this happen.
Thomas was a first-round pick for a reason, and his rookie season is still a reminder of the ceiling he possesses. However, teams cannot ignore what has happened since then. His declining production and recent reduction in playing time should affect his trade value, particularly when there is no guarantee that his early-career success will return.
I would be interested in exploring a deal built around a Day 2 or conditional draft pick, depending on what the front office learns about his development and the asking price. Giving up a premium selection without understanding the reasons behind his struggles would be a gamble.
Landing him for a more manageable price, on the other hand, could make the risk worthwhile.
There is also the financial side of the decision. The Chargers would need to evaluate his contract, future commitments and how a potential acquisition fits into their longer-term plans. Adding another receiver is only worthwhile if it does not prevent the team from addressing other needs. Still, the potential reward is hard to overlook. Thomas has already demonstrated that he can produce at an elite level, and he is young enough that a turnaround could benefit a team for years rather than just a few weeks.
The Bolts need to be confident that the problems are correctable and that the price makes sense. But if those conditions are met, this is a conversation worth having. Thomas might not be the guaranteed solution some fans are looking for, but he could represent an opportunity to add legitimate upside to Herbert’s supporting cast without paying the price normally associated with a receiver coming off a breakout season.

title: A Wyatt Teller Trade Clearly Makes Sense for the Chargers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have spent years trying to put the right pieces around Justin Herbert. Herbert has shown he can make plays against just about any defense in the league, but even the best quarterbacks are going to have a difficult time when the pocket constantly collapses around them.
That is why a potential trade for Wyatt Teller is worth taking seriously.
The biggest reason this potential trade makes sense is pretty simple. Teller is having a clear down year with the Texans, and the Bolts have a crucial need at the offensive line position.
There is only so much a quarterback can do when he does not have enough time to operate.
The Chargers need to make sure their offensive line is capable of holding up against the best defensive fronts in football. That becomes especially important when facing teams that can generate pressure with their front four and force the quarterback to make quick decisions. Against those defenses, even a small weakness along the interior can become a major problem.
That is where Teller could potentially fit in. As a guard, he would give them another experienced option in the middle of the offensive line. His physical style of play and years of NFL experience make him a name worth evaluating. Another benefit would be the potential impact on the running game. Interior offensive linemen play a major role in creating running lanes. Which could be more of a dependable presence at guard. Establishing that balance would take some pressure off Herbert and give the offense more ways to attack opposing defenses.
Teller lost his starting position early this year after siging a two-year deal with Houston. Things have not worked the way both parties wanted it too, so a trade would make complete sense.
The Chargers also have to think about depth. Injuries are part of the game, and a team can quickly find itself in trouble when it does not have enough reliable options up front. Adding an experienced lineman could give the coaching staff more flexibility over the course of a long season. There is a financial side to consider as well. The Bolts should not give up valuable draft capital or take on an unreasonable contract just to make a move. If the Texans are willing to negotiate a deal that makes sense for both teams, however, the conversation becomes much more interesting.
They do not need to make a splash just for the sake of making one. They need to make smart decisions that improve the roster where it matters most. If Teller can help strengthen the offensive line, give Justin Herbert more time and making the offense more balanced. Bringing him aboard could be a move that makes a lot of sense.
