title: Why the Raiders Missed Out on Opportunity to Improve Future of Roster
full_text:
Just a month ago, we were talking about the Las Vegas Raiders as a legitimate playoff contender.
Fast forward to the present day, and the Raiders have had a rude awakening, losing four consecutive games and falling to 3-4 in the blink of an eye. Because Las Vegas was off to such a hot start in the first month of the season, it was featured in discussions of a team potentially being a buyer at the trade deadline. Now, with the current losing streak, the Raiders could be sellers at the deadline . That being said, it doesn't mean Las Vegas shouldn't consider acquiring a player for now and the future.
On Tuesday, the Indianapolis Colts traded eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Based on that information, here's why it was a missed opportunity for general manager John Spytek to improve the offensive line .
Yes, the Raiders' draft picks will be much higher on the board than Seattle's, but giving up a Day 2 2027 pick and a Day 3 2028 pick is not expensive at all for one of the best guards in the league. Yes, Las Vegas is trending toward not competing this season, but that doesn't disqualify them from making moves in the near future.
Let's say the front office and coaching staff still believe this team is playing for something this season; then vastly improving the offensive line, especially the interior, isn't the worst idea. Pairing Nelson with Tyler Linderbaum would be an excellent start to rebuilding the interior of the offensive line. Now, Spytek may really value picks in this upcoming draft, especially if the Raiders are picking near the top of each round. However, it never hurts to negotiate and assess the market.
As we've seen countless times over the years, without a formidable offensive line, it's virtually impossible to operate cohesively as an offense. At times, we’ve seen that with Las Vegas, as their run game has been inept due to struggles up front.
It's important to note that Nelson is in the final year of his contract and is a pending free agent. So, you may be asking, 'Why would the Raiders, who are a rebuilding team, trade for a 30-year-old guard on an expiring contract?' It's certainly a fair question, but as mentioned earlier, this move wouldn't be just about this season. Las Vegas is trying to set the foundation for the future .
It would be an interesting situation for the Raiders' front office to navigate, as Linderbaum is already the highest-paid center in the league. Meanwhile, Nelson's current contract is valued at $20 million annually, and he would likely want more money than Peter Skoronski and Tyler Smith, who are each earning at least $24 million per year. So again, it may be perplexing to think why Las Vegas would invest that much money in the interior of the offensive line. Quite simple: it’s feasible.
The Raiders aren't paying substantial money to several of their top, future pieces. Ashton Jeanty and Brock Bowers are still on their rookie contracts. Meanwhile, Mendoza won't be making significant money for the foreseeable future. This is the time to overspend a little and ensure the future franchise quarterback has as many resources as possible to succeed.
Throughout the offseason, the Raiders' ownership, Spytek, and head coach Klint Kubiak have preached the plan to build and develop this team patiently. But if an opportunity presents itself to acquire high-end players who can help the team now and in the future at a relatively affordable price, those situations should always be considered.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Raiders GM John Spytek Surprises With Bold Roster Move
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—Say whatever you like about the Las Vegas Raiders (3-4) GM John Spytek, but you can’t avoid using the word bold.
Despite taking the high road and taking all the blame for the team’s collapse in 2025 , for the record, absolutely none of the responsibility for the collapse had to do with him; ever since his voice grew louder and he took the wheel late last season, he has been superb.
There have been some questions, prematurely in some cases, in this reporter’s opinion, about the 2025 NFL Draft class, but he has been bold and aggressive.
I first learned of him when he interned with the Detroit Lions in 2004, when Lions executives gave him the nickname “The Whiz Kid” because of his analytical nature.
Spytek bristled at my use of analytical, but the reality is that he leaves no stone unturned, like his head coach, Klint Kubiak, and owner, Tom Brady. We talked about that earlier this year when he selected Klint Kubiak as head coach.
“I would not say that I am analytical, just thorough and a lot of depth. You’re always looking for an edge. Your ability to process, maintain, and use a lot of information is huge at my job, or quarterback, or a head coach. It was cool to see the depths that Klint would go, just like Tom (Brady) would go to as a player."
"Like what is required, and how much you can process and maintain, and use. We could throw a book at a player or coach, if they can’t. It’s really about what they can use and kind of value in that process, kind of value in that process to help bring it to life.”
Spytek announced today that he was activating WR Dont’e Thornton, Jr. (DTJ) from injured reserve back to the 53-man roster.
Spytek selected DTJ in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, 108th overall. The 6’5” wideout weighs 205 pounds and runs a blazing 4.3 forty-yard dash.
Physically and athletically, he looks like a prototypical elite NFL WR. Looks can be deceiving.
He came to the Raiders during the mini-camp and OTA portion of the 2025 offseason looking like the steal of the NFL Draft. He made enormous plays and shone.
On August 14, 2025, everything changed. DTJ literally disappeared once the San Francisco 49ers arrived in Henderson. The great plays and the constant showing up, day after day, just stopped.
Teammates wondered what happened, and early in the season, even some on the staff did, too. The once-promising rookie couldn’t seem to, in the words of one coach no longer with the team, “Get any traction.”
In this reporter’s opinion, and in the view of others around the organization, nothing has changed.
A wonderful young man, I have stated many times, no one was rooting against him, just the opposite, but nothing was popping.
Just last Friday, on a team desperate for WR help, Kubiak was asked about DTJ, and his answer was interesting. “He’s making big progress. He’s done a lot of good things in practice. Still working back into getting his football legs back after missing a lot of time. But I’ve been really pleased with his effort, with his detail. He’s close.”
In deciding to elevate DTJ to the 53-man roster, Spytek let Las Vegas native DT Jonah Laulu go. Laulu was inactive against the Chiefs and the Rams, and with his former defensive line coach now the defensive coordinator, that is telling.
DTJ played in 15 games last year, caught 10 passes, and scored no touchdowns.
Laulu has started 22 games for the Raiders, including seven during his rookie year in 2024 and 15 last year. His production this year has been, at best, suspect.
Many, including me, thought DTJ might not make the initial 53-man roster, which he did, and I certainly thought that, with Jack Bech presumably coming back this week, DTJ’s days were either numbered or he was heading to the IR for the remainder of the season.
The reality is that if you trust Spytek (and he has earned it) or Kubiak (and he has earned it), they believe in DTJ at least for now, and the sophomore WR needs to seize the moment of public endorsement and turn things around.
In the NFL, a player's third year is called the money year. In that belief, DTJ is far too young to give up on, and Spytek and Kubiak are again making the statement we told you before the season.
This is a youth-movement Raiders rebuild, and keeping DTJ in the fold once again shows that while Laulu was in the money year and they clearly didn’t like what he offered comparatively, they value DTJ more.
The analytical-excuse me, “thorough” John Spytek yet again made a bold move. You can’t fault him for that, and in a year when this team isn’t going to a Super Bowl, trusting WR coach Zach Azzanni and Kubiak to develop DTJ and finding out whether he can turn it around is the correct move.
If the Raiders move on from DTJ at some point, that won’t be the story. The story will be that Spytek continues to do what he has since last December: methodically lead the franchise in a disciplined way, trust the process, and not cut corners.
No one would have complained or been shocked if Spytek cut DTJ or at least relegated him to the IR for the rest of the season. Unless he signed with the Chiefs and the young man with all of the intangibles became great.
The story isn’t whether or not DTJ turns out to be great; it is that in the early stages of a rebuild, a franchise that was once known as the team with a lack of patience who constantly let players go to thrive elsewhere, showed discipline and a commitment to the plan.
Or as they say in these parts, “Committed to Excellence.”
Who knows if DTJ will be excellent, but discipline and commitment to a proven plan clearly exemplify “Commitment to Excellence.”
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: The Perfect Trade Target for Raiders If They Become Available
full_text:
Even after wholesale changes to its coaching staff and roster, the Las Vegas Raiders are still struggling with several of the same things that have plagued them in recent seasons. This is to be expected, as the Raiders are in the early stages of rebuilding their roster.
For as much progress as the Raiders made on their roster this offseason, they have equally as much work to do moving forward. The season's first seven games have solidified the offensive line as Las Vegas' most significant issue at the midway point of the season.
The Raiders' offensive line should undoubtedly be the front office's top priority this offseason. Adding Tyler Linderbaum was a start. However, there are no guarantees for any player on the unit beyond that, except possibly DJ Glaze, who has proven dependable for multiple seasons.
Still, after their Week 7 loss, it's no secret that the Raiders don't have a line that can consistently protect a quarterback who cannot move well in the pocket. Las Vegas has to switch its offensive linemen or its quarterback, and Klint Kubiak refuses to choose the latter .
Las Vegas' issues are wide-ranging, but largely center on an inefficient offense after they hired Kubiak for his offensive prowess. Following their loss to the Los Angeles Rams, Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins shared his thoughts on the loss and what went wrong for his unit.
"I don't know that we've – We didn't finish drives well enough I think. I would think if you go back and look at the wins, we probably were a little better in the red zone or in finishing drives coming away with six points instead of three. Or in this case today, we got down coming to zero, going for it on fourth down. So that probably is one of the differences is just those four point moments in the game where you could go from a field goal to touchdown,” Cousins said after the game.
Las Vegas has more than a few shortcomings on its roster. Plenty of blame to go around for their four-game losing streak. Still, the Raiders' offensive issues stem from their offensive line. The Raiders have little they can do to help the unit, as any available options likely wouldn't suffice.
However, the trade deadline is approaching and, in theory, Las Vegas could swing a trade to help its offensive line. Given that it would require the Raiders to trade away a player or draft capital, I don't think they will make a trade. If they do, it will not be a big one.
Kubiak knows the answers the Raiders are looking for are within the building. The coaching staff will have to get the most out of the revamped roster they have been given. Sure, the roster needs more, but it started this season with the most it has had in years; a trade is unlikely.
Las Vegas' offensive line struggles have affected the unit on the ground and through the air. The Raiders have been one of the worst rushing teams in the league for the fourth consecutive season. Cousins' immobility has only made the unit's issues worse while pass-blocking.
"Well, I think the number one thing guys is when teams can play that much man against you it's because we're not a threat running the football right now. So, we’ve got to make teams more –we got to be more of a well-rounded offensive football club right now. And again, those are things that we're working on," Kubiak said.
"But when you are down multiple scores, it is not a running game, and we've been giving up way too many points right now to put ourselves in position to be balanced in the fourth quarter, to be balanced in the third quarter. So, I like the strides that our guys have made in practice. I've seen it in the games, I've seen how our runners are breaking tackles. I do like that, but we've got to call runs and be in competitive games in the second half."
There are a few offensive guards the Raiders could trade for, but I personally think it would be unrealistic for them to pull it off, and if they were to make a trade, it would need to be worth their time. Players such as Wyatt Teller and Landon Dickerson would be solid options.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Keys Raiders Couldn't Execute in Loss to Rams
full_text:
It's been 30 days since the Las Vegas Raiders last won, as they lost their fourth consecutive game on Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams.
Los Angeles defeated Las Vegas 35-21, but that score doesn't accurately depict the game. This game wasn't that close, and that's saying something, as it was still a 14-point loss. At one point, the Rams led 28-3. This was a complete mismatch , even with Los Angeles operating in less-than-ideal circumstances. Before we reveal too much, here are three things I got wrong in this matchup.
We've essentially covered this in the excerpt above. However, there's context for why I believed the Raiders would win this game . Considering Davante Adams, Trent McDuffie, Kobie Turner, Poona Ford, and Myles Garrett were all out, I was shocked by how dominant they were against Las Vegas.
Those injuries were the main reason I thought the Raiders would end their three-game losing streak on Sunday. Obviously, that wasn't the case, and I was clearly wrong, as this game wasn't even competitive.
The majority of my opinions in this game were correlated with Los Angeles' slew of injuries. That included believing the run game would be unleashed against the Rams' undermanned defensive line. Well, that was far from the case, as Ashton Jeanty had eight carries for 15 yards, while Mike Washington Jr. produced 27 yards on six carries.
Part of the reason the Raiders couldn't even attempt to establish the run was that they fell behind 14-3 early in the second quarter. Another factor in this abysmal output is simply that the offensive line was horrendous in creating lanes for the running backs. That should have been feasible with the lack of personnel the Rams had available in the trenches. This game was a glaring indictment of this offensive line and rushing attack.
Again, my opinions entering this game centered on the Rams being decimated by injuries. With their top cornerback and the majority of their starting defensive line out, this was a spot for Cousins to exploit. However, the offensive line was also poor in pass protection, as the 38-year-old quarterback was pressured 16 times and sacked twice.
Also, defenses have forced anyone other than Brock Bowers to beat them, doubling or bracketing the superstar tight end. Because the Raiders lack a true WR1, it's very easy for defenses to carry out this plan effectively. Tre Tucker has taken advantage of that, compiling 19 targets, 10 receptions, 200 yards, and three touchdowns over the last two weeks. However, the bulk of that production has come in garbage time.
Cousins attempted 44 passes, which isn't what head coach Klint Kubiak wants to implement in his scheme consistently. That said, this is the third game this season Cousins has thrown 40+ passes. This passing attack is supposed to be opened up by the run game, but as mentioned earlier, that aspect of the offense has been a non-factor.
The shortcomings in the air boil down to several factors, including the lack of a run game, the offensive line failing in multiple facets, and the Raiders' lack of a bona fide WR1.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Denial Won't Change What Is Blatantly Apparent for Raiders
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders endured a terrible 3-14 season in 2025 and earned the No. 1 overall pick in this year's draft. That pick secured Fernando Mendoza as the team's future franchise quarterback. Mendoza has played one series in seven regular-season games.
The Raiders' 3-0 start made it a no-brainer to stick with their plan to develop Mendoza in the background while Kirk Cousins led the team. A four-game losing streak makes it fair to wonder how far along Mendoza's development is and when the Raiders will play him more.
Head coach Klint Kubiak made it clear that Cousins is still the team's quarterback and that, to him, there is no quarterback controversy.
“I want to let you guys know that Kirk [Cousins] is our starting quarterback. There is no controversy there. He’s playing at a very high level, and he’s got to continue to do that for us to win. And we’ve got to keep helping all the areas around him. So, excited for him to go play here against the [New York] Jets,” Kubiak said Monday morning following his team’s fourth straight loss.
Las Vegas has several other problems on both sides of the ball besides the quarterback, but the quarterback is the most critical position on the field. With the obvious issues the Raiders have along their offensive line, leaving Cousins as a sitting duck behind it makes little sense.
Cousins' experience is negated by his own physical deficiencies and those of the offensive line and Las Vegas' group of wide receivers. Cousins' inability to move around in the pocket makes the Raiders' aforementioned deficiencies even worse.
An immobile quarterback behind a shaky offensive line, a questionable group of wide receivers, and no running game is a recipe for disaster. None of those are Cousins' fault.
However, they undeniably have a quarterback, albeit a rookie, who has a skill set to help negate Las Vegas' roster issues on offense. The Raiders just used the No. 1 overall pick in the draft on a quarterback who excels at many of the things Cousins struggles with.
Kubiak is right. There is no quarterback controversy, but there are quarterback facts. Mendoza is more mobile, more accurate, and has more zip on his passes than Cousins does. Cousins only has one thing over Mendoza: experience, and the rookie won't get that on the bench.
It is fair to note that rebuilds and development take time. It is also fair to note that only so much development can happen in practice.
Kubiak has correctly noted that Cousins has played some of the best football of any quarterback in the league, which is fair. However, it is also fair to point out that a decent portion of his best stats have come with the Raiders already out of reach of realistically winning a game.
Throwing for a bunch of yards while down double digits in the fourth quarter to Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, and Matthew Stafford isn't the same as doing so earlier in the game with a realistic chance of winning.
Scoring six, 10, and 13 points through three quarters of four different games, then attempting to rally late in the fourth quarter is not winning football. That's losing football, as their four-game losing streak shows.
By then, the quarterback's stats are irrelevant. Since the offense did nothing for three quarters , the quarterback should put up big numbers with his team down by multiple scores in the fourth quarter.
However, their four-game losing streak, while Cousins has apparently put up great numbers, is confirmation that Cousins' stats do not equate to winning football unless they are playing the likes of the winless Los Angeles Chargers, the 1-5 Miami Dolphins, or the 2-5 New Orleans Saints.
But alas, here we are. Even with Mendoza primed for this very moment, Kubiak believes Cousins is the man for the job. Kubiak is saying the right things, as throwing his starting quarterback under the bus is far from the right answer. That does not change the reality of the situation.
Soon, players in the locker room will begin to second-guess their new coaching staff if not hurting feelings matters more than on-field performance when deciding who starts. No amount of denial can wash away what is painfully apparent.
Deny it all you want. If the Raiders want a better chance of beating the league's best teams this season, it is time for Mendoza . Otherwise, the past four weeks will be what the rest of the season will look like for Las Vegas, and we can all start looking forward to the 2027 NFL Draft.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Big Issues Raiders May Not Resolve This Season
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have lost four consecutive games after starting the year 3-0.
Two of the Raiders' losses have come by three points, while two more were lost by 14 or more points, including their recent game against the Los Angeles Rams. The biggest difference in most of these games is that the team has remained competitive and is fighting to win instead of lacking so much talent that it could not come close in past years.
However, Las Vegas is in a tough spot, trying to stay disciplined in the team's rebuild while knowing they are a win away from 4-4 and staying in the thick of the wild-card race in the AFC. Some of the issues they face, though, may not be resolved during the season. Three areas will need improvement next offseason.
The Raiders have a mixture of youth and veterans who are working together well, but there is a lack of difference-makers at key spots such as defensive tackle and No. 2 edge rusher. I think Las Vegas and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard are rolling with the punches at cornerback and safety with rookies Hezekiah Masses and Treydan Stukes, both of whom have shown immense flashes but also had rough moments.
Tonka Hemingway is the Raiders' best defensive tackle, but after that, it is bleak. Maxx Crosby is still searching for a quality pass rusher opposite him, with Malcolm Koonce and Kwity Paye failing to meet expectations at the moment. Again, I don't think Las Vegas makes a move here to fix some of these issues; they may wait until March and April to address the defensive flaws.
Jackson Powers-Johnson and Caleb Rogers have been going back and forth at right guard for much of the season, but it is becoming clear they are not the answer at this spot. It might be worth a shot to give rookie Trey Zuhn III some opportunities here, but this is another area the Raiders may have to let play out for the offseason.
Powers-Johnson and Rogers could be potential trade assets at the deadline from my perspective, though Rogers is unlikely as a second-year player. Powers-Johnson provides more of that, which would give the Raiders more ammo for this year's or next year's NFL Draft.
The Raiders (74.7 YPG) have the second-worst rushing offense in the NFL, behind the Green Bay Packers (59.9 YPG). Running back Ashton Jeanty has been both hurt and inconsistent as a runner, while rookie Mike Washington has flashed but runs into the same issues. The offensive line, specifically the guards, is failing to hit their marks on gap or zone blocking concepts.
Head coach and play-caller Klint Kubiak , along with offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko, will attempt every avenue they can to find some consistency in the run game, which could mean an offensive line scuffle and a change in approach with the blocking scheme Kubiak and Janocko are deploying. Still, don't expect this key issue to be resolved anytime soon.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Raiders' Rookie, Sophomore Power Rankings: Up and Down We Go
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' plan all along was to depend on several rookies and second-year players they have drafted under John Spytek to be productive this season. Las Vegas loaded its roster with young, talented players at positions of need, knowing there would be growing pains.
The Raiders' Week 7 loss to the Los Angeles Rams further confirmed what the previous three losses already made clear: Las Vegas' dependence on young players would inevitably cost them games. This is normal in the type of rebuild the Raiders have embarked on under Spytek and Klint Kubiak.
Las Vegas has a long way to go to consistently compete with and beat the league's best. Below are the power rankings for the Raiders' rookies and second-year players.
The rookie quarterback's stock is through the roof right now, and he didn't even play a down on Sunday against the Rams. Las Vegas spent months evaluating every facet of Mendoza before using the No. 1 overall draft pick in this year's draft on him. Sunday's loss makes it clear his time is now.
Mendoza's skill set can help Las Vegas offset its limitations on its offensive line and at wide receiver. Still, Kubiak explained that Mendoza will see the field sometime this season, just not during their Week 8 road trip.
“Eventually Fernando [Mendoza] is going to play football. We have a plan. We don’t have a timeline for that. Kirk [Cousins] is playing really well, and we’re in the hunt. It’s really important that we keep playing really well behind him and continue to develop Fernando, but Fernando is going to play at some point. It’s not going to be this week," Kubiak said.
Sure, Las Vegas has a winnable road game against the New York Jets, followed by a tough game against the San Francisco 49ers. Starting the rookie in either game would be questionable. However, even if the Raiders split those two games, Mendoza should start after that.
The Raiders' ground game has continued to struggle. However, these issues have long existed before Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington arrived. Las Vegas has finished with the fewest rushing yards in the league in two of the past three seasons.
They finished with the third-fewest rushing yards in the third of those three seasons. Through seven games this season, the Raiders have the second-fewest rushing yards in the league. Las Vegas has swapped out multiple running backs during that time, while largely keeping the same offensive line.
Despite his ankle injury and the clear lack of the explosion that led Las Vegas to draft him No. 6 overall, he has shown his versatility by making an impact in the passing game. The Raiders have plenty to figure out, as their ground game has been largely rendered useless by their offensive line.
Overall, Las Vegas' defensive backfield struggled against Matthew Stafford and the Rams. The unit, largely composed of rookies and second-year players, was simply outmatched by a more experienced quarterback and group of Rams wide receivers.
Stafford completed 23 of his 29 passes, with the longest gain of the day being 15 yards. Although the Raiders' defensive backfield eliminated the big plays, they failed to slow down the Rams' passing attack enough to give their offense a chance to work their issues out.
Still, the unit is about where they were expected to be at the start of the season.
The Raiders started Rogers over Jackson Powers-Johnson again on Sunday. The second-year offensive guard continued to show a need for improvement, routinely missing critical blocks that led to negative plays. There were multiple plays where Rogers looked lost on the field.
Las Vegas must seriously consider adding help at offensive guard, as they don't get quality play at either guard position at a starting-caliber level. They also lack depth behind their shaky starting guards.
Rogers needs further development, as many second-year players do. However, his poor play only highlights a larger issue for the Raiders. The team may make offensive guard its top priority after the season. Las Vegas' offensive guards are holding the offense back.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Hondo’s Raiders Report Card: The Unfiltered Truth on Team Performance
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders' (3-4) performance on Sunday was the worst of the season for the Silver and Black, and what made it worse was that it was at home against a battered team that was the unquestioned Super Bowl favorite coming into the season, whom the Raiders had a chance to knock out.
Instead, the Los Angeles Rams (3-4) leave Allegiant Stadium with not only a win, but a new breath of life for their once nearly certain Super Bowl chances.
This one hurt Raider Nation. Bad.
Each week, I offer my report on the game after watching copious amounts of film, drawing on my years of experience and sources both inside and outside the Raiders franchise, from around the world of football.
That was by far the hardest grade I will give in this report.
Raiders QB Kirk Cousins leads the NFL in passing touchdowns (16) and ranks third with nearly 1,900 yards. Kirk Cousins isn’t playing well; he is playing terrific.
Every player, including Raiders owner Tom Brady, the best QB in the history of the game, can go back to every game he ever played and find one or two plays he could have done better. The other team is full of high-priced millionaire players, too
The reality is that I predicted the Raiders would be sitting here today at 2-5 instead of 3-4, and there is no way the Raiders have the success they do without Cousins.
Of course, the elephant in the room is that the Silver and Black selected the man NFL executives ranked the best QB prospect of the last four NFL Drafts, Fernando Mendoza, waiting in the wings.
I totally understand the mindset of fans who recognize what I told you all offseason: this is not a Super Bowl team, and they want to turn the page.
Cousins is not just a man I cover, but a friend. That said, when the time comes, I also look forward to seeing the Nandoloarian, but when it comes to QB development, I trust Brady, Kubiak, and the way Cousins is executing their plan.
But the aforementioned Brady, who knew more about being a QB in the NFL long before he was an owner, talked about how sitting and watching helped him, and the franchise is sticking to the plan.
The plan is that as long as Cousins is playing well and the team is in NFL Playoff contention, Cousins is the man.
The made-up media frenzy this offseason that we told you was a farce, and the one now, isn’t reality. Kubiak pulled out a hammer and nails and put those rumors and speculation to death on Monday.
“I want to let you guys know that Kirk [Cousins] is our starting quarterback. There is no controversy there. He’s playing at a very high level, and he’s got to continue to do that for us to win. And we’ve got to keep helping all the areas around him. So, excited for him to go play here against the Jets.”
Credit Kubiak; he knows what he has on his bench, and he signed off on him. Kubiak and I agree that Mendoza looks exactly like what they wanted, but not today.
I have said since last May that the feeling I got from people in the building was probably around the Cleveland game. That changes if the team continues to overachieve, but at some point this year, I expect Mendoza to start. Kubiak talked more about the Mendoza factor and, as usual, took it head-on.
“Eventually Fernando [Mendoza] is going to play football. We have a plan. We don’t have a timeline for that. Kirk [Cousins] is playing really well, and we’re in the hunt. It’s really important that we keep playing really well behind him and continue to develop Fernando, but Fernando is going to play at some point. It’s not going to be this week.”
But despite Cousins' terrific play, the reality is that the offensive line, as a unit, is struggling and, frankly, is brutal.
The guard play on the right side has not been good all season, and on the left side has been up and down like a roller coaster at your favorite amusement park.
Watching the film and seeing input, Kolton Miller was not elite, or even top-ten at the NFL level, but did an adequate job.
Tyler Linderbaum is a star, and the Bills game was a disaster. He has had some struggles, but as one NFL executive told me about the Rams game, “There are some plays that he is getting blamed for that has more to do with the pathetic play from the guys next to him. Was he great? No, but who the hell can be great when the two guys next to him are playing like that? He has to be able to trust those guys next to him, and he can’t trust (excrement) right now.”
Delmar “DJ” Glaze, The Mule, looks like the emerging star we thought he could be. He was a problem for the Rams, who found very few along the Raiders' OL, and he played as a steady foundational piece who looks like a fan favorite and a long-term solution for a franchise with a history of elite OL play. I asked Kubiak about “The Mule” on Monday, and he didn’t hold back.
"Yeah, DJ [Glaze] was a team captain for us this week, so that tells you how highly we believe how high of a level he's playing at, how good of a teammate that he is, and how he's taking the next step in his career. And the thing about DJ is that he's not satisfied, and he's continuing to get better, which he's a very self-motivated young man."
I asked Kubiak bluntly if the poor play at guard was going to get Trey Zuhn III and Bryce Cabeldue consideration for reps this week, and without hesitation, he said, “Yes.”
They deserve the chance. They have to earn them, but players know what is going on, and Kubiak’s locker room trusts him and Rick Dennison.
Neither Dennison nor Kubiak is the problem; they are the answer, and hopefully the three young men who have been playing guard can grow into the spots, but they aren't good enough now. After Sunday's performance, Zuhn, the rookie, and Cabeldue can do no worse and deserve a chance on a team that prides itself on competition.
Ashton Jeanty continues to shine in the passing game, but rookie Mike Washington Jr., who was injured last week before the game, continues to rack up impressive plays and earn more carries.
The tight ends aren't the issue, but the wide receivers, as a unit, haven't been good. Dont’e Thornton Jr. appears to be headed out of town later this week, and Jack Bech should be back this week, but that doesn’t change the fact that Cousins has to throw quick because the pressure is on him nearly as fast as Tyler Linderbaum puts the ball in his hand.
We knew coming into the season the Raiders don’t have a WR1, and credit GM John Spytek and Kubiak for dealing with it in a rebuilding year, rather than wasting picks or money on Elmer’s Glue and Scotch tape fixes, as this franchise has relied on for the last two-plus decades.
Their discipline may infuriate some fans who don’t understand it now, but they'll thank them down the road in 2028.
I will get more into coaching later, but for now, the Raiders' defense had some players playing at a good level. Still, even with a terrific player (injured) at WR, Puka Nacua, and a future Hall of Fame QB in Matthew Stafford, they have no excuse for embarrassing themselves as they did, hindered as they were.
Missed tackles, missed assignments, and an inability in the first half should have embarrassed the men wearing the Raiders patch. They are good men, they are proud men, and many of them are better players than they looked on Sunday, but I am grading Sunday, and it was terrible.
True to his character, Kubiak didn’t hold back any punches when discussing why his team continues to struggle against the run, and teams are literally doing whatever they want to them on the ground.
"It's all team. It's all phases. It's tackling, it's at the front, it's putting them in situations to be successful as coaches, so we're all accountable."
The reality is that this defense is struggling for legitimate reasons; it is a rebuilding year. But these men are paid a lot of money, and missed tackles, especially those executed terribly, are inexcusable. These men are paid a lot of money to do a job, and Brady, Mark Davis, GM John Spytek, and Kubiak are not being unrealistic in asking…

title: The Biggest Decisions Kubiak, Raiders Got Wrong vs. Rams
full_text:
The first mistake the Raiders made on Sunday was winning the coin toss and electing to receive the ball. Las Vegas starting the game on defense has worked better for them in each game this season. Overall, they played better with their defense on the field first, even in losses.
In each of their three wins, Las Vegas' defense was on the field first. The Raiders forced a punt or a turnover on downs on the opponent's first drive in each of those three games. In those three wins, the Raiders' defense held opposing offenses to six points combined in the first quarter.
Even during their three wins, the Raiders' offense started slowly. In those three wins, Las Vegas' offense scored a total of 10 points in the first quarter. That is why electing to receive the ball against the Rams was a mistake.
In theory, getting the ball first, marching down the field, and scoring first against a reeling Rams team sounds good. However, that only works if your offense can actually execute in the first quarter. Or execute in general. Once the offense doesn't score, you're essentially behind a possession.
Not only are you down by a possession because the other team got the ball first after halftime, but you are also down by a possession to Matthew Stafford. The Raiders got the ball first, gained one yard in three plays, and punted the ball to Stafford and the Rams.
Luckily, the Raiders' defense forced a punt. Las Vegas' offense got the ball back and essentially did the same thing it did on the first drive. However, this time, a missed field goal after a 39-yard defensive pass interference call against the Rams helped the unit move downfield.
This is why electing to receive may seem insignificant, but it wasn't. The Raiders' offense took the field and quickly showed that they had nothing. They were not going to do anything that day. Their teammates on defense knew early on that they had no run support, no matter how well they played.
They made plenty of mistakes, but the attempt to gain a mental edge backfired spectacularly. After the Raiders' missed field goal, the Rams scored a touchdown on all of their next four possessions, while Las Vegas kicked two field goals. Las Vegas needs to start games on defense.
Still, the Raiders' biggest mistake was fooling themselves into thinking the game was more competitive than it was and not giving Fernando Mendoza any playing time.
"No, we made it a competitive game in the third quarter, so no, to answer your question," Kubiak said after the game when asked if he and the coaching staff considered playing the rookie in the second half.
Sure, Las Vegas' defense turned things up a notch, but the Raiders were down 28-6 heading into the fourth. The Raiders' offense scored zero points in the third quarter for the third time in four weeks. I am not sure how competitive that is.
If being down by 21 to Stafford and the Rams entering the fourth quarter, with your offense having scored only two field goals that day, is competitive, then their decision not to play Mendoza even one play makes perfect sense. However, the nearly 63,000 fans in attendance know what they saw.
Other position groups need attention, but the quarterback position is the most critical position on the field. Kubiak added that although his coaching staff did not consider making the move during the game, all options are on the table moving forward.
“I think we have to go watch the film, and I think at this point we're thinking about everything, how to fix our problems, how to fix our issues in the red zone, in the third quarter, and personnel, scheme. We've got to talk about all of it," Kubiak said.
It would be understandable if the coaching staff waited until after their matchup against the San Francisco 49ers to start Mendoza, but at the rate they were going on Sunday, he should have gotten on the field at some point. The game was already over .
Still, it is time for Las Vegas' coaching staff to begin the succession plan from Cousins to Mendoza.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: What to Know About the Latest Wave of Dolphins Tryout Players
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' 53-man roster remains a work in progress, as GM Jon-Eric Sullivan has indicated on multiple occasions since the spring, so it was only natural to have more player tryouts Tuesday.
Especially since the team has an opening on the roster.
The Dolphins brought in eight players for tryouts Tuesday, with a heavy emphasis on the tight end position. Four of the players brought played that position, along with two defensive tackles, one quarterback and one defensive end.
As has been the case for most of the tryouts this year for Miami, the list was comprised of young players with little or no NFL game experience.
The list: QB Derek Robertson, Monmouth TE Jaheim Bell, Florida State TE Devin Culp, Washington TE Rivaldo Fairweather, Auburn TE Joshua Simon, South Carolina DE Anthony Goodlow, Oklahoma State DT Cole Brevard, Texas DT Jay Toia, UCLA
Of those eight players, Bell, Culp, Goodlow and Toia are the only ones with NFL game experience, those it ranges from five to 18 games for Culp.
Bell, Culp and Toia entered the NFL as seventh-round draft picks, while the other five were undrafted rookie free agents, including Brevard and Robertson this year. Robertson's only NFL exposure came when he attended the Jacksonville Jaguars rookie minicamp as a tryout player.
This tryout, like all the ones before, shouldn't be viewed as a precursor to a signing, though it has happened this year, most recently with Zane Gonzalez beating out three other kickers to land a spot on the practice squad after the team released incumbent Riley Patterson.
The Dolphins didn't replace Patterson the 53, which is why they have an opening, but Gonzalez can only be elevated for a game two more times before the Dolphins have to put him on the 53-man roster or find another kicker.
The likelihood is this latest tryout was about gathering intel on potential future signings. If we're looking at tight ends, the Dolphins already have three rookies at the position with third-round pick Will Kacmarek, fifth-round pick Seydou Traore and waiver wire pick-up Justin Joly, himself a fifth-round pick of the Denver Broncos.
In a full-circle moment, outside linebacker/edge defender Andre Jones Jr. rejoined the Buffalo Bills practice squad, which is where the Dolphins got him for their 53-man roster before eventually waiving him after three games.
Jones played 45 games on special teams for Miami in those three games.
Elsewhere: -- Former Dolphins punter Matt Haack had a tryout with the Tennessee Titans. -- Tackle Charlie Heck, who failed to make Miami's 53-man roster after signing as an unrestricted free agent in the offseason, had a tryout with the New York Jets. -- Tight end Ben Sims, who was waived/injured after also signing as a UFA in the offseason, had a tryout with the Seattle Seahawks.

title: Examining the Impact of the Nelson Trade on the Dolphins
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is now two weeks away, but there was a significant trade Tuesday.
The immediate impact for the Miami Dolphins of the Indianapolis Colts beginning their expected fire sale by sending perennial Pro Bowl Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks is that their Week 10 game at Lucas Oil Stadium might become a lot more winnable than it once was.
There are potentially other implications beyond that game on November 15, though.
The reported return for Nelson, who will become a free agent after the season and no doubt will get a massive free agent deal, was a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL draft along with a fifth-round selection in 2028.
The trade compensation is important to note as a comparison point for all the teams looking or willing to deal players before the trade deadline November 10.
While they're coming off a victory, the Dolphins remain — or at least should remain — focused on the big picture and treat their personnel with the future in mind, meaning they should listen to offers for any players and maybe seek deals for those they don't see as part of the team beyond this season.
Tackle Austin Jackson has long been assumed on the way out because he's a pretty expensive player in the final year of his contract, he's not having a great year and the Dolphins have their future right tackle on the roster with Kadyn Proctor if they decide to switch him there instead of keeping him at left guard where he's showing great promise as a rookie.
While the Nelson trade compensation doesn't really apply when it comes to Jackson — as it doesn't to a whole lot of offensive linemen around the NFL — maybe it becomes a better barometer for someone like defensive tackle Zach Sieler.
The question, of course, is whether the Dolphins even want to trade Sieler, who's not only a good player in the middle of the defensive line but a leader on a team with an abundance of young players.
While Sieler isn't an All-Pro like Nelson, he is under contract through the next three years after this one, though with no guaranteed salary, giving an acquiring team flexiblity in terms of how to proceed forward with him.
If Nelson fetched a third and a fifth in a trade, what could the Dolphins get for Sieler? The obvious answer is whatever a team — say, the New York Giants — needing help at defensive tackle is willing to give up,
Realistically, it's always felt as though maybe the best the Dolphins could do was get a third-round pick and that likely would entail them giving up a late-round pick in addition to Sieler.
Jackson, because his contract expires, he has a long injury history and has had issues in pass protection, probably wouldn't fetch more than a late-round pick.
That game against the Colts will come five days after the trade deadline, and it's entirely possible that Nelson won't be the only star player gone from Indy by then.
After GM Chris Ballard was fired following the Colts' loss against the Tennessee Titans, it looks like the team is headed for a full rebuild and players like Jonathan Taylor and DeForrest Buckner also could be moved.
One thing for sure, that Colts team isn't going to look the same as the one the Dolphins saw in the 2025 opener when they left Indianapolis with a 33-8 loss.

title: What the Week 7 Film Told Us About the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins tallied their first win of 2026 against the New York Jets, and the All-22 film shows both triumph and room for improvement. Here’s a look at the key developments from this game along with breakdowns of some of the biggest plays.
The Dolphins’ passing game was operating as cleanly as we’ve seen it in 2026. Their 0.41 EPA per pass ranked third in the league in Week 7, and their passing yards per play was fifth at 8.9.
For the first time all season, the route concepts consistently fit the players on the field. They sent more of their eligibles on routes, found ways to space out zone coverages, and were on the same page in blitz situations.
Miami set the tone early, as Malik Willis’ first three pass attempts looked relatively similar: four or more players out on routes, no play-action, and opportunities for Willis to get to the back side of his progression.
pic.twitter.com/Q9YTDETNUW
He did so beautifully on each of the three, casually sliding from one read to the next, and capping off a 3-for-3 opening drive with a touchdown strike to the returning Caleb Douglas.
Through the first five games of the season, Bobby Slowik’s passing offense looked clunky and congested. As I’ve chronicled in the previous film breakdowns, far too many of Miami’s dropbacks involved simple two-man route concepts and shot plays. They were sprinkled into this game as well, but looked more like a changeup to the quick-game fastball.
The quick, ball-control style of the Dolphins’ passing game dominated the Jets’ blitzes. Malik Willis finished 8-for-10 for 128 yards passing when Aaron Glenn sent extra rushers, and his 14.6 EPA was the best mark in football for any quarterback against the blitz.
pic.twitter.com/dtZ2JtusmF
The only thing better than Slowik’s timely play calling was the execution from Miami’s most important pieces. On Caleb Douglas’ second touchdown, he notices the cornerback blitz, and, knowing his route is where Willis would have to go with the ball, he stops short and throws his hands up. Willis sees him in space, takes a shot on a sidearm delivery that whips around Brandon Stephens, and Douglas takes it 63 yards thanks to a crucial block from Malik Washington.
That single play was a glimpse of what could be for the future of the Miami Dolphins. Caleb Douglas looked smooth and athletic in his return, and if Willis keeps making cerebral plays in key moments, he’ll look more and more like a franchise quarterback.
Miami’s run game was just as impressive as their passing attack. EPA per rush was seventh in the league, success rate was 11th, and Ollie Gordon logged his second 100-yard game of the season.
In De’Von Achane’s absence, Bobby Slowik has maximized this unit, largely due to the amount of gap scheme runs he’s worked in. In previous years, Mike McDaniel worked almost exclusively with outside zone and toss looks, but Miami’s power and counter runs might be their best concepts in 2026.
pic.twitter.com/RDlidmHBzc
On Miami’s final drive, they ran the same power play three times in a row, and hit a 14-yard gain on their first attempt. Will Kacmarek and Austin Jackson obliterate their down-block at the point-of-attack, Kadyn Proctor’s pull makes contact with two defenders, and Ollie Gordon hurdles into the second level.
Every aspect of this rushing game looks dangerous right now. The revamped scheme simplifies reads for Gordon, while allowing Miami’s massive guards to use their strength to their advantage. Bobby Slowik’s attention to detail, timely calls, and wrinkles with motion and alignment have all created advantages that the players have capitalized on.
The Dolphins’ defense was able to get enough stops to win, but they struggled down to down. Geno Smith went 23-of-30 passing for 308 yards, including two deep shots that targeted Miami’s youth.
pic.twitter.com/SJBMzyou0A
Smith’s first pass of the game went for 52 yards, with nobody taking Omar Cooper Jr. deep down the field. In man coverage, Chris Johnson appears to signal to Jason Marshall Jr. that he'll take the outside man, but at the snap of the ball, both players play Garrett Wilson, and neither can recover before Cooper makes the catch.
pic.twitter.com/cZ4qIxWgJW
Later in the game, Cooper made another big play. With Johnson in man coverage, the Jets’ receiver fired off the line, stayed physical with Johnson, and quickly stacked him. Dante Trader Jr., who was occupied with Garrett Wilson on the near sideline, can’t get over in time, and the ball splits the defenders for a 60-yard chunk.
Compounding mistakes, especially in man-to-man looks, result in big plays. If Johnson plays through the receiver and doesn’t slow up or Trader drops closer to the middle of the field, that second explosive likely is erased.
Miami’s defense was feast or famine, making a few momentum-swinging plays that proved sufficient in eking out a victory. When challenging opponents with one-on-one situations, though, Hafley’s young secondary has plenty to clean up.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Dolphins Week 7 Report Card: A Big Step Forward
full_text:
Whether you wanted them to or not, the Miami Dolphins have finally put one in the win column, beating the New York Jets 28-25 at MetLife Stadium on Sunday.
For a team supposedly setting football back a few decades, they’ve kept knocking on the door. Competitive losses against Minnesota and Cincinnati showed signs of progress, but costly mistakes kept Miami winless heading into its bye.
This time, the Dolphins gave themselves a chance and actually did something with it. Malik Willis delivered his best performance of the season, the running game showed it’s here to stay, and the defense made enough timely stops to survive New York’s late push.
Here’s how each position group graded out in Miami’s first win of the season.
Willis completed 14 of 21 passes for 208 yards and two touchdowns without an interception, adding 37 yards and another score on eight carries. He finished with a 130.7 passer rating.
The numbers reflect Willis’ growing comfort processing the defense. He’s moving through his progressions more naturally and showing he can create openings as well as recognize them.
On his 32-yard completion to Greg Dulcich up the seam, Willis did more than work through his reads. He turned his feet and shoulders to the right, where Caleb Douglas and Seydou Traore were running quick outs. That movement drew the safety toward the sideline, opening a window up the seam for Dulcich.
Similarly, on Douglas’ first touchdown, Willis resisted the urge to scramble or throw the ball away when his first two reads weren’t available. He stayed with the play, allowing the routes to develop and clear space before finding Douglas late in his progression on an in-breaking route.
Offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik favors 12 personnel (one back, two tight ends), but Willis’ mobility also makes a case for spreading the field. Empty sets and formations with three or four receivers can widen the defense and open running lanes through the middle, giving Willis another way to punish the coverage with his legs.
At this point, we’re out of fluke territory. We’ve all heard the legends of Ollie Gordon II’s Doak Walker year at Oklahoma State and the mysterious drought that followed, but it appears the Dolphins have unlocked that version of him again.
Gordon finished with 103 yards and a touchdown on 25 carries, giving him his second 100-yard game in his last three starts.
The 4.1 yards per carry doesn’t jump off the page, but New York knew Miami wanted to run late. Gordon still ripped off gains of 14 and seven yards on consecutive carries during the final drive.
Jaylen Wright, meanwhile, continued struggling to find running room, finishing with 8 yards on six carries before leaving with a quad injury.
Welcome back, Caleb Douglas.
After quickly winning over Dolphins fans, the rookie had barely gotten involved in Week 2 before an ankle injury sidelined him. His return gave Miami the length and athleticism it had been missing on the outside.
He caught just two passes, but both went for touchdowns, totaling 70 yards.
On his goal-line touchdown, Douglas drove vertically at full speed to get on Azareye’h Thomas’ toes, then used a hard jab step with his right foot to get the corner leaning before breaking inside.
Malik Washington remained a reliable target, catching all three of his targets for 27 yards, while Chris Bell added three catches for 25.
Miami also used Bell on shallow crossing routes out of mesh concepts, giving him opportunities to use his strength and speed against man coverage. It was a familiar look for Bell, who turned a similar drag route into a touchdown for Louisville against Miami.
After going without a target in Miami’s loss to Cincinnati, Greg Dulcich has now drawn five in back-to-back games as the Dolphins steadily work him into the passing attack.
He caught all five for 86 yards, all in the first half.
Dulcich had a 32-yard catch on Miami’s opening touchdown drive, converted a third-and-7 on the next possession and later added gains of 15 and 16 yards during the 91-yard touchdown drive before halftime.
Rookie Will Kacmarek continued to handle his blocking assignments well, but Dulcich finally delivered the receiving production Miami has been waiting for from the position.
The offensive line has had their fair share of ugly moments this season, but this wasn’t one of them.
Miami ran for 156 yards, held the ball for more than 34 minutes and, most importantly, was able to run the ball when even the people using the bathroom at MetLife stadium knew it was coming
That final possession was probably the best example. Miami lined up and ran it over and over again with a three-point lead, and the Jets never got the ball back.
Austin Jackson still had his moment, let’s not be unrealistic here, giving up a sack late in the third quarter that killed a possession, but overall this was one of the unit’s better games.
If you want one sequence to describe this unit, just watch the goal-line stand.
New York was sitting on Miami’s doorstep on first-and-goal when the Dolphins responded with a Zach Sieler tackle for loss, another stop by Josh Uche and then a Chop Robinson sack on third down.
Robinson continues to create pressure even when the sacks aren’t piling up, generating four pressures.
Malik Herring also sacked Geno Smith with 11:36 in the 3rd quarter.
That said, the run defense was less than ideal, as Braelon Allen finished with 104 yards on just 17 carries.
Jordyn Brooks did what Jordyn Brooks usually does, finishing with nine tackles and two tackles for loss.
Jacob Rodriguez, meanwhile, had his quietest game of the season with four tackles.
Here’s my weekly Pro Football Focus disclaimer: they charged Rodriguez with allowing a completion to Jets running back Isaiah Davis, but Rodriguez appeared to communicate that Jason Marshall needed to pick up the crossing route, which makes it difficult to pin the breakdown solely on Rodriguez
Mason Taylor caught two touchdowns, but both came with defensive backs in coverage, Jason Marshall and Michael Taaffe.
Miami’s rookie defensive backs continue to ride the NFL roller coaster.
Michael Taaffe read Geno Smith the entire way on his second-quarter interception, jumping Mason Taylor’s route to end a Jets scoring threat. Taylor got him back in the fourth quarter, beating him for a 12-yard touchdown.
Chris Johnson also intercepted Smith, but his own defensive holding penalty wiped out the takeaway. He later surrendered a 60-yard completion to Omar Cooper Jr. on a deep crossing route with safety Dante Trader Jr. also in the coverage area.
Smith completed 23 of 30 passes for 287 yards and three touchdowns, while Cooper finished with 115 yards on five catches.
Jason Marshall Jr. had his struggles, too. On Taylor’s first touchdown, Marshall was draped over the tight end near the pylon but couldn’t break up the pass and never looked back for the ball.
For once, there wasn’t much to complain about.
Wright averaged 26.2 yards on five kickoff returns and had a 39-yarder that helped set up Miami’s second touchdown drive.
Bradley Pinion also did his job, averaging 44.2 yards per punt with a 42.5 net.
The wind was briefly knocked out of everybody’s stomach when Wright muffed the final kickoff before recovering it, because apparently Miami can’t go an entire game without making a kickoff stressful, but this was a major improvement from the first month of the season.
For the first time this season, Miami actually made the plays necessary to win a close game.
Taaffe got the interception, the defense made the goal-line stand, and Douglas and Gordon  supplied the offensive punch the Dolphins had been thirsting for.
After spending six weeks finding increasingly creative ways to lose, the Dolphins finally figured out how to finish one.
Tyler M. Carmona is a Miami native whose work has appeared in the Miami Herald and Associated Press. He previously worked as a local television news reporter. He recently graduated from Columbia University’s Graduate School of…

title: Poup's Perspective: Why This First Dolphins Win Indeed Was a Very Big Deal
full_text:
No, the Miami Dolphins are not suddenly going to make a playoff push because they got off the schneid and got their first victory of the 2026 season Sunday.
Or let's just say it's extraordinarily unlikely because we never want to say never.
And, yes, that elusive victory did come against the New York Jets, an organization about as dysfunctional as any in the NFL, as evidenced by the fact it's got the longest playoff drought (appearance, not win because that one belongs to the Dolphins).
But, make no mistake, it was cause for celebration, not just for the players and coaches who have been working hard under difficult circumstances to become at a minimum competitive and it most definitely was cause for celebration for anybody who cares about the Miami Dolphins.
Belief. Step inside the locker room after our Week 7 win 🔊 pic.twitter.com/i20aJA405x
The video of the Dolphins' locker room celebration was something, capturing the kind of excitement you normally see when a team clinches a playoff berth or even more.
But it actually was similar for the Dolphins and not just because it was Jeff Hafley's first win as an NFL head coach.
It was the first tangible reward for the vision that Jon-Eric Sullivan and Hafley have implemented, with strong performances by quarterback Malik Willis and members of a 2026 draft class that has looked promising from the start, with Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, Caleb Douglas, Will Kacmarek, Chris Bell and Michael Taaffe all contributing to one degree or another to that 28-25 win against the New York Jets.
In that Dolphins video, we saw Hafley talk about asking his offensive linemen about going for it on that late fourth-down to clinch the victory and making the call to proceed after getting the response he wanted.
Truth is, it was the only acceptable response from the big guys up front because the second an offensive lineman suggests at that time it would be more prudent to punt and let the defense hold the lead, that's the time to replace the head coach, that offensive lineman or both.
We still like the idea of Hafley there showing he was going to trust his players to deliver after they accept a challenge, and that's a big part of what this season is for the Dolphins.
Jets or not, the Dolphins played their best game of the season Sunday and just like that any talk of an 0-17 season disappeared.
That it was there in the first place only was evidence of just how massive a rebuilding project the Dolphins undertook by dumping so many high-end players and taking on so much dead cap space in one year.
But the Dolphins, with Sullivan in charge, sure look like they've done a pretty good job of restocking the roster, to the extent that they could do it in the first year with their cap restrictions.
As we've said before, this 2026 season for the Dolphins isn't about wins and losses, it's about progress and developments and being able to identify a nice group of young players with whom the team can move forward as part of the nucleus.
At this point, it sure looks as thought the Dolphins have a decent number of those core pieces to keep watching and the hope is we'll see more performances like we saw against the Jets.
That absolutely includes Willis, who accomplished more against the Jets by actually trying to do less — if that makes sense. It probably wasn't an accident that he was more efficient than in any other previous while not going downfield nearly as much.
Look at Willis' stat line against the Jets and you'll notice an uncanny resemblance to that of his second start with the Green Bay Packers in 2024.
Against the Jets on Sunday: 14-for-21, 208 yards, 2 TD, 0 INT, 130.7 passer rating, 37 rushing yards, 1 TD
Against the Titans in 2024: 13-for-19, 202 yards, 1 TD, 0 INT, 120.9 passer rating, 73 rushing yards, 1 TD
That was just one game, of course, and the key will be for Willis to do it again and then again after that.
And if there are more games like from Willis, there will be more wins.
And then the first 2027 draft pick will get lower and lower, and the same goes for more performances like we saw from Douglas or Taaffe or Ollie Gordon II or Greg Dulcich.
And that should be the goal for the Dolphins and the hope for Dolphins fans.
If the Dolphins can go, say, 5-12 and have to settle for eighth or ninth overall pick, it would be more favorable for the future health of the franchise than going 2-15 or 1-16 and having the second or even first pick.
The difference between two picks within the top 10 isn't nearly as significant as having found a group of key pieces with whom to move forward.
The win against the Jets was big. And the hope should be there are more to come, even if they're not that frequent.
The focus needs to stay on the 2026 season, not the 2027 draft. And that's how it should have been all along.

title: Four Winners And Four Losers From Miami's First Win Of 2026
full_text:
Rejoice if you'd like, as the Miami Dolphins are no longer winless, taking down the New York Jets in a 28-25 thriller. If you're on the side of the room that thinks going winless would be better for "draft capital," please chill out.
No team deserves to go an entire season without winning a game. The way things are shaping up, the Dolphins are still in contention for a top pick regardless, with the only winless team remaining being the Los Angeles Chargers.
So how did Miami pull it off? The best performance of the season by their offense from the jump, alongside doing just enough on the defense to slow the Jets down. It wasn't easy, but the idea of Jeff Hafley not getting drenched in Gatorade this season has been officially put to rest.
This has to feel great for Willis, coming off a shoddy performance against Cincinnati. Instead, he shushed a lot of the doubters with a strong performance - 208 yards and two touchdowns through the air, and 37 yards and a score on the ground. Make fun of the Jets all you want, but their secondary was generally considered a tough unit.
Nothing Willis did physically stands out from what we know about his skill set. Instead, the bigger difference is what he did mentally - he was much smarter with his decision-making in this game. Whether he had to pin the ball in the right spot or escape the pocket, he made the right call more often than not.
It's a very positive sign for the Dolphins. Their quarterback looks like he has confidence again, and the big question is whether he can keep it up against tougher competition, with New England and Detroit coming to town. If he can, the idea of Miami going for a quarterback in the 2027 draft gets a bit muddled.
The offensive line played fine, but not thanks to Jackson. One mistake stands out - a missed block on third down at midfield, which led to defensive end Nate Lynn's first career sack with less than a minute to go in the third quarter. Miami looked poised to get to field goal range, but instead were forced to punt. The Jets responded with a lengthy drive, going all the way to the 1-yard line.
That was the only major negative play Jackson caused, but every play matters more when the game comes down to the wire. It's no secret that he's been a liability more often than not for the Dolphins - Pro Football Focus certainly thinks so, as he's earned a 43.7 grade. Out of all 71 eligible tackles, that's the lowest of the group.
It really seems like the future of the offensive line is bright with the consistent performances that Aaron Brewer, Jonah Savaiinaea, Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor have orchestrated this season. But Jackson hasn't proven himself worthy of being mentioned in that group, and that missed block might be bulletin-board material for the Dolphins to consider going somewhere else at right tackle.
Douglas walked into the land of questionable turf and proved he was the most explosive player on the field. He wasn't targeted much - only three times - but made the most of his opportunities with two touchdowns on two receptions.
The first score was great, creating separation from Azareye'h Thomas in the back of the end zone to give the Dolphins their first lead of the season. However, his second touchdown was stellar - a 63-yard sprint down the left side of the field, narrowly getting by Nahshon Wright while staying in bounds for the score, giving Miami the 11-point cushion they needed in the end.
Believing that the outlook of this game changed the moment it was announced that Douglas would play was justified. He's a natural difference-maker even as a rookie, and a red zone weapon that Willis and the Dolphins could rely on for years to come.
Unfortunately, it's almost obligatory at this point to include Wright in these lists, as he's just not reliable for the Dolphins. Once again, he failed to get past New York's defensive line, settling for 8 yards on six carries. Wide receiver Malik Washington somehow managed the same amount of yards in just TWO carries.
At this point, what's the excuse for not giving another running back on the roster a shot to back up Ollie Gordon II? Whether it's Kaytron Allen, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers back on October 9,  or Carlos Washington Jr., currently on their practice squad, how can it be any worse?
It feels bad to hammer Wright this much, especially because there was a small chance he wasn't able to play in this game due to a nagging foot injury. But the production at running back falls off so much when he's on the field that it's almost become a guarantee. Having two reliable running backs instead of one would do wonders for this offense.
It might not look like Taaffe had a major game just by the box score - three tackles and a pass deflection is just OK. But the major highlight on defense for Miami came at the hands of Taaffe - a clutch interception, considering the Jets were knocking on Miami's red zone in the second quarter.
Despite the achievement, it was a pretty standard play. Geno Smith targeted Mason Taylor right off the play action, never looking away, even when shuffling to the right before throwing the ball. Taaffe read it the whole way, jumping the route and denying the Jets another score for the rest of the half.
Taffee is in elite company, being one of three rookies with multiple picks this season (Hezekiah Masses and Genesis Smith). He's the first member of the Dolphins to do so in the first six games of his career, since Patrick Surtain in 1998. You can't ask for much more from the 158th overall pick.
Overall, this was a successful day for the Dolphins in terms of getting to the quarterback, especially when compared to their earlier struggles to do so this season. Geno Smith took a beating, with two sacks and six confirmed QB hits. However, these came at the hands of guys like Chop Robinson, Malik Herring, Chris Johnson, and Zach Sieler.
Phillips, in comparison, had a very quiet performance - just one solo tackle, stopping Omar Cooper Jr. in his tracks after a 3-yard gain in the fourth quarter. Of all the playmakers in the trenches, he was the most pedestrian. He didn't hurt the Dolphins in the long run, partially because of Sieler's contributions, but it was disappointing to see nonetheless.
We debuted the first coach on one of these lists in Week 5, with STC Chris Tabor being named a loser. It's only fair to flip the script this week, and Hafley gets the honor for having his team ready to play from the start all the way to the finish.
It was a near-complete game on offense, defense, and special teams. Even with a 0-5 record, Hafley made sure his team gave everything they had against a division rival, and they did just enough to get the job done. It wasn't always perfect - the Dolphins committed five penalties but had no turnovers at the same time.
His signature moment was the decision to go for it on fourth down on the Dolphins' final drive to ice the game as opposed to punting the ball, which would have been the safer choice. Hafley noted postgame that he asked the offensive line if they wanted to do it, and trusted them when they said yes. It turned out to be the right decision as it was the prior two times they went for it on fourth down in this game.
This was overall a mediocre performance by Marshall. He was the victim of a ridiculous snag by Mason Taylor (son of Dolphins legend Jason Taylor) in the end zone for New York's sole touchdown in the first half.
The coverage on the play by Marshall wasn't bad, though he made the mistake of never looking back for the ball. Taylor simply went up and made a remarkable catch on National Tight Ends Day, no less. It was a quiet performance by Marshall all around, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but he'll definitely want to have that one play back.
Jake Gibson is a writer for the Miami Dolphins on SI. He began his sports journalism career with PantherNOW, the student newspaper at his alma mater, Florida International University, where he began as a sportswriter…

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 7 Snap Counts Stories: Tight End Time, Rookie Revelations
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 28-25 victory against the New York Jets on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by veterans Jalen Tolbert and Wille Gay Jr., the latter being kept out after missing practice time this week because of illness.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Kyle McCord and tight end Justin Joly. The rookie was active for only the second time this season.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies with the return of Caleb Douglas, even though he did replace fellow rookie Chris Bell as a starter. But fullback DJ Herman was back as a starter, joining Will Kacmarek at tight end, guard Kadyn Proctor, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- While it was Kacmarek who got the start, Greg Dulcich led all tight ends in offensive snaps with 42 compared to 29 for Kacmarek and 11 for rookie Seydou Traore. Before this game, Traore had played only one snap on offense, though head coach Jeff Hafley indicated he liked the progress he had seen from the fifth-round pick.
-- In his first game since the Week 2 loss at San Francisco, Douglas ended up playing 44 of the Dolphins' 65 offensive snaps, which wasn't as much as Malik Washington's 52 snaps but still a got play count in his first game back. And he sure made the most of his time on the field with his two touchdown catches.
-- With the Dolphins controlling the ball more than in any previous game (season-high 34:36 time of possession), Herman played a career-high 29 snaps on offense, topping the 27 he had against the Kansas City Chiefs in the home opener in Week 3.
-- Ollie Gordon II had his second 100-yard rushing outing in his third start and it came on 54 offensive snaps, which actually wasn't his highest total of the season. He played 61 snaps in the loss against Kansas City when he took over as the lead back following De'Von Achane's season-ending knee injury. The good news here is that Gordon clearly didn't slow down because he did some of his best work in the fourth quarter.
-- Newcomer Jared Wayne, claimed off waivers from the Houston Texans during the bye week, got 10 offensive snaps, the same number as Kevin Coleman Jr. Wayne's superior size and physicality makes him a more ideal option to help out with run blocking.
-- The Dolphins used Caedan Wallace as a sixth offensive lineman on five snaps, with mixed results.
-- With Douglas back, Chris Bell wound up with his second-lowest percentage of offensive snaps, his lowest since Week 2. Bell was on the field on offense for 31 snaps, less than half of the team's total.
-- Four players were on the field for all the team's 59 defensive snaps — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe and CB Chris Johnson.
-- Cornerback JuJu Brents was close as well, finishing with 53 snaps, but he left the game temporarily because of an injury. Brents opened with Jason Marshall Jr. on the outside and Johnson as the nick corner, a lineup the Dolphins used on about 50 percent of their defensive snaps.
-- Safety Dante Trader Jr. also left the game temporarily with an injury (shoulder), which led to Zayne Anderson getting 14 snaps on defense after he played only two against Cincinnati in Week 5.
-- Josh Uche, who continues what quietly has been a very solid season, again led the edge defenders with 43 snaps, compared to 38 for Chop Robinson. Malik Herring was next with 14, while Rodney McGraw was limited to seven snaps in his first game since being signed to the active roster.
-- On the interior of the defensive line, it's worth noting that Kenneth Grant played only 22 snaps in his second game of the season, the lowest total in the position group. Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips were pretty even with 31 and 29 snaps, with Zach Sieler as expected leading the way with 49.
-- In his return from injured reserve, rookie safety Kyle Louis saw his only action on special teams, which pretty much was to be expected (and we predicted it Saturday).
-- Speaking of special teams, Traore again led the way with 19 snaps, followed by 15 for Louis, Jackson Woodard, Julius Wood and Shaka Heyward. With Gay out of action, Woodard also got 29 snaps on defense when the Dolphins had a three-linebacker alignment.
