title: 3 Positions the Patriots May Address at the Trade Deadline
full_text:
After seven weeks, the New England Patriots are sitting in the thick of the AFC postseason race. They're 4-3, coming off a hard-fought TNF game against the Chicago Bears and now have a long break before their divisional battle with the Miami Dolphins.
But this team is far from perfect, and there are some holes that could be plugged up by the Nov. 10 trade deadline. Could the Patriots swing a trade to add some new help for the late-season push?
Here are three positions that the Patriots could potentially look at to bring a new face in via trade.
The Patriots have three running backs on the roster right now, so it might not make a lot of sense to add another one to the mix. But other than Rhamondre Stevenson, the Patriots haven't been able to get consistent week-after-week production from their backups.
TreVeyon Henderson, who was expected to have a large role this year in the passing attack, has really struggled on the ground — and carried the ball just three times on Thursday. Corey Kiner, a hard runner, just doesn't have the NFL experience yet for a larger workload.
So maybe the Patriots look to find some help with a receiving option. Tony Pollard, who was rumored to potentially join the Patriots through a trade last season, has 349 yards and one touchdown on a bad Tennessee Titans team. He fits the mold of a Josh McDaniels running back in this offense.
Injuries have depleted the interior of New England's offensive line . Mike Onwenu broke his ankle, Greg Van Roten was placed on IR one week later, Aliijah Vera-Tucker was just placed on IR this week and Ben Brown is dealing with an ankle injury. It's not a deep unit right now.
The Patriots have gotten inspiring play from backups Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse, but that pair — one that wasn't even with the team during the preseason — could be improved on ahead of the postseason. So maybe the Patriots try to swing for the fences with a new starter.
This one might be a pipe dream, but Quenton Nelson has been one of the league's top guards since being drafted by the Indianapolis Colts. If the Patriots want to try and get some additional protection for Drake Maye once the weather turns colder, finding a starting guard could help.
Another position banged up, the Patriots were without Carlton Davis , Channing Canada and Karon Prunty against the Bears. Charles Woods has stepped up in Davis' absence, and both Marcus Jones and Christian Gonzalez have been their usual selves. Kindle Vildor is also on the 53-man roster, rounding out that position group for now.
There is always room to try and bring in some new blood to shut down some of the receivers coming up on the Patriots' schedule. They're tasked to go against Justin Jefferson, Jaylen Waddle, D.J. Moore, Christian Watson and Garrett Wilson later this year, and while those guys will certainly be lined up against Gonzalez, another injury could be dangerous.
There are several guys who have seen their names tossed around trade talks, including Philadelphia's Kelee Ringo and Riq Woolen, Tampa Bay's Zyon McCollum and Los Angeles' Donte Jackson. A lot of this would depend on the health of Davis , who's dealt with a neck injury for the last few games.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: 3 Takeaways From Saints' Loss to Steelers: Same Problems, Different Country
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints traveled across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to build momentum heading into their bye week and salvage their season. Instead, they returned home with its fourth loss in five games and it just seems like another repeating nightmare for Who Dat Nation.
New Orleans fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in Paris, dropping to 2-5 through seven games under second-year coach Kellen Moore . It was the NFL's first regular-season game in France.
Despite another efficient passing performance from quarterback Tyler Shough , the Saints struggled to establish their rushing attack, failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities and couldn't get off the field defensively when it mattered most.
The loss marked New Orleans' third one-possession defeat this season, reinforcing concerns about the team's ability to execute in critical situations.
Here are three takeaways from another disappointing performance from the Saints performance.
For all the attention surrounding Shough's development, New Orleans' inability to run the football continues to undermine its offense.
Sunday's performance might have been its most concerning yet.
The Saints finished with just 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts, averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Even more alarming, Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards on three attempts. However, he is a quarterback and that is not his job.
But for Alvin Kamara (six carries for five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries for six yards) to have more carries than rushing yards is disgusting.
It shows the lack of life in a running back room without a primary option, compounded by an offensive line struggling to create leverage.
That level of production is unacceptable for any offense regardless of the level of play, especially one relying on a young quarterback to consistently move the ball.
Pittsburgh's defense shut down the run, forcing Shough to carry nearly the entire offensive load.
Although Shough completed nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans could not consistently finish drives because it lacked balance.
The problems extend beyond one disappointing performance.
New Orleans has struggled to generate consistent production on the ground throughout the season, making the offense increasingly predictable against physical defensive fronts.
Because of the rushing problems, the Saints had to rely on Shough again.
Shough did everything you could ask of him, completing 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards and a touchdown. However, one costly mistake ultimately changed the game's complexion.
Trailing 13-10 at the start of the second half, New Orleans put together a 13-play drive that moved the offense inside Pittsburgh's 10-yard line as the Saints appeared positioned to take their first lead of the afternoon.
Instead, Shough threw a pass intended for Chris Olave , which Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson intercepted at the Pittsburgh 11-yard line.
The turnover erased a scoring opportunity and let Pittsburgh respond with a field goal, extending its lead to 16-10.
The interception proved costly, but it also highlighted the impossible position Shough has found himself in because of New Orleans' offensive struggles.
Despite completing nearly 79% of his passes, the quarterback could not afford even one mistake because the Saints had virtually no rushing attack to complement him.
That is an unrealistic expectation for any quarterback, much less one still developing at the NFL level.
Shough showed he could move the football against a Pittsburgh defense, distributing the ball effectively and keeping New Orleans competitive despite a one-dimensional offensive approach.
However, his play reinforced a troubling reality: when Shough plays well, the Saints can win; when he makes one mistake, the operation unravels.
Until Moore builds a credible run game and finishes drives, Shough bears an unreasonable load and New Orleans must create an offense where its quarterback does not need to be perfect to win.
Unless the Saints give Shough a credible rushing attack and adequate protection, they risk repeating a familiar chapter in franchise history: asking a talented young quarterback to overcome problems far beyond his control, much like Archie Manning decades ago.
Daniel Carlson 's fourth missed field goal in 11 attempts this season — a 52-yarder in the fourth quarter — kept New Orleans trailing in a 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, highlighting a critical special teams weakness for the 2-5 Saints.
The missed 52-yard attempt came while the Saints trailed 16-10 in the fourth quarter, keeping Pittsburgh's lead at six points. Carlson's 63.6% success rate contrasts with Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who converted all three attempts (28, 47 and 39 yards) for nine points.
The fourth-quarter miss was especially costly as New Orleans had already squandered a promising red-zone drive earlier in the second half. Instead of entering the final minutes needing only a field goal to tie or lead, the Saints remained six points behind.
Carlson's kicking struggles add to head coach Kellen Moore's bye-week concerns. For a team hampered by offensive inefficiency, defensive lapses and turnovers, unreliable special teams further shrink a narrow margin for error.
With three one-score losses this season, New Orleans cannot afford missed points. Sunday's loss highlights that the Saints lack the margin for error to overcome recurring scoring mistakes in tight games.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

title: Saints vs. Steelers: Injury Concerns Mount Ahead of Historic Paris Showdown
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints face several injury concerns as they prepare for Sunday's historic international matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France in Paris.
Running back Alvin Kamara and starting offensive guard Cesar Ruiz headline New Orleans' injury report, while Pittsburgh is monitoring several key defensive players, including T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
According to the Saints' official Thursday injury report , 11 New Orleans players were listed Thursday, with three missing practice and three participating on a limited basis.
The Saints (2-4) are looking to build momentum following Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped a three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Pittsburgh (4-2) enters the matchup seeking its second consecutive victory.
Both teams have several injury situations worth monitoring before Friday's final practice report.
The Saints' biggest offensive concerns involve Kamara and Ruiz, who have been dealing with back and knee injuries, respectively.
Kamara was limited for the second consecutive practice Thursday, leaving his availability worth monitoring heading into Sunday's game.
The veteran running back remains an important part of Kellen Moore's offense, particularly as New Orleans attempts to establish a more consistent rushing attack.
Ruiz's situation is potentially more concerning. The veteran offensive lineman missed practice Wednesday and Thursday because of a knee injury, raising questions about his availability against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
However, Jeremiah Wright played well in his absence during New Orleans’ win over the Giants last week.
Meanwhile, linebacker Kaden Elliss (calf) and edge rusher Anfernee Jennings (knee) were limited for the second consecutive day. During today's player roundtable , Elliss was asked if he would be available to play Sunday, and he said, "Yes."
There was some encouraging news for New Orleans.
Shough, who appeared on the report with a left-hand injury, participated fully in both practices. Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (head) and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd (illness) also practiced without limitations.
Running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) improved from limited participation Wednesday to a full practice Thursday.
Kicker Daniel Carlson missed his second consecutive practice because of a personal matter unrelated to injury (he and his wife are having a baby), while defensive lineman Davon Godchaux received a rest day Thursday.
Backup quarterback Spencer Rattler was added to Thursday's report with a knee injury but participated fully.
Pittsburgh is also dealing with significant injury concerns, particularly on defense.
The most notable development Thursday was star edge rusher T.J. Watt, who was limited with a calf injury after sitting out Wednesday's practice for rest.
Watt's status matters, given the Saints' offensive line concerns. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks through six games.
Fellow pass rusher Alex Highsmith remained limited with a groin injury, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward missed his second straight practice for rest.
The Steelers also received encouraging news about star cornerback Jalen Ramsey, who returned to practice on Thursday, albeit in a limited capacity. He missed Wednesday's session with a wrist injury.

title: Saints Stock Up: 3 Heroes From New Orleans' Win Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints earned a much-needed victory over the New York Giants as they broke a three-game losing streak.
Now, the Saints are in Paris as they turn their attention to the Pittsburgh Steelers to win consecutive games for the first time this season. However, it will be a tough task: Pittsburgh still has a solid quarterback in Aaron Rodgers at 42, and the offense has plenty of weapons; on defense, they have a solid pass rush.
After fully reviewing the Saints’ win over New York and looking at which players have been trending upward, here are three players whose stock is rising.
The Saints historically produce standout special teams performers, including Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis , and Steve Gleason .
Linebacker Isaiah Stalbird has continued that tradition this year, keying special teams unit success and executing the decisive sequence of the game.
Down 10-3 late in the second quarter, New Orleans seemed poised for a halftime deficit before Stalbird made a game-altering play on coverage.
The second-year backer stripped the ball from Charlie Jones on a kickoff return, which tight end Oscar Delp recovered to set up New Orleans inside the red zone.
Shough converted the takeaway into points, finding rookie Bryce Lance for a game-tying touchdown right before the break.
That turnover shifted game momentum entirely and helped spark a 31-point unanswered run that gave New Orleans a 34-10 lead before the Giants mounted a furious fourth-quarter comeback.
Cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. posted his top outing of the year in the 34-27 victory, accumulating seven tackles, two interceptions, and four pass breakups.
His effort earned an 88.4 defensive rating and a 90.2 coverage rating from Pro Football Focus, leading all team defenders in Week 6. Emerson was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his efforts.
Emerson held opponents to four catches on 10 targeted passes while picking off throws from Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy . The performance provided valuable depth after Kool-Aid McKinstry exited due to a migraine.
Rookie guard Jeremiah Wright capitalized on unexpected playing time against New York, filling in when starter Cesar Ruiz left with a knee injury in the second quarter.
If one thing is certain, the run game started to click when Wright went into the game as he added toughness to the interior line, anchoring a run game that piled up a season-best 175 yards. If you want to know how much of an impact Wright had? When the Saints ran to the right, they averaged just over 5 yards per carry. When they ran to the left? 3.1-yards a clip.
The fourth-round selection surrendered just a single QB pressure in his most extensive action of the season.

title: Banged Up but Winning: Giants Hold the NFC East Lead at the Bye
full_text:
Franchise quarterback. Elite pass rusher. Anchor middle linebacker. Let's start with how season-ending injuries in critical spots have created numerous obstacles for the New York Giants , who enter their bye week atop the NFC East.
Sure, they haven't always painted a pretty picture in fighting their way to a 4-2-1 record, but NFL teams don't get any extra credit for style points. The reality is that the Giants have already beaten the second-place Dallas Cowboys (3-4) and are one of five NFC teams to have two or fewer losses this season.
Piece by piece, coach John Harbaugh has called upon the depth chart built by general manager Joe Schoen to navigate significant detours along the way.
"It's just a matter of keep growing and keep building our execution and our ability to do things the right way at a high level. It takes that; it's a race," Harbaugh said this week.
"It's a marathon, but a marathon - I've been told - is a series of sprints, one after another. That's really what we're doing, a series of sprints, so we'll get a little bit of a break here, grab some Gatorade and a granola bar at the table, and then we'll be back into the race when we get back."
General managers usually say the season is the easiest part of their jobs because they're in charge of offseason roster building. It's clear Schoen and Harbaugh collaborated to improve the Giants' depth from the moment the new coach was hired, and it didn't come only through the draft with the likes of linebacker Arvel Reese and Francis Maguinoa.
The retention of middle linebacker Micah McFadden in his comeback from a broken foot, the signing of veteran cornerback Greg Newsome and the return of former Giants safety Jason Pinnock are just a few of the significant moves that have paid dividends.
Yet none may be more important than the early-season trade that sent a fifth-round draft choice to the Minnesota Vikings for quarterback J.J. McCarthy, who was sensational in his first Giants start while beating the Houston Texans on the road in overtime.
QB Jaxson Dart, LBs Brian Burns and Tremaine Edmunds, DL Chauncey Golston and Roy Robertson-Harris, WR Calvin Austin, and RET Gunner Olszewski. Each was expected to play a key role, but season-ending injuries have forced the Giants to rely on improved depth to maintain their preseason goal of challenging for the playoffs.
Schoen explained how the team expects to move forward in the second half of the season in his annual state-of-the-team address during the bye week. title: After Buckner Trade to 49ers, Two More D-Line Trade Targets for the Giants
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ biggest need ahead of the trade deadline remains their defensive line.
Despite pouring so many resources into the unit since the offseason, including the recent signing of veteran Dean Lowry to the practice squad, the depth behind starters Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader remains suspect, particularly against the run.
When either or both of Harris and Reader are on the field, opposing offenses have averaged 4.4 yards per carry. When one or both are off the field, that average has jumped to 5.2 yards per carry.
Their absences have also been felt on third down. When either or both of Harris and Reader have been on the field, opponents have converted 64.3% of their third-down attempts. When both have been off the field, that percentage has increased to 71.4%.
If the Giants are all in on making a run for the NFC East title this year, and they clearly are, it may be worth trading for a veteran defensive lineman who can provide more consistency, particularly against the run, where the defense has been erratic.
With DeForest Buckner traded from the Colts back to the San Francisco 49ers for a fourth-round draft pick , here are a couple of other options the Giants could consider to upgrade their defensive line depth.
The Dolphins are going nowhere this season as they work their way out from under the salary cap mess created in part by releasing quarterback Tua Tagovailoa.
So it’s fair to wonder whether they might embark on a fire sale to add to their nine picks in 2027.
Zach Sieler, in the first year of a three-year, $64 million deal signed with Miami this past offseason, has historically been a solid defensive lineman, according to his PFF grades . This year, that hasn’t been the case, but then again, few Dolphins players can be described as solid.
Sieler, a seventh-round pick of the Ravens under Harbaugh in 2018, has 13 quarterback pressures and 13 stops through six games. He has missed only three tackles.
If the Giants were to acquire Sieler, they would be on the hook this year for $76,470 for each week he is on their roster. Per reports, Sieler would prefer to stay with Miami .
As for compensation, Buckner, a three-time Pro Bowler and two-time All-Pro, fetched a fourth-round pick, so the Giants could ask the Dolphins for one of their two sixth-rounders in 2027, the second of which they acquired in the trade that sent offensive lineman Daniel Faalele to the Jaguars.
Or, if the Giants don’t want to keep draining their 2027 draft picks, they might offer a 2028 pick instead.
Like Sieler, Dalvin Tomlinson has a connection to Giants head coach John Harbaugh, albeit through Harbaugh’s brother, Jim, the Chargers' head coach.
Tomlinson, 6-foot-3 and 317 pounds, began his career as the Giants' second-round pick in 2017. He spent his first four seasons with Big Blue, then signed with the Vikings as an unrestricted free agent. After two seasons in Minnesota, Tomlinson spent two years with the Browns and one with the Cardinals.
He signed with the Chargers this past offseason on a one-year deal worth up to $6.5 million.
Tomlinson is another player who could potentially be worth a sixth-round pick in a trade. If the Giants acquired him, he would cost a cap-friendly $158,235 per week.
He can also earn $30,000 for each week he is active, with playtime incentives of up to $1 million based on cumulative game snaps and a $300,000 weight clause, according to Spotrac .

title: Giants Place RB Tyrone Tracy Jr. on IR; Add Former Chargers Runner to Roster
full_text:
Another week, another New York Giants player is heading to injured reserve.
Running back Tyrone Tracy Jr., who injured his hamstring in the second quarter of Sunday’s game against the Houston Texans, will be placed on IR this week, general manager Joe Schoen announced ahead of his annual bye-week press briefing.
Tracy, the team’s fifth-round draft pick in 2024, has appeared in all seven games this season without making a start.
He has 19 rushing attempts for 55 yards and two touchdowns and has caught five of seven targets for 54 yards and a touchdown. He was looking to record his third straight season with 1,000 scrimmage yards, but that goal now appears to be a long shot.
Taking Tracy’s spot on the 53-man roster is running back Greg Desrosiers, whom the Giants signed off the Chargers’ practice squad. Desrosiers, 5-foot-11 and 200 pounds, signed with the Chargers as an undrafted free agent out of Memphis after this year’s draft.
Desrosiers had a six-year college career, playing two seasons each for Louisville, Massachusetts and Memphis. He finished with 211 carries for 1,302 yards and 16 touchdowns, and 76 receptions for 612 yards and seven touchdowns as a receiver.
This past summer, Desrosiers appeared in all three preseason games for the Chargers, rushing for 166 yards on 23 carries with one touchdown and catching one of two targets for eight yards.

title: Giants Make Long Anticipated Practice Squad Signing
full_text:
The New York Giants are finally signing defensive lineman Dean Lowry to their practice squad, general manager Joe Schoen confirmed.
Lowry, who played for the Steelers until they released him after this past summer’s training camp, was first linked to the Giants in September , but the chatter died down quickly when the move didn’t materialize.
Lowry suffered a torn ACL in August 2025, so the Giants may have waited to see how his rehab progressed this past summer.
Either way, Lowry, 6-foot-6 and 300 pounds, brings veteran experience to a defensive line group that, outside of starters D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris, has been inconsistent, especially against the run.
The Packers selected Lowry in the fourth round of the 2016 draft out of Northwestern. He played for Green Bay until the 2022 season before moving on to the Vikings for one season and then to the Steelers.
Lowry, 32, has appeared in 132 regular-season games with 85 starts and has 271 career tackles, 23 tackles for loss, 16.5 sacks, one interception and five fumble recoveries.
His best season came in 2021 with Green Bay, when he recorded five sacks in 17 starts.
Lowry’s skill set likely aligns with what the Giants previously had Chauncey Golston doing on the defensive line: a rotational pass rusher at 5-technique, or at 3-technique in an odd front.
Golston is on season-ending injured reserve with a neck ailment.
The Giants released receiver Jason Brownlee fromt he practice squad to make room for Lowry.

title: What Giants’ Week 7 Win Changed About Their Trade Deadline Plans
full_text:
Maybe, just maybe, the New York Giants ’ roster needs aren’t what they thought they were.
Ahead of their Week 7 game against the Houston Texans, the Giants were thought to need a running back to boost a sagging rushing attack. The unit ranked 22nd in the league at a dismal 3.8 yards per carry, its 629 rushing yards ranked 16th, and its offensive success rate of 43.2% ranked 20th.
But after head coach John Harbaugh challenged his running backs to step up, they delivered a historic performance. For the first time since October 1950, four different runners scored a touchdown in a 27-21 overtime win over the Texans.
With the rushing game delivering 188 yards on 34 carries against what had been the league’s third-ranked run defense, New York has quelled the calls for a trade for a running back such as Colts star Jonathan Taylor, who is believed to be among those the Colts are considering moving by the November 10 trade deadline.
This isn’t to say that the Giants won’t need to add to the running back group at some point. New York is undoubtedly holding its collective breath that the hamstring injuries suffered by Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy Jr. heal up over the bye.
But with the running game boosted not just by the backs themselves but also by the insertion of quarterback J.J. McCarthy, who brings back the RPO threat, the need to trade for a running back isn’t as great as it once was.
That all being said, the Giants still need to watch the future.
Running back Devin Singletary is in the final year of his contract, and there is no guarantee he’ll be back with the team after this year.
Skattebo, despite the energy he brings to the game, is still part of a rotation that has seen him primarily handle the early-down and goal-line duties, casting doubt on whether he’s a legitimate RB1 or just someone who, by virtue of the Giants’ running back room, has been thrust into that role.
And Tracy is more of a change-of-pace back than the bell cow Harbaugh seems to want in the offense.
Remember, it wasn’t that long ago when the Giants reportedly had strong interest in former Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love, who was taken one pick before the Giants went on the clock this past April.
It also wasn’t that long ago that Harbaugh yearned for a workhorse running back like the one he had in Baltimore with Derrick Henry. He said he “would love for us” to have “a Derrick Henry circumstance.”
But Harbaugh and the Giants must honestly answer whether they are one running back away from not only making the postseason but also staying there once they do.
If their current running backs keep delivering as they did against the Texans, they could defer adding a workhorse running back until next offseason, when they can get someone either in free agency or on a rookie contract via the draft.

title: Giants Rookie Report: Reese, Mauigoa and Fields Shine in Overtime Win Over Texans
full_text:
Earning a hard-fought road win one week after an embarrassing home performance marks a rising, maturing football team. When rookies overcome the same circumstances, then you really have something cooking. John Harbaugh is building a culture on the New York Giants .
Big Blue’s first-timers responded after a Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, playing a key role in Sunday’s 27-21 overtime win over the Houston Texans.
Several rookies dazzled, but a couple of outings were underwhelming. Let’s check in on the rookies after a jubilant Week 7.
The former Ohio State star linebacker has had some lows in his first NFL season, but the highs have been far more frequent and mighty impressive.
Arvell Reese demonstrated his superb athleticism and excellent hustle on one play, pressuring Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud before running downfield to make the tackle. Only a select few can cover the field that swiftly, and they are not typically rookies.
Reese contributed to a relentless defensive attack, posting half a sack and seven total tackles. A No. 5 overall pick should have exceptional physical gifts, but there is no guarantee he will play with a high motor. Reese is fulfilling both categories so far.
Miami powerhouse Francis “Sisi” Mauigoa has occasionally looked like a weak link on the offensive line, which is understandable given his move from tackle. Still, at other times he has carried himself like a seasoned pro. His showing in Houston definitely falls under the latter.
Mauigoa recorded a 100 percent pass-block win rate, per Pro Football Focus, providing stalwart protection for J.J. McCarthy in his first Giants start and creating more opportunities for the Cam Skattebo-led backfield.
His continued development could determine just how good this O-line and offense become.
Malachi Fields officially introduced himself to fans with a breakout game at NRG Stadium. The 6-foot-4 wide receiver used his size and strength to punish Houston. He recorded a career-high four receptions for 83 yards.
With tremendous sideline awareness, Fields created space and then shook off the defense for 40 yards after the catch. He was every bit the deep threat that Joe Schoen and John Harbaugh invested in at the NFL Draft. And he is just getting started.
The Giants will not achieve meaningful success unless the defensive tackle group is solid. Bobby Jamison-Travis may be the missing link the team has been searching for over the last couple of years. He added an indisputable boost in Week 7.
The sixth-round selection was an active member of a run defense that held Woody Marks to a meager 3.5 yards per carry. He logged 24 snaps , six more than he did against the Saints, and could get even more after the bye.
Jamison-Travis does not need to be a Day 3 gem. Competent play will more than suffice.
The returning Paulson Adebo filled in for the injured Greg Newsome II, leaving no room for Colton Hood in the secondary. He did help out on special teams, however.
The No. 37 overall pick played 14 snaps and appeared to hold his own. Until he learns the nuances of being an NFL cornerback, Hood will have to make the most of his chances in the third phase of the game.
J.C. Davis added immediate value at left tackle in Week 6, when Andrew Thomas was evaluated for a concussion. With Thomas back this week, Davis did not see time on the line and instead got some work on special teams.
The unit was sharper than it was against New Orleans, and the 6-foot-4, 322-pounder did his part. If needed, Harbaugh should feel comfortable giving the AP All-Big Ten first-team selection more opportunities on the O-line.
Generally a reliable special teams contributor, sixth-rounder Jack Kelly took a slight step back in Houston. He missed a tackle , which is always a concern in coverage situations.
Still, Kelly deserves some trust given the film he has put together for New York in 2026.
The undrafted kicker is in free fall. Dominic Zvada is surely running out of chances after missing 56- and 44-yard field goals against the Texans. Those blunders could easily have been the difference in the game if the squad hadn’t excelled in most other areas.
Zvada is still in a precarious position. All the goodwill he stored by nailing his first nine field goal attempts has nearly evaporated.
Harbaugh is not ready to make a change yet, though, so the 2024 Big Ten Kicker of the Year must straighten out during the bye week.

title: Giants Defense Review: Banks, Reese and McFadden Lead a Best-of-the-Year Showing in Houston
full_text:
Just when the Houston Texans offense thought it had finally found its stride, the New York Giants defense showed up.
Big Blue held the Texans to just 153 passing yards in their Week 7 game, their lowest allowed by the Giants defense this season.
A big reason was the stellar play of the defensive secondary, especially cornerback Deonte Banks, who is having a banner year.
Banks wasn’t alone. Linebacker Abdul Carter was a pesky presence in the pass rush, and Micah McFadden took up Tremaine Edmunds’ mantle as a tracking machine, leading the team with 10 tackles (all solo).
It wasn’t a perfect showing, but it was a lot better than the week before, with the defense stepping up to answer defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson’s challenge to play better. And the unit certainly did.
Let’s dive into the player-by-player grades for the defense and for special teams.
The gap in effectiveness between Reader and his D-line mates seems to be widening by the week.
Reader wasn’t only the pit’s best run defender Sunday; he was easily the interior’s best pass rusher, with a handful of quick moves around his man that hurried the quarterback into quicker decisions.
One of Reader’s inside wins turned into a hit on the quarterback and forced a big fourth-quarter incompletion.
Reader pitched in with 2 more tackles, holding his turf as well as we’ve seen any nose tackle do, or at least since Dexter Lawrence’s heyday with the team.
Active again after sitting out last week, Okoye received some rotation snaps inside and flashed on one run play, but otherwise he was pushed around and was slow to react.
Getting another start at defensive end, the veteran Harris made a couple of flash moves attacking the gap, but he remained ineffective holding his ground at the point of attack.
Harris earned one of the defense’s few hits on the quarterback when he shot up the gap, and he contributed 2 tackles on run downs.
Falling back into his non-factor shell against the run, Alexander got credit for a half-sack when he helped chase a scrambling quarterback out of bounds for no gain.
Alexander then chirped at the quarterback as if he’d made a play, which was hardly an athletic football play. He did manage to work his way into a run-game tackle, but he remains a big body with a lack of feel for D-line play.
One of the few D-line highlights was this rookie's active role.
Jamison-Travis looks like a keeper, holding his point of attack against double teams more stoutly than most.
He also has shown enough mobility to get into plays on the edge, which is where most nose tackles fear to tread. The kid finished with 3 total tackles and showed up around some other piles, too.
The leader of the front seven continues to disrupt things around the edges at a high rate.
He drew two holding calls, and there should have been two more, his biggest coming in overtime on third down, when he flew around the edge.
Though he didn’t finish any sacks, he was once again a major disruptive force on a front group that is sorely lacking them.
Carter finished with 4 total tackles, continuing to contribute against the run and short edge coverage in the flat in pursuit, but when he attacks the line of scrimmage, you really ought to lean forward and enjoy the show.
He was electric out there once again.
The polar opposite of Carter on the edge, Thibodeaux has settled into a power defensive end role with very little attack mobility in his arsenal.
His pass rushes were the bull-rush variety, but he lacks the power to beat his man.
He also lacks the foot speed to make any plays in space. He dropped a “sure” interception in overtime on a drop back into zone coverage, the ball hitting him right in the hands. For some reason, he started to run with the ball before securing it.
The one thing he does well these days is hold his edge with power against the run and close down in pursuit when unblocked.
Thibodeaux did this well enough to earn 4 total tackles against the run. Against the pass, he was a non-factor.
Getting plenty of edge snaps, Ford played with effort but only got in on 1 tackle.
Against double teams of tight ends on several occasions, he was easily swallowed up and lost his edge.
His pass rush game has petered off, though he did draw a holding penalty on an edge play.
Getting a handful of snaps on the edge as a power contain guy, Harrison held his ground firmly and kept everything inside of him, where it belonged.
Continuing his march to the Defensive Rookie of the Year award, Reese added 7 more tackles, including a half-sack, a tackle against a screen pass for a loss of 4 yards, and a handful of definitive finishes on plays that seemed like threats until Reese arrived and ended them. He also drew a holding penalty on a tight end he overpowered in his block attempt. He is such an enforcer.
Reese also just missed a sack after beating his man on an inside blitz. He is particularly dangerous on these blitzes because he can beat his blocker with speed, power, or both.
The defense’s surprise leading tackler was McFadden, who stepped up after Tremaine Edmunds finished for the season.
McFadden’s 10 solo tackles included 2 in the backfield, one of which came close to a forced fumble and return for a touchdown, as McFadden’s hit bent the RB over.
McFadden’s quick reads were on point all over the place. If he can teach Reese the secret of his quick reads, then Reese may have to be outlawed.
For McFadden to be so effective despite his size, short arms, and mediocre speed and athleticism, it goes to show how far you can go with a lightning-fast processing chip in your brain.
McFadden gave up plays in coverage because he can’t make those plays. The miss in the back of the end zone for a Houston touchdown was one of them. But his on-point control of cutbacks and reads was sharp throughout.
McFadden also factored into the blitz, drawing a hold on one of them and recording a quarterback hit on another (on Houston’s last offensive snap in OT).
Talk about depth: the defense just lost its play-caller, Edmunds; his replacement steps in, and the defense plays its best game of the year.
Playing his best game of the year (which is saying something, since he’s excelled from the get-go), Banks took Houston’s leading receiver, Nico Collins, with his three successive 1,000-yard seasons, put him in his back pocket, and kept him there for the duration.
Collins finished with 2 catches for 6 yards, and one of those catches wasn’t even against Banks. Suffice it to say that Banks continues to play the best football of his career in coverage.
He also added 2 tackles and 2 passes defensed. He’s even showing up for his contain on the edge and not flinching away from contact (baby steps).
Banks is a strange one. He shows great courage returning kicks, yet has long shied away from contact on defense.
Regardless, he’s playing top-shelf press coverage right now, and it’s a perfect fit in this defense.
This hard-tackling slot cornerback kept getting isolated in coverage, and it resulted in two flags: one for holding (a very iffy call) and one legit pass interference for grabbing his man’s hand while in trail technique.
If he continues to be a liability in coverage, the coaches will have no choice but to get him off the field on passing downs.
His blitzes came up empty, and he wasn’t around the ball often enough to record more than his one lone tackle.
The return of this veteran boundary corner helped make up for the absence of Greg Newsome II (concussion). With Adebo back in the fold, Phillips should lose significant playing time.
Adebo’s coverage was sharp and deep most of the day. He has an aversion to getting beat deep, so he usually and willingly gives up the short stuff. That didn’t happen Sunday.
It will be interesting to watch how this veteran settles into a defensive backs group that has excelled playing an aggressive style. That doesn’t seem to fit Adebo’s style much, but his length and long speed are legit factors in his game.

title: Cowboys or Eagles? Giants Fans Face a Rooting Dilemma on Monday Night
full_text:
In a cruel twist, New York Giants fans face a rooting dilemma ahead of Monday Night Football that, no matter which way they lean, feels a bit like a betrayal.
With Big Blue comfortably in first place, fans could be forgiven this week if they root for one divisional opponent to beat the other, right?
That’s the dilemma Giants fans face regarding the Monday night matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles, who square off at Lincoln Financial Field.
Both teams are 2-4, behind the Giants, who sit atop the NFC East at 4-2-1 and will remain there regardless of what happens on Monday night. (The Commanders, at 1-4-1, have a bye this week.)
So who should Giants fans root for in the Monday night game? On the one hand, the answer should be the Eagles, whose roster has been significantly gutted. An Eagles win over the Cowboys would drop Dallas, widely regarded as the Giants’ biggest competition for the division crown, to 2-5 on the year.
Then there is the argument that Giants fans would be better off rooting for the Cowboys, who, if they win, would improve to 3-4 and move into second place in the division, while dropping the Eagles to 2-5.
The answer may come down to personal preference, but outside of rooting for a tie, it probably makes more sense for Big Blue faithful to root for the Cowboys.
Remember, the Giants already have a 1-0 head-to-head advantage over Dallas, which gives them a tiebreaker edge.
Meanwhile, the Giants haven’t faced the Eagles yet. That game is on tap after the bye, and it will take place at Philadelphia’s “House of Horrors,” a.k.a. Lincoln Financial Field, where the Giants have not won a game (regular season or postseason) since Oct. 27, 2013.
To put that dry spell into perspective, since that last win as led by Eli Manning, the Giants have used 12 different starting quarterbacks.
This is a new era of Giants football, and head coach John Harbaugh has the players believing they can beat anyone at any place and any time.
That was evident in how they went after a Houston Texans team that, despite entering the Week 7 game with a 2-4 record, boasted a top defense and a surging offense, neither of which did much to stop a determined Giants team.
And did we mention the Giants won that game without their starting quarterback (Jaxson Dart), their starting inside linebacker (Tremaine Edmunds), one of their starting cornerbacks (Greg Newsome II), and one of their starting safeties (Jevon Holland)?
So maybe at the end of the day, it doesn’t matter who Giants fans root for tonight, unless it’s for the Eagles and Cowboys to somehow beat up each other physically.

title: John Harbaugh Offers Update on Giants’ Kicker Plans
full_text:
Despite missing field goals in two of his last three games, New York Giants placekicker Dominic Zvada does not appear to be in danger of losing his job.
That’s the word from head coach John Harbaugh, who, when asked if there were plans to try out new kickers, said, “We’re not going to be doing that right now, no.”
Zvada, a rookie who impressed the coaches with his strong leg and long-distance accuracy, started the season going 9-of-9.
But the magic seemed to run out on him in Week 4, in a rain-soaked game at Washington, when he missed three of his five field goal attempts.
He steadied himself last week in the loss to the Saints, a game after which Harbaugh cited a technique issue with Zvada’s plant leg as the culprit behind the Washington misses.
Against the Texans, though, Zvada was off target again, missing both attempts in the win.
All of Zvada’s misses have come from 50-plus yards, where he is 5-of-8 this season. Against the Texans, after he showed signs of struggle again, the Giants decided to punt rather than attempt another long-distance field goal after reaching the Texans’ 37-yard line.
Zvada and the Giants lead the league in field goal attempts from 50 or more yards. Zvada’s 62.5% conversion rate on those long-distance field goals ranks 18th among kickers, but his overall field goal conversion rate (72.2%) ranks 27th.
"I think from a confidence standpoint, I believe you don't have to check in with him, you just got to remind him that he is damn good," assistant head coach/special teams coordiantor Chris Horton said of Zvada two weeks ago.
"That's one of the things I think when you believe in your players again, and you remind them that they're here for a reason and you trust in them. You’ve just got to remind them of those things. From a confidence standpoint, that's solely on him and him understanding that I can go out there and I can do this."
The Giants are on their bye this week. Harbaugh said the players were in on Monday for a film review session and will be in again on Tuesday for a light workout before being given Wednesday through Sunday off for the bye.
“We’ll take advantage of that as much as we can; we have five full days plus a little bit for them to rest, recover, all three phases, you know, mind, spirit, body. And then we’ll be back Monday afternoon to start on the Eagles.”

title: Giants Offensive Player Grades: McCarthy Stays in Control as Run Game Rolls
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ 27-21 overtime win against the Houston Texans was a masterclass in “slow and steady wins the race.”
Led by quarterback J.J. McCarthy, who made his first start for Big Blue, the Giants offense dominated a very good Houston Texans defense, racking up 420 yards and 22 first downs while averaging an impressive 6.5 yards per play.
The Giants running attack, challenged by head coach John Harbaugh to step up, did just that, totaling 188 yards on 34 carries (5.5 yards per carry). And all four of the Giants’ scores came on the ground.
The Giants pulled off an inspiring win, though many thought they were heading into the lion’s den without a chance; instead, they emerged with a win to improve to 4-2-1 and strengthen their hold on first place in the division.
Let’s get into this week’s grades.
After last week’s scintillating fourth-quarter performance, McCarthy came out as the team’s new starter, slinging it again, though in a much more controlled manner.
To throw the ball into so many tight places and never once put it in danger is mind-boggling, but that’s what this kid has done through five-plus quarters with the Giants.
McCarthy’s first half, while still playing in a new offense, in enemy territory, against one of the league’s best defenses, was close to spectacular. His 9-of-12 first-half throws show he wasn’t throwing it all over the ballyard; he threw it under control, with timing, accuracy, and audacity.
On his third throw of the game, he went up top to Malik Nabers for 42 yards on the throw that truly opened up the field. He then threw another 17 yards to Nabers, 49 yards to Malachi Fields, 29 yards to tight end Thomas Fidone, and another 27 yards to Nabers.
What did all this downfield throwing do? It opened up things for the running game (188 yards total on the day), and they were legit rushing yards with not a single scramble to pad the total.
Why did the Giants run the ball so well against the league’s third-ranked run defense? How did the Giants earn a 35:50-to-26:45 time-of-possession edge and a total net-yard advantage (420 to 237)?
With McCarthy attacking Houston’s vaunted corners downfield early and often, the entire defense had to back off.
The quarterback’s second half wasn’t quite as sharp, but it wasn’t needed. And when it was needed, McCarthy answered the bell.
A favorite throw by McCarthy was the 3rd-and-9 deep out, where he hit Fields in stride to beat a blitz and get the first down, right before Cam Skattebo’s touchdown run took a fourth-quarter lead.
This week wasn’t one of those crazy up-and-down passing affairs that seem to dominate the league. It was a controlled demolition by the Giants, with their quarterback managing the game smartly, making every throw that had to be made, and quarterbacking a running attack that wore down the Texans by game’s end.
When you have a quarterback who can make every throw, and isn’t afraid to try every throw, then you have a chance to open up the defense and win any way you like. McCarthy won Sunday’s game from the pocket, and that’s where we prefer to keep him.
However, he also has the mobility to run an RPO (two this week, both successful handoffs) and scramble away from pressure and hurt the defense with his legs. He truly is a quarterback for the modern game and looks like a real value for the Giants, who gave up a fifth-round pick to get him.
Contributing four successful “tush-pushes” (including a touchdown) and one nifty handoff to Cam Skattebo on another fake tush-push that went for 19 yards on a key second-half 4th-and-1 is pretty good production for the team’s backup quarterback.
Also, give credit to the coaches for keeping Winston in the offense and recognizing one thing he does quite well: short-yardage quarterbacking.
It boggled the mind that Skattebo was flagged for unnecessary roughness for lowering his head in traffic and annihilating a safety, who also lowered his head on the play. Incredibly, the officials can throw this flag and yet ignore the scores of defensive players lowering their heads into tackles.
Skattebo’s sin is that he does it so aggressively and finishes his hits with a toughness not often seen from the running back position that it doesn’t seem fair to the defense.
You know what? Too bad. Physicality is what Skattebo does best. You rarely see the NFL write rules that so clearly favor the defense, but this is one of them.
As for Skattebo’s game, it was classic ground-and-pound. He was responsible for three big yardage plays: the 19-yard fake tush-push, the 16-yard fourth-quarter rushing touchdown (his best run of the day, in which he broke and shed at least five tackles on his way into the end zone), and his 42-yard burst in overtime that set up the Giants for the winning score.
The big plays are huge, but the little plays into the teeth of the defense eventually wore the Texans down. It was power running at its purest, a style that Skattebo is built for.
He came up gimpy at the end of that overtime run after tweaking his hamstring, which hopefully will heal over the bye week.
Also in need of some bye-week R&R, Tracy was forced out of the game late in the second quarter after suffering a hamstring pull that ended his day.
Before that, Tracy made a couple of solid plays with the ball in his hands, the best one a neat cut near the goal line to avoid a tackler and get into the end zone for the team’s opening score.
Tracy’s numbers were modest: 6 carries for 15 yards and 1 catch for 2 yards. He seems to have locked down the third-down role while also serving as a rotation back.
With the other two backs suffering in-game injuries, “Mr. Reliable” had to step into the breach and calm everyone down.
Singletary caught 3 balls out of the backfield for 14 yards and had another 41 yards on the ground, the big play being his 30-yard game-winning jaunt around left end to finish things off for the big underdog visiting team.
This veteran always brings an often-needed calming presence to his many younger teammates.
With him logging his fourth straight 100-plus-yard receiving game, Nabers has become one of this team’s go-to players who always wants the ball in big situations.
We were thrilled early on when he beat single coverage deep and came down with the long ball for a 42-yard punch-in-the-mouth moment to the Texans.
Nabers never quite got deep again, but the threat opened up space for catches of 17 and 27 yards, plus a bunch of short but positive completions.
Nabers finished with 7 catches for 111 yards as he continued to take the league by storm.
He did have a rare drop over the middle on one of those J.J. McCarthy bullet throws, but Nabers’ route-running remains as clean and reliable as it gets.
Having his best game as a pro, the hard-blocking rookie (watch his take-out of two Houston defensive backs on the game-winning run) finished with 4 catches for 83 yards.
The big play was a clean down-and-out route: the quarterback got the ball to him right out of his break, with just enough time to shrug off his man.
Fields then took the ball upfield along the sideline for another north-south 20 yards after contact, refusing to go down; he never did go out of bounds. This big chunk play was the offense’s longest of the day (47 yards).
Fields also caught balls for 14 and 20 yards. Though we’re still waiting on those downfield, boundary jump balls that he allegedly specializes in, Fields continues to run clean routes and make his quarterback look good by catching everything that comes his way, including low throws.
It’s so nice to have reliable receivers who actually catch the ball. Fields is also showing some intriguing yards-after-contact running ability that wasn’t previously advertised.
Still struggling to find his way into this offense, Mooney is a player we think the coaches need to force the ball to, as his speed is undeniable.
The problem is that Mooney is so slight that he doesn’t seem able to take a hit.
He was bulldozed on his lone 4-yard catch and failed…

title: 3 2027 First-Round Prospects Should Be on Jets' Radar as Another Losing Season Seems Inevitable
full_text:
With losses piling up, it isn't too early to think about the Jets' 2027 NFL Draft outlook .
New York currently holds three first-round picks for next year's draft. As it stands, those three picks all fall within the first 12 selections , according to Tankathon . The Colts' pick from the Sauce Gardner trade is currently No. 7 , the Jets' own pick is No. 10 and the Cowboys' selection—coming from the Quinnen Williams trade—is No. 12.
The Jets have a chance to get high-level talent, and plenty of it, but with the way the season is going, Gang Green will look to shore up holes in the roster, making these options even more important.
The Jets are 2-5 after seven weeks, leaving the team and fans looking ahead to next year. As the Jets look to drift into another year of mediocrity, these three college prospects should be on general manager Darren Mougey's radar as potential first-round targets.
The Jets have a quarterback problem that has plagued them for generations. Geno Smith has looked serviceable on the stat sheet, but he isn't the long-term answer for success. Darian Mensah may be the answer for a team that has been looking for a franchise player at the position since the days of Joe Namath.
Mensah has been one of the nation's best players through the 2026 college football season. The 21-year-old has 2,155 yards and 22 touchdowns over seven games. Pro Football Focus also has the Miami Hurricanes' QB graded the best in the nation in that time . Mensah has produced everywhere he's been, which earned him a $6.5 million NIL deal with the Canes .
Mensah has shown that he can do it at every level in college football. Now the QB is thriving in Coral Gables. He has shown he can keep a number-one receiver like Malachi Toney sufficiently fed while spreading the ball around effectively. Mensah boasts inhuman accuracy and an arm strong enough to handle windy days at MetLife.
Whether he falls into New York's lap or they have to trade up, the Jets must look to bring in the player who looks like the best quarterback in the draft.
The Jets' defense has improved from the past season, but that does not mean that there aren't holes to be filled on that side of the ball. Guys like Demario Davis were brought back in the offseason, but the 37-year-old is in the tail end of his career.
With that in mind, Georgia linebacker Chris Cole could be a welcome addition to the defense come April.
The junior linebacker has 39 tackles, 2.5 sacks, and 3 passes defended this season. Cole has shown that he can play around the line while also being competent in coverage. He could fit into New York's linebacker room immediately, and the current Bulldog could learn from an aging superstar in Davis and could slot in with a resurging Jamien Sherwood .
Cole could be the next great linebacking for the Jets. A franchise that boasts the likes of David Harris and Bart Scott could use another freak at the position. Cole has the ability to make an impact as soon as he steps on an NFL field. New York should do its due diligence to see whether those first steps should be in Gotham green.
The Jets' secondary has still been a problem through the 2026 season, with the cornerback position being one of the most glaring issues . New York will likely look to bolster the position group through the offseason, which brings the spotlight onto a player like Ashton Hampton.
Hampton has been one of the lone bright spots for Clemson this season. The junior cornerback has been lockdown this season, recording nine passes defended to go along with one interception so far. He's also allowed only 40.6% of passes thrown his way to be completed, according to Pro Football Focus , resulting in a career-high 85.4 coverage grade— third-best among 108 CBs to take at least 400 snaps this season .
Hampton has thrived in man coverage. The Clemson product would fit in perfectly with the press-man scheme the Jets have run the past two seasons.
Gang Green has an opportunity that 31 other teams don't have in the upcoming draft. With three picks in Round 1, the Jets must do work to shore up a roster that seems better than their record suggests.
These three options should be high on the Jets' board as they continue to map out their draft plans between now and April.

title: One Jets WR's Outlook Couldn't Be Worse After Omar Cooper Jr.'s Breakout Continues
full_text:
First-year Jets wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. showed up and showed out again in Week 7's unfortunate loss to the Dolphins .
The rookie wide receiver finished his second full game in the NFL with 5 receptions, 115 yards, and a trip to the end zone. Cooper has made a name for himself , but his success means less work for other receivers looking to stake a claim in the Jets' WR room.
In fact, Isaiah Williams has been one of the casualties of Cooper's success.
The 25-year-old made a name for himself as one of the best punt returners in the league in 2025. Unfortunately for him, Williams has not been able to parlay his return ability into a cemented spot as a receiver for New York. Throw in his lackluster numbers and Cooper's recent performances, and Williams has been sent into even more of a background role.
So, what could his future in Gotham look like?
Williams slotted into the receiver core after Cooper got hurt in Week 1. The former Illinois receiver saw 137 pass snaps during the four weeks Cooper missed, according to Pro Football Focus . He has seen only 10 since the rookie's return. Williams ranks second among the Jets' receivers in snaps so far this season (255), trailing only Garrett Wilson (385).
That ranking seems fleeting as the Jets' receiver core gets healthier, though.
Clearly, Williams has become one of the odd men out in the Jets' receiver room. Even gadget plays that Williams once received have gone to Cooper instead. His future with the Jets is coming into question as Cooper continues to cement his role, and the team could be open to a split since Williams will become a restricted free agent in March.
Williams saw only seven passing snaps in the Week 7 game against Miami. This was a game that the Jets were trailing throughout, and Williams still could not get on the field. The former Pro Bowl alternate has still seen some special teams action, but even then, he has zero kick returns in the last two games, while his only punt return in that stretch went for seven yards.
The writing seems to be on the wall.
Williams has been frozen out of the target conversation as well. The third-year receiver has not seen a target since Week 5, which was a 16-yard gain. There is a clear correlation between Cooper's ascension and Williams's decline as an offensive asset.
The former Bengal and Lion saw 15 targets through the first five weeks of the season. Fourteen of those targets came in while Cooper wasn't lacing up on Sundays after he suffered a high ankle sprain against Tennessee in Week 1. Now the rookie has taken over Williams's spot in the pecking order, even outpacing Garrett Wilson in targets against the Dolphins.
Cooper has been a revelation for a struggling Jets team since returning from injury. He has looked to grab the starting role in the slot and isn't looking back. The Jets will benefit from his emerging stardom, but players like Williams will see their roles shrink. The promising returner is being reduced to just that as Cooper takes hold of the Jets' receiver room and fans alike.
With the trade deadline less than two weeks ago, Williams might not have much time remaining in Gotham.

title: Sauce Gardner Trade Keeps Aging Like Fine Wine for Jets After Quenton Nelson News
full_text:
The Colts are in fire-sale mode. After dropping to 2-5, they traded away All-Pro Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks and look to continue to sell as their season falls apart. Although they weren't involved in this deal, the Jets might come out the biggest winner in all of the Colts' trades as the season continues.
Sauce Gardner was supposed to be the piece that pushed the Colts over the edge last season. That was one of the reasons the Jets were able to get two first-round picks for the cornerback. Instead, the Colts have fired their GM and are 2-5 this season.
As the weeks go on, the trade looks more and more like a Darren Mougey masterclass.
Gardner started his career hot. The former Jet was rookie of the year and had multiple All-Pro selections. That success hasn't followed Sauce to Indianapolis this season. The Colts have only won two games since acquiring the former All-Pro. To make matters worse, Gardner is having the worst year of his career in his first full year as a Colt.
Pro Football Focus has graded Gardner at 60.3 this season —the lowest mark in his career. This grade ranks lower than both Azareye'h Thomas and Brandon Stephens, despite struggles this season . Gardner was supposed to be a lockdown addition for the Colts.
Instead, he has been a thorn in the side of a struggling Indianapolis squad. The Jets seem to have gotten rid of Gardner at the perfect time. He is no longer a corner to be feared; he's become one to target.
Gardner has allowed a 113.6 passer rating and 21.7 yards per reception. New York has been on the better side of the trade for draft capital, and also on the field. As Gardner's performance has declined , this trade has the Jets making out like bandits.
The Jets got two first-round picks and Adonai Mitchell for Gardner. Mitchell has been fine for New York, and Kenyon Sadiq has been a welcome addition to the team. That said, the best part of the trade may be yet to come with the second first-rounder in the upcoming draft.
The Jets hold the Colts' first pick this season, which looks to be a top-10 selection (barring Indianapolis winning out the year).
The Colts' pick currently sits at No. 7 in the 2027 NFL Draft , according to Tankathon , and they have also lost three games straight. Indianapolis looks headed towards a rebuild, which means losing football games. A top-10 pick would be a welcome addition to a Jets team that still has holes in the roster.
New York landed a budding star in Sadiq with the Colts' pick last year, and they will have the chance to pick another if the Colts keep losing. The Jets also have their own first-rounder to use (currently No. 10), as well as whichever of the Cowboys' or Packers' picks is earlier, due to the Quinnen Williams trade. As of Tuesday, that would be the Dallas selection (No. 12).
Getting two first-round picks for any player is usually a good trade. That trade gets even better when the team you trade the player to underperforms. The Gardner deal just keeps getting better, with the Colts looking like a team with no identity and the Jets getting rid of Gardner's bloated contract.
In a season that hasn't gone as planned for New York, this trade continues to be one of the best things to happen to Gang Green in a long time, and time will tell just how much better it gets.

title: D'Angelo Ponds Could Force Jets to Rethink Jarvis Brownlee's Future Before Trade Deadline
full_text:
At first glance, it seemed like the Jets wanted to see what they had in second-round rookie cornerback D'Angelo Ponds when they gave him his first NFL start Sunday against the Dolphins .
It turns out that wasn't always the plan.
New York made previously starting cornerback Jarvis Brownlee Jr. a healthy scratch going into the Week 7 AFC East showdown . Head coach Aaron Glenn clarified that the decision is one the team is handling internally with Brownlee.
In short, the Jets benched Brownlee for a reason outside of just injuries. So how did Ponds look in his debut start? Do the Jets still see Brownlee as part of their plans going forward?
It's time to break all of those questions down now.
Context is important when judging Ponds' first NFL start. Remember, this is a player who didn't get a training camp and had to learn a brand-new position at nickel on the fly. He received limited practice reps and has been thrust onto the field.
So it should come as no surprise that Ponds had a mixed day on Sunday.
Ponds was targeted three times, giving up one catch for five yards, according to Pro Football Focus . Still, he didn't have the best day tackling and was charged with a pass interference penalty in the end zone during Miami's touchdown drive before the half ended. PFF graded his game out to a respectable 64.6 on 30 defensive snaps, ranking 38th-best among 77 cornerbacks to play at least 20 snaps in Week 7.
The idea is that Ponds will get better with time and more reps.
And because of that, New York's other slot corner becomes even more expendable with each passing day.
The moment the Jets drafted Ponds in the 2026 NFL Draft's second round , it seemed like Brownlee's future was going to be in question.
The veteran CB was one of the unit's best players over the course of the last few weeks, but fast-forward to when he was benched after a miscommunication on a touchdown pass in New York's loss to New England, which opened the door for Ponds to play. It doesn't help that opposing QBs have a 78.6% completion rate when targeting Brownlee since Week 4, per PFF .
However, it's clear that the Jets want to see more out of Ponds. If they were focused solely on winning games, then it's clear Brownlee should be on the field some more. Teams have targeted New York's secondary more and more, and viable veterans are needed when that happens.
But that isn't the total end goal anymore. At least not after the team's loss to Miami.
Whatever the reason Brownlee was benched, it's clear he could be one of several players the Jets move for future draft capital ahead of the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10. Brownlee is under contract through 2027, according to Spotrac , with cap hits of $1.085 million this season and $1.19 million next . While the Jets should be rethinking their plans in the secondary, potential trades are still something that the team needs to focus on.
And that leaves Brownlee expendable for the future as Ponds gets more reps going forward.
