title: 10 Best Aaron Glenn Replacement Options If Jets Fire Head Coach
full_text:
It seems like we have come to the inevitable following the Jets' Week 7 defeat at the hands of the previously winless Dolphins . It's hard to imagine head coach Aaron Glenn getting a third year with the team now 2-5.
And so, here we are again. On the precipice of a team seemingly in need of a new head coach once again.
This time, though, the Jets should focus on young offensive minds who understand how to elevate talent from a play-calling perspective, as well as someone who can get the most out of quarterbacks. Gone are the days when the team should focus on defensive-minded individuals or retread leaders. It's time for innovation and modernity.
Here's my "way too early but not really" list of 10 head coaching candidates the Jets should look to target once they turn the page on Glenn.
I'm definitely lower on Webb after his struggles in getting the Broncos' offense going at the beginning of the year. It's never a good thing for a team to have a head coach take back play-calling duties because the OC is not up to the task. I would argue Webb is the weakest candidate on this list.
Still, he fits the mold as a former quarterback with an understanding of how offenses should be run. For that reason, he makes the list.
I'm higher on Brian Johnson than most other people. The former offensive coordinator for Philadelphia had the unit as a top-10 offense in almost every category in 2023. He was scapegoated because of a poor defense and an overbearing head coach.
Since his departure, he helped develop Jayden Daniels in a historic rookie season, and now is working under Sean McVay in Los Angeles. He's someone who has play-calling and quarterback development experience and could be a dark-horse candidate.
If you checked in on Rees before Week 4, you could argue he was more likely to be fired than promoted to head coach. Since Atlanta got competent quarterback play, though, Rees has found plenty of deserving success. He has Atlanta's offense ranked sixth in yards and 10th in points. He understands the importance of the quarterback and can shift a scheme for one.
He's another dark-horse candidate.
The Commanders aren't a good football team, but I don't think that's because of their offensive play-caller. If anything, it seems like the rash of injuries suffered by their quarterback, offensive line and receiving corps highlights how solid Blough has been.
Washington was able to beat the Seahawks with a backup QB because of the design from Blough. He also happens to be one of the few offensive coordinators on this list with play-calling experience. I wouldn't look past this candidate because of the team he is on. He's doing a lot better than most would give credit for.
McCown has never called plays or led an offensive huddle as a coach. He's only been a passing game coordinator andf quarterbacks coach. Still, I can't help but think he could be the next Andy Reid-type coach—someone who knows how to do the top job without actually having experience at it.
As a former quarterback, McCown has had success as a leader and developer. He's someone who won't be a favorite for the top job, but someone who could end up getting it as a former Jet and who understands what the team needs.
Before Lamar Jackson got hurt, it looked like Declan Doyle was dominating as a play-caller and designer. Since the quarterback's injury, though, it's clear that while the design is good, Doyle is lacking experience as an adjuster.
That's okay, though. This is something that will be tested for him over the next few games this season. This will be a viable learning curve for the young play-caller before he inevitably gets a coaching job in the near future. As a designer, he could scheme some fun plays for New York's excellent weapons.
Unlike most people on this list, Scheelhaase is not someone who owns offensive coordinator duties alone. He shares that position with Dave Ragone. The latter, though, is older and has more of a history of coaching solely quarterbacks. Scheelhaase is younger, has worked under Sean McVay for longer, and understands the finer points of what the team's offense must be in the modern game.
It seems like this year is the time for him to get a top job.
Here's an option that will be debated plenty. Who gets credit for the rebound of Bryce Young? Is it just head coach Dave Canales or does offensive coordinator Brad Idzik deserve some flowers?
In reality, it's a little bit of both.
Idzik is a quality offensive mind that has taken on more responsibility this season. He's deserving of a top job considering he's someone currently calling plays and has found success in doing it.  If anything, the fact that he has found even more success as a play-caller with Young should lead many to see him as a legitimate option for a team like the Jets.
I love Udinski. So does Jacksonville Jaguars head coach Liam Coen and quarterback Trevor Lawrence.
" He made a huge impact—just the amount of work he puts in, how smart he is ," Lawrence said of Udinski (h/t Jaguars). "He's really good at finding weaknesses in defenses, just breaking down the defenses and presenting them to us. He just brings a standard to the room. He never misses an opportunity to coach. He takes away a lot of the gray on Sunday and reduces the unknowns."
He may not be calling plays, but he's an offensive-minded coach with a philosophy that fits the modern game and a history of developing quarterbacks. I think Udinski and who's next on my list would be slam-dunk hires.
Unlike his brother, Kubiak doesn't have the same kind of play-calling experience that would make him a slam-dunk hire. However, the work he has done in helping Kyle Shanahan right the ship in San Francisco, despite so many injuries, cannot be overlooked.
The Kubiak coaching lineage has plenty of success. He doesn't have play-calling experience, but he knows how to do it and understands the importance of developing quarterbacks. As of this posting, he is my top choice for the Jets going into 2027.

title: Brandon Stephens Is Slowly Becoming an Unnecessary Jets Headache
full_text:
Fresh off a humiliating 28-25 loss to the previously winless Dolphins on Sunday, the Jets find themselves at 2-5 as they continue to struggle to put positive results together with a much-improved roster on paper.
In that loss alone, the Jets had a 100-yard rusher, a 100-yard receiver, a defense that surrendered just seven second-half points and a quarterback who went for 287 yards and three touchdowns. That ultimately did not matter in a rock-bottom performance that featured another poorly executed game plan from the coaching staff.
While head coach Aaron Glenn deserves much of the blame for his continued struggles with game management, it is still up to the players on the field to do their part and make a strong impression.
Now in his second season with Gang Green, cornerback Brandon Stephens is one of those examples: he's someone who is exceptional against the run and versatile at multiple positions, but has struggled to create turnovers in his career.
In his last four games alone, Stephens has allowed opposing QBs to go 11-of-16 (68.8%) for 167 yards and a TD when targeted, which is good for an average of 15.2 yards per catch. For reference, he only allowed seven completions on 13 targets for 78 yards (11.1 yards per catch) in his first three games.
With a career average of 12.1 yards per catch allowed, that is not exactly the type of performance he needs to be displaying in Year 2 of a three-year contract.
It's safe to say, Stephens needs to step up—and soon.
To his credit, Stephens does have three broken-up passes in the last four games, but he has also failed to come away with a single interception this season and none at all since he recorded the only two picks of his career in 2023 with the Ravens.
Sure, the Jets have only one interception as a team this season (Minkah Fitzpatrick), so it is not like Stephens is alone in that regard. This was also a defense that gave up 28 points to a team that hadn't led this season and couldn't stop the run if it tried, in a disappointing all-around performance by the entire group against the Dolphins.
That said, a lot more is expected from Stephens as a starting corner alongside Azareye'h Thomas. For comparison, Thomas has 33 tackles, two tackles for loss and five passes defended. Stephens, meanwhile, has 19 tackles, one tackle for loss, six passes defended and one fumble recovery in the same number of games.
While a player's success is not solely determined by those respective stats, there is clearly some room for improvement for a starting corner with the talent that Stephens possesses. According to Pro Football Focus , Stephens has the 38th-ranked overall grade (65.1), as well as the 27th-ranked coverage grade (68.1) and 53rd-ranked run-defense grade (61.8) out of 103 qualified CBs.
That is an indication of the potential that Stephens brings, but it has not been enough as of late with the Jets facing an uphill climb the rest of the season.
He is still under contract with a $14 million cap hit in 2027 , per Spotrac , but the Jets have a $12 million out in the offseason that they can use if they feel he hasn't done enough to justify keeping him at that cap hit for his final year. Adding that to the over $96.8 million that New York is projected to have would help general manager Darren Mougey be one of the most powerful spenders in March.
Along with his durability and run-defense skills, Stephens has shown flashes of high-level play in heavy man-coverage schemes throughout his career, but he has mostly been inconsistent when he is isolated without any safety help. That said, he has the prototypical size (6'1", 215 lbs) for his position and the athletic traits suited for press-man when those opportunities arise.
While Fitzpatrick has the team's lone interception this season and safety Dane Belton has proved to be the best offseason signing with a team-high 56 tackles, the rest of the secondary has not really stood out on a consistent basis. Even Jarvis Brownlee Jr., who has been a bright spot for the defense but was a healthy scratch in Week 7, ranks lower than Stephens in overall grade (60.3), coverage grade (63.1) and run-defense grade (58.2) from PFF .
That alone should not measure a player's success, but it does show things could be a lot worse for Stephens.
With that in mind, he will likely get more opportunities coming his way against the Raiders' sixth-ranked scoring attack (26.1 ppg) on Sunday. If Stephens cannot figure out how to create some turnovers and get more consistent stops, he may not be around Gotham much longer.

title: Biggest Decision Aaron Glenn Got Wrong vs. Dolphins (And What Needs to Change in Week 8)
full_text:
Just when it looked like things could not get much worse for the Jets this season, a humiliating 28-25 loss to the previously winless Dolphins took place on Sunday and dropped them to 2-5 in what is shaping up to be another season to forget in Gotham.
While injuries to key players like running back Breece Hall (groin) continue to plague this roster , the Jets finally had their top-three receivers on the field with Adonai Mitchell returning from a finger injury and appeared poised to take care of business on Sunday.
Even though rookie Omar Cooper Jr. shined once again (five catches, 115 yards, one touchdown) and running back Braelon Allen impressed (17 carries, 104 yards), the Jets immediately fell behind and never recovered after allowing the Dolphins to score on each of their first two possessions.
Coming into Week 7, the Dolphins were the only team that had not led at any point this season and lost RB1 De'Von Achane (torn ACL) for the season. On Sunday, they never trailed and Ollie Gordon II went for 103 yards and a TD on 23 carries, which proved vital in one of the key matchups going into the game .
That said, this was still a game the Jets were in position to win if they executed better in key moments. Look no further than the end-of-half TD from the Dolphins prior to the break, and how Glenn once again paid the price for his baffling clock management.
Following a punt, the Jets had the Dolphins backed up at their own nine-yard line, only trailing by seven points with 8:44 remaining in the first half. Not only did the defense allow quarterback Malik Willis to convert a fourth-and-two to keep the drive going, but they also let the Dolphins take the clock all the way down to six seconds and stretch their lead to 21-7.
Despite having all three timeouts in his pocket, Glenn refused to use either of them. It was one thing to allow Miami to go all the way down the field in methodical fashion, but why not start using the timeouts following the two-minute warning to at least give your offense enough time to try to score some points?
Instead, Willis ran in for the two-yard score (h/t NFL) and extended the Dolphins' lead to 14 just before the break.
Malik Willis lowers his shoulder for the touchdown MIAvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/TVRwL1sULm
Glenn is now 0-8 against divisional opponents and has been outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of the first half in his 24 games as HC of the Jets. Chalk this up to the latest instance of him fumbling a game away on the sidelines and the clock management woes that have plagued his tenure in Gang Green.
To make matters worse, Glenn called a timeout within the first five minutes of the second half to prevent his offense from getting a delay of game. A back-breaking 63-yard TD pass from Willis to rookie WR Caleb Douglas put the finishing touches on the game late in the fourth quarter, but the bizarre timeout usage—or lack thereof at the end of the first half—helped put the Jets in that predicament and made Glenn's seat even hotter than it was entering the day .
The frustration did not reside solely on Glenn's shoulders as offensive coordinator Frank Reich once again failed to get WR1 Garrett Wilson involved in the game plan. Worst of all, the Jets had a first-and-goal at the one-yard line, but had to settle for a 33-yard field goal instead of tying the game. Gang Green was an improved 3-of-4 in the red zone, but not without some more issues that simply cannot happen in a close game at home.
That said, this was a game in which the Dolphins were in control throughout, which only made Glenn's decision to hang onto the timeouts that much more puzzling when he had the opportunity to at least give the offense the ball back on a day that a lot of positive things were happening compared to recent weeks.
As the Jets remain home to face the 3-4 Raiders on Sunday, the pressure remains firmly on Glenn after reaching a new low against the Dolphins . Although Las Vegas has been competitive so far, its defense is 29th in the league in points allowed per game (28.1 PPG), so perhaps the Jets can find something and take advantage of that weakness.
However, as ESPN' s Rich Cimini noted after the Week 7 loss, Glenn is the ninth coach since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger "to begin his career with eight straight division losses" and "the fifth coach to do it in the last 30 seasons (Jim Schwartz, Matt Eberflus, Pat Shurmur, Leslie Frazier)."
Aaron Glenn becomes the 9th head coach since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger to begin his career with eight straight division losses. He’s the 5th coach to do it in the last 30 seasons (Jim Schwartz, Matt Eberflus, Pat Shurmur, Leslie Frazier). ESPN Research. #Jets
While that only applies to divisional opponents, that is not the type of list you want to be on, and it's another reason why Glenn's seat continues to reach a boiling point . Going forward, his focus must be on getting off to better starts, executing key plays and being more aggressive with his game and clock management.
After all, the offense was not bad on Sunday, especially when you consider the bad spot it was put in, with the defense surrendering the TD drives to begin the game. Glenn simply needs to be more aggressive with his play-calling and come out of the gates swinging with something to prove.
If not, it could be more of the same with a tougher schedule on the horizon as another season slips away for the Jets.

title: Jets Week 7 Awards Paint Grim Picture for What's to Come in Gotham
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Another season. Another year for Jets fans to tune out the organization before Halloween .
Of course, can you really blame them after Sunday's loss?
New York went into a home contest against a winless Miami team and got outplayed and coached for the entire contest. The Jets' 28-25 loss not only dropped them to 2-5 , but it made people wonder whether they will ever become a winning organization again.
As always, we have some Jets awards to hand out after a humiliating loss like that. Let's get to it.
After the 2025 season, the excuse was that Glenn was a first-year coach. He just needed time to get players who fit his scheme. After Week 2, the excuse was that it was just a single loss and the team was competing at a high level. In Week 6, the excuse was that the Jets' losses came at the hands of playoff teams, not inferior opponents.
The reality is that the Jets under Aaron Glenn are what their record is. They are not just 5-19 in a year and a half, but they are 0-8 in the AFC East. They have lost blowouts and close games. They never seem to make the right play or call to win.
That is the lone takeaway under Glenn as a head coach. After Sunday's loss to Miami, in which the team was outcoached by a first-year staff and outplayed by a 0-5 roster, the question of whether Glenn can turn around the team has been answered .
And it seems like it will lead to an inevitable coaching search again.
Omar Cooper Jr. is a future star in the NFL. All he has to do is stay healthy.
New York watched their 30th overall pick lead the team in targets for a second straight game, and he was rewarded with a six-catch (h/t NFL), 115-yard game and a score. Along the way, he was the first Jets rookie to record back-to-back 100-yard games since Al Toon in 1985.
Here comes Omar Cooper Jr. 👀 MIAvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dSXEZjYYD4
Quarterback Geno Smith shared high praise for rookie WR after the game.
"(Cooper) played a great game," Smith said. "Obviously, we all can do a lot better in some areas, but (he) made plays when necessary. We all fought to the end, but it just wasn’t enough."
So long as Cooper continues to make big plays and be hard to bring down after the catch, he must be New York's second receiving option behind Garrett Wilson .
It's inconceivable. Superstar receivers across the NFL are all schemed open and targeted more than other players around them. Garrett Wilson seems to be the only receiver whose offense is deliberately looking the other way when he's open .
Wilson saw just three targets all game on Sunday and recorded two receptions. Throughout the contest, he was running open over the middle of the field, but either the quarterback's read or final decision went to a different player.
That cannot happen in the modern NFL. If the star receiver is open, the team needs to get him the ball because it's the best chance they have at winning. It should be no coincidence that the team's offense has failed in key areas each of the last two weeks, with Wilson coming behind Braelon Allen in targets and touches.
Offensive coordinator Frank Reich and Smith have a role in this. Even if Smith touted his chemistry with New York's top wideout.
"I think we’ve got great chemistry," Smith said. "When we get our opportunities, the plays are there. We’re still building. That’s just a part of the process, but so far, I think we have tremendous chemistry."
Smith can tout his chemistry with Wilson all he wants. The tape says something different . And it's completely unthinkable to see how the Jets are the lone team struggling to get the ball to their best player.
Going into Sunday, the Dolphins were the second-worst passing offense in the league and the eighth-best rushing unit. The goal for New York's defense was simple: get pressure on Malik Willis and get extra guys in the box to fortify their run defense.
What happened? The exact opposite. Willis picked apart New York's defense from the very first snap and the Dolphins ran for 156 yards on the ground. In their last two games played, the Jets have given up 304 yards to the Dolphins and Patriots.
This unit has regressed all season. They don't have a semblance of tackle depth to generate pressure in the pocket; they aren't getting consistent pass rush from their edge rushers, and their secondary is taxed because of it.
Despite all the talk about Glenn's "superpower" being play-calling , this entire group was outclassed throughout Sunday. Miami averaged over five yards per play and dominated at the point of attack.
"That’s really puzzling to me," Glenn said. "It just seemed like they were falling forward on everything. And even the ones that we had them knocked back, they still fell forward for three or four yards, and you can’t have any leaky yardage like that."
This group is in serious trouble with the Bills and Chiefs coming up on their schedule.
Jets fans deserve better. There's really no reason the fanbase should expect Gang Green to magically beat some of the high-powered teams on the schedule. The team has proven that even games against "inferior" competition aren't exactly safe.
That leaves the fanbase watching a team out of the running before Halloween ... again. It means fans must choose between rooting for the team to win games and hurt their draft stock, or lose out and secure the rights to a top rookie quarterback.
New York fans have been here before. They are looking at a playoff drought that will extend to 16 years this season and an 11-year run of finishing below .500. After the game, Glenn even tried to curry favor with the fans by showing understanding of their pain.
Fans don't care about improvement on the field, though, if it means the end results aren't changing. And there is the issue.
Without changed results, the Jets are the same as they have ever been.
And the fans deserve better.

title: Jets' Garrett Wilson Malpractice Should Cost Frank Reich His Job After Loss vs. Dolphins
full_text:
Another Sunday, another disappointing Jets loss. This, however, came at the hands of their winless division rival, the Dolphins, who beat Gang Green 28-25 at MetLife Stadium .
Recurring mistakes have plagued Gang Green’s season, with poor coaching decisions and an inability to capitalize in the red zone and on short-yardage at the forefront of the team’s issues. Another concern is offensive coordinator Frank Reich’s inability to consistently utilize star wide receiver Garrett Wilson .
Although the former Ohio State Buckeye leads the team in receptions (37), receiving yards (444), and touchdowns (3), the majority of that production came during the first three games. His involvement in the offense has decreased over the past four weeks:
Garrett Wilson first 3 games
Garrett Wilson last 4 games
Even worse, in the last four games, Wilson has been targeted more than six times just once, posting seven receptions for 104 yards and a touchdown against the Browns in Week 6. In the other three games combined, Wilson has logged just nine receptions (13 targets) for 97 yards. For a receiver of his caliber, this is unacceptable.
With New York sitting at 2-5 and Wilson’s frustration becoming increasingly apparent (h/t Glenn Naughton), Reich’s inability to get his best offensive weapon involved raises questions about whether he should stay in the position.
A frustrated Garrett Wilson has some words for Geno Smith on the @nyjets sideline as he's been a non-factor with the Jets trailing the winless Dolphins 21-14. Smith appears unmoved. pic.twitter.com/esmJHlbXi7
Reich knows Wilson is a special talent. Earlier this month, he compared Wilson to a "masterpiece" (h/t Jets), explaining that he and the coaching staff continue to discover new ways Wilson can impact a game.
“If it’s a masterpiece of art that you’re looking at, if it’s a true masterpiece, you kind of keep coming back and looking at it, and you see it and appreciate different aspects of it every time you look at it,” Reich said. “But also to learn to try to figure out, ‘Oh, he can do this, he can do that. How do we fully utilize the things that he can do?’”
Garrett Wilson 🤝 masterpiece pic.twitter.com/4bPQ7t4ntk
Reich also emphasized the importance of spreading the ball around while acknowledging that he wants Wilson to get a lot of targets. However, the Jets’ offense hasn’t operated as if it were trying to get Wilson involved, and the unit’s production has been underwhelming.
Although New York is averaging more total yards per game than it did through seven games last season, its scoring average has barely increased, rising from 18.4 to 19.6 points per game. Reich’s approach, particularly his inconsistency involving Wilson, has played a key role in the team’s lack of wins.
The recipe that’s resulted in wins for New York is when the offense feeds Wilson. When Wilson is targeted seven or more times, the Jets are 2-2 this season. When he receives fewer than that, New York is 0-3.
Although targets alone won’t determine the game’s outcome, the Jets have a better chance when Wilson is involved. Even head coach Aaron Glenn recognizes the importance of committing to Wilson.
Last week, Reich acknowledged that Glenn regularly reminds him to get him the ball , reported by Sports Illustrated 's Nick Faria.
“AG (Glenn) is always in my ear if Garrett hasn’t gotten the ball for a little bit,” Reich said. “He’s like, ‘Hey, don’t forget, boom, get our playmakers the ball.’”
The fact that Glenn has to remind Reich to get him involved raises serious concerns about the offensive coordinator’s game planning and in-game adjustments. While Glenn takes the blame for Wilson’s low usage (h/t SNY Jets ), it’s Reich’s responsibility to create opportunities for him.
He had the right plan on the opening drive against Cleveland . Wilson recorded three receptions (four targets) for 70 yards and a touchdown. Reich used Wilson creatively, moving him between the slot and outside to give different looks and opportunities to make a play.
This is what Reich needed to replicate. Instead, he failed to do so in the past two games.
Now, Wilson is starting to become visibly frustrated with his lack of targets and the offense’s poor play. If this continues, Wilson’s patience with the franchise could eventually wear thin and end in a departure as soon as the Nov. 10 trade deadline .
While that’s unlikely, the Jets can’t let this continue any further . Reich’s tenure with the Jets could end sooner rather than later if he doesn’t start making Wilson the focal point of the passing game.

title: Faria's Focus Week 7: 5 Jets Thoughts After Loss to Dolphins Drops Gang Green to 2-5
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — It isn't even Halloween, yet the Jets' season is effectively over .
Gang Green's struggles reached their pinnacle in Sunday's 28-25 loss to the Dolphins , a team that was 0-5 going into the contest and hadn't even recorded a lead at any point this season. The Jets had a 100-yard rusher, a 100-yard receiver, and a quarterback throw for nearly 300 yards and it wasn't enough.
Bad teams always make mistakes when it matters most. The Jets are a bad team, no matter what they say or the talent on the roster shows.
Jets fans are rightfully furious after a loss such as Sundays. It's time to give my five thoughts moving forward for the organization.
Last season, Aaron Glenn got the Jets job because the general consensus believed him to be a culture setter, someone who could hire great coordinators, and could even call plays if needed on defense.
Through a year and a half, where has that gone?
Well, New York is 5-19 with Glenn at the helm, and 0-8 in AFC East play. The Dolphins, a team obviously looking to soft-tank the season, still found a way to beat Gang Green's improved roster. No matter what Glenn has said, it's hard to build a culture with results like that .
As for hiring coordinators, the Jets repeatedly struggle to get the ball to start wideout Garrett Wilson —a fact that has left their head coach and quarterback flummoxed when asked about it on Sunday.
"I think we all can do a better job of finding ways to get him more targets and more touches," Geno Smith said. "But again, the ball has to go where it goes based on the coverage, and hats off to them for the game plan they had."
Offensive coordinator Frank Reich's inability to scheme up touches for Wilson has left fans frustrated beyond belief. It also didn't help that when Wilson was open, the quarterback didn't get him the ball either. In both cases, Glenn has taken the mantle of blame for that.
The numbers are what they are, though. New York has found big plays in their offense, but has struggled to find consistency throughout a game. That is a play-calling failure and, in turn, a failure of the head coach as he struggles to find someone to run his offense.
Then there are his own play-calling issues. New York went into Sunday against a Dolphins team hoping to secure a top pick this year in the 2027 draft to get a quarterback. Instead, the Jets defense was shelled by Miami, giving up 156 yards on the ground and failing to record a turnover.
Glenn's play-calling "superpower" was nonexistent on Sunday.
That leads us to the reality of where the Jets are. Glenn's superpower isn't what New York wants it to be. Unfortunately, any superpower starts and ends with his inability to turn the ship around. It's not exactly hard to picture this team entering a new coaching search after this season is over.
If you told me at the beginning of the season that a Jets star was going to be "Wally Pipp'd," my first guess would have been that something happened to Geno Smith. I could never have predicted Braelon Allen would become the most productive running back the Jets have seen so far this year.
Allen ran 17 times for 104 yards on the ground while gaining over six yards per carry. He also added six catches for 30 yards during the game while leading all pass catchers in targets. We've already talked about how insane that is with Wilson on the team, but still. This season, Allen has rushed for 418 yards on 91 carries. That's a projected 1,000-yard season and a healthy 4.6-yard-per-carry average.
Breece Hall has been a star for the Jets offense for years now, but the writing is on the wall. As the second-round running back works his way back from an injury suffered in Week 3, the Jets have no other choice to make. They need to split carries or even feature Allen more when Hall is 100% .
For those who don't remember, Wally Pipp was the Yankees' first baseman who got a headache and sat out a game for Lou Gehrig . Pipp never got his job back and watched as Gehrig became one of the greatest baseball players of all time.
Allen is probably not going to be a superstar like Gehrig, but it's clear he's earned a starting role for the Jets ahead of Hall.
The Jets had a really bad day yesterday. No one is going to dispute that. However, the team should feel great about their future.
And a first-round rookie's performance remains a big reason why.
When the Jets inevitably draft a future rookie quarterback in 2027, they'll do so knowing they have a collection of receivers who can get the most out of the young signal-caller right away. Garrett Wilson is an obvious star, but Omar Cooper Jr.'s performance over the last two weeks has been one for the record books.
Cooper caught six passes for 115 yards and a touchdown (h/t NFL) on Sunday, including two passes that went beyond 50 yards. His work after the catch is a perfect complement to Wilson's pass-catching ability over the middle of the field.
The @nyjets rookie Omar Cooper Jr. finds the end zone for the second-straight week MIAvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/TqzjdFlxY4
Not many rebuilding teams have two receivers with the ability to record 1,000-yard seasons on their own. It's obvious, though, that the Jets are in a great place with their offensive talent and any rookie should find success early with that.
If you thought the Jets' defensive performance has been bad recently, just wait. It's about to get a whole lot worse.
New York's biggest problem this season has been an inability to stop the run. While many people will point to their edge rushers and their consistent struggles against rushing offenses, the reality is much more alarming.
The Jets don't have the defensive tackles needed to win with this type of alignment they want to run.
Darrell Jackson Jr. is a late-round rookie and has been thrust into the lineup more due to injuries. Harrison Phillips and Jowon Briggs have both struggled mightily so far this season. Then there are the players unable to perform due to injuries. David Onyemata has been effectively lost for the season and T'Vondre Sweat left Sunday's game with a knee injury.
So where does that leave New York? With a massive gap in the middle of the field and a defensive tackle room that is one of the worst in the NFL.
Until this position group gets fixed, the Jets' defense will continue to get gashed by their opponents. In their last two games combined, the front seven has given up 304 yards rushing.
It's also going to get a lot worse moving forward.
We've already touched on how much Glenn has failed as Jets head coach, but I think it's also obvious to point out that the team is going to inevitably move on from this staff after this season. It's hard to envision a path in which the Jets somehow win six of their final nine contests.
That leaves the Jets in familiar territory: at the outset of another head coaching search and looking through mock drafts to see who could end up with Gang Green in 2027.
There are a lot of lessons to learn from Glenn's failings over the last two seasons. The chief point, though, must be that the organization desperately needs to find an offensive-minded head coach with experience in developing young quarterbacks. Gone are the days when the team should hire "culture-setters" because they "know what it takes to succeed."
New York needs fresh ideas.
Coaches who understand the modern NFL are about out-scheming an opponent rather thanf someone who can keep a locker room together. They need someone who can control an offense and overwhelm the opposition on that end, not someone who coaches with the sole idea of building through the defense.
If Glenn's failings are going to teach the Jets anything it's this: offense breeds wins. Wins breed culture.

title: 3 Potential Moro Ojomo Trade Destinations That Make Most Sense for Eagles
full_text:
A five-game losing streak and a laundry list of injuries put the Eagles in line to be sellers at the upcoming NFL trade deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10. It's not a familiar spot for general manager Howie Roseman to be in, but one he can use to put Philadelphia in position to compete for a Super Bowl in 2027 and beyond.
Trading away veteran players on expiring contracts is the easiest way to increase Philly's draft capital. That includes pros like cornerback Tariq Woolen and wide receiver Hollywood Brown . What's more intriguing is trading away a high-upside player on an expiring deal like defensive tackle Moro Ojomo.
Ojomo has risen from a seventh-round draft selection in 2023 to an impactful pass-rusher on a defensive line rotation that hoisted the Lombardi Trophy. He is entering his prime at 25 years old. The Nigerian native has logged 79 tackles, eight tackles for loss and six sacks through 49 career games.
Here are three trade destinations for Ojomo that make the most sense from the Eagles' perspective.
It would be logical to send Ojomo out of the NFC in hopes that he doesn't sign a long-term deal with a direct competitor of the Eagles. Jacksonville is no stranger to trades with Philly. Roseman acquired running back Tank Bigsby and offensive lineman Fred Johnson from the Jaguars just last year.
Jacksonville currently sits atop the AFC South with a 4-2 record. A menacing run defense has been the backbone of their success, giving up a league-leading 72.2 rushing yards per game. The same defensive line has struggled to frustrate quarterbacks, though, ranking 22nd in sacks per game (1.8).
Ojomo has posted a 17% pass-rush win rate , according to ESPN analytics. That has him ranked 17th among defensive tackles. It's only a matter of time before those strong reps turn into game-changing sacks. Pairing Ojomo with Arik Armstead would give the Jaguars a dangerous duo in the trenches.
The Browns were not expected to be buyers at the deadline entering the season; however, they boast a 5-2 record, with four of their next six games coming against teams with a losing record. There's a path to a playoff spot and opportunities to improve via trades. The Eagles should take advantage.
Cleveland's defensive line depth took a hit when Mason Graham suffered a left MCL sprain and an ankle sprain on Oct. 1. He returned to the field in Week 7, playing limited snaps and even limping off at one point. Head coach Todd Monken said it will be a while before Graham is 100% healthy (h/t Daryl Ruiter).
Acquiring Ojomo would be a way for Cleveland to give Graham and other defensive tackles crucial rest. Ojomo's quick first step and violent hands would fit in well on a disruptive defense. The Browns own a combined 18 picks in the 2027 and 2028 NFL Drafts. They can create quite an enticing offer.
There's an avenue Roseman can take other than simply selling Ojomo for draft capital. Acquiring a young player capable of helping the Eagles for years to come would be ideal. It would just take some finessing, like packaging Ojomo with an early or mid-round pick to a team in complete win-now mode.
The Lions' Super Bowl window is open with quarterback Jared Goff and running back Jahmyr Gibbs playing at an elite level. There have been reported contract disputes between Detroit and tight end Sam LaPorta. The Iowa product is in the final year of his rookie contract and is seeking a long-term deal.
LaPorta is exactly the kind of player Roseman should target and satisfy with a new deal. The 25-year-old has averaged 50.8 receiving yards and scored 23 touchdowns in 48 career games. LaPorta could form a compelling one-two punch with Eli Stowers, assuming the Eagles move on from Dallas Goedert.
As for Detroit, Ojomo would solidify a defensive line that already has Aidan Hutchinson tormenting opposing quarterbacks. The Lions could sign Ojomo to a multi-year deal if things work out, or earn a compensatory pick by letting him leave in free agency. It's a home run swing Howie should take.

title: Kracz: Eagles Facing a Harsh Saquon Barkley Reality After Loss to Cowboys
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — Membership fees to the 2,000-yard rusher’s club are coming due for Saquon Barkley.
Perhaps that 2024 season is catching up to him . It was fun in the moment and a big reason the Eagles claimed their second Lombardi Trophy, but now it feels like playing 20 games that season, counting the playoffs—logging 446 carries and 2,504 yards—has taken its toll.
Barkley has played five games this season, and he has three different injuries: a stinger, a hamstring injury, and on Monday night, his back was added to the list. Not many players—maybe not any players—invest more time and money in their fitness regimen than Barkley.
But sometimes that isn’t even enough to fend off injuries, and he wouldn’t be the first running back to find the going more difficult after running for 2,000 yards.
“Every injury is its own injury,” Barkley said after the Eagles lost their fifth straight game on Monday. “For me, it's just unfamiliar territory. I've never really done anything like this to my hamstring. I've had little, small strains and stuff like, but all my other injuries have been, like, football, like someone tackling me or I tore my ACL.”
Now, this isn’t meant to pick on Barkley. Not in the least. He was one of the few who showed heart in what became a 38-21 loss to the Cowboys on Monday night. He knew his team needed a spark, and he tried to ignite it. He nearly did. His mind was willing; his body wasn’t.
Still, Barkley did what leaders do. They give effort then they take accountability.
While many of his teammates, such as Zack Baun, Jalen Carter, and Riq Woolen, declined to talk, Barkley was one of the few who stood tall in the locker room after their fifth straight loss to answer questions, something he did for nearly 15 minutes.
Barkley is battling with everything he has. Maybe he shouldn’t have played, but he tried. He laid it on the line. It added up to 10 snaps, and he touched the ball on nine of them, including the first two the Eagles’ offense ran. He turned a short throw into a 12-yard gain and then ripped off a 29-yard run. He capped it with an 8-yard scoring run that gave the Eagles their first touchdown of the first quarter this season and a 7-3 lead.
It was on that run when Barkley said he felt his hamstring grab. Then, he said, he tried to overcompensate, leading to his back locking up.
“Your back ever locked on you?” Barkley asked a swarm of reporters. “It's like, that's the only way I can explain it. Your body overcompensates. I'm not trying to get too much into the injury, but your body, that's how the body protects itself a little bit; something's a little banged up, so something's gotta work a little harder."
When Barkley has stayed healthy, he has shown he still has juice, a home run hitter in waiting. It’s just that those healthy moments appear to be diminishing.
Or maybe he comes back next year fully healthy, stays that way, and bangs out another 1,000-yard season.
But Barkley's 29 now, and typically NFL running backs don’t get better at that age unless they're a freak like Derrick Henry, who is in the 2,000-yard rushing club with Barkley, along with seven others.
Of the nine to rush for more than 2,000 yards in a season, Barkley and Adrian Peterson were the second oldest at the time of the feat.
Barkley ran his way into the club at the age of 27. Peterson was also 27 when he did it in 2012. Five of his next seven seasons were plagued with injury. Only Barry Sanders was older when he did it. Sanders was 29. He played one more year after his 2,000-yard masterpiece, then abruptly retired.
“It sucks when it's not going the way you want it to go,” Barkley said. “It's kinda like the school of thought I come from. I truly love this game, and I feel like if you're able to go, sometimes you gotta push your body to the limit, and I'm trying. It's just not responding the way I want it to respond right now, and it sucks because trying to be the best leader I wanna be, and it's hard when you're not able to be out there and perform for your team.”

title: McMullen: Potential Eagles Defensive Concerns Emerged After MNF Loss vs. Cowboys
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. - For one night, at least, the Eagles' offense looked like it had found something workable .
Tanner McKee went 23-of-35 for 211 yards and a touchdown in Monday's loss to Dallas; the unit put together a 17-play, 84-yard drive that ate nine-plus minutes to open the second half and briefly grab a 21-20 lead, and Saquon Barkley punched in a touchdown before his hamstring and back derailed things.
It wasn’t aesthetic or explosive outside of Barkley, and a late interception by the Cowboys' DeMarvion Overshown ended any real comeback hopes, but it was competent.
Given the injuries, the missing pieces, and the reality that McKee is a career backup, this may have been close to the top end of what this version of the offense can do right now.
And that still wasn’t enough. In fact, it wasn’t even close.
Dallas walked out of the Linc with a 38-21 win, 416 total yards, with 204 of those coming on the ground.
Javonte Williams went for a career-high 155 rushing yards and a score. Dak Prescott threw three touchdowns without being sacked or even meaningfully harassed for most of the night. The Eagles generated zero sacks, zero quarterback hits, no tackles for loss and essentially no consistent pressure on a Cowboys offense that had been struggling.
Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio’s unit, the one built with significant investment up front and expected to carry this team while the offense figured itself out, got pushed around on the interior and couldn’t get off the field.
This is the story of the 2-5 season in one night.
The offense—short-handed and operating with a limited ceiling—scraped together three touchdowns and kept the game within reach into the fourth quarter. The defense, the side that was supposed to be the identity, let a division rival run the ball at will and score on most of its possessions.
When the offense needs the defense to make a stand, force a turnover, or simply limit the damage, it has too often failed to show up. Monday night was one of the clearest examples yet.
McKee isn’t going to morph into a high-end starter overnight , and the skill-position group remains thinned out. If this is roughly the offensive floor-to-ceiling range for the foreseeable future, then the margin for error is small. An underachieving defense that can’t generate pressure or stop the run removes that margin entirely.
The Eagles are not just dealing with the absence of franchise QB Jalen Hurts . They’re dealing with a defensive unit that has the names, the salary commitments and the reputation, but not the results.
That’s the gap that is turning a tough season into a free fall.

title: Eagles Stock Report: Defensive Concerns Rising, Offense Showing Life Ahead of Week 8
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — The Eagles offense showed as much life as it has all season, but the defense faltered by allowing 416 total yards in a 38-21 loss to the Cowboys on Monday night , Philadelphia's fifth consecutive setback after starting the season 2-0.
The Eagles (2-5)  went ahead 21-20 after an impressive touchdown drive to start the third quarter but were outscored 18-0 the rest of the way, including touchdowns by Cowboys' playmakers CeeDee Lamb, who tortured the Eagles' cornerbacks at times, and Javonte Williams, who ran for a career-high 155 yards.
Dallas (3-4) had come into the game, No. 31 in the NFL when it came to running the football, avergaing just 76.0 yards per game.
"It's never just one thing when you give up a bunch of yards like that," Eagles coach Nick Sirianni said when discussing the run game. "We've got to do a better job coaching. We've got to do a better job executing, getting off blocks, tackling. We had a couple missed tackles, but it's always going to be about block destruction, playing on their side of the line of scrimmage, and then us putting them in positions to succeed. I give them credit. They played a good game. "
The Eagles are now in third place in the NFC East, outpaced by the Giants (4-2-1) and the Cowboys. Washington, at 1-4-1, is at the bottom of the division and will host Philadelphia in Week 8. The Eagles will then finish a three-game stretch in the division by hosting the Giants on Nov. 8.
Here is the weekly stock market from the game:
The Saquon Barkley-led running game: Down their top two receivers—DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks—due to injury, the Eagles needed what had been a moribund running game of their own to get going. It did due to the return of Barkley to the backfield, as well as Drew Kendall and Landon Dickerson on the offensive line. However, on the second play of the game, a 29-yard run by Barkley, the dynamic runner felt a tweak in his hamstring, and his back locked up while he favored the injury.
Barkley tried to stay loose and in the game but each time he entered in the second half he left after one run, finishing with 62 yards and a touchdown on just seven carries. Backup Dameon Pierce was also somewhat effective, gaining 47 yards and a TD on 14 carries, although he was also forced to leave with an injury in the fourth quarter.
Tempo: Down 20-14 at halftime, the Eagles came out in the third quarter with tempo, getting Dallas in its nickel defense to strain a back seven that has had a lot of problems communicating this season. The result produced the best drive of the season for Sean Mannion's offense, a 17-play, 84-yard marathon that took over nine minutes off the clock. It was Philadelphia's first TD in the third quarter this season and Makai Lemon's first NFL score.
The drive also shortened the game against the more talented Cowboys but the Philadelphia could not finish the deal.
Makai Lemon: Without Smith and Wicks, necessity forced Mannion to use Lemon in better ways. Difficult catches over the middle of the field and run-after-catch opportunities on shallow crossing routes—things that Lemon excelled at in college at Southern California were a sight for the sore eyes of Eagles fans. Lemon finished with a career-high seven receptions for 67 yards and his first professional TD.
The Philly fans: There was some thought that Eagles fans might boo Jeffrey Lurie when the Eagles owner was inducted into the organization's Hall of Fame at halftime. That stemmed from the messaging and closed-door approach to the handling of Jalen Hurts's health . The popular QB1 had to be shut down after a superficial blood clot turned into pulmonary emboli, something neither Lurie nor general manager Howie Roseman has addressed to date.
Typically, when individuals are inducted into the team's HOF, they are made available to the media, and that was not the case with Lurie. Despite that obfuscation, Lurie is easily the best owner in franchise history and perhaps the history of Philadelphia sports.
The usually tough-minded Eagles fans were able to compartmentalize and show class while honoring Lurie.
Dirty kicks: After losing Britain Covey to a knee injury, the Eagles were forced to use Pierce and Elijah Mitchell on kickoff returns and each had a very difficult time handling Brandon Aubrey's kickoffs, often forcing a limited offense to take the long road too many times in the game.
The defensive front: The production simply doesn't match the reputation so far this season. Considering the expectations, there might be no more disappointing unit in the NFL than this Eagles defensive front.
Jalen Carter often flashes his enormous talent but is not consistent enough. Jordan Davis remains a two-down player despite being paid like a three-down star; Moro Ojomo has regressed recently and the edge rushers—Jonathan Greenard, Jalyx Hunt and Nolan Smith (out Monday night with a concussion)— have all battled injuries and haven't produced at the level expected when on the field.
Against the Cowboys, the front managed just five pressures as Dak Prescott got very comfortable en route to a three-touchdown performance.
Fiver: The last time the Eagles lost five straight games was during the 2016 season (Weeks 10 through 14) under then-first-year head coach Doug Pederson and then-rookie quarterback Carson Wentz. Philadelphia is not used to losing like this, and it will be interesting to see how the organization reacts to this kind of adversity with the trade deadline approaching on Nov. 10 .

title: 4 Winners & 4 Losers From Eagles' 38-21 Monday Night Football Loss to Cowboys
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA – The Eagles took some baby steps toward turning around their season, but the fact is, they need to start taking giant steps if they want to extend their playoff streak to six straight seasons.
Sitting at 2-5 after their fifth straight loss, this one, 38-21, to the Dallas Cowboys on Monday Night Football, they are now three games behind the NFC East Division-leading New York Giants in the loss column.
The last time the Eagles lost five in a row was 2016 in Weeks 11 through 15 when Carson Wentz was a rookie quarterback.
They will play two more games until the trade deadline—next Sunday night in primetime against the Washington Commanders on the road, and the following week at home against the Giants.
The Eagles offense operated better in Tanner McKee’s second straight start of the season, and that was one little step forward. So were third downs. The Eagles converted over 40 percent at 5-for-12 and was 2-for-3 on fourth downs.
Offensive coordinator Sean Mannion had some decent moments calling plays, and the offense managed to score their first touchdowns of the season in the first and third quarters.
The quarterback, however, threw a costly interception with the Eagles moving the ball into Cowboys territory down 10 with 7:47 to play.
Saquon Barkley returned, but his hamstring flared up, then his back acted up, and he played just 10 snaps. They were productive, though. He ran for 62 yards on seven runs (8.9 yards per carry) and had his first touchdown of the season with an 8-yard run in the first.
McKee settled in well enough to complete 23 passes in 35 attempts for 211 yards, a touchdown on a 4-yard strike to rookie Makai Lemon, and a pick. The QB finished with a 79.6 passer rating.
The defense was gashed all night, allowing the Cowboys to pile up 416 yards of offense and to convert 8-of-13 third downs.
Landon Dickerson was a big boost here. Getting the left guard back after missing the previous five games with a bone bruise was a big benefit. Pierce’s 5-yard touchdown run went through a hole Dickerson helped pave. The Eagles ran for 86 yards on the first half on 13 runs but fizzled a bit in the second half and ended with 109 yards on 21 runs.
The rookie sparked an 84-yard drive that used 9 minutes, 16 seconds, and spanned 17 plays, with a fourth-and-one catch for 15 yards, then made his first career TD catch on the same drive—a 4-yarder on third down that gave the Eagles a 21-20 lead with 5:49 to go in the third quarter. He finished with career highs in catches (7) and yards (67).
He has been with the Eagles for just two weeks, but he’s already ascended to the backup job, ahead of rookie Cole Payton, who served as the emergency quarterback. If McKee can’t find a way to win a game these next two weeks, Milton could rise to the starter when the Eagles emerge from their bye week to host the Pittsburgh Steelers on Nov. 22.
The owner was inducted into the Eagles Hall of Fame at halftime, and it was well-deserved. He has the second-most wins (317) and division titles (12) in the salary cap era that began the same year he bought the team, on May 6, 1994. His induction, however, was marred by another loss for his team.
It was invisible once again, even with Jonathan Greenard playing. It entered the game with eight sacks and left with the same number. Dak Prescott had all day to throw the ball and made the Eagles pay, especially on third downs. If you’re looking for an area the Eagles need to address in the first round of the draft, look no further than an edge rusher.
Entering the fourth quarter, the Eagles had just three pressures – two from Arnold Ebiketie and one from Greenard.
Defensive tackles Jordan Davis, Jalen Carter, and Moro Ojomo didn’t do much to stop the run. The Cowboys were ranked 30th in the league in running the ball, averaging just 76 yards per game. Against the porous Eagles, they pounded out 204 with Javonte Williams getting a career-high 155 on 25 carries.
The defensive back has taken a big step back this season, and he was victimized by CeeDee Lamb for a 9-yard TD on third-and-two to give Dallas a 10-7 lead with 5:32 to play in the first quarter. DeJean was also called for a pass interference penalty early in the fourth quarter to ignite another Cowboys drive.
The Eagles would probably be wise to trade him and get whatever they can . The cornerback hasn’t found the rookie year magic he had years ago.
His missed tackles were glaring and so were some of his busted coverages, like on the double move Lamb laid on him for a wide-open 30-yard catch to the 9-yard line with 12 seconds left that led to a field goal as time expired in the half. The 27-yard field goal from Brandon Aubrey made it 20-14 at halftime.
Woolen’s breakdown would have been a walk-in touchdown if Prescott had made a better throw. He also committed a costly holding penalty that gave the Cowboys a first down and kept a drive alive that led to the go-ahead touchdown after the Eagles took a 21-20 lead.
Woolen was beaten by Lamb and Prescott on a 16-yard throw with 1:30 to play in the third quarter to take a 28-21 lead after Prescott easily ran for the 2-point conversion.

title: Final Week 7 Injury Report Gives Desperate Eagles Offense a Huge Boost
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — It’s not exactly the cavalry riding to the Eagles’ offensive rescue for Monday night’s home game against the Cowboys , but it’s better than nothing.
Just hours before kickoff, Philly filled its three spots on the 53-man roster, adding:
Calcaterra and Stowers have yet to play this season after being placed on injured reserve before the season opener. What’s interesting about these three names is that Zach Ertz is not among them . The thinking had been that the Eagles made a deal with the veteran tight end to return to Philly in exchange for adding him to the roster at some point.
This feels like the point, yet it didn’t happen.
Ertz is out of practice squad elevations, so the only way he can play again for the Eagles is to be added to the roster. Clearly, the team is higher on Calcaterra and the rookie Stowers right now.
Speaking of the practice squad, the Eagles elevated outside linebacker Keyshawn James-Newby for a second straight game and running back Elijah Mitchell.
Meanwhile, Saquon Barkley is expected to return to the lineup after missing two games with a hamstring injury. Adding Mitchell gives the Eagles three running backs for Monday’s game, as he and Barkley join Dameon Pierce.
The return of Barkley and Dickerson should help the Eagles find some traction in the running game, and that would help Tanner McKee, who will make his second straight start in place of injured Jalen Hurts.
In last week’s loss to the Panthers, McKee attempted 45 passes while running the ball just 12 times against a Panthers defense that was one of the worst at stopping the run in the league. The Bay Buccaneers showed the Eagles how bad that run defense was on Sunday when the Bucs torched Carolina on the ground, with 49 runs for 258 yards. Baker Mayfield threw just 11 passes.
Yet, the Eagles insisted on letting McKee throw the ball and never took advantage of the Panthers’ inability to stop the run.
A more balanced attack against the Cowboys might help the Eagles snap a four-game losing streak. Having McKee throw the ball another 40-plus times doesn’t feel like a recipe for success, especially with the Eagles missing their top two playmakers—DeVonta Smith (hamstring) and Tay Wicks (ankle).
That leaves the Eagles with a decimated receiver corps that includes rookie Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore.
Dickerson will be playing his first game since the season-opening win over the Washington Commanders. He was placed on injured reserve the day after the game with a bone bruise.
Cornerback Jakorian Bennett (knee) was ruled out for the game against Dallas.
In addition to Smith and Wicks being ruled out in Saturday’s final injury report, the Eagles ruled out defensive back Michael Carter (abdomen) and OLB Nolan Smith (concussion).
Outside linebacker Jonathan Greenard was listed as questionable with an ankle injury, but he is expected to play. Outside linebacker Jalyx Hunt (knee/ankle) was questionable on the final injury report , but he has yet to be ruled out at the time of writing.

title: 3 Eagles in Danger of Landing on the Trade Block With a Dud vs. Cowboys in Week 7
full_text:
Given the way the season has gone for the Eagles, there's a real chance they could be sellers leading up to the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10 .
If the Eagles continue to slide down the standings in the NFC, they may look to recoup some value for guys that they don't view as long-term pieces.
They have three games remaining before the deadline, starting with a Monday night matchup with the rival Cowboys in Week 7. Here's a look at three Eagles players who could potentially be on the trade block after an underwhelming performance against Dallas.
Hollywood Brown has been a complete nonfactor for the Eagles through six weeks of the 2026 season. He's appeared in just one game for Philly and hasn't logged a single reception. But if he's ever going to have an impact for the Eagles, it will be against the Cowboys on Monday night when Philadelphia will be missing its top two receivers, DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks.
Without Smith and Wicks, the Eagles and backup quarterback Tanner McKee will be forced to rely on the rest of the receivers on the roster, including Brown. If he doesn't play much or make an impact with the Eagles—who are in desperate need of production at the receiver spots—that should tell you all you need to know about his standing within the team.
Brown could already be considered a trade candidate heading into the deadline, and another quiet performance against Dallas will only hammer that home.
Pretty much the exact same logic that was applied above to Brown could also be applied to wide receiver Elijah Moore, who has also been a non-factor for Philly. Moore has appeared in four games this season, but he has just one reception for four yards.
Again, there should be increased opportunity for other receivers like Moore (and Brown) to step up against Dallas and fill the void left by Smith and Wicks. If Moore is unable to do so, then there's no reason for the Eagles not to try to move him prior to the deadline.
On the other hand, if he can demonstrate some value, perhaps the Eagles would want to hang onto him for the rest of the season.
Tariq Woolen won a ring as a cornerback for the Seahawks last season, and when the Eagles signed him to a one-year deal in free agency, they probably envisioned him filling a similar role in Philadelphia.
However, at this point it's pretty clear that the Eagles probably won't be competing for the Super Bowl this season, and Woolen could potentially fetch a decent return in a trade . If the Eagles don't view him as a piece that they're likely to bring back in free agency next year, it would make sense to try to get some value for him while they still can.
